## The Type System — 4.2. Propositions {#manual-the-type-system-42-propositions}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Type-System/Propositions/

Propositions are meaningful statements that admit proof. 
Nonsensical statements are not propositions, but false statements are.
All propositions are classified by `Prop`.

Propositions have the following properties:

Definitional proof irrelevance
:   Any two proofs of the same proposition are completely interchangeable.

Run-time irrelevance
:   Propositions are erased from compiled code.

Impredicativity
:   Propositions may quantify over types from any universe whatsoever.

Restricted Elimination
:   With the exception of [subsingletons](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Type-System/Inductive-Types/#--tech-term-subsingleton), propositions cannot be eliminated into non-proposition types.

Extensionality
:   Any two logically equivalent propositions can be proven to be equal with the `[propext]](#manual-propext)` axiom.

axiom

```lean
[propext]](#manual-propext) {a b : Prop} : [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Iff___intro)a [↔](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Iff___intro) b[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Iff___intro) → a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) b



[propext]](#manual-propext) {a b : Prop} : [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Iff___intro)a [↔](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Iff___intro) b[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Iff___intro) → a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) b
```

The [axiom](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=axioms) of **propositional extensionality**. It asserts that if
propositions `a` and `b` are logically equivalent (that is, if `a` can be proved from `b` and vice
versa), then `a` and `b` are *equal*, meaning `a` can be replaced with `b` in all contexts.

The standard logical connectives provably respect propositional extensionality. However, an axiom is
needed for higher order expressions like `P a` where `P : Prop → Prop` is unknown, as well as for
equality. Propositional extensionality is intuitionistically valid.

---



## The Type System — 4.3. Universes {#manual-the-type-system-43-universes}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Type-System/Universes/

Types are classified by *universes*. Universes are also referred to as *sorts*.
Each universe has a *level*,  which is a natural number.
The `Sort` operator constructs a universe from a given level. 
If the level of a universe is smaller than that of another, the universe itself is said to be smaller.
With the exception of propositions (described later in this chapter), types in a given universe may only quantify over types in smaller universes.
`Sort 0` is the type of propositions, while each `Sort (u + 1)` is a type that describes data.

Every universe is an element of the next larger universe, so `Sort 5` includes `Sort 4`.
This means that the following examples are accepted:

```lean
example : Sort 5 := Sort 4
example : Sort 2 := Sort 1
```

On the other hand, `Sort 3` is not an element of `Sort 5`:

```lean
example : Sort 5 := Sort 3
```

```lean
Type mismatch
  Type 2
has type
  Type 3
of sort `Type 4` but is expected to have type
  Type 4
of sort `Type 5`
```

Similarly, because `[Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)` is in `Sort 1`, it is not in `Sort 2`:

```lean
example : Sort 1 := [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)
```

```lean
example : Sort 2 := [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)
```

```lean
Type mismatch
  [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)
has type
  Type
of sort `Type 1` but is expected to have type
  Type 1
of sort `Type 2`
```

Because propositions and data are used differently and are governed by different rules, the abbreviations `Type` and `Prop` are provided to make the distinction more convenient.  
`Type u` is an abbreviation for `Sort (u + 1)`, so `Type 0` is `Sort 1` and `Type 3` is `Sort 4`.
`Type 0` can also be abbreviated `Type`, so `Unit : Type` and `Type : Type 1`.
`Prop` is an abbreviation for `Sort 0`.

### 4.3.1. Predicativity {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The-Type-System--Universes--Predicativity}

Each universe contains dependent function types, which additionally represent universal quantification and implication.
A function type's universe is determined by the universes of its argument and return types.
The specific rules depend on whether the return type of the function is a proposition.

Predicates, which are functions that return propositions (that is, where the result of the function is some type in `Prop`) may have argument types in any universe whatsoever, but the function type itself remains in `Prop`.
In other words, propositions feature *impredicative*  quantification, because propositions can themselves be statements about all propositions (and all other types).

**Example: Impredicativity**

Proof irrelevance can be written as a proposition that quantifies over all propositions:

```lean
example : Prop := ∀ (P : Prop) (p1 p2 : P), p1 = p2
```

A proposition may also quantify over all types, at any given level:

```lean
example : Prop := ∀ (α : Type), ∀ (x : α), x = x
example : Prop := ∀ (α : Type 5), ∀ (x : α), x = x
```

For universes at [level]](#manual---tech-term-level) `1` and higher (that is, the `Type u` hierarchy), quantification is *predicative*. 
For these universes, the universe of a function type is the least upper bound of the argument and return types' universes.

**Example: Universe levels of function types**

Both of these types are in `Type 2`:

```lean
example (α : Type 1) (β : Type 2) : Type 2 := α → β
example (α : Type 2) (β : Type 1) : Type 2 := α → β
```

**Example: Predicativity of Type**

This example is not accepted, because `α`'s level is greater than `1`. In other words, the annotated universe is smaller than the function type's universe:

```lean
example (α : Type 2) (β : Type 1) : Type 1 := α → β
```

```lean
Type mismatch
  α → β
has type
  Type 2
of sort `Type 3` but is expected to have type
  Type 1
of sort `Type 2`
```

Lean's universes are not cumulative; a type in `Type u` is not automatically also in `Type (u + 1)`.
Each type inhabits precisely one universe.

**Example: No cumulativity**

This example is not accepted because the annotated universe is larger than the function type's universe:

```lean
example (α : Type 2) (β : Type 1) : Type 3 := α → β
```

```lean
Type mismatch
  α → β
has type
  Type 2
of sort `Type 3` but is expected to have type
  Type 3
of sort `Type 4`
```

### 4.3.2. Polymorphism {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The-Type-System--Universes--Polymorphism}

Lean supports *universe polymorphism*,   which means that constants defined in the Lean environment can take universe parameters.
These parameters can then be instantiated with universe levels when the constant is used.
Universe parameters are written in curly braces following a dot after a constant name.

**Example: Universe-polymorphic identity function**

When fully explicit, the identity function takes a universe parameter `u`. Its signature is:

```lean
id.{u} {α : Sort u} (x : α) : α
```

Universe variables may additionally occur in [universe level expressions]](#manual-level-expressions), which provide specific universe levels in definitions.
When the polymorphic definition is instantiated with concrete levels, these universe level expressions are also evaluated to yield concrete levels.

**Example: Universe level expressions**

In this example, `Codec` is in a universe that is one greater than the universe of the type it contains:

```lean
structure Codec.{u} : Type (u + 1) where
type : Type u
encode : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [UInt32](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt32___ofBitVec) → type → [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [UInt32](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt32___ofBitVec)
decode : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [UInt32](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt32___ofBitVec) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (type × [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

Lean automatically infers most level parameters.
In the following example, it is not necessary to annotate the type as `Codec.{0}`, because `[Char](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___mk)`'s type is `Type 0`, so `u` must be `0`:

```lean
def Codec.char : Codec where
[type]](#manual-Codec___type-_LPAR_in-Universe-level-expressions_RPAR_) := [Char](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___mk)
[encode]](#manual-Codec___encode-_LPAR_in-Universe-level-expressions_RPAR_) buf ch := buf.[push](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___push) ch.[val](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___mk)
[decode]](#manual-Codec___decode-_LPAR_in-Universe-level-expressions_RPAR_) buf i := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let v ← buf[i]?
if h : v.[isValidChar](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt32___isValidChar) then
let ch : [Char](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___mk) := ⟨v, h⟩
return (ch, i + 1)
else
failure
```

Universe-polymorphic definitions in fact create a *schematic definition* that can be instantiated at a variety of levels, and different instantiations of universes create incompatible values.

**Example: Universe polymorphism and definitional equality**

This can be seen in the following example, in which `[T]](#manual-T-_LPAR_in-Universe-polymorphism-and-definitional-equality_RPAR_)` is a gratuitously-universe-polymorphic function that always returns `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.
Because it is marked `opaque`, Lean can't check equality by unfolding the definitions.
Both instantiations of `[T]](#manual-T-_LPAR_in-Universe-polymorphism-and-definitional-equality_RPAR_)` have the parameters and the same type, but their differing universe instantiations make them incompatible.

```lean
opaque T.{u} (_ : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
(fun (α : Sort u) => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) [PUnit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit).{u}
set_option pp.universes true
def test.{u, v} : [T]](#manual-T-_LPAR_in-Universe-polymorphism-and-definitional-equality_RPAR_).{u} 0 = [T]](#manual-T-_LPAR_in-Universe-polymorphism-and-definitional-equality_RPAR_).{v} 0 := [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
```

```lean
Type mismatch
  [rfl.{?u.5}](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
has type
  [Eq.{?u.5}](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) ?m.7 ?m.7
but is expected to have type
  [Eq.{1}](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) ([T.{u}]](#manual-T-_LPAR_in-Universe-polymorphism-and-definitional-equality_RPAR_) 0) ([T.{v}]](#manual-T-_LPAR_in-Universe-polymorphism-and-definitional-equality_RPAR_) 0)
```

Auto-bound implicit arguments are as universe-polymorphic as possible.
Defining the identity function as follows:

```lean
def id' (x : α) := x
```

results in the signature:

```lean
[id']](#manual-id___).{u} {α : Sort u} (x : α) : α
```

**Example: Universe monomorphism in auto-bound implicit parameters**

On the other hand, because `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is in universe `Type 0`, this function automatically ends up with a concrete universe level for `α`, because `m` is applied to both `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and `α`, so both must have the same type and thus be in the same universe:

```lean
partial def count [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] (p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) (act : m α) : m [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
if p (← act) then
return 1 + (← [count]](#manual-count-_LPAR_in-Universe-monomorphism-in-auto-bound-implicit-parameters_RPAR_) p act)
else
return 0
```

#### 4.3.2.1. Level Expressions {#manual-level-expressions}

Levels that occur in a definition are not restricted to just variables and addition of constants.
More complex relationships between universes can be defined using level expressions.

```
Level ::= 0 | 1 | 2 | ...  -- Concrete levels
        | u, v             -- Variables
        | Level + n        -- Addition of constants
        | max Level Level  -- Least upper bound
        | imax Level Level -- Impredicative LUB
```

Given an assignment of level variables to concrete numbers, evaluating these expressions follows the usual rules of arithmetic.
The `imax` operation is defined as follows:

`\mathtt{imax}\ u\ v = \begin{cases}0 & \mathrm{when\ }v = 0\\\mathtt{max}\ u\ v&\mathrm{otherwise}\end{cases}`

`imax` is used to implement [impredicative]](#manual---tech-term-impredicative) quantification for `Prop`.
In particular, if `A : Sort u` and `B : Sort v`, then `(x : A) → B : Sort (imax u v)`.
If `B : Prop`, then the function type is itself a `Prop`; otherwise, the function type's level is the maximum of `u` and `v`.

#### 4.3.2.2. Universe Variable Bindings {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The-Type-System--Universes--Polymorphism--Universe-Variable-Bindings}

Universe-polymorphic definitions bind universe variables.
These bindings may be either explicit or implicit.
Explicit universe variable binding and instantiation occurs as a suffix to the definition's name.
Universe parameters are defined or provided by suffixing the name of a constant with a period (`.`) followed by a comma-separated sequence of universe variables between curly braces.

**Example: Universe-polymorphic map**

The following declaration of `[map]](#manual-map-_LPAR_in-Universe-polymorphic--map_RPAR_)` declares two universe parameters (`u` and `v`) and instantiates the polymorphic `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` with each in turn:

```lean
def map.{u, v} {α : Type u} {β : Type v}
(f : α → β) :
[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil).{u} α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil).{v} β
| [] => []
| x :: xs => f x :: [map]](#manual-map-_LPAR_in-Universe-polymorphic--map_RPAR_) f xs
```

Just as Lean automatically instantiates implicit parameters, it also automatically instantiates universe parameters.
When [automatic implicit parameter insertion](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Headers-and-Signatures/#automatic-implicit-parameters) is enabled (i.e. the `[autoImplicit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Headers-and-Signatures/#autoImplicit)` option is set to `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, which is the default), it is not necessary to explicitly bind universe variables; they are inserted automatically.
When it is set to `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, then they must be added explicitly or declared using the `universe` command.

**Example: Automatic Implicit Parameters and Universe Polymorphism**

When `autoImplicit` is `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` (which is the default setting), this definition is accepted even though it does not bind its universe parameters:

```lean
set_option [autoImplicit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Headers-and-Signatures/#autoImplicit) true
def map {α : Type u} {β : Type v} (f : α → β) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) β
| [] => []
| x :: xs => f x :: map f xs
```

When `autoImplicit` is `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, the definition is rejected because `u` and `v` are not in scope:

```lean
set_option [autoImplicit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Headers-and-Signatures/#autoImplicit) false
def map {α : Type u} {β : Type v} (f : α → β) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) β
| [] => []
| x :: xs => f x :: map f xs
```

```lean
unknown universe level `u`
```

```lean
unknown universe level `v`
```

In addition to using `autoImplicit`, particular identifiers can be declared as universe variables in a particular [section scope](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#--tech-term-section-scope) using the `universe` command.

syntaxUniverse Parameter Declarations

```lean
command ::= ...
    | universe ident ident*
```

Declares one or more universe variables for the extent of the current scope.

Just as the `variable` command causes a particular identifier to be treated as a parameter with a particular type, the `universe` command causes the subsequent identifiers to be implicitly quantified as universe parameters in declarations that mention them, even if the option `autoImplicit` is `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.

**Example: The universe command when autoImplicit is false**

```lean
set_option [autoImplicit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Headers-and-Signatures/#autoImplicit) false
[universe]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___universe-next) u
def id₃ (α : Type u) (a : α) := a
```

Because the automatic implicit parameter feature only inserts parameters that are used in the declaration's [header](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Headers-and-Signatures/#--tech-term-header), universe variables that occur only on the right-hand side of a definition are not inserted as arguments unless they have been declared with `universe` even when `autoImplicit` is `true`.

**Example: Automatic universe parameters and the universe command**

This definition with an explicit universe parameter is accepted:

```lean
def L.{u} := [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) (Type u)
```

Even with automatic implicit parameters, this definition is rejected, because `u` is not mentioned in the header, which precedes the `:=`:

```lean
set_option [autoImplicit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Headers-and-Signatures/#autoImplicit) true
def L := [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) (Type u)
```

```lean
unknown universe level `u`
```

With a universe declaration, `u` is accepted as a parameter even on the right-hand side:

```lean
[universe]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___universe-next) u
def L := [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) (Type u)
```

The resulting definition of `L` is universe-polymorphic, with `u` inserted as a universe parameter.

Declarations in the scope of a `universe` command are not made polymorphic if the universe variables do not occur in them or in other automatically-inserted arguments.

```lean
[universe]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___universe-next) u
def L := [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) (Type 0)
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) L
```

#### 4.3.2.3. Universe Lifting {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The-Type-System--Universes--Polymorphism--Universe-Lifting}

When a type's universe is smaller than the one expected in some context, *universe lifting* operators can bridge the gap.
These are wrappers around terms of a given type that are in larger universes than the wrapped type.
There are two lifting operators:

- `[PLift]](#manual-PLift___up)` can lift any type, including [propositions]](#manual---tech-term-Propositions), by one level. It can be used to include proofs in data structures such as lists.
- `[ULift]](#manual-ULift___up)` can lift any non-proposition type by any number of levels.

structure

```lean
[PLift.{u}]](#manual-PLift___up) (α : Sort u) : Type u



[PLift.{u}]](#manual-PLift___up) (α : Sort u) : Type u
```

Lifts a proposition or type to a higher universe level.

`[PLift]](#manual-PLift___up) α` wraps a proof or value of type `α`. The resulting type is in the next largest universe
after that of `α`. In particular, propositions become data.

The related type `[ULift]](#manual-ULift___up)` can be used to lift a non-proposition type by any number of levels.

Examples:

- `([False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) : Prop)`
- `([PLift]](#manual-PLift___up) [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) : Type)`
- `([[.up]](#manual-PLift___up) (by [trivial](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#trivial)), [.up]](#manual-PLift___up) (by [simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)), [.up]](#manual-PLift___up) (by [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide))] : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) ([PLift]](#manual-PLift___up) [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)))`
- `([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) : Type 0)`
- `([PLift]](#manual-PLift___up) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) : Type 1)`

Constructor

```lean
[PLift.up]](#manual-PLift___up).{u}
```

Wraps a proof or value to increase its type's universe level by 1.

Fields

```lean
down : α
```

Extracts a wrapped proof or value from a universe-lifted proposition or type.

structure

```lean
[ULift.{r, s}]](#manual-ULift___up) (α : Type s) : Type (max s r)



[ULift.{r, s}]](#manual-ULift___up) (α : Type s) : Type (max s r)
```

Lifts a type to a higher universe level.

`[ULift]](#manual-ULift___up) α` wraps a value of type `α`. Instead of occupying the same universe as `α`, which would be
the minimal level, it takes a further level parameter and occupies their maximum. The resulting type
may occupy any universe that's at least as large as that of `α`.

The resulting universe of the lifting operator is the first parameter, and may be written explicitly
while allowing `α`'s level to be inferred.

The related type `[PLift]](#manual-PLift___up)` can be used to lift a proposition or type by one level.

Examples:

- `([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) : Type 0)`
- `([ULift]](#manual-ULift___up) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) : Type 0)`
- `([ULift]](#manual-ULift___up) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) : Type 1)`
- `([ULift]](#manual-ULift___up) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) : Type 5)`
- `([ULift]](#manual-ULift___up).{7} ([PUnit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit) : Type 3) : Type 7)`

Constructor

```lean
[ULift.up]](#manual-ULift___up).{r, s}
```

Wraps a value to increase its type's universe level.

Fields

```lean
down : α
```

Extracts a wrapped value from a universe-lifted type.

---



## The Type System — 4.4. Inductive Types {#manual-the-type-system-44-inductive-types}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Type-System/Inductive-Types/

*Inductive types* are the primary means of introducing new types to Lean.
While [universes]](#manual---tech-term-universes), [functions]](#manual---tech-term-Functions), and [quotient types](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Type-System/Quotients/#--tech-term-Quotient-types) are built-in primitives that could not be added by users, every other type in Lean is either an inductive type or defined in terms of universes, functions, and inductive types.
Inductive types are specified by their *type constructors*  and their *constructors*;  their other properties are derived from these.
Each inductive type has a single type constructor, which may take both [universe parameters]](#manual---tech-term-universe-parameters) and ordinary parameters.
Inductive types may have any number of constructors; these constructors introduce new values whose types are headed by the inductive type's type constructor.

Based on the type constructor and the constructors for an inductive type, Lean derives a *recursor*.
Logically, recursors represent induction principles or elimination rules; computationally, they represent primitive recursive computations.
The termination of recursive functions is justified by translating them into uses of the recursors, so Lean's kernel only needs to perform type checking of recursor applications, rather than including a separate termination analysis.
Lean additionally produces a number of helper constructions based on the recursor,The term *recursor* is always used, even for non-recursive types. which are used elsewhere in the system.

*Structures* are a special case of inductive types that have exactly one constructor.
When a structure is declared, Lean generates helpers that enable additional language features to be used with the new structure.

This section describes the specific details of the syntax used to specify both inductive types and structures, the new constants and definitions in the environment that result from inductive type declarations, and the run-time representation of inductive types' values in compiled code.

### 4.4.1. Inductive Type Declarations {#manual-inductive-declarations}

syntaxInductive Type Declarations

```lean
command ::= ...
    | [declModifiers](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Modifiers/#Lean___Parser___Command___declModifiers)
      inductive declId [optDeclSig](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Headers-and-Signatures/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeclSig) where
        (| [declModifiers](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Modifiers/#Lean___Parser___Command___declModifiers) ident [optDeclSig](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Headers-and-Signatures/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeclSig))*
      ([deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) ident,*)?
```

Declares a new inductive type.
The meaning of the `declModifiers` is as described in the section [on declaration modifiers](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Modifiers/#declaration-modifiers).

After declaring an inductive type, its type constructor, constructors, and recursor are present in the environment.
New inductive types extend Lean's core logic—they are not encoded or represented by some other already-present data.
Inductive type declarations must satisfy [a number of well-formedness requirements]](#manual-well-formed-inductives) to ensure that the logic remains consistent.

The first line of the declaration, from `inductive` to `where`, specifies the new [type constructor]](#manual---tech-term-type-constructors)'s name and type.
If a type signature for the type constructor is provided, then its result type must be a [universe]](#manual---tech-term-universes), but the parameters do not need to be types.
If no signature is provided, then Lean will attempt to infer a universe that's just big enough to contain the resulting type.
In some situations, this process may fail to find a minimal universe or fail to find one at all, necessitating an annotation.

The constructor specifications follow `where`.
Constructors are not mandatory, as constructorless inductive types such as `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)` and `[Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty)` are perfectly sensible.
Each constructor specification begins with a vertical bar (`'|'`, Unicode `'VERTICAL BAR' (U+007c)`), declaration modifiers, and a name.
The name is a [raw identifier](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Source-Files-and-Modules/#--tech-term-raw-identifier).
A declaration signature follows the name.
The signature may specify any parameters, modulo the well-formedness requirements for inductive type declarations, but the return type in the signature must be a saturated application of the type constructor of the inductive type being specified.
If no signature is provided, then the constructor's type is inferred by inserting sufficient implicit parameters to construct a well-formed return type.

The new inductive type's name is defined in the [current namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#--tech-term-current-namespace).
Each constructor's name is in the inductive type's namespace.

#### 4.4.1.1. Parameters and Indices {#manual-inductive-datatypes-parameters-and-indices}

Type constructors may take two kinds of arguments: *parameters*  and *indices*.
Parameters must be used consistently in the entire definition; all occurrences of the type constructor in each constructor in the declaration must take precisely the same argument.
Indices may vary among the occurrences of the type constructor.
All parameters must precede all indices in the type constructor's signature.

Parameters that occur prior to the colon (`':'`) in the type constructor's signature are considered parameters to the entire inductive type declaration.
They are always parameters that must be uniform throughout the type's definition.
Generally speaking, parameters that occur after the colon are indices that may vary throughout the definition of the type.
However, if the option `[inductive.autoPromoteIndices]](#manual-inductive___autoPromoteIndices)` is `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, then syntactic indices that could have been parameters are made into parameters.
An index could have been a parameter if all of its type dependencies are themselves parameters and it is used uniformly as an uninstantiated variable in all occurrences of the inductive type's type constructor in all constructors.

option

```lean
inductive.autoPromoteIndices
```

Default value: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

Promote indices to parameters in inductive types whenever possible.

Indices can be seen as defining a *family* of types.
Each choice of indices selects a type from the family, which has its own set of available constructors.
Type constructors with indices are said to specify *indexed families*  of types.

#### 4.4.1.2. Example Inductive Types {#manual-example-inductive-types}

**Example: A constructorless type**

`[Vacant]](#manual-Vacant-_LPAR_in-A-constructorless-type_RPAR_)` is an empty inductive type, equivalent to Lean's `[Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty)` type:

```lean
inductive Vacant : Type where
```

Empty inductive types are not useless; they can be used to indicate unreachable code.

**Example: A constructorless proposition**

`[No]](#manual-No-_LPAR_in-A-constructorless-proposition_RPAR_)` is a false [proposition]](#manual---tech-term-Propositions), equivalent to Lean's `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)`:

```lean
inductive No : Prop where
```

**Example: A unit type**

`[Solo]](#manual-Solo-_LPAR_in-A-unit-type_RPAR_)` is equivalent to Lean's `[Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)` type:

```lean
inductive Solo where
| solo
```

It is an example of an inductive type in which the signatures have been omitted for both the type constructor and the constructor.
Lean assigns `[Solo]](#manual-Solo-_LPAR_in-A-unit-type_RPAR_)` to `Type`:

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) [Solo]](#manual-Solo-_LPAR_in-A-unit-type_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[Solo]](#manual-Solo-_LPAR_in-A-unit-type_RPAR_) : Type
```

The constructor is named `[Solo.solo]](#manual-Solo___solo-_LPAR_in-A-unit-type_RPAR_)`, because constructor names are in the type constructor's namespace.
Because `[Solo]](#manual-Solo-_LPAR_in-A-unit-type_RPAR_)` expects no arguments, the signature inferred for `[Solo.solo]](#manual-Solo___solo-_LPAR_in-A-unit-type_RPAR_)` is:

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) [Solo.solo]](#manual-Solo___solo-_LPAR_in-A-unit-type_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[Solo.solo]](#manual-Solo___solo-_LPAR_in-A-unit-type_RPAR_) : [Solo]](#manual-Solo-_LPAR_in-A-unit-type_RPAR_)
```

**Example: A true proposition**

`[Yes]](#manual-Yes-_LPAR_in-A-true-proposition_RPAR_)` is equivalent to Lean's `[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)` proposition:

```lean
inductive Yes : Prop where
| intro
```

Unlike `One`, the new inductive type `[Yes]](#manual-Yes-_LPAR_in-A-true-proposition_RPAR_)` is specified to be in the `Prop` universe.

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) [Yes]](#manual-Yes-_LPAR_in-A-true-proposition_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[Yes]](#manual-Yes-_LPAR_in-A-true-proposition_RPAR_) : Prop
```

The signature inferred for `[Yes.intro]](#manual-Yes___intro-_LPAR_in-A-true-proposition_RPAR_)` is:

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) [Yes.intro]](#manual-Yes___intro-_LPAR_in-A-true-proposition_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[Yes.intro]](#manual-Yes___intro-_LPAR_in-A-true-proposition_RPAR_) : [Yes]](#manual-Yes-_LPAR_in-A-true-proposition_RPAR_)
```

**Example: A type with parameter and index**

An `[EvenOddList]](#manual-EvenOddList-_LPAR_in-A-type-with-parameter-and-index_RPAR_) α b` is a list where `α` is the type of the data stored in the list and `b` is `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` when there are an even number of entries:

```lean
inductive EvenOddList (α : Type u) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → Type u where
| nil : [EvenOddList]](#manual-EvenOddList-_LPAR_in-A-type-with-parameter-and-index_RPAR_) α [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| cons : α → [EvenOddList]](#manual-EvenOddList-_LPAR_in-A-type-with-parameter-and-index_RPAR_) α isEven → [EvenOddList]](#manual-EvenOddList-_LPAR_in-A-type-with-parameter-and-index_RPAR_) α ([not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not) isEven)
```

This example is well typed because there are two entries in the list:

```lean
example : [EvenOddList]](#manual-EvenOddList-_LPAR_in-A-type-with-parameter-and-index_RPAR_) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
[.cons]](#manual-EvenOddList___cons-_LPAR_in-A-type-with-parameter-and-index_RPAR_) "a" ([.cons]](#manual-EvenOddList___cons-_LPAR_in-A-type-with-parameter-and-index_RPAR_) "b" [.nil]](#manual-EvenOddList___nil-_LPAR_in-A-type-with-parameter-and-index_RPAR_))
```

This example is not well typed because there are three entries in the list:

```lean
example : [EvenOddList]](#manual-EvenOddList-_LPAR_in-A-type-with-parameter-and-index_RPAR_) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
[.cons]](#manual-EvenOddList___cons-_LPAR_in-A-type-with-parameter-and-index_RPAR_) "a" ([.cons]](#manual-EvenOddList___cons-_LPAR_in-A-type-with-parameter-and-index_RPAR_) "b" ([.cons]](#manual-EvenOddList___cons-_LPAR_in-A-type-with-parameter-and-index_RPAR_) "c" [.nil]](#manual-EvenOddList___nil-_LPAR_in-A-type-with-parameter-and-index_RPAR_)))
```

```lean
Type mismatch
  [EvenOddList.cons]](#manual-EvenOddList___cons-_LPAR_in-A-type-with-parameter-and-index_RPAR_) "a" ([EvenOddList.cons]](#manual-EvenOddList___cons-_LPAR_in-A-type-with-parameter-and-index_RPAR_) "b" ([EvenOddList.cons]](#manual-EvenOddList___cons-_LPAR_in-A-type-with-parameter-and-index_RPAR_) "c" [EvenOddList.nil]](#manual-EvenOddList___nil-_LPAR_in-A-type-with-parameter-and-index_RPAR_)))
has type
  [EvenOddList]](#manual-EvenOddList-_LPAR_in-A-type-with-parameter-and-index_RPAR_) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) [!](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not)[!](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not)[!](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not)[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
but is expected to have type
  [EvenOddList]](#manual-EvenOddList-_LPAR_in-A-type-with-parameter-and-index_RPAR_) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

In this declaration, `α` is a [parameter]](#manual---tech-term-parameters), because it is used consistently in all occurrences of `[EvenOddList]](#manual-EvenOddList-_LPAR_in-A-type-with-parameter-and-index_RPAR_)`.
`b` is an [index]](#manual---tech-term-indices), because different `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` values are used for it at different occurrences.

**Example: Parameters before and after the colon**

In this example, both parameters are specified before the colon in `[Either]](#manual-Either-_LPAR_in-Parameters-before-and-after-the-colon_RPAR_)`'s signature.

```lean
inductive Either (α : Type u) (β : Type v) : Type (max u v) where
| left : α → [Either]](#manual-Either-_LPAR_in-Parameters-before-and-after-the-colon_RPAR_) α β
| right : β → [Either]](#manual-Either-_LPAR_in-Parameters-before-and-after-the-colon_RPAR_) α β
```

In this version, there are two types named `α` that might not be identical:

```lean
inductive Either' (α : Type u) (β : Type v) : Type (max u v) where
| left : {α : Type u} → {β : Type v} → α → [Either']](#manual-Either___-_LPAR_in-Parameters-before-and-after-the-colon_RPAR_) α β
| right : β → Either' α β
```

```lean
Mismatched inductive type parameter in
  Either' α β
The provided argument
  α
is not definitionally equal to the expected parameter
  α✝

Note: The value of parameter `α✝` must be fixed throughout the inductive declaration. Consider making this parameter an index if it must vary.
```

Placing the parameters after the colon results in parameters that can be instantiated by the constructors:

```lean
inductive Either'' : Type u → Type v → Type (max u v + 1) where
| left : {α : Type u} → {β : Type v} → α → [Either'']](#manual-Either______-_LPAR_in-Parameters-before-and-after-the-colon_RPAR_) α β
| right : β → [Either'']](#manual-Either______-_LPAR_in-Parameters-before-and-after-the-colon_RPAR_) α β
```

A larger universe is required for this type because [constructor parameters must be in universes that are smaller than the inductive type's universe]](#manual-inductive-type-universe-levels).
`[Either''.right]](#manual-Either_________right-_LPAR_in-Parameters-before-and-after-the-colon_RPAR_)`'s type parameter is discovered via Lean's ordinary rules for [automatic implicit parameters](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Headers-and-Signatures/#--tech-term-automatic-implicit-parameters).

#### 4.4.1.3. Anonymous Constructor Syntax {#manual-anonymous-constructor-syntax}

If an inductive type has just one constructor, then this constructor is eligible for *anonymous constructor syntax*.
Instead of writing the constructor's name applied to its arguments, the explicit arguments can be enclosed in angle brackets (`'⟨'` and `'⟩'`, Unicode `MATHEMATICAL LEFT ANGLE BRACKET (U+0x27e8)` and `MATHEMATICAL RIGHT ANGLE BRACKET (U+0x27e9)`) and separated with commas.
This works in both pattern and expression contexts.
Providing arguments by name or converting all implicit parameters to explicit parameters with `@` requires using the ordinary constructor syntax.

syntaxAnonymous Constructors

Constructors can be invoked anonymously by enclosing their explicit arguments in angle brackets, separated by commas.

```lean
term ::= ...
    | ⟨ term,* ⟩
```

**Example: Anonymous constructors**

The type `[AtLeastOne]](#manual-AtLeastOne-_LPAR_in-Anonymous-constructors_RPAR_) α` is similar to `List α`, except there's always at least one element present:

```lean
inductive AtLeastOne (α : Type u) : Type u where
| mk : α → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([AtLeastOne]](#manual-AtLeastOne-_LPAR_in-Anonymous-constructors_RPAR_) α) → [AtLeastOne]](#manual-AtLeastOne-_LPAR_in-Anonymous-constructors_RPAR_) α
```

Anonymous constructor syntax can be used to construct them:

```lean
def oneTwoThree : [AtLeastOne]](#manual-AtLeastOne-_LPAR_in-Anonymous-constructors_RPAR_) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
⟨1, [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ⟨2, [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ⟨3, [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)⟩⟩⟩
```

and to match against them:

```lean
def AtLeastOne.head : [AtLeastOne]](#manual-AtLeastOne-_LPAR_in-Anonymous-constructors_RPAR_) α → α
| ⟨x, _⟩ => x
```

Equivalently, traditional constructor syntax could have been used:

```lean
def oneTwoThree' : [AtLeastOne]](#manual-AtLeastOne-_LPAR_in-Anonymous-constructors_RPAR_) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[.mk]](#manual-AtLeastOne___mk-_LPAR_in-Anonymous-constructors_RPAR_) 1 ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([.mk]](#manual-AtLeastOne___mk-_LPAR_in-Anonymous-constructors_RPAR_) 2 ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([.mk]](#manual-AtLeastOne___mk-_LPAR_in-Anonymous-constructors_RPAR_) 3 [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)))))
def AtLeastOne.head' : [AtLeastOne]](#manual-AtLeastOne-_LPAR_in-Anonymous-constructors_RPAR_) α → α
| [.mk]](#manual-AtLeastOne___mk-_LPAR_in-Anonymous-constructors_RPAR_) x _ => x
```

#### 4.4.1.4. Deriving Instances {#manual-inductive-declarations-deriving-instances}

The optional `deriving` clause of an inductive type declaration can be used to derive instances of type classes.
Please refer to [the section on instance deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#deriving-instances) for more information.

### 4.4.2. Structure Declarations {#manual-structures}

syntaxStructure Declarations

```lean
command ::= ...
    | [declModifiers](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Modifiers/#Lean___Parser___Command___declModifiers)
      structure declId bracketedBinder* (: term)?
        (extends (ident : )?term,*)?
        where
        ([declModifiers](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Modifiers/#Lean___Parser___Command___declModifiers) ident ::)?
        structFields
      ([deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) derivingClass,*)?
```

Declares a new structure type.

Structures are inductive types that have only a single constructor and no indices.
In exchange for these restrictions, Lean generates code for structures that offers a number of conveniences: projection functions are generated for each field, an additional constructor syntax based on field names rather than positional arguments is available, a similar syntax may be used to replace the values of certain named fields, and structures may extend other structures.
Just like other inductive types, structures may be recursive; they are subject to the same restrictions regarding strict positivity.
Structures do not add any expressive power to Lean; all of their features are implemented in terms of code generation.

#### 4.4.2.1. Structure Parameters {#manual-structure-params}

Just like ordinary inductive type declarations, the header of the structure declaration contains a signature that may specify both parameters and a resulting universe.
Structures may not define [indexed families]](#manual---tech-term-indexed-families).

#### 4.4.2.2. Fields {#manual-structure-fields}

Each field of a structure declaration corresponds to a parameter of the constructor.

**Example: Inferring Universes**

The structure `[MyProd]](#manual-MyProd-_LPAR_in-Inferring-Universes_RPAR_)` is the same as `[Prod](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)`.

```lean
structure MyProd (α β : Type _) where
fst : α
snd : β
```

The two parameters and the two fields are constructor parameters:

```lean
MyProd.mk.{u, v}
{α : Type u}
{β : Type v}
(fst : α)
(snd : β)
: [MyProd]](#manual-MyProd-_LPAR_in-Inferring-Universes_RPAR_).{u, v} α β
```

Additionally, the constructor is [universe polymorphic]](#manual---tech-term-universe-polymorphism); the type constructor `[MyProd]](#manual-MyProd-_LPAR_in-Inferring-Universes_RPAR_)` takes two universe parameters:

```lean
[MyProd]](#manual-MyProd-_LPAR_in-Inferring-Universes_RPAR_).{u, v} (α : Type u) (β : Type v) : Type (max u v)
```

The universe level of each type of each field must be less than or equal to the universe level of the structure.
Lean infers that `Type (max u v)` is the least universe that can accommodate both `Type u` and `Type v`.

Auto-implicit arguments are inserted in each field separately, even if their names coincide, and the fields become constructor parameters that quantify over types.

**Example: Auto-Implicit Parameters in Structure Fields**

The structure `[MyStructure]](#manual-MyStructure-_LPAR_in-Auto-Implicit-Parameters-in-Structure-Fields_RPAR_)` contains fields whose types have auto-implicit parameters:

```lean
structure MyStructure where
field1 : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n
field2 : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n
```

Each fields in the constructor `MyStructure.mk` takes its own implicit parameter `n` of type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`:

```lean
MyStructure.mk
(field1 : {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n)
(field2 : {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n)
: [MyStructure]](#manual-MyStructure-_LPAR_in-Auto-Implicit-Parameters-in-Structure-Fields_RPAR_)
```

The type constructor `[MyStructure]](#manual-MyStructure-_LPAR_in-Auto-Implicit-Parameters-in-Structure-Fields_RPAR_)` takes no universe parameters, and the resulting type is in `Type`,
which is the universe for `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n`:

```lean
[MyStructure]](#manual-MyStructure-_LPAR_in-Auto-Implicit-Parameters-in-Structure-Fields_RPAR_) : Type
```

For each field, a projection function is generated that extracts the field's value from the underlying type's constructor.
This function is in the structure's name's namespace.
Structure field projections are handled specially by the elaborator (as described in the [section on structure inheritance]](#manual-structure-inheritance)), which performs extra steps beyond looking up a namespace.
When field types depend on prior fields, the types of the dependent projection functions are written in terms of earlier projections, rather than explicit pattern matching.

**Example: Dependent projection types**

The structure `[ArraySized]](#manual-ArraySized-_LPAR_in-Dependent-projection-types_RPAR_)` contains a field whose type depends on both a structure parameter and an earlier field:

```lean
structure ArraySized (α : Type u) (length : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) where
array : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α
size_eq_length : array.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) = length
```

The signature of the projection function `[size_eq_length]](#manual-ArraySized___size_eq_length-_LPAR_in-Dependent-projection-types_RPAR_)` takes the structure type's parameter as an implicit parameter and refers to the earlier field using the corresponding projection:

```lean
[ArraySized.size_eq_length]](#manual-ArraySized___size_eq_length-_LPAR_in-Dependent-projection-types_RPAR_).{u}
{α : Type u} {length : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)}
(self : [ArraySized]](#manual-ArraySized-_LPAR_in-Dependent-projection-types_RPAR_) α length)
: self.[array]](#manual-ArraySized___array-_LPAR_in-Dependent-projection-types_RPAR_).[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) = length
```

Structure fields may have default values, specified with `:=`.
These values are used if no explicit value is provided.

**Example: Default values**

An adjacency list representation of a graph can be represented as an array of lists of `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
The size of the array indicates the number of vertices, and the outgoing edges from each vertex are stored in the array at the vertex's index.
Because the default value `#[]` is provided for the field `[adjacency]](#manual-Graph___adjacency-_LPAR_in-Default-values_RPAR_)`, the empty graph `[Graph.empty]](#manual-Graph___empty-_LPAR_in-Default-values_RPAR_)` can be constructed without providing any field values.

```lean
structure Graph where
adjacency : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) ([List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) := #[]
def Graph.empty : [Graph]](#manual-Graph-_LPAR_in-Default-values_RPAR_) := {}
```

Structure fields may additionally be accessed via their index, using dot notation.
Fields are numbered beginning with `1`.

#### 4.4.2.3. Structure Constructors {#manual-structure-constructors}

Structure constructors may be explicitly named by providing the constructor name and `::` prior to the fields.
If no name is explicitly provided, then the constructor is named `mk` in the structure type's namespace.
[Declaration modifiers](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Modifiers/#declaration-modifiers) may additionally be provided along with an explicit constructor name.

**Example: Non-default constructor name**

The structure `[Palindrome]](#manual-Palindrome-_LPAR_in-Non-default-constructor-name_RPAR_)` contains a string and a proof that the string is the same when reversed:

```lean
structure Palindrome where
ofString ::
text : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
is_palindrome : text.data.[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse) = text.data
```

Its constructor is named `[Palindrome.ofString]](#manual-Palindrome___ofString-_LPAR_in-Non-default-constructor-name_RPAR_)`, rather than `Palindrome.mk`.

**Example: Modifiers on structure constructor**

The structure `[NatStringBimap]](#manual-NatStringBimap-_LPAR_in-Modifiers-on-structure-constructor_RPAR_)` maintains a finite bijection between natural numbers and strings.
It consists of a pair of maps, such that the keys each occur as values exactly once in the other map.
Because the constructor is private, code outside the defining module can't construct new instances and must use the provided API, which maintains the invariants of the type.
Additionally, providing the default constructor name explicitly is an opportunity to attach a [documentation comment](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Modifiers/#--tech-term-Documentation-comments) to the constructor.

```lean
structure NatStringBimap where
/--
Build a finite bijection between some
natural numbers and strings
-/
private mk ::
natToString : [Std.HashMap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Maps-and-Sets/#Std___HashMap) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
stringToNat : [Std.HashMap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Maps-and-Sets/#Std___HashMap) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
def NatStringBimap.empty : [NatStringBimap]](#manual-NatStringBimap-_LPAR_in-Modifiers-on-structure-constructor_RPAR_) := ⟨{}, {}⟩
def NatStringBimap.insert
(nat : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (string : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray))
(map : [NatStringBimap]](#manual-NatStringBimap-_LPAR_in-Modifiers-on-structure-constructor_RPAR_)) :
[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [NatStringBimap]](#manual-NatStringBimap-_LPAR_in-Modifiers-on-structure-constructor_RPAR_) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) map.[natToString]](#manual-NatStringBimap___natToString-_LPAR_in-Modifiers-on-structure-constructor_RPAR_).[contains](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Maps-and-Sets/#Std___HashMap___contains) nat ||
map.[stringToNat]](#manual-NatStringBimap___stringToNat-_LPAR_in-Modifiers-on-structure-constructor_RPAR_).[contains](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Maps-and-Sets/#Std___HashMap___contains) string [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) <|
[NatStringBimap.mk]](#manual-_private___Manual___Language___InductiveTypes___Structures___0___NatStringBimap___mk-_LPAR_in-Modifiers-on-structure-constructor_RPAR_)
(map.[natToString]](#manual-NatStringBimap___natToString-_LPAR_in-Modifiers-on-structure-constructor_RPAR_).[insert](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Maps-and-Sets/#Std___HashMap___insert) nat string)
(map.[stringToNat]](#manual-NatStringBimap___stringToNat-_LPAR_in-Modifiers-on-structure-constructor_RPAR_).[insert](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Maps-and-Sets/#Std___HashMap___insert) string nat)
```

Because structures are represented by single-constructor inductive types, their constructors can be invoked or matched against using [anonymous constructor syntax]](#manual---tech-term-anonymous-constructor-syntax).
Additionally, structures may be constructed or matched against using *structure instance* notation, which includes the names of the fields together with values for them.

syntaxStructure Instances

```lean
term ::= ...
    | { structInstField,*
        (: term)? }
```

Constructs a value of a constructor type given values for named fields.
Field specifiers may take two forms:

```lean
structInstField ::= ...
    | structInstLVal := private? term
```

```lean
structInstField ::= ...
    | ident
```

A `structInstLVal` is a field name (an identifier), a field index (a natural number), or a term in square brackets, followed by a sequence of zero or more subfields.
Subfields are either a field name or index preceded by a dot, or a term in square brackets.

This syntax is elaborated to applications of structure constructors.
The values provided for fields are by name, and they may be provided in any order.
The values provided for subfields are used to initialize fields of constructors of structures that are themselves found in fields.
Terms in square brackets are not allowed when constructing a structure; they are used in structure updates.

Field specifiers that do not contain `:=` are field abbreviations.
In this context, the identifier `f` is an abbreviation for `f := f`; that is, the value of `f` in the current scope is used to initialize the field `f`.

Every field that does not have a default value must be provided.
If a tactic is specified as the default argument, then it is run at elaboration time to construct the argument's value.

In a pattern context, field names are mapped to patterns that match the corresponding projection, and field abbreviations bind a pattern variable that is the field's name.
Default arguments are still present in patterns; if a pattern does not specify a value for a field with a default value, then the pattern only matches the default.

When a field definition contains the `private` modifier, the value is placed in the current module's [private scope](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Source-Files-and-Modules/#--tech-term-private-scope), even if the structure value is itself in the public scope.
The value is wrapped in a public but non-exposed helper definition.
This is particularly useful with instances of type classes, because the implementation of [methods](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/#--tech-term-methods) in public [instances](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/#--tech-term-instances) of type classes are [exposed](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Source-Files-and-Modules/#--tech-term-exposed) by default.
This modifier allows them to be made private.

The optional type annotation allows the structure type to be specified in contexts where it is not otherwise determined.

**Example: Patterns and default values**

The structure `[AugmentedIntList]](#manual-AugmentedIntList-_LPAR_in-Patterns-and-default-values_RPAR_)` contains a list together with some extra information, which is empty if omitted:

```lean
structure AugmentedIntList where
list : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)
augmentation : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) := ""
```

When testing whether the list is empty, the function `[isEmpty]](#manual-AugmentedIntList___isEmpty-_LPAR_in-Patterns-and-default-values_RPAR_)` must explicitly match the `[augmentation]](#manual-AugmentedIntList___augmentation-_LPAR_in-Patterns-and-default-values_RPAR_)` field, even though it has a default value:

```lean
def AugmentedIntList.isEmpty : [AugmentedIntList]](#manual-AugmentedIntList-_LPAR_in-Patterns-and-default-values_RPAR_) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| {[list]](#manual-AugmentedIntList___list-_LPAR_in-Patterns-and-default-values_RPAR_) := [], [augmentation]](#manual-AugmentedIntList___augmentation-_LPAR_in-Patterns-and-default-values_RPAR_) := ""} => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| _ => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) {[list]](#manual-AugmentedIntList___list-_LPAR_in-Patterns-and-default-values_RPAR_) := [], [augmentation]](#manual-AugmentedIntList___augmentation-_LPAR_in-Patterns-and-default-values_RPAR_) := "extra" : [AugmentedIntList]](#manual-AugmentedIntList-_LPAR_in-Patterns-and-default-values_RPAR_)}.[isEmpty]](#manual-AugmentedIntList___isEmpty-_LPAR_in-Patterns-and-default-values_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

**Example: Private Field Values**

Even when a definition of a structure is [exposed](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Source-Files-and-Modules/#--tech-term-exposed), individual fields may be hidden using the field-level `private` modifier.
In this module, the exposed public definition of `x` may use the private definition `secret` because the `imaginary` field's value is not exposed:

`Main.lean`

```lean
module
public structure Complex where
real : [Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float___ofModel)
imaginary : [Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float___ofModel)
private def secret := 2.3
@[expose]
public def x : [Complex]](#manual-Complex-_LPAR_in-Private-Field-Values_RPAR_) := {
[real]](#manual-Complex___real-_LPAR_in-Private-Field-Values_RPAR_) := 5.0
[imaginary]](#manual-Complex___imaginary-_LPAR_in-Private-Field-Values_RPAR_) := private 2 * [secret]](#manual-_private___0___secret-_LPAR_in-Private-Field-Values_RPAR_)
}
```

**Example: Private Methods**

In this module, the existence of the `State` structure is public, but its constructor and field are private.
The function `State.toString` is also private, and is intended to be accessed via the `ToString` instance.
However, because the implementations of [methods](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/#--tech-term-methods) are exposed for public instances, this is not allowed:

`Main.lean`

```lean
module
public structure State where
private mk ::
private count : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
private def State.toString (s : State) : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
s!"⟨{s.count}⟩"
public instance : ToString State where
toString s := s.toString
```

```lean
Invalid field `toString`: The environment does not contain `State.toString`, so it is not possible to project the field `toString` from an expression
  s
of type `State`

Note: A private declaration `State.toString` (from the current module) exists but would need to be public to access here.
```

Marking the implementation of `toString` as `private` removes it from the module's [public scope](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Source-Files-and-Modules/#--tech-term-public-scope), giving it access to private functions:

`Main.lean`

```lean
module
public structure State where
private mk ::
private count : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
private def State.toString (s : State) : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
s!"⟨{s.count}⟩"
public instance : ToString State where
toString s := private s.toString
```

syntaxStructure Updates

```lean
term ::= ...
    | {term with
        structInstField,*
        (: term)?}
```

Updates a value of a constructor type.
The term that precedes the `with` clause is expected to have a structure type; it is the value that is being updated.
A new instance of the structure is created in which every field not specified is copied from the value that is being updated, and the specified fields are replaced with their new values.
When updating a structure, array values may also be replaced by including the index to be updated in square brackets.
This updating does not require that the index expression be in bounds for the array, and out-of-bounds updates are discarded.

**Example: Updating arrays**

Updating structures may use array indices as well as projection names.
Updates at indices that are out of bounds are ignored:

```lean
structure AugmentedIntArray where
array : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)
augmentation : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) := ""
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr]](#manual-Repr___mk)
def one : [AugmentedIntArray]](#manual-AugmentedIntArray-_LPAR_in-Updating-arrays_RPAR_) := {[array]](#manual-AugmentedIntArray___array-_LPAR_in-Updating-arrays_RPAR_) := #[1]}
def two : [AugmentedIntArray]](#manual-AugmentedIntArray-_LPAR_in-Updating-arrays_RPAR_) := {[one]](#manual-one-_LPAR_in-Updating-arrays_RPAR_) with [array]](#manual-AugmentedIntArray___array-_LPAR_in-Updating-arrays_RPAR_) := #[1, 2]}
def two' : [AugmentedIntArray]](#manual-AugmentedIntArray-_LPAR_in-Updating-arrays_RPAR_) := {[two]](#manual-two-_LPAR_in-Updating-arrays_RPAR_) with [array]](#manual-AugmentedIntArray___array-_LPAR_in-Updating-arrays_RPAR_)[0] := 2}
def two'' : [AugmentedIntArray]](#manual-AugmentedIntArray-_LPAR_in-Updating-arrays_RPAR_) := {[two]](#manual-two-_LPAR_in-Updating-arrays_RPAR_) with [array]](#manual-AugmentedIntArray___array-_LPAR_in-Updating-arrays_RPAR_)[99] := 3}
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ([one]](#manual-one-_LPAR_in-Updating-arrays_RPAR_), [two]](#manual-two-_LPAR_in-Updating-arrays_RPAR_), [two']](#manual-two___-_LPAR_in-Updating-arrays_RPAR_), [two'']](#manual-two______-_LPAR_in-Updating-arrays_RPAR_))
```

```lean
({ array := #[1], augmentation := "" },
 { array := #[1, 2], augmentation := "" },
 { array := #[2, 2], augmentation := "" },
 { array := #[1, 2], augmentation := "" })
```

Values of structure types may also be declared using `where`, followed by definitions for each field.
This may only be used as part of a definition, not in an expression context.

**Example: where for structures**

The product type in Lean is a structure named `[Prod](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)`.
Products can be defined using their projections:

```lean
def location : [Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float___ofModel) × [Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float___ofModel) where
[fst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) := 22.807
[snd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) := -13.923
```

#### 4.4.2.4. Structure Inheritance {#manual-structure-inheritance}

Structures may be declared as extending other structures using the optional `extends` clause.
The resulting structure type has all of the fields of all of the parent structure types.
If the parent structure types have overlapping field names, then all overlapping field names must have the same type.

The resulting structure has a *field resolution order* that affects the values of fields.
When possible, this resolution order is the [C3 linearization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C3_linearization) of the structure's parents.
Essentially, the field resolution order should be a total ordering of the entire set of parents such that every `extends` list is in order.
When there is no C3 linearization, a heuristic is used to find an order nonetheless.
Every structure type is first in its own field resolution order.

The field resolution order is used to compute the default values of optional fields.
When the value of a field is not specified, the first default value defined in the resolution order is used.
References to fields in the default value use the field resolution order as well; this means that child structures that override default fields of parent constructors may also change the computed default values of parent fields.
Because the child structure is the first element of its own resolution order, default values in the child structure take precedence over default values from the parent structures.

When the new structure extends existing structures, the new structure's constructor takes the existing structure's information as additional arguments.
Typically, this is in the form of a constructor parameter for each parent structure type.
This parent value contains all of the parent's fields.
If the parents' fields overlap, however, then the subset of non-overlapping fields from one or more of the parents is included instead of an entire value of the parent structure to prevent duplicating field information.

There is no subtyping relation between a parent structure type and its children.
Even if structure `B` extends structure `A`, a function expecting an `A` will not accept a `B`.
However, conversion functions are generated that convert a structure into each of its parents.
These conversion functions are called *parent projections*.
Parent projections are in the child structure's namespace, and their name is the parent structure's name preceded by `to`.

**Example: Structure type inheritance with overlapping fields**

In this example, a `[Textbook]](#manual-Textbook-_LPAR_in-Structure-type-inheritance-with-overlapping-fields_RPAR_)` is a `[Book]](#manual-Book-_LPAR_in-Structure-type-inheritance-with-overlapping-fields_RPAR_)` that is also an `[AcademicWork]](#manual-AcademicWork-_LPAR_in-Structure-type-inheritance-with-overlapping-fields_RPAR_)`:

```lean
structure Book where
title : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
author : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
structure AcademicWork where
author : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
discipline : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
structure Textbook extends [Book]](#manual-Book-_LPAR_in-Structure-type-inheritance-with-overlapping-fields_RPAR_), [AcademicWork]](#manual-AcademicWork-_LPAR_in-Structure-type-inheritance-with-overlapping-fields_RPAR_)
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) Textbook.toBook
```

Because the field `author` occurs in both `[Book]](#manual-Book-_LPAR_in-Structure-type-inheritance-with-overlapping-fields_RPAR_)` and `[AcademicWork]](#manual-AcademicWork-_LPAR_in-Structure-type-inheritance-with-overlapping-fields_RPAR_)`, the constructor `Textbook.mk` does not take both parents as arguments.
Its signature is:

```lean
Textbook.mk (toBook : [Book]](#manual-Book-_LPAR_in-Structure-type-inheritance-with-overlapping-fields_RPAR_)) (discipline : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [Textbook]](#manual-Textbook-_LPAR_in-Structure-type-inheritance-with-overlapping-fields_RPAR_)
```

The conversion functions are:

```lean
Textbook.toBook (self : [Textbook]](#manual-Textbook-_LPAR_in-Structure-type-inheritance-with-overlapping-fields_RPAR_)) : [Book]](#manual-Book-_LPAR_in-Structure-type-inheritance-with-overlapping-fields_RPAR_)
```

```lean
Textbook.toAcademicWork (self : [Textbook]](#manual-Textbook-_LPAR_in-Structure-type-inheritance-with-overlapping-fields_RPAR_)) : [AcademicWork]](#manual-AcademicWork-_LPAR_in-Structure-type-inheritance-with-overlapping-fields_RPAR_)
```

The latter combines the `author` field of the included `[Book]](#manual-Book-_LPAR_in-Structure-type-inheritance-with-overlapping-fields_RPAR_)` with the unbundled `Discipline` field, and is equivalent to:

```lean
def toAcademicWork (self : [Textbook]](#manual-Textbook-_LPAR_in-Structure-type-inheritance-with-overlapping-fields_RPAR_)) : [AcademicWork]](#manual-AcademicWork-_LPAR_in-Structure-type-inheritance-with-overlapping-fields_RPAR_) :=
let .mk book discipline := self
let .mk _title author := book
.mk author discipline
```

The resulting structure's projections can be used as if its fields are simply the union of the parents' fields.
The Lean elaborator automatically generates an appropriate projection when fields are used.
Likewise, the field-based initialization and structure update notations hide the details of the encoding of inheritance.
The encoding is, however, visible when using the constructor's name, when using [anonymous constructor syntax]](#manual---tech-term-anonymous-constructor-syntax), or when referring to fields by their index rather than their name.

**Example: Field Indices and Structure Inheritance**

```lean
structure Pair (α : Type u) where
fst : α
snd : α
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr]](#manual-Repr___mk)
structure Triple (α : Type u) extends [Pair]](#manual-Pair-_LPAR_in-Field-Indices-and-Structure-Inheritance_RPAR_) α where
thd : α
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr]](#manual-Repr___mk)
def coords : [Triple]](#manual-Triple-_LPAR_in-Field-Indices-and-Structure-Inheritance_RPAR_) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := {[fst]](#manual-Pair___fst-_LPAR_in-Field-Indices-and-Structure-Inheritance_RPAR_) := 17, [snd]](#manual-Pair___snd-_LPAR_in-Field-Indices-and-Structure-Inheritance_RPAR_) := 2, [thd]](#manual-Triple___thd-_LPAR_in-Field-Indices-and-Structure-Inheritance_RPAR_) := 95}
```

Evaluating the first field index of `[coords]](#manual-coords-_LPAR_in-Field-Indices-and-Structure-Inheritance_RPAR_)` yields the underlying `[Pair]](#manual-Pair-_LPAR_in-Field-Indices-and-Structure-Inheritance_RPAR_)`, rather than the contents of the field `fst`:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [coords]](#manual-coords-_LPAR_in-Field-Indices-and-Structure-Inheritance_RPAR_).1
```

```lean
{ fst := 17, snd := 2 }
```

The elaborator translates `[coords]](#manual-coords-_LPAR_in-Field-Indices-and-Structure-Inheritance_RPAR_).[fst]](#manual-Pair___fst-_LPAR_in-Field-Indices-and-Structure-Inheritance_RPAR_)` into `[coords]](#manual-coords-_LPAR_in-Field-Indices-and-Structure-Inheritance_RPAR_).toPair.[fst]](#manual-Pair___fst-_LPAR_in-Field-Indices-and-Structure-Inheritance_RPAR_)`.

**Example: No structure subtyping**

Given these definitions of even numbers, even prime numbers, and a concrete even prime:

```lean
structure EvenNumber where
val : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
isEven : 2 ∣ val := by [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)
structure EvenPrime extends [EvenNumber]](#manual-EvenNumber-_LPAR_in-No-structure-subtyping_RPAR_) where
notOne : val ≠ 1 := by [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)
isPrime : ∀ n, n ≤ val → n ∣ val → n = 1 ∨ n = val
def two : [EvenPrime]](#manual-EvenPrime-_LPAR_in-No-structure-subtyping_RPAR_) where
[val]](#manual-EvenNumber___val-_LPAR_in-No-structure-subtyping_RPAR_) := 2
```
