The `#print` command displays the most important information about structure types, including the [parent projections]](#manual---tech-term-parent-projections), all the fields with their default values, the constructor, and the [field resolution order]](#manual---tech-term-field-resolution-order).
When working with deep hierarchies that contain inheritance diamonds, this information can be very useful.

**Example: #print and Structure Types**

This collection of structure types models a variety of bicycles, both electric and non-electric and both ordinary-sized and large family bicycles.
The final structure type, `[ElectricFamilyBike]](#manual-ElectricFamilyBike-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_)`, contains a diamond in its inheritance graph, because both `[FamilyBike]](#manual-FamilyBike-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_)` and `[ElectricBike]](#manual-ElectricBike-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_)` extend `[Bicycle]](#manual-Bicycle-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_)`.

```lean
structure Vehicle where
wheels : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
structure Bicycle extends [Vehicle]](#manual-Vehicle-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_) where
[wheels]](#manual-Vehicle___wheels-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_) := 2
structure ElectricVehicle extends [Vehicle]](#manual-Vehicle-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_) where
batteries : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := 1
structure FamilyBike extends [Bicycle]](#manual-Bicycle-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_) where
[wheels]](#manual-Vehicle___wheels-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_) := 3
structure ElectricBike extends [Bicycle]](#manual-Bicycle-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_), [ElectricVehicle]](#manual-ElectricVehicle-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_)
structure ElectricFamilyBike
extends [FamilyBike]](#manual-FamilyBike-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_), [ElectricBike]](#manual-ElectricBike-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_) where
batteries := 2
```

The `#print` command displays the important information about each structure type:

```lean
#print [ElectricBike]](#manual-ElectricBike-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_)
```

```lean

number of parameters: 0
parents:
  ElectricBike.toBicycle : [Bicycle]](#manual-Bicycle-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_)
  ElectricBike.toElectricVehicle : [ElectricVehicle]](#manual-ElectricVehicle-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_)
fields:
  [Vehicle.wheels]](#manual-Vehicle___wheels-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
    2
  [ElectricVehicle.batteries]](#manual-ElectricVehicle___batteries-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
    1
constructor:
  ElectricBike.mk (toBicycle : [Bicycle]](#manual-Bicycle-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_)) (batteries : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [ElectricBike]](#manual-ElectricBike-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_)
field notation resolution order:
  [ElectricBike]](#manual-ElectricBike-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_), [Bicycle]](#manual-Bicycle-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_), [ElectricVehicle]](#manual-ElectricVehicle-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_), [Vehicle]](#manual-Vehicle-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_)
```

An `[ElectricFamilyBike]](#manual-ElectricFamilyBike-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_)` has three wheels by default because `[FamilyBike]](#manual-FamilyBike-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_)` precedes `[Bicycle]](#manual-Bicycle-_LPAR_in-___print--and-Structure-Types_RPAR_)` in its resolution order:

### 4.4.3. Logical Model {#manual-inductive-types-logical-model}

#### 4.4.3.1. Recursors {#manual-recursors}

Every inductive type is equipped with a [recursor]](#manual---tech-term-recursor).
The recursor is completely determined by the signatures of the type constructor and the constructors.
Recursors have function types, but they are primitive and are not definable using `fun`.

##### 4.4.3.1.1. Recursor Types {#manual-recursor-types}

The recursor takes the following parameters:

The inductive type's [parameters]](#manual---tech-term-parameters)
:   Because parameters are consistent, they can be abstracted over the entire recursor.

The *motive*
:   The motive determines the type of an application of the recursor. The motive is a function whose arguments are the type's indices and an instance of the type with these indices instantiated. The specific universe for the type that the motive determines depends on the inductive type's universe and the specific constructors—see the section on [[subsingleton]](#manual---tech-term-subsingleton) elimination](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Type-System/Inductive-Types/#subsingleton-elimination) for details.

A *minor premise* for each constructor
:   For each constructor, the recursor expects a function that satisfies the motive for an arbitrary application of the constructor.
    Each minor premise abstracts over all of the constructor's parameters.
    If the constructor's parameter's type is the inductive type itself, then the minor premise additionally takes a parameter whose type is the motive applied to that parameter's value—this will receive the result of recursively processing the recursive parameter.

The *major premise*, or target
:   Finally, the recursor takes an instance of the type as an argument, along with any index values.

The result type of the recursor is the motive applied to these indices and the major premise.

**Example: The recursor for Bool**

`[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`'s recursor `Bool.rec` has the following parameters:

- The motive computes a type in any universe, given a `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.
- There are minor premises for both constructors, in which the motive is satisfied for both `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` and `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.
- The major premise is some `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.

The return type is the motive applied to the major premise.

```lean
Bool.rec.{u} {motive : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → Sort u}
(false : motive [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false))
(true : motive [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false))
(t : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : motive t
```

**Example: The recursor for List**

`[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`'s recursor `List.rec` has the following parameters:

- The parameter `α` comes first, because the motive, minor premises, and major premise need to refer to it.
- The motive computes a type in any universe, given a `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α`. There is no connection between the universe levels `u` and `v`.
- There are minor premises for both constructors:

  - The motive is satisfied for `[List.nil](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`
  - The motive should be satisfiable for any application of `[List.cons](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`, given that it is satisfiable for the tail. The extra parameter `motive tail` is because `tail`'s type is a recursive occurrence of `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`.
- The major premise is some `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α`.

Once again, the return type is the motive applied to the major premise.

```lean
List.rec.{u, v} {α : Type v} {motive : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → Sort u}
(nil : motive [])
(cons : (head : α) → (tail : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) → motive tail →
motive (head :: tail))
(t : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : motive t
```

**Example: Recursor with parameters and indices**

Given the definition of `[EvenOddList]](#manual-EvenOddList-_LPAR_in-Recursor-with-parameters-and-indices_RPAR_)`:

```lean
inductive EvenOddList (α : Type u) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → Type u where
| nil : [EvenOddList]](#manual-EvenOddList-_LPAR_in-Recursor-with-parameters-and-indices_RPAR_) α [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| cons : α → [EvenOddList]](#manual-EvenOddList-_LPAR_in-Recursor-with-parameters-and-indices_RPAR_) α isEven → [EvenOddList]](#manual-EvenOddList-_LPAR_in-Recursor-with-parameters-and-indices_RPAR_) α ([not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not) isEven)
```

The recursor `EvenOddList.rec` is very similar to that for `List`.
The difference comes from the presence of the index:

- The motive now abstracts over any arbitrary choice of index.
- The minor premise for `[nil]](#manual-EvenOddList___nil-_LPAR_in-Recursor-with-parameters-and-indices_RPAR_)` applies the motive to `[nil]](#manual-EvenOddList___nil-_LPAR_in-Recursor-with-parameters-and-indices_RPAR_)`'s index value `true`.
- The minor premise `[cons]](#manual-EvenOddList___cons-_LPAR_in-Recursor-with-parameters-and-indices_RPAR_)` abstracts over the index value used in its recursive occurrence, and instantiates the motive with its negation.
- The major premise additionally abstracts over an arbitrary choice of index.

```lean
EvenOddList.rec.{u, v} {α : Type v}
{motive : (isEven : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) → [EvenOddList]](#manual-EvenOddList-_LPAR_in-Recursor-with-parameters-and-indices_RPAR_) α isEven → Sort u}
(nil : motive [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) [EvenOddList.nil]](#manual-EvenOddList___nil-_LPAR_in-Recursor-with-parameters-and-indices_RPAR_))
(cons : {isEven : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)} →
(head : α) →
(tail : [EvenOddList]](#manual-EvenOddList-_LPAR_in-Recursor-with-parameters-and-indices_RPAR_) α isEven) → motive isEven tail →
motive (!isEven) ([EvenOddList.cons]](#manual-EvenOddList___cons-_LPAR_in-Recursor-with-parameters-and-indices_RPAR_) head tail)) :
{isEven : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)} → (t : [EvenOddList]](#manual-EvenOddList-_LPAR_in-Recursor-with-parameters-and-indices_RPAR_) α isEven) → motive isEven t
```

When using a predicate (that is, a function that returns a `Prop`) for the motive, recursors express induction.
The minor premises for non-recursive constructors are the base cases, and the additional arguments supplied to minor premises for constructors with recursive arguments are the induction hypotheses.

###### 4.4.3.1.1.1. Subsingleton Elimination {#manual-subsingleton-elimination}

Proofs in Lean are computationally irrelevant.
In other words, having been provided with **some** proof of a proposition, it should be impossible for a program to check **which** proof it has received.
This is reflected in the types of recursors for inductively defined propositions or predicates.
For these types, if there's more than one potential proof of the theorem then the motive may only return another `Prop`.
If the type is structured such that there's only at most one proof anyway, then the motive may return a type in any universe.
A proposition that has at most one inhabitant is called a *subsingleton*.
Rather than obligating users to *prove* that there's only one possible proof, a conservative syntactic approximation is used to check whether a proposition is a subsingleton.
Propositions that fulfill both of the following requirements are considered to be subsingletons:

- There is at most one constructor.
- Each of the constructor's parameter types is either a `Prop`, a parameter, or an index.

**Example: True is a subsingleton**

`[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)` is a subsingleton because it has one constructor, and this constructor has no parameters.
Its recursor has the following signature:

```lean
True.rec.{u} {motive : [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) → Sort u}
(intro : motive [True.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro))
(t : [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)) : motive t
```

**Example: False is a subsingleton**

`[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)` is a subsingleton because it has no constructors.
Its recursor has the following signature:

```lean
False.rec.{u} (motive : [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) → Sort u) (t : [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)) : motive t
```

Note that the motive is an explicit parameter.
This is because it is not mentioned in any further parameters' types, so it could not be solved by unification.

**Example: And is a subsingleton**

`[And](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)` is a subsingleton because it has one constructor, and both of the constructor's parameters' types are propositions.
Its recursor has the following signature:

```lean
And.rec.{u} {a b : Prop} {motive : a ∧ b → Sort u}
(intro : (left : a) → (right : b) → motive ([And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) left right))
(t : a ∧ b) : motive t
```

**Example: Or is not a subsingleton**

`[Or](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl)` is not a subsingleton because it has more than one constructor.
Its recursor has the following signature:

```lean
Or.rec {a b : Prop} {motive : a ∨ b → Prop}
(inl : ∀ (h : a), motive ([.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) h))
(inr : ∀ (h : b), motive ([.inr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) h))
(t : a ∨ b) : motive t
```

The motive's type indicates that `Or.rec` can only be used to produce proofs.
A proof of a disjunction can be used to prove something else, but there's no way for a program to inspect *which* of the two disjuncts was true and used for the proof.

**Example: Eq is a subsingleton**

`[Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl)` is a subsingleton because it has just one constructor, `[Eq.refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl)`.
This constructor instantiates `[Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl)`'s index with a parameter value, so all arguments are parameters:

```lean
[Eq.refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl).{u} {α : Sort u} (x : α) : [Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x x
```

Its recursor has the following signature:

```lean
Eq.rec.{u, v} {α : Sort v} {x : α}
{motive : (y : α) → x = y → Sort u}
(refl : motive x ([.refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x))
{y : α} (t : x = y) : motive y t
```

This means that proofs of equality can be used to rewrite the types of non-propositions.

##### 4.4.3.1.2. Reduction {#manual-iota-reduction}

In addition to adding new constants to the logic, inductive type declarations also add new reduction rules.
These rules govern the interaction between recursors and constructors; specifically recursors that have constructors as their major premise.
This form of reduction is called *ι-reduction* (iota reduction).

When the recursor's major premise is a constructor with no recursive parameters, the recursor application reduces to an application of the constructor's minor premise to the constructor's arguments.
If there are recursive parameters, then these arguments to the minor premise are found by applying the recursor to the recursive occurrence.

#### 4.4.3.2. Well-Formedness Requirements {#manual-well-formed-inductives}

Inductive type declarations are subject to a number of well-formedness requirements.
These requirements ensure that Lean remains consistent as a logic when it is extended with the inductive type's new rules.
They are conservative: there exist potential inductive types that do not undermine consistency, but that these requirements nonetheless reject.

##### 4.4.3.2.1. Universe Levels {#manual-inductive-type-universe-levels}

Type constructors of inductive types must either inhabit a [universe]](#manual---tech-term-universes) or a function type whose return type is a universe.
Each constructor must inhabit a function type that returns a saturated application of the inductive type.
If the inductive type's universe is `Prop`, then there are no further restrictions on universes, because `Prop` is [impredicative]](#manual---tech-term-impredicative).
If the universe is not `Prop`, then the following must hold for each parameter to the constructor:

- If the constructor's parameter is a parameter (in the sense of parameters vs indices) of the inductive type, then this parameter's type may be no larger than the type constructor's universe.
- All other constructor parameters must be smaller than the type constructor's universe.

**Example: Universes, constructors, and parameters**

`[Either]](#manual-Either-_LPAR_in-Universes___-constructors___-and-parameters_RPAR_)` is in the greater of its arguments' universes, because both are parameters to the inductive type:

```lean
inductive Either (α : Type u) (β : Type v) : Type (max u v) where
| inl : α → [Either]](#manual-Either-_LPAR_in-Universes___-constructors___-and-parameters_RPAR_) α β
| inr : β → [Either]](#manual-Either-_LPAR_in-Universes___-constructors___-and-parameters_RPAR_) α β
```

`[CanRepr]](#manual-CanRepr-_LPAR_in-Universes___-constructors___-and-parameters_RPAR_)` is in a larger universe than the constructor parameter `α`, because `α` is not one of the inductive type's parameters:

```lean
inductive CanRepr : Type (u + 1) where
| mk : (α : Type u) → [[Repr]](#manual-Repr___mk) α] → [CanRepr]](#manual-CanRepr-_LPAR_in-Universes___-constructors___-and-parameters_RPAR_)
```

Constructorless inductive types may be in universes smaller than their parameters:

```lean
inductive Spurious (α : Type 5) : Type 0 where
```

It would, however, be impossible to add a constructor to `[Spurious]](#manual-Spurious-_LPAR_in-Universes___-constructors___-and-parameters_RPAR_)` without changing its levels.

##### 4.4.3.2.2. Strict Positivity {#manual-strict-positivity}

All occurrences of the type being defined in the types of the parameters of the constructors must be in *strictly positive* positions.
A position is strictly positive if it is not in a function's argument type (no matter how many function types are nested around it) and it is not an argument of any expression other than type constructors of inductive types.
This restriction rules out unsound inductive type definitions, at the cost of also ruling out some unproblematic ones.

**Example: Non-strictly-positive inductive types**

The type `Bad` would make Lean inconsistent if it were not rejected:

```lean
inductive Bad where
| bad : (Bad → Bad) → Bad
```

```lean
(kernel) arg #1 of 'Bad.bad' has a non positive occurrence of the datatypes being declared
```

This is because it would be possible to write a circular argument that proves `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)` under the assumption `Bad`.
`Bad.bad` is rejected because the constructor's parameter has type `Bad → Bad`, which is a function type in which `Bad` occurs as an argument type.

This declaration of a fixed point operator is rejected, because `Fix` occurs as an argument to `f`:

```lean
inductive Fix (f : Type u → Type u) where
| fix : f ([Fix]](#manual-Fix-_LPAR_in-Non-strictly-positive-inductive-types_RPAR_) f) → [Fix]](#manual-Fix-_LPAR_in-Non-strictly-positive-inductive-types_RPAR_) f
```

```lean
(kernel) arg #2 of 'Fix.fix' contains a non valid occurrence of the datatypes being declared
```

`Fix.fix` is rejected because `f` is not a type constructor of an inductive type, but `Fix` itself occurs as an argument to it.
In this case, `Fix` is also sufficient to construct a type equivalent to `Bad`:

```lean
def Bad : Type := [Fix]](#manual-Fix-_LPAR_in-Non-strictly-positive-inductive-types_RPAR_) fun t => t → t
```

##### 4.4.3.2.3. Prop vs Type {#manual-prop-vs-type}

Lean rejects universe-polymorphic types that could not, in practice, be used polymorphically.
This could arise if certain instantiations of the universe parameters would cause the type itself to be a `Prop`.
If this type is not a [subsingleton]](#manual---tech-term-subsingleton), then its recursor can only target propositions (that is, the [motive]](#manual---tech-term-motive) must return a `Prop`).
These types only really make sense as `Prop`s themselves, so the universe polymorphism is probably a mistake.
Because they are largely useless, Lean's inductive type elaborator has not been designed to support these types.

When such universe-polymorphic inductive types are indeed subsingletons, it can make sense to define them.
Lean's standard library defines `[PUnit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit)` and `[PEmpty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#PEmpty)`.
To define a subsingleton that can inhabit `Prop` or a `Type`, set the option `[bootstrap.inductiveCheckResultingUniverse]](#manual-bootstrap___inductiveCheckResultingUniverse)` to `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.

option

```lean
bootstrap.inductiveCheckResultingUniverse
```

Default value: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

by default the `inductive`/`structure` commands report an error if the resulting universe is not zero, but may be zero for some universe parameters. Reason: unless this type is a subsingleton, it is hardly what the user wants since it can only eliminate into `Prop`. In the `Init` package, we define subsingletons, and we use this option to disable the check. This option may be deleted in the future after we improve the validator

**Example: Overly-universe-polymorphic Bool**

Defining a version of `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` that can be in any universe is not allowed:

```lean
inductive PBool : Sort u where
| true
| false
```

```lean
Invalid universe polymorphic resulting type: The resulting universe is not `Prop`, but it may be `Prop` for some parameter values:
  Sort u

Hint: A possible solution is to use levels of the form `max 1 _` or `_ + 1` to ensure the universe is of the form `Type _`
```

#### 4.4.3.3. Constructions for Termination Checking {#manual-recursor-elaboration-helpers}

In addition to the type constructor, constructors, and recursors that Lean's core type theory prescribes for inductive types, Lean constructs a number of useful helpers.
First, the equation compiler (which translates recursive functions with pattern matching in to applications of recursors) makes use of these additional constructs:

- `recOn` is a version of the recursor in which the major premise is prior to the minor premise for each constructor.
- `casesOn` is a version of the recursor in which the major premise is prior to the minor premise for each constructor, and recursive arguments do not yield induction hypotheses. It expresses case analysis rather than primitive recursion.
- `below` computes a type that, for some motive, expresses that *all* inhabitants of the inductive type that are subtrees of the major premise satisfy the motive. It transforms a motive for induction or primitive recursion into a motive for strong recursion or strong induction.
- `brecOn` is a version of the recursor in which `below` is used to provide access to all subtrees, rather than just immediate recursive parameters. It represents strong induction.
- `noConfusion` is a general statement from which injectivity and disjointness of constructors can be derived.
- `noConfusionType` is the motive used for `noConfusion` that determines what the consequences of two constructors being equal would be. For separate constructors, this is `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)`; if both constructors are the same, then the consequence is the equality of their respective parameters.

These constructions follow the description in McBride, Goguen, and McKinna (2004)Conor McBride, Healfdene Goguen, and James McKinna, 2004. [“A Few Constructions on Constructors”](https://doi.org/10.1007/11617990_12). In *Types for Proofs and Programs, International Workshop, TYPES 2004.* (LNCS 3839).

For [well-founded recursion](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#--tech-term-well-founded-recursion), it is frequently useful to have a generic notion of size available.
This is captured in the `[SizeOf]](#manual-SizeOf___mk)` class.

type class

```lean
[SizeOf.{u}]](#manual-SizeOf___mk) (α : Sort u) : Sort (max 1 u)



[SizeOf.{u}]](#manual-SizeOf___mk) (α : Sort u) : Sort (max 1 u)
```

`[SizeOf]](#manual-SizeOf___mk)` is a typeclass automatically derived for every inductive type,
which equips the type with a "size" function to `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
The default instance defines each constructor to be `1` plus the sum of the
sizes of all the constructor fields.

This is used for proofs by well-founded induction, since every field of the
constructor has a smaller size than the constructor itself,
and in many cases this will suffice to do the proof that a recursive function
is only called on smaller values.
If the default proof strategy fails, it is recommended to supply a custom
size measure using the `termination_by` argument on the function definition.

Instance Constructor

```lean
[SizeOf.mk]](#manual-SizeOf___mk).{u}
```

Methods

```lean
sizeOf : α → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

The "size" of an element, a natural number which decreases on fields of
each inductive type.

### 4.4.4. Run-Time Representation {#manual-run-time-inductives}

An inductive type's run-time representation depends both on how many constructors it has, how many arguments each constructor takes, and whether these arguments are [relevant]](#manual---tech-term-relevant).

#### 4.4.4.1. Exceptions {#manual-inductive-types-runtime-special-support}

Not every inductive type is represented as indicated here—some inductive types have special support from the Lean compiler:

- The representation of the fixed-width integer types `[UInt8](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt8___ofBitVec)`, …, `[UInt64](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt64___ofBitVec)`, `[Int8](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#Int8___ofUInt8)`, …, `[Int64](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#Int64___ofUInt64)`, and `[USize](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#USize___ofBitVec)` depends on whether the code is compiled for a 32- or 64-bit architecture.
  Their representation is described [in a dedicated section](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#fixed-int-runtime).
- `[Char](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___mk)` is represented by `uint32_t`. Because `[Char](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___mk)` values never require more than 21 bits, they are always unboxed.
- `[Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float___ofModel)` is represented by a pointer to a Lean object that contains a “double”.
- An *enum inductive* type of at least 2 and at most `2^{32}` constructors, each of which has no parameters, is represented by the first type of `uint8_t`, `uint16_t`, `uint32_t` that is sufficient to assign a unique value to each constructor. For example, the type `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` is represented by `uint8_t`, with values `0` for `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` and `1` for `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.
- `[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) α` is represented the same way as `Bool`
- `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)` are represented by `lean_object *`.
  Their representations are described in more detail in [the section on natural numbers](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#nat-runtime) and [the section on integers](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#int-runtime).

#### 4.4.4.2. Relevance {#manual-inductive-types-runtime-relevance}

Types and proofs have no run-time representation.
That is, if an inductive type is a `Prop`, then its values are erased prior to compilation.
Similarly, all theorem statements and types are erased.
Types with run-time representations are called *relevant*, while types without run-time representations are called *irrelevant*.

**Example: Types are irrelevant**

Even though `[List.cons](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` has the following signature, which indicates three parameters:

```lean
[List.cons](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil).{u} {α : Type u} : α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α
```

its run-time representation has only two, because the type argument is run-time irrelevant.

**Example: Proofs are irrelevant**

Even though `[Fin.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)` has the following signature, which indicates three parameters:

```lean
[Fin.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} (val : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : val < n → [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n
```

its run-time representation has only two, because the proof is erased.

In most cases, irrelevant values simply disappear from compiled code.
However, in cases where some representation is required (such as when they are arguments to polymorphic constructors), they are represented by a trivial value.

#### 4.4.4.3. Trivial Wrappers {#manual-inductive-types-trivial-wrappers}

An inductive type is a trivial wrapper if it has has exactly one constructor and that constructor has exactly one run-time relevant parameter.
Trivial wrappers are represented identically to their constructor's parameter in the following circumstances:

- The inductive type is private.
- The type is public, and the [public scope](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Source-Files-and-Modules/#--tech-term-public-scope) of the module in which it is defined contains enough information to determine that it is a trivial wrapper.
- The type is defined in a source file that is not a [module](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Source-Files-and-Modules/#--tech-term-module).

**Example: Zero-Overhead Subtypes**

The structure `[Subtype](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Subtypes/#Subtype___mk)` bundles an element of some type with a proof that it satisfies a predicate.
Its constructor takes four arguments, but three of them are irrelevant:

```lean
[Subtype.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Subtypes/#Subtype___mk).{u} {α : Sort u} {p : α → Prop}
(val : α) (property : p val) : [Subtype](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Subtypes/#Subtype___mk) p
```

Thus, subtypes impose no runtime overhead in compiled code, and are represented identically to the type of the `[val](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Subtypes/#Subtype___mk)` field.

**Example: Signed Integers**

The signed integer types `[Int8](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#Int8___ofUInt8)`, ..., `[Int64](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#Int64___ofUInt64)`, `[ISize](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#ISize___ofUSize)` are structures with a single field that wraps the corresponding unsigned integer type.
They are represented by the unsigned C types `uint8_t`, ..., `uint64_t`, `size_t`, respectively, because they have a trivial structure.

#### 4.4.4.4. Other Inductive Types {#manual-inductive-types-standard-representation}

If an inductive type doesn't fall into one of the categories above, then its representation is determined by its constructors.
Constructors without relevant parameters are represented by their index into the list of constructors, as unboxed unsigned machine integers (scalars).
Constructors with relevant parameters are represented as an object with a header, the constructor's index, an array of pointers to other objects, and then arrays of scalar fields sorted by their types.
The header tracks the object's reference count and other necessary bookkeeping.

Recursive functions are compiled as they are in most programming languages, rather than by using the inductive type's recursor.
Elaborating recursive functions to recursors serves to provide reliable termination evidence, not executable code.

##### 4.4.4.4.1. FFI {#manual-inductive-types-ffi}

From the perspective of C, these other inductive types are represented by `lean_object *`.
Each constructor is stored as a `lean_ctor_object`, and `lean_is_ctor` will return true.

There are no guarantees about the exact layout of fields in a constructor object; the compiler is free to select any layout.
Thus, constructor objects should only be created or unpacked by functions defined in Lean code.
These functions can be made available to C via the [`export`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Run-Time-Code/Foreign-Function-Interface/#Lean___Parser___Attr___export) attribute.
Because the resulting C and Lean code call symbols defined in each other, they should be linked together.
Each C should be compiled to an object file using a custom target in Lake and added to the Lean library configuration's `[moreLinkObjs](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Lake/#Lake___LeanLibConfig-moreLinkObjs)` field.

### 4.4.5. Mutual Inductive Types {#manual-mutual-inductive-types}

Inductive types may be mutually recursive.
Mutually recursive definitions of inductive types are specified by defining the types in a `mutual ... end` block.

**Example: Mutually Defined Inductive Types**

The type `EvenOddList` in a prior example used a Boolean index to select whether the list in question should have an even or odd number of elements.
This distinction can also be expressed by the choice of one of two mutually inductive types `[EvenList]](#manual-EvenList-_LPAR_in-Mutually-Defined-Inductive-Types_RPAR_)` and `[OddList]](#manual-OddList-_LPAR_in-Mutually-Defined-Inductive-Types_RPAR_)`:

```lean
[mutual](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
inductive EvenList (α : Type u) : Type u where
| nil : [EvenList]](#manual-EvenList-_LPAR_in-Mutually-Defined-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) α
| cons : α → [OddList]](#manual-OddList-_LPAR_in-Mutually-Defined-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) α → [EvenList]](#manual-EvenList-_LPAR_in-Mutually-Defined-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) α
inductive OddList (α : Type u) : Type u where
| cons : α → [EvenList]](#manual-EvenList-_LPAR_in-Mutually-Defined-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) α → [OddList]](#manual-OddList-_LPAR_in-Mutually-Defined-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) α
[end](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
example : [EvenList]](#manual-EvenList-_LPAR_in-Mutually-Defined-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) := [.cons]](#manual-EvenList___cons-_LPAR_in-Mutually-Defined-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) "x" ([.cons]](#manual-OddList___cons-_LPAR_in-Mutually-Defined-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) "y" [.nil]](#manual-EvenList___nil-_LPAR_in-Mutually-Defined-Inductive-Types_RPAR_))
example : [OddList]](#manual-OddList-_LPAR_in-Mutually-Defined-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) := [.cons]](#manual-OddList___cons-_LPAR_in-Mutually-Defined-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) "x" ([.cons]](#manual-EvenList___cons-_LPAR_in-Mutually-Defined-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) "y" ([.cons]](#manual-OddList___cons-_LPAR_in-Mutually-Defined-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) "z" [.nil]](#manual-EvenList___nil-_LPAR_in-Mutually-Defined-Inductive-Types_RPAR_)))
```

```lean
example : [OddList]](#manual-OddList-_LPAR_in-Mutually-Defined-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) := [.cons]](#manual-OddList___cons-_LPAR_in-Mutually-Defined-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) "x" ([.cons]](#manual-EvenList___cons-_LPAR_in-Mutually-Defined-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) "y" .nil)
```

```lean
Unknown constant `OddList.nil`

Note: Inferred this name from the expected resulting type of `.nil`:
  [OddList]](#manual-OddList-_LPAR_in-Mutually-Defined-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
```

#### 4.4.5.1. Requirements {#manual-mutual-inductive-types-requirements}

The inductive types declared in a `mutual` block are considered as a group; they must collectively satisfy generalized versions of the well-formedness criteria for non-mutually-recursive inductive types.
This is true even if they could be defined without the `mutual` block, because they are not in fact mutually recursive.

##### 4.4.5.1.1. Mutual Dependencies {#manual-mutual-inductive-types-dependencies}

Each type constructor's signature must be able to be elaborated without reference to the other inductive types in the `mutual` group.
In other words, the inductive types in the `mutual` group may not take each other as arguments.
The constructors of each inductive type may mention the other type constructors in the group in their parameter types, with restrictions that are a generalization of those for recursive occurrences in non-mutual inductive types.

**Example: Mutual inductive type constructors may not mention each other**

These inductive types are not accepted by Lean:

```lean
[mutual](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
inductive FreshList (α : Type) (r : α → α → Prop) : Type where
| nil : FreshList α r
| cons (x : α) (xs : FreshList α r) (fresh : Fresh r x xs)
inductive Fresh
(r : α → FreshList α → Prop) :
α → FreshList α r → Prop where
| nil : Fresh r x .nil
| cons : r x y → (f : Fresh r x ys) → Fresh r x (.cons y ys f)
[end](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

The type constructors may not refer to the other type constructors in the `mutual` group, so `FreshList` is not in scope in the type constructor of `Fresh`:

```lean
Unknown identifier `FreshList`
```

##### 4.4.5.1.2. Parameters Must Match {#manual-mutual-inductive-types-same-parameters}

All inductive types in the `mutual` group must have the same [parameters]](#manual---tech-term-parameters).
Their indices may differ.

**Example: Differing numbers of parameters**

Even though `Both` and `Optional` are not mutually recursive, they are declared in the same `mutual` block and must therefore have identical parameters:

```lean
[mutual](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
inductive Both (α : Type u) (β : Type v) where
| mk : α → β → Both α β
inductive Optional (α : Type u) where
| none
| some : α → Optional α
[end](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

```lean
Invalid mutually inductive types: `Optional` has 1 parameter(s), but the preceding type `Both` has 2

Note: All inductive types declared in the same `mutual` block must have the same parameters
```

**Example: Differing parameter types**

Even though `Many` and `Optional` are not mutually recursive, they are declared in the same `mutual` block and must therefore have identical parameters.
They both have exactly one parameter, but `Many`'s parameter is not necessarily in the same universe as `Optional`'s:

```lean
[mutual](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
inductive Many (α : Type) : Type u where
| nil : Many α
| cons : α → Many α → Many α
inductive Optional (α : Type u) where
| none
| some : α → Optional α
[end](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

```lean
Invalid mutually inductive types: Parameter `α` has type
  Type u
of sort `Type (u + 1)` but is expected to have type
  Type
of sort `Type 1`
```

##### 4.4.5.1.3. Universe Levels {#manual-mutual-inductive-types-same-universe}

The universe levels of each inductive type in a mutual group must obey the same requirements as non-mutually-recursive inductive types.
Additionally, all the inductive types in a mutual group must be in the same universe, which implies that their constructors are similarly limited with respect to their parameters' universes.

**Example: Universe mismatch**

These mutually-inductive types are a somewhat complicated way to represent run-length encoding of a list:

```lean
[mutual](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
inductive RLE : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → Type where
| nil : RLE []
| run (x : α) (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :
n ≠ 0 → [PrefixRunOf]](#manual-PrefixRunOf-_LPAR_in-Universe-mismatch_RPAR_) n x xs ys → RLE ys → RLE xs
inductive PrefixRunOf : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → Type where
| zero
(noMore : ¬∃zs, xs = x :: zs := by [simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)) :
[PrefixRunOf]](#manual-PrefixRunOf-_LPAR_in-Universe-mismatch_RPAR_) 0 x xs xs
| succ :
[PrefixRunOf]](#manual-PrefixRunOf-_LPAR_in-Universe-mismatch_RPAR_) n x xs ys →
[PrefixRunOf]](#manual-PrefixRunOf-_LPAR_in-Universe-mismatch_RPAR_) (n + 1) x (x :: xs) ys
[end](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
example : RLE [1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 1, 1] :=
[.run]](#manual-RLE___run-_LPAR_in-Universe-mismatch_RPAR_) 1 2 (by⊢ 2 ≠ 0 [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)All goals completed! 🐙) ([.succ]](#manual-PrefixRunOf___succ-_LPAR_in-Universe-mismatch_RPAR_) ([.succ]](#manual-PrefixRunOf___succ-_LPAR_in-Universe-mismatch_RPAR_) [.zero]](#manual-PrefixRunOf___zero-_LPAR_in-Universe-mismatch_RPAR_))) <|
```

Specifying `[PrefixRunOf]](#manual-PrefixRunOf-_LPAR_in-Universe-mismatch_RPAR_)` as a `Prop` would be sensible, but it cannot be done because the types would be in different universes:

```lean
[mutual](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
inductive RLE : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → Type where
| nil : RLE []
| run
(x : α) (n : Nat) :
n ≠ 0 → PrefixRunOf n x xs ys → RLE ys →
RLE xs
inductive PrefixRunOf : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → Prop where
| zero
(noMore : ¬∃zs, xs = x :: zs := by [simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)) :
PrefixRunOf 0 x xs xs
| succ :
PrefixRunOf n x xs ys →
PrefixRunOf (n + 1) x (x :: xs) ys
[end](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

```lean
Invalid mutually inductive types: The resulting type of this declaration
  Prop
differs from a preceding one
  Type

Note: All inductive types declared in the same `mutual` block must belong to the same type universe
```

This particular property can be expressed by separately defining the well-formedness condition and using a subtype:

```lean
def RunLengths α := [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) (α × [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))

| [_] => [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)
| (x, _) :: ((y, n) :: xs) =>
x ≠ y ∧ [NoRepeats]](#manual-NoRepeats-_LPAR_in-Universe-mismatch_RPAR_) ((y, n) :: xs)

| (x, n) :: xs, ys =>
ys.[take](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___take) n = [List.replicate](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___replicate) n x ∧

| _, _ => [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)

| (_, n) :: xs => n ≠ 0 ∧ [NonZero]](#manual-NonZero-_LPAR_in-Universe-mismatch_RPAR_) xs

rle : [RunLengths]](#manual-RunLengths-_LPAR_in-Universe-mismatch_RPAR_) α

runsMatch : [RunsMatch]](#manual-RunsMatch-_LPAR_in-Universe-mismatch_RPAR_) rle xs
nonZero : [NonZero]](#manual-NonZero-_LPAR_in-Universe-mismatch_RPAR_) rle
```

##### 4.4.5.1.4. Positivity {#manual-mutual-inductive-types-positivity}

Each inductive type that is defined in the `mutual` group may occur only strictly positively in the types of the parameters of the constructors of all the types in the group.
In other words, in the type of each parameter to each constructor in all the types of the group, none of the type constructors in the group occur to the left of any arrows, and none of them occur in argument positions unless they are an argument to an inductive type's type constructor.

**Example: Mutual strict positivity**

In the following mutual group, `Tm` occurs in a negative position in the argument to `Binding.scope`:

```lean
[mutual](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
inductive Tm where
| app : [Tm]](#manual-Tm-_LPAR_in-Mutual-strict-positivity_RPAR_) → [Tm]](#manual-Tm-_LPAR_in-Mutual-strict-positivity_RPAR_) → [Tm]](#manual-Tm-_LPAR_in-Mutual-strict-positivity_RPAR_)
| lam : [Binding]](#manual-Binding-_LPAR_in-Mutual-strict-positivity_RPAR_) → [Tm]](#manual-Tm-_LPAR_in-Mutual-strict-positivity_RPAR_)
inductive Binding where
| scope : ([Tm]](#manual-Tm-_LPAR_in-Mutual-strict-positivity_RPAR_) → [Tm]](#manual-Tm-_LPAR_in-Mutual-strict-positivity_RPAR_)) → [Binding]](#manual-Binding-_LPAR_in-Mutual-strict-positivity_RPAR_)
[end](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

Because `Tm` is part of the same mutual group, it must occur only strictly positively in the arguments to the constructors of `Binding`.
It occurs, however, negatively:

```lean
(kernel) arg #1 of 'Binding.scope' has a non positive occurrence of the datatypes being declared
```

**Example: Nested positions**

The definitions of `[LocatedStx]](#manual-LocatedStx-_LPAR_in-Nested-positions_RPAR_)` and `[Stx]](#manual-Stx-_LPAR_in-Nested-positions_RPAR_)` satisfy the positivity condition because the recursive occurrences are not to the left of any arrows and, when they are arguments, they are arguments to inductive type constructors.

```lean
[mutual](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
inductive LocatedStx where
| mk (line col : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (val : [Stx]](#manual-Stx-_LPAR_in-Nested-positions_RPAR_))
inductive Stx where
| atom (str : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray))
| node (kind : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) (args : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [LocatedStx]](#manual-LocatedStx-_LPAR_in-Nested-positions_RPAR_))
[end](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

#### 4.4.5.2. Recursors {#manual-mutual-inductive-types-recursors}

Mutual inductive types are provided with primitive recursors, just like non-mutually-defined inductive types.
These recursors take into account that they must process the other types in the group, and thus will have a motive for each inductive type.
Because all inductive types in the `mutual` group are required to have identical parameters, the recursors still take the parameters first, abstracting them over the motives and the rest of the recursor.
Additionally, because the recursor must process the group's other types, it will require cases for each constructor of each of the types in the group.
The actual dependency structure between the types is not taken into account; even if an additional motive or constructor case is not really required due to there being fewer mutual dependencies than there could be, the generated recursor still requires them.

**Example: Even and odd**

```lean
[mutual](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
inductive Even : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prop where
| zero : [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) 0
| succ : [Odd]](#manual-Odd-_LPAR_in-Even-and-odd_RPAR_) n → [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) (n + 1)
inductive Odd : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prop where
| succ : [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) n → [Odd]](#manual-Odd-_LPAR_in-Even-and-odd_RPAR_) (n + 1)
[end](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

```lean
Even.rec
{motive_1 : (a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) a → Prop}
{motive_2 : (a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → [Odd]](#manual-Odd-_LPAR_in-Even-and-odd_RPAR_) a → Prop}
(zero : motive_1 0 [Even.zero]](#manual-Even___zero-next))
(succ : {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → (a : [Odd]](#manual-Odd-_LPAR_in-Even-and-odd_RPAR_) n) → motive_2 n a → motive_1 (n + 1) ([Even.succ]](#manual-Even___succ-_LPAR_in-Even-and-odd_RPAR_) a)) :
(∀ {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} (a : [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) n), motive_1 n a → motive_2 (n + 1) ([Odd.succ]](#manual-Odd___succ-_LPAR_in-Even-and-odd_RPAR_) a)) →
∀ {a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} (t : [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) a), motive_1 a t
```

```lean
Odd.rec
{motive_1 : (a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) a → Prop}
{motive_2 : (a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → [Odd]](#manual-Odd-_LPAR_in-Even-and-odd_RPAR_) a → Prop}
(zero : motive_1 0 [Even.zero]](#manual-Even___zero-next))
(succ : ∀ {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} (a : [Odd]](#manual-Odd-_LPAR_in-Even-and-odd_RPAR_) n), motive_2 n a → motive_1 (n + 1) ([Even.succ]](#manual-Even___succ-_LPAR_in-Even-and-odd_RPAR_) a)) :
(∀ {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} (a : [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) n), motive_1 n a → motive_2 (n + 1) ([Odd.succ]](#manual-Odd___succ-_LPAR_in-Even-and-odd_RPAR_) a)) → ∀ {a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} (t : [Odd]](#manual-Odd-_LPAR_in-Even-and-odd_RPAR_) a), motive_2 a t
```

**Example: Spuriously mutual types**

The types `[Two]](#manual-Two-_LPAR_in-Spuriously-mutual-types_RPAR_)` and `[Three]](#manual-Three-_LPAR_in-Spuriously-mutual-types_RPAR_)` are defined in a mutual block, even though they do not refer to each other:

```lean
[mutual](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
inductive Two (α : Type) where
| mk : α → α → [Two]](#manual-Two-_LPAR_in-Spuriously-mutual-types_RPAR_) α
inductive Three (α : Type) where
| mk : α → α → α → [Three]](#manual-Three-_LPAR_in-Spuriously-mutual-types_RPAR_) α
[end](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

`[Two]](#manual-Two-_LPAR_in-Spuriously-mutual-types_RPAR_)`'s recursor, `Two.rec`, nonetheless requires a motive and a case for `[Three]](#manual-Three-_LPAR_in-Spuriously-mutual-types_RPAR_)`:

```lean
Two.rec.{u} {α : Type}
{motive_1 : [Two]](#manual-Two-_LPAR_in-Spuriously-mutual-types_RPAR_) α → Sort u}
{motive_2 : [Three]](#manual-Three-_LPAR_in-Spuriously-mutual-types_RPAR_) α → Sort u}
(mk : (a a_1 : α) → motive_1 ([Two.mk]](#manual-Two___mk-_LPAR_in-Spuriously-mutual-types_RPAR_) a a_1)) :
((a a_1 a_2 : α) → motive_2 ([Three.mk]](#manual-Three___mk-_LPAR_in-Spuriously-mutual-types_RPAR_) a a_1 a_2)) → (t : [Two]](#manual-Two-_LPAR_in-Spuriously-mutual-types_RPAR_) α) → motive_1 t
```

#### 4.4.5.3. Run-Time Representation {#manual-mutual-inductive-types-run-time}

Mutual inductive types are represented identically to [non-mutual inductive types]](#manual-run-time-inductives) in compiled code and in the runtime.
The restrictions on mutual inductive types exist to ensure Lean's consistency as a logic, and do not impact compiled code.

#### 4.4.5.4. Nested Inductive Types {#manual-nested-inductive-types}

*Nested inductive types* are inductive types in which recursive occurrences of the type being defined are parameters to other inductive type constructors.
These recursive occurrences are “nested” underneath the other type constructors.
Nested inductive types that satisfy certain requirements can be translated into mutual inductive types; this translation demonstrates that they are sound.
Internally, the [kernel]](#manual---tech-term-kernel) performs this translation; if it succeeds, then the *original* nested inductive type is accepted.
This avoids performance and usability issues that would arise from details of the translation surfacing.

Nested recursive occurrences must satisfy the following requirements:

- They must be nested *directly* under an inductive type's type constructor.
  Terms that reduce to such nested occurrences are not accepted.
- Local variables such as the constructor's parameters may not occur in the arguments to the nested occurrence.
- The nested occurrences must occur strictly positively. They must occur strictly positively in the position in which they are nested, and the type constructor in which they are nested must itself occur in a strictly positive position.
- Constructor parameters whose types include nested occurrences may not be used in ways that rely on the specific choice of outer type constructor. The translated version will not be usable in those contexts.
- Nested occurrences may not be used as parameters to the outer type constructor that occur in the types of the outer type's indices.

**Example: Nested Inductive Types**

Instead of using two constructors, the natural numbers can be defined using `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`:

```lean
inductive ONat : Type where
| mk (pred : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [ONat]](#manual-ONat-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_))
```

Arbitrarily-branching trees, also known as *rose trees*, are nested inductive types:

```lean
inductive RTree (α : Type u) : Type u where
| empty
| node (val : α) (children : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) ([RTree]](#manual-RTree-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) α))
```

**Example: Invalid Nested Inductive Types**

This declaration of arbitrarily-branching rose trees declares an alias for `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`, rather than using `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` directly:

```lean
abbrev Children := [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
inductive RTree (α : Type u) : Type u where
| empty
| node (val : α) (children : [Children]](#manual-Children-_LPAR_in-Invalid-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) ([RTree]](#manual-RTree-_LPAR_in-Invalid-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) α))
```

```lean
(kernel) arg #3 of 'RTree.node' contains a non valid occurrence of the datatypes being declared
```

This declaration of arbitrarily-branching rose trees tracks the depth of the tree using an index.
The constructor `DRTree.node` has an [automatic implicit parameter](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Headers-and-Signatures/#--tech-term-automatic-implicit-parameters) `n` that represents the depths of all sub-trees.
However, local variables such as constructor parameters are not permitted as arguments to nested occurrences:

```lean
inductive DRTree (α : Type u) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Type u where
| empty : [DRTree]](#manual-DRTree-_LPAR_in-Invalid-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) α 0
| node (val : α) (children : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) ([DRTree]](#manual-DRTree-_LPAR_in-Invalid-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) α n)) : [DRTree]](#manual-DRTree-_LPAR_in-Invalid-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) α (n + 1)
```

This declaration includes a non-strictly-positive occurrence of the inductive type, nested under an `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`:

```lean
inductive WithCheck where
| done
| check (f : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [WithCheck]](#manual-WithCheck-_LPAR_in-Invalid-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false))
```

```lean
(kernel) arg #1 of 'WithCheck.check' has a non positive occurrence of the datatypes being declared
```

This rose tree has a branching factor that's limited by its parameter:

```lean
inductive BRTree (branches : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (α : Type u) : Type u where
| mk :
(children : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) ([BRTree]](#manual-BRTree-_LPAR_in-Invalid-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) branches α)) →
children.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) < branches →
[BRTree]](#manual-BRTree-_LPAR_in-Invalid-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) branches α
```

Only nested inductive types that can be translated to mutual inductive types are allowed.
However, translating this type would require a translation of `[List.length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length)` to the translated types, but function definitions may not occur in mutual blocks with inductive types.
The resulting error message shows that the function was not translated, but was applied to a term of the translated type:

```lean
(kernel) application type mismatch
  [List.length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) children
argument has type
  @_nested.List_1 branches α
but function has type
  List (@BRTree branches α) → Nat
```

It is acceptable to use the parameter with the nested occurrence with fully polymorphic functions, such as `id`:

```lean
inductive RTree'' (α : Type u) : Type u where
| mk :
(children : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) ([BRTree]](#manual-BRTree-_LPAR_in-Invalid-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) branches α)) →
id children = children →
[BRTree]](#manual-BRTree-_LPAR_in-Invalid-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) branches α
```

In this case, the function applies equally well to the translated version as it does to the original.

The translation from nested inductive types to mutual inductive types proceeds as follows:

Nested occurrences become inductive types
:   Nested occurrences of the inductive type are translated into new inductive types in the same mutual group, which replace the original nested occurrences.
    These new inductive types have the same constructors as the outer inductive type, except the original parameters are instantiated by the translated version of the type.
    The original inductive type becomes an alias for the version in which the nested occurrences have been rewritten.
    This process is repeated if the resulting type is also a nested inductive type (e.g. a type nested under `[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk)` becomes a type nested under `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`, because `[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk)`'s constructor takes a `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`).

Conversions to and from the nested types
:   Conversions between the outer inductive type applied to the new alias and the generated auxiliary types are generated.
    These conversions are then proved to be mutual inverses.

Constructor reconstruction
:   Each constructor of the original type is defined as a function that returns the constructor of the translated type, after applying the appropriate conversions.

Recursor reconstruction
:   The recursor for the nested inductive type is constructed from the recursor for the translated type.
    In the translation, the motives for the nested occurrences are composed with the conversion functions and the [minor premises]](#manual---tech-term-minor-premise) use them as needed.
    The proofs that the conversion functions are mutually inverse are needed because the encoded constructors convert in one direction, but end up applied to the result of the conversion in the other direction.

**Example: Translating Nested Inductive Types**

This nested inductive type represents the natural numbers:

```lean
inductive ONat where
| mk (pred : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ONat) : ONat
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) [ONat.rec]](#manual-ONat___rec-_LPAR_in-Translating-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_)
```

The first step in the internal translation is to replace the nested occurrences with auxiliary inductive types that “inline” the resulting type.
In this case, the nested occurrence is under `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`; thus, the auxiliary type has the constructors of `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, with `[ONat']](#manual-ONat___-_LPAR_in-Translating-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_)` substituted for the type parameter:

```lean
[mutual](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
inductive ONat' where
| mk (pred : [OptONat]](#manual-OptONat-_LPAR_in-Translating-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_)) : [ONat']](#manual-ONat___-_LPAR_in-Translating-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_)
inductive OptONat where
| none
| some : [ONat']](#manual-ONat___-_LPAR_in-Translating-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) → [OptONat]](#manual-OptONat-_LPAR_in-Translating-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_)
[end](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

`[ONat']](#manual-ONat___-_LPAR_in-Translating-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_)` is the encoding of `ONat`:

```lean
def ONat := [ONat']](#manual-ONat___-_LPAR_in-Translating-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_)
```

The next step is to define conversion functions that translate the original nested type to and from the auxiliary type:

```lean
def OptONat.ofOption : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ONat → [OptONat]](#manual-OptONat-_LPAR_in-Translating-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_)
| [Option.none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [OptONat.none]](#manual-OptONat___none-_LPAR_in-Translating-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_)
| [Option.some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) o => [OptONat.some]](#manual-OptONat___some-_LPAR_in-Translating-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) o
def OptONat.toOption : [OptONat]](#manual-OptONat-_LPAR_in-Translating-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ONat
| [OptONat.none]](#manual-OptONat___none-_LPAR_in-Translating-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) => [Option.none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [OptONat.some]](#manual-OptONat___some-_LPAR_in-Translating-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) o => [Option.some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) o
```
