The original constructor is translated to an application of the translation's corresponding constructor, with the appropriate conversion applied for the nested occurrence:

```lean
def ONat.mk (pred : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ONat) : ONat :=
[ONat'.mk]](#manual-ONat______mk-_LPAR_in-Translating-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) ([.ofOption]](#manual-OptONat___ofOption-_LPAR_in-Translating-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) pred)
```

Finally, the original type's recursor can be translated.
The translated recursor uses the translated type's recursor.
The original nested occurrences are translated using the conversions, and the proofs that the conversions are mutually inverse are used to rewrite types as needed.

```lean
noncomputable def ONat.rec
{motive1 : ONat → Sort u}
{motive2 : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ONat → Sort u}
(h1 :
(pred : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ONat) → motive2 pred →
motive1 (ONat.mk pred))
(h2 : motive2 [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none))
(h3 : (o : ONat) → motive1 o → motive2 ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) o)) :
(t : ONat) → motive1 t :=
@ONat'.rec motive1 (motive2 ∘ [OptONat.toOption]](#manual-OptONat___toOption-_LPAR_in-Translating-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_))
(fun pred ih =>
[OptONat.of_to_eq_id]](#manual-OptONat___of_to_eq_id-_LPAR_in-Translating-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) pred ▸ h1 pred.[toOption]](#manual-OptONat___toOption-_LPAR_in-Translating-Nested-Inductive-Types_RPAR_) ih)
h2
h3
```

#### 4.4.5.5. Lattice-Theoretic Inductive and Coinductive Predicates {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The-Type-System--Inductive-Types--Mutual-Inductive-Types--Lattice-Theoretic-Inductive-and-Coinductive-Predicates}

The syntax of inductive type declarations can be used to specify both inductive and coinductive predicates.
These are not a built-in feature of Lean's type system, but are instead elaborated to a suitable encoding.
They are described in [a dedicated section](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#coinductive-predicates).

---



## The Type System — 4.5. Quotients {#manual-the-type-system-45-quotients}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Type-System/Quotients/

*Quotient types* allow a new type to be formed by decreasing the granularity of an existing type's [propositional equality](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#--tech-term-Propositional-equality).
In particular, given a type `A` and an equivalence relation `\sim`, the quotient `A / \sim` contains the same elements as `A`, but every pair of elements that are related by `\sim` are considered equal.
Equality is respected universally; nothing in Lean's logic can observe any difference between two equal terms.
Thus, quotient types provide a way to build an impenetrable abstraction barrier.
In particular, all functions from a quotient type must prove that they respect the equivalence relation.

def

```lean
[Quotient.{u}]](#manual-Quotient) {α : Sort u} (s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α) : Sort u



[Quotient.{u}]](#manual-Quotient) {α : Sort u} (s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α) :
  Sort u
```

Quotient types coarsen the propositional equality for a type so that terms related by some
equivalence relation are considered equal. The equivalence relation is given by an instance of
`[Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk)`.

Set-theoretically, `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s` can seen as the set of equivalence classes of `α` modulo the
`[Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk)` instance's relation `s.[r]](#manual-Setoid___mk)`. Functions from `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s` must prove that they respect `s.[r]](#manual-Setoid___mk)`:
to define a function `f : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s → β`, it is necessary to provide `f' : α → β` and prove that
for all `x : α` and `y : α`, `s.[r]](#manual-Setoid___mk) x y → f' x = f' y`. `[Quotient.lift]](#manual-Quotient___lift)` implements this operation.

The key quotient operators are:

- `[Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk)` places elements of the underlying type `α` into the quotient.
- `[Quotient.lift]](#manual-Quotient___lift)` allows the definition of functions from the quotient to some other type.
- `[Quotient.sound]](#manual-Quotient___sound)` asserts the equality of elements related by `r`
- `[Quotient.ind]](#manual-Quotient___ind)` is used to write proofs about quotients by assuming that all elements are
  constructed with `[Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk)`.

`[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)` is built on top of the primitive quotient type `[Quot]](#manual-Quot)`, which does not require a proof
that the relation is an equivalence relation. `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)` should be used instead of `[Quot]](#manual-Quot)` for
relations that actually are equivalence relations.

A proof that two elements of the underlying type are related by the equivalence relation is sufficient to prove that they are equal in the `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)`.
However, [definitional equality]](#manual---tech-term-definitional-equality) is unaffected by the use of `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)`: two elements in the quotient are definitionally equal if and only if they are definitionally equal in the underlying type.

Quotient types are not widely used in programming.
However, they occur regularly in mathematics:

Integers
:   The integers are traditionally defined as a pair of natural numbers `(n, k)` that encodes the integer `n - k`.
    In this encoding, two integers `(n_1, k_1)` and `(n_2, k_2)` are equal if `n_1 + k_2 = n_2 + k_1`.

Rational Numbers
:   The number `\frac{n}{d}` can be encoded as the pair `(n, d)`, where `d \neq 0`.
    Two rational numbers `\frac{n_1}{d_1}` and `\frac{n_2}{d_2}` are equal if `n_1 d_2 = n_2 d_1`.

Real Numbers
:   The real numbers can be represented as a Cauchy sequence, but this encoding is not unique.
    Using a quotient type, two Cauchy sequences can be made equal when their difference converges to zero.

Finite Sets
:   Finite sets can be represented as lists of elements.
    With a quotient types, two finite sets can be made equal if they contain the same elements; this definition does not impose any requirements (such as decidable equality or an ordering relation) on the type of elements.

One alternative to quotient types would be to reason directly about the equivalence classes introduced by the relation.
The downside of this approach is that it does not allow *computation*: in addition to knowing *that* there is an integer that is the sum of 5 and 8, it is useful for `5 + 8 = 13` to not be a theorem that requires proof.
Defining functions out of sets of equivalence classes relies on non-computational classical reasoning principles, while functions from quotient types are ordinary computational functions that additionally respect an equivalence relation.

### 4.5.1. Alternatives to Quotient Types {#manual-quotient-alternatives}

While `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)` is a convenient way to form quotients with reasonable computational properties, it is often possible to define quotients in other ways.

In general, a type `Q` is said to be the quotient of `A` by an equivalence relation `\sim` if it respects the universal property of quotients: there is a function `q:A\to Q` with the property that `q(a)=q(b)` if and only if `a\sim b` for all `a` and `b` in `A`.

Quotients formed with `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)` have this property up to [propositional equality](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#--tech-term-Propositional-equality): elements of `A` that are related by `\sim` are equal, so they cannot be distinguished.
However, members of the same equivalence class are not necessarily [definitionally equal]](#manual---tech-term-definitional-equality) in the quotient.

Quotients may also be implemented by designating a single representative of each equivalence class in `A` itself, and then defining `Q` as pair of elements in `A` with proofs that they are such a canonical representative.
Together with a function that maps each `a` in `A` to its canonical representative, `Q` is a quotient of `A`.
Due to [proof irrelevance]](#manual---tech-term-proof-irrelevance), representatives in `Q` of the same equivalence class are [definitionally equal]](#manual---tech-term-definitional-equality).

Such a manually implemented quotient `Q` can be easier to work with than `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)`.
In particular, because each equivalence class is represented by its single canonical representative, there's no need to prove that functions from the quotient respect the equivalence relation.
It can also have better computational properties due to the fact that the computations give normalized values (in contrast, elements of `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)` can be represented in multiple ways).
Finally, because the manually implemented quotient is an [inductive type]](#manual---tech-term-Inductive-types), it can be used in contexts where other kinds of types cannot, such as when defining a [nested inductive type]](#manual-nested-inductive-types).
However, not all quotients can be manually implemented.

**Example: Manually Quotiented Integers**

When implemented as pairs of `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`s, each equivalence class according to the desired equality for integers has a canonical representative in which at least one of the `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`s is zero.
This can be represented as a Lean structure:

```lean
structure Z where
a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
b : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
canonical : a = 0 ∨ b = 0
```

Due to [proof irrelevance]](#manual---tech-term-proof-irrelevance), every value of this structure type that represents the same integer is *already* equal.
Constructing a `[Z]](#manual-Z-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_)` can be made more convenient with a wrapper that uses the fact that subtraction of natural numbers truncates at zero to automate the construction of the proof:

```lean
def Z.mk' (n k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Z]](#manual-Z-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_) where
[a]](#manual-Z___a-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_) := n - k
[b]](#manual-Z___b-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_) := k - n
[canonical]](#manual-Z___canonical-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_) := byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)k:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ n [-](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk) k [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) k [-](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk) n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 [omega](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#omega)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [[Z.mk']](#manual-Z___mk___-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_)]n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)k:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)n':[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)k':[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ n [-](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk) k [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n' [-](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk) k' [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) k [-](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk) n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) k' [-](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk) n' [↔](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Iff___intro) n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) k' [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n' [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) k
```

To use this type in examples, it's convenient to have `[Neg](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Neg___mk)`, `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)`, and `ToString` instances.
These instances make it easier to read or write examples.

```lean
instance : [Neg](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Neg___mk) [Z]](#manual-Z-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_) where
[neg](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Neg___mk) n := [Z.mk']](#manual-Z___mk___-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_) n.[b]](#manual-Z___b-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_) n.[a]](#manual-Z___a-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_)
instance : [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [Z]](#manual-Z-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_) n where
[ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) := [Z.mk']](#manual-Z___mk___-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_) n 0
instance : ToString [Z]](#manual-Z-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_) where
toString n :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) n.[a]](#manual-Z___a-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_) = 0 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) n.[b]](#manual-Z___b-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_) = 0 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) "0"
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) s!"-{n.[b]](#manual-Z___b-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_)}"
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) toString n.[a]](#manual-Z___a-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_)
```

Addition is addition of the underlying `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`s:

```lean
instance : [Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) [Z]](#manual-Z-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_) where
[add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) n k := [Z.mk']](#manual-Z___mk___-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_) (n.[a]](#manual-Z___a-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_) + k.[a]](#manual-Z___a-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_)) (n.[b]](#manual-Z___b-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_) + k.[b]](#manual-Z___b-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_))
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (-5 + 22: [Z]](#manual-Z-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_))
```

```lean
17
```

Because each equivalence class is uniquely represented, there's no need to write a proof that these functions from `[Z]](#manual-Z-_LPAR_in-Manually-Quotiented-Integers_RPAR_)` respect the equivalence relation.
However, in practice, the [API for quotients]](#manual-quotient-api) should be implemented for manually-constructed quotients and proved to respect the universal property.

**Example: Built-In Integers as Quotients**

Lean's built-in integer type `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)` satisfies the universal property of quotients, and can thus be thought of as a quotient of pairs of `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`s.
The canonical representative of each equivalence class can be computed via comparison and subtraction:This `[toInt]](#manual-toInt-_LPAR_in-Built-In-Integers-as-Quotients_RPAR_)` function is called `[Int.subNatNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___subNatNat)` in the standard library.

```lean
def toInt (n k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) n < k [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) - (k - n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) n = k [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) 0
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) (n - k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

It satisfies the universal property.
Two pairs of `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`s represent the same integer if and only if `[toInt]](#manual-toInt-_LPAR_in-Built-In-Integers-as-Quotients_RPAR_)` computes the same `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)` for both pairs:

### 4.5.2. Setoids {#manual-setoids}

Quotient types are built on setoids.
A *setoid* is a type paired with a distinguished equivalence relation.
Unlike a quotient type, the abstraction barrier is not enforced, and proof automation designed around equality cannot be used with the setoid's equivalence relation.
Setoids are useful on their own, in addition to being a building block for quotient types.

type class

```lean
[Setoid.{u}]](#manual-Setoid___mk) (α : Sort u) : Sort (max 1 u)



[Setoid.{u}]](#manual-Setoid___mk) (α : Sort u) : Sort (max 1 u)
```

A setoid is a type with a distinguished equivalence relation, denoted `≈`.

The `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)` type constructor requires a `[Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk)` instance.

Instance Constructor

```lean
[Setoid.mk]](#manual-Setoid___mk).{u}
```

Methods

```lean
r : α → α → Prop
```

`x ≈ y` is the distinguished equivalence relation of a setoid.

```lean
iseqv : [Equivalence]](#manual-Equivalence___mk) [Setoid.r]](#manual-Setoid___mk)
```

The relation `x ≈ y` is an equivalence relation.

theorem

```lean
[Setoid.refl.{u}]](#manual-Setoid___refl) {α : Sort u} [[Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α] (a : α) : a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) a



[Setoid.refl.{u}]](#manual-Setoid___refl) {α : Sort u} [[Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α]
  (a : α) : a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) a
```

A setoid's equivalence relation is reflexive.

theorem

```lean
[Setoid.symm.{u}]](#manual-Setoid___symm) {α : Sort u} [[Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α] {a b : α} (hab : a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b) : b [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) a



[Setoid.symm.{u}]](#manual-Setoid___symm) {α : Sort u} [[Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α]
  {a b : α} (hab : a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b) : b [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) a
```

A setoid's equivalence relation is symmetric.

theorem

```lean
[Setoid.trans.{u}]](#manual-Setoid___trans) {α : Sort u} [[Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α] {a b c : α} (hab : a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b)
  (hbc : b [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) c) : a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) c



[Setoid.trans.{u}]](#manual-Setoid___trans) {α : Sort u} [[Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α]
  {a b c : α} (hab : a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b)
  (hbc : b [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) c) : a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) c
```

A setoid's equivalence relation is transitive.

### 4.5.3. Equivalence Relations {#manual-equivalence-relations}

An *equivalence relation* is a relation that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

syntaxEquivalence Relations

Equivalence according to some canonical equivalence relation for a type is written using `≈`, which is overloaded using the [type class](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/#--tech-term-type-class) `[HasEquiv]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk)`.

```lean
term ::= ...
    | term ≈ term
```

type class

```lean
[HasEquiv.{u, v}]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) (α : Sort u) : Sort (max u (v + 1))



[HasEquiv.{u, v}]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) (α : Sort u) :
  Sort (max u (v + 1))
```

`[HasEquiv]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) α` is the typeclass which supports the notation `x ≈ y` where `x y : α`.

Instance Constructor

```lean
[HasEquiv.mk]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk).{u, v}
```

Methods

```lean
Equiv : α → α → Sort v
```

`x ≈ y` says that `x` and `y` are equivalent. Because this is a typeclass,
the notion of equivalence is type-dependent.

Conventions for notations in identifiers:

- The recommended spelling of `≈` in identifiers is `equiv`.

The fact that a relation `r` is actually an equivalence relation is stated `[Equivalence]](#manual-Equivalence___mk) r`.

structure

```lean
[Equivalence.{u}]](#manual-Equivalence___mk) {α : Sort u} (r : α → α → Prop) : Prop



[Equivalence.{u}]](#manual-Equivalence___mk) {α : Sort u}
  (r : α → α → Prop) : Prop
```

An equivalence relation `r : α → α → Prop` is a relation that is

- reflexive: `r x x`,
- symmetric: `r x y` implies `r y x`, and
- transitive: `r x y` and `r y z` implies `r x z`.

Equality is an equivalence relation, and equivalence relations share many of the properties of
equality.

Constructor

```lean
[Equivalence.mk]](#manual-Equivalence___mk).{u}
```

Fields

```lean
refl : ∀ (x : α), r x x
```

An equivalence relation is reflexive: `r x x`

```lean
symm : ∀ {x y : α}, r x y → r y x
```

An equivalence relation is symmetric: `r x y` implies `r y x`

```lean
trans : ∀ {x y z : α}, r x y → r y z → r x z
```

An equivalence relation is transitive: `r x y` and `r y z` implies `r x z`

Every `[Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk)` instance leads to a corresponding `[HasEquiv]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk)` instance.

### 4.5.4. Quotient API {#manual-quotient-api}

The quotient API relies on a pre-existing `[Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk)` instance.

#### 4.5.4.1. Introducing Quotients {#manual-quotient-intro}

The type `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)` expects an instance of `[Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk)` as an ordinary parameter, rather than as an [instance implicit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/#--tech-term-instance-implicit) parameter.
This helps ensure that the quotient uses the intended equivalence relation.
The instance can be provided either by naming the instance or by using `[inferInstance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance)`.

A value in the quotient is a value from the setoid's underlying type, wrapped in `[Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk)`.

def

```lean
[Quotient.mk.{u}]](#manual-Quotient___mk) {α : Sort u} (s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α) (a : α) : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s



[Quotient.mk.{u}]](#manual-Quotient___mk) {α : Sort u}
  (s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α) (a : α) : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s
```

Places an element of a type into the quotient that equates terms according to an equivalence
relation.

The setoid instance is provided explicitly. `[Quotient.mk']](#manual-Quotient___mk___)` uses instance synthesis instead.

Given `v : α`, `[Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s v : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s` is like `v`, except all observations of `v`'s value
must respect `s.[r]](#manual-Setoid___mk)`. `[Quotient.lift]](#manual-Quotient___lift)` allows values in a quotient to be mapped to other types, so long
as the mapping respects `s.[r]](#manual-Setoid___mk)`.

def

```lean
[Quotient.mk'.{u}]](#manual-Quotient___mk___) {α : Sort u} [s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α] (a : α) : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s



[Quotient.mk'.{u}]](#manual-Quotient___mk___) {α : Sort u}
  [s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α] (a : α) : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s
```

Places an element of a type into the quotient that equates terms according to an equivalence
relation.

The equivalence relation is found by synthesizing a `[Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk)` instance. `[Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk)` instead expects
the instance to be provided explicitly.

Given `v : α`, `[Quotient.mk']](#manual-Quotient___mk___) v : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s` is like `v`, except all observations of `v`'s value
must respect `s.[r]](#manual-Setoid___mk)`. `[Quotient.lift]](#manual-Quotient___lift)` allows values in a quotient to be mapped to other types, so long
as the mapping respects `s.[r]](#manual-Setoid___mk)`.

**Example: The Integers as a Quotient Type**

The integers, defined as pairs of natural numbers where the represented integer is the difference of the two numbers, can be represented via a quotient type.
This representation is not unique: both `(4, 7)` and `(1, 4)` represent `-3`.

Two encoded integers should be considered equal when they are related by `[Z.eq]](#manual-Z___eq-_LPAR_in-The-Integers-as-a-Quotient-Type_RPAR_)`:

```lean
def Z' : Type := [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
def Z.eq (n k : [Z']](#manual-Z___-_LPAR_in-The-Integers-as-a-Quotient-Type_RPAR_)) : Prop :=
n.[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) + k.[2](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) = n.[2](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) + k.[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)
```

This relation is an equivalence relation:


Thus, it can be used as a `[Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk)`:

```lean
instance Z.instSetoid : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) [Z']](#manual-Z___-_LPAR_in-The-Integers-as-a-Quotient-Type_RPAR_) where
[r]](#manual-Setoid___mk) := [Z.eq]](#manual-Z___eq-_LPAR_in-The-Integers-as-a-Quotient-Type_RPAR_)
[iseqv]](#manual-Setoid___mk) := [Z.eq.eqv]](#manual-Z___eq___eqv-_LPAR_in-The-Integers-as-a-Quotient-Type_RPAR_)
```

The type `[Z]](#manual-Z-_LPAR_in-The-Integers-as-a-Quotient-Type_RPAR_)` of integers is then the quotient of `[Z']](#manual-Z___-_LPAR_in-The-Integers-as-a-Quotient-Type_RPAR_)` by the `[Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk)` instance:

```lean
def Z : Type := [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) [Z.instSetoid]](#manual-Z___instSetoid-_LPAR_in-The-Integers-as-a-Quotient-Type_RPAR_)
```

The helper `[Z.mk]](#manual-Z___mk-_LPAR_in-The-Integers-as-a-Quotient-Type_RPAR_)` makes it simpler to create integers without worrying about the choice of `[Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk)` instance:

```lean
def Z.mk (n : [Z']](#manual-Z___-_LPAR_in-The-Integers-as-a-Quotient-Type_RPAR_)) : [Z]](#manual-Z-_LPAR_in-The-Integers-as-a-Quotient-Type_RPAR_) := [Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) _ n
```

However, numeric literals are even more convenient.
An `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` instance allows numeric literals to be used for integers:

```lean
instance : [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [Z]](#manual-Z-_LPAR_in-The-Integers-as-a-Quotient-Type_RPAR_) n where
[ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) := [Z.mk]](#manual-Z___mk-_LPAR_in-The-Integers-as-a-Quotient-Type_RPAR_) (n, 0)
```

#### 4.5.4.2. Eliminating Quotients {#manual-quotient-elim}

Functions from quotients can be defined by proving that a function from the underlying type respects the quotient's equivalence relation.
This is accomplished using `[Quotient.lift]](#manual-Quotient___lift)` or its binary counterpart `[Quotient.lift₂]](#manual-Quotient___lift___)`.
The variants `[Quotient.liftOn]](#manual-Quotient___liftOn)` and `[Quotient.liftOn₂]](#manual-Quotient___liftOn___)` place the quotient parameter first rather than last in the parameter list.

def

```lean
[Quotient.lift.{u, v}]](#manual-Quotient___lift) {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} {s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α}
  (f : α → β) : (∀ (a b : α), a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b → f a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f b) → [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s → β



[Quotient.lift.{u, v}]](#manual-Quotient___lift) {α : Sort u}
  {β : Sort v} {s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α}
  (f : α → β) :
  (∀ (a b : α), a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b → f a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f b) →
    [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s → β
```

Lifts a function from an underlying type to a function on a quotient, requiring that it respects the
quotient's equivalence relation.

Given `s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α` and a quotient `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s`, applying a function `f : α → β` requires a proof
`h` that `f` respects the equivalence relation `s.[r]](#manual-Setoid___mk)`. In this case, the function
`[Quotient.lift]](#manual-Quotient___lift) f h : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s → β` computes the same values as `f`.

`[Quotient.liftOn]](#manual-Quotient___liftOn)` is a version of this operation that takes the quotient value as its first explicit
parameter.

def

```lean
[Quotient.liftOn.{u, v}]](#manual-Quotient___liftOn) {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} {s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α}
  (q : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s) (f : α → β) (c : ∀ (a b : α), a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b → f a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f b) : β



[Quotient.liftOn.{u, v}]](#manual-Quotient___liftOn) {α : Sort u}
  {β : Sort v} {s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α}
  (q : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s) (f : α → β)
  (c : ∀ (a b : α), a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b → f a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f b) : β
```

Lifts a function from an underlying type to a function on a quotient, requiring that it respects the
quotient's equivalence relation.

Given `s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α` and a quotient value `q : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s`, applying a function `f : α → β` requires
a proof `c` that `f` respects the equivalence relation `s.[r]](#manual-Setoid___mk)`. In this case, the term
`[Quotient.liftOn]](#manual-Quotient___liftOn) q f h : β` reduces to the result of applying `f` to the underlying `α` value.

`[Quotient.lift]](#manual-Quotient___lift)` is a version of this operation that takes the quotient value last, rather than
first.

def

```lean
[Quotient.lift₂.{uA, uB, uC}]](#manual-Quotient___lift___) {α : Sort uA} {β : Sort uB} {φ : Sort uC}
  {s₁ : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α} {s₂ : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) β} (f : α → β → φ)
  (c :
    ∀ (a₁ : α) (b₁ : β) (a₂ : α) (b₂ : β),
      a₁ [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) a₂ → b₁ [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b₂ → f a₁ b₁ [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f a₂ b₂)
  (q₁ : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s₁) (q₂ : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s₂) : φ



[Quotient.lift₂.{uA, uB, uC}]](#manual-Quotient___lift___) {α : Sort uA}
  {β : Sort uB} {φ : Sort uC}
  {s₁ : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α} {s₂ : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) β}
  (f : α → β → φ)
  (c :
    ∀ (a₁ : α) (b₁ : β) (a₂ : α) (b₂ : β),
      a₁ [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) a₂ →
        b₁ [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b₂ → f a₁ b₁ [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f a₂ b₂)
  (q₁ : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s₁) (q₂ : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s₂) :
  φ
```

Lifts a binary function from the underlying types to a binary function on quotients. The function
must respect both quotients' equivalence relations.

`[Quotient.lift]](#manual-Quotient___lift)` is a version of this operation for unary functions. `[Quotient.liftOn₂]](#manual-Quotient___liftOn___)` is a version
that take the quotient parameters first.

def

```lean
[Quotient.liftOn₂.{uA, uB, uC}]](#manual-Quotient___liftOn___) {α : Sort uA} {β : Sort uB} {φ : Sort uC}
  {s₁ : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α} {s₂ : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) β} (q₁ : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s₁) (q₂ : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s₂)
  (f : α → β → φ)
  (c :
    ∀ (a₁ : α) (b₁ : β) (a₂ : α) (b₂ : β),
      a₁ [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) a₂ → b₁ [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b₂ → f a₁ b₁ [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f a₂ b₂) :
  φ



[Quotient.liftOn₂.{uA, uB, uC}]](#manual-Quotient___liftOn___)
  {α : Sort uA} {β : Sort uB}
  {φ : Sort uC} {s₁ : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α}
  {s₂ : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) β} (q₁ : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s₁)
  (q₂ : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s₂) (f : α → β → φ)
  (c :
    ∀ (a₁ : α) (b₁ : β) (a₂ : α) (b₂ : β),
      a₁ [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) a₂ →
        b₁ [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b₂ → f a₁ b₁ [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f a₂ b₂) :
  φ
```

Lifts a binary function from the underlying types to a binary function on quotients. The function
must respect both quotients' equivalence relations.

`[Quotient.liftOn]](#manual-Quotient___liftOn)` is a version of this operation for unary functions. `[Quotient.lift₂]](#manual-Quotient___lift___)` is a version
that take the quotient parameters last.

**Example: Integer Negation and Addition**

Given the encoding `Z` of integers as a quotient of pairs of natural numbers, negation can be implemented by swapping the first and second projections:

```lean
def neg' : Z' → Z
| (x, y) => .mk (y, x)
```

This can be transformed into a function from `Z` to `Z` by proving that negation respects the equivalence relation:

```lean
instance : [Neg](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Neg___mk) Z where
```

Similarly, `[Quotient.lift₂]](#manual-Quotient___lift___)` is useful for defining binary functions from a quotient type.
Addition is defined point-wise:

```lean
def add' (n k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : Z :=
.mk (n.[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) + k.[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk), n.[2](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) + k.[2](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk))
```

Lifting it to the quotient requires a proof that addition respects the equivalence relation:

When the function's result type is a [subsingleton]](#manual---tech-term-subsingleton), `[Quotient.recOnSubsingleton]](#manual-Quotient___recOnSubsingleton)` or `[Quotient.recOnSubsingleton₂]](#manual-Quotient___recOnSubsingleton___)` can be used to define the function.
Because all elements of a subsingleton are equal, such a function automatically respects the equivalence relation, so there is no proof obligation.

def

```lean
[Quotient.recOnSubsingleton.{u, v}]](#manual-Quotient___recOnSubsingleton) {α : Sort u} {s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α}
  {motive : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s → Sort v}
  [h : ∀ (a : α), [Subsingleton](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Subsingleton___intro) (motive ([Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s a))]
  (q : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s) (f : (a : α) → motive ([Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s a)) : motive q



[Quotient.recOnSubsingleton.{u, v}]](#manual-Quotient___recOnSubsingleton)
  {α : Sort u} {s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α}
  {motive : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s → Sort v}
  [h :
    ∀ (a : α),
      [Subsingleton](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Subsingleton___intro)
        (motive ([Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s a))]
  (q : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s)
  (f :
    (a : α) → motive ([Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s a)) :
  motive q
```

An alternative recursion or induction principle for quotients that can be used when the target type
is a subsingleton, in which all elements are equal.

In these cases, the proof that the function respects the quotient's equivalence relation is trivial,
so any function can be lifted.

`[Quotient.rec]](#manual-Quotient___rec)` does not assume that the target type is a subsingleton.

def

```lean
[Quotient.recOnSubsingleton₂.{uA, uB, uC}]](#manual-Quotient___recOnSubsingleton___) {α : Sort uA} {β : Sort uB}
  {s₁ : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α} {s₂ : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) β}
  {motive : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s₁ → [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s₂ → Sort uC}
  [s :
    ∀ (a : α) (b : β),
      [Subsingleton](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Subsingleton___intro) (motive ([Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s₁ a) ([Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s₂ b))]
  (q₁ : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s₁) (q₂ : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s₂)
  (g :
    (a : α) → (b : β) → motive ([Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s₁ a) ([Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s₂ b)) :
  motive q₁ q₂



[Quotient.recOnSubsingleton₂.{uA, uB, uC}]](#manual-Quotient___recOnSubsingleton___)
  {α : Sort uA} {β : Sort uB}
  {s₁ : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α} {s₂ : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) β}
  {motive :
    [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s₁ → [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s₂ → Sort uC}
  [s :
    ∀ (a : α) (b : β),
      [Subsingleton](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Subsingleton___intro)
        (motive ([Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s₁ a)
          ([Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s₂ b))]
  (q₁ : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s₁) (q₂ : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s₂)
  (g :
    (a : α) →
      (b : β) →
        motive ([Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s₁ a)
          ([Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s₂ b)) :
  motive q₁ q₂
```

An alternative induction or recursion operator for defining binary operations on quotients that can
be used when the target type is a subsingleton.

In these cases, the proof that the function respects the quotient's equivalence relation is trivial,
so any function can be lifted.

#### 4.5.4.3. Proofs About Quotients {#manual-quotient-proofs}

The fundamental tools for proving properties of elements of quotient types are the soundness axiom and the induction principle.
The soundness axiom states that if two elements of the underlying type are related by the quotient's equivalence relation, then they are equal in the quotient type.
The induction principle follows the structure of recursors for inductive types: in order to prove that a predicate holds for all elements of a quotient type, it suffices to prove that it holds for an application of `[Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk)` to each element of the underlying type.
Because `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)` is not an [inductive type]](#manual---tech-term-Inductive-types), tactics such as `[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases)` and `[induction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#induction)` require that `[Quotient.ind]](#manual-Quotient___ind)` be specified explicitly with the `using` modifier.

theorem

```lean
[Quotient.sound.{u}]](#manual-Quotient___sound) {α : Sort u} {s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α} {a b : α} :
  a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b → [Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s b



[Quotient.sound.{u}]](#manual-Quotient___sound) {α : Sort u}
  {s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α} {a b : α} :
  a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b →
    [Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s b
```

The **quotient axiom**, which asserts the equality of elements related in the setoid.

Because `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)` is built on a lower-level type `[Quot]](#manual-Quot)`, `[Quotient.sound]](#manual-Quotient___sound)` is implemented as a
theorem. It is derived from `[Quot.sound]](#manual-Quot___sound)`, the soundness axiom for the lower-level quotient type
`[Quot]](#manual-Quot)`.

theorem

```lean
[Quotient.ind.{u}]](#manual-Quotient___ind) {α : Sort u} {s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α}
  {motive : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s → Prop} :
  (∀ (a : α), motive ([Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s a)) → ∀ (q : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s), motive q



[Quotient.ind.{u}]](#manual-Quotient___ind) {α : Sort u}
  {s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α}
  {motive : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s → Prop} :
  (∀ (a : α), motive ([Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s a)) →
    ∀ (q : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s), motive q
```

A reasoning principle for quotients that allows proofs about quotients to assume that all values are
constructed with `[Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk)`.

**Example: Proofs About Quotients**

Given the definition of integers as a quotient type from the prior examples, `[Quotient.ind]](#manual-Quotient___ind)` and `[Quotient.sound]](#manual-Quotient___sound)` can be used to prove that negation is an additive inverse.
First, `[Quotient.ind]](#manual-Quotient___ind)` is used to replace instances of `n` with applications of `[Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk)`.
Having done so, the left side of the equality becomes definitionally equal to a single application of `[Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk)`, via unfolding definitions and the computation rule for `[Quotient.lift]](#manual-Quotient___lift)`.
This makes `[Quotient.sound]](#manual-Quotient___sound)` applicable, which yields a new goal: to show that both sides are related by the equivalence relation.
This is provable using `[simp_arith](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp_arith)`.

```lean
theorem Z.add_neg_inverse (n : Z) : n + (-n) = 0 := byn:Z⊢ n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) [-](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Neg___mk)n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0
[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases) n [using](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases) [Quotient.ind]](#manual-Quotient___ind)aa✝:Z'⊢ [Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) instSetoid a✝ [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) [-](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Neg___mk)[Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) instSetoid a✝ [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0
```

For more specialized use cases, `[Quotient.rec]](#manual-Quotient___rec)`, `[Quotient.recOn]](#manual-Quotient___recOn)`, and `[Quotient.hrecOn]](#manual-Quotient___hrecOn)` can be used to define dependent functions from a quotient type to a type in any other universe.
Stating that a dependent function respects the quotient's equivalence relation requires a means of dealing with the fact that the dependent result type is instantiated with different values from the quotient on each side of the equality.
`[Quotient.rec]](#manual-Quotient___rec)` and `[Quotient.recOn]](#manual-Quotient___recOn)` use the `[Quotient.sound]](#manual-Quotient___sound)` to equate the related elements, inserting the appropriate cast into the statement of equality, while `[Quotient.hrecOn]](#manual-Quotient___hrecOn)` uses heterogeneous equality.

def

```lean
[Quotient.rec.{u, v}]](#manual-Quotient___rec) {α : Sort u} {s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α}
  {motive : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s → Sort v}
  (f : (a : α) → motive ([Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s a))
  (h : ∀ (a b : α) (p : a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b), ⋯ ▸ f a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f b) (q : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s) :
  motive q



[Quotient.rec.{u, v}]](#manual-Quotient___rec) {α : Sort u}
  {s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α}
  {motive : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s → Sort v}
  (f : (a : α) → motive ([Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s a))
  (h :
    ∀ (a b : α) (p : a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b),
      ⋯ ▸ f a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f b)
  (q : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s) : motive q
```

A dependent recursion principle for `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)`. It is analogous to the
[recursor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=recursors) for a structure, and can be used when the resulting type
is not necessarily a proposition.

While it is very general, this recursor can be tricky to use. The following simpler alternatives may
be easier to use:

- `[Quotient.lift]](#manual-Quotient___lift)` is useful for defining non-dependent functions.
- `[Quotient.ind]](#manual-Quotient___ind)` is useful for proving theorems about quotients.
- `[Quotient.recOnSubsingleton]](#manual-Quotient___recOnSubsingleton)` can be used whenever the target type is a `[Subsingleton](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Subsingleton___intro)`.
- `[Quotient.hrecOn]](#manual-Quotient___hrecOn)` uses heterogeneous equality instead of rewriting with `[Quotient.sound]](#manual-Quotient___sound)`.

`[Quotient.recOn]](#manual-Quotient___recOn)` is a version of this recursor that takes the quotient parameter first.

def

```lean

  {motive : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s → Sort v} (q : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s)
  (f : (a : α) → motive ([Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s a))
  (h : ∀ (a b : α) (p : a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b), ⋯ ▸ f a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f b) : motive q



[Quotient.recOn.{u, v}]](#manual-Quotient___recOn) {α : Sort u}
  {s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α}
  {motive : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s → Sort v}
  (q : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s)
  (f : (a : α) → motive ([Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s a))
  (h :
    ∀ (a b : α) (p : a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b),
      ⋯ ▸ f a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f b) :
  motive q
```

A dependent recursion principle for `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)`. It is analogous to the
[recursor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=recursors) for a structure, and can be used when the resulting type
is not necessarily a proposition.

While it is very general, this recursor can be tricky to use. The following simpler alternatives may
be easier to use:

- `[Quotient.lift]](#manual-Quotient___lift)` is useful for defining non-dependent functions.
- `[Quotient.ind]](#manual-Quotient___ind)` is useful for proving theorems about quotients.
- `[Quotient.recOnSubsingleton]](#manual-Quotient___recOnSubsingleton)` can be used whenever the target type is a `[Subsingleton](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Subsingleton___intro)`.
- `[Quotient.hrecOn]](#manual-Quotient___hrecOn)` uses heterogeneous equality instead of rewriting with `[Quotient.sound]](#manual-Quotient___sound)`.

`[Quotient.rec]](#manual-Quotient___rec)` is a version of this recursor that takes the quotient parameter last.

def

```lean
[Quotient.hrecOn.{u, v}]](#manual-Quotient___hrecOn) {α : Sort u} {s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α}
  {motive : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s → Sort v} (q : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s)
  (f : (a : α) → motive ([Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s a))
  (c : ∀ (a b : α), a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b → f a [≍](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#HEq___refl) f b) : motive q



[Quotient.hrecOn.{u, v}]](#manual-Quotient___hrecOn) {α : Sort u}
  {s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α}
  {motive : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s → Sort v}
  (q : [Quotient]](#manual-Quotient) s)
  (f : (a : α) → motive ([Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s a))
  (c : ∀ (a b : α), a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b → f a [≍](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#HEq___refl) f b) :
```

A dependent recursion principle for `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)` that uses [heterogeneous
equality](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=HEq), analogous to a [recursor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=recursors) for
a structure.

`[Quotient.recOn]](#manual-Quotient___recOn)` is a version of this recursor that uses `[Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl)` instead of `[HEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#HEq___refl)`.

If two elements of a type are equal in a quotient, then they are related by the setoid's equivalence relation.
This property is called `[Quotient.exact]](#manual-Quotient___exact)`.

theorem

```lean
[Quotient.exact.{u}]](#manual-Quotient___exact) {α : Sort u} {s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α} {a b : α} :
  [Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s b → a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b



[Quotient.exact.{u}]](#manual-Quotient___exact) {α : Sort u}
  {s : [Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk) α} {a b : α} :
  [Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [Quotient.mk]](#manual-Quotient___mk) s b →
    a [≈]](#manual-HasEquiv___mk) b
```

If two values are equal in a quotient, then they are related by its equivalence relation.

### 4.5.5. Logical Model {#manual-quotient-model}

Like functions and universes, quotient types are a built-in feature of Lean's type system.
However, the underlying primitives are based on the somewhat simpler `[Quot]](#manual-Quot)` type rather than on `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)`, and `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)` is defined in terms of `[Quot]](#manual-Quot)`.
The primary difference is that `[Quot]](#manual-Quot)` is based on an arbitrary relation, rather than a `[Setoid]](#manual-Setoid___mk)` instance.
The provided relation need not be an equivalence relation; the rules that govern `[Quot]](#manual-Quot)` and `[Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl)` automatically extend the provided relation into its reflexive, transitive, symmetric closure.
When the relation is already an equivalence relation, `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)` should be used instead of `[Quot]](#manual-Quot)` so Lean can make use of the fact that the relation is an equivalence relation.

The fundamental quotient type API consists of `[Quot]](#manual-Quot)`, `[Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk)`, `[Quot.lift]](#manual-Quot___lift)`, `[Quot.ind]](#manual-Quot___ind)`, and `[Quot.sound]](#manual-Quot___sound)`.
These are used in the same way as their `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)`-based counterparts.

primitive

```lean
[Quot.{u}]](#manual-Quot) {α : Sort u} (r : α → α → Prop) : Sort u



[Quot.{u}]](#manual-Quot) {α : Sort u} (r : α → α → Prop) :
  Sort u
```

Low-level quotient types. Quotient types coarsen the propositional equality for a type `α`, so that
terms related by some relation `r` are considered equal in `[Quot]](#manual-Quot) r`.

Set-theoretically, `[Quot]](#manual-Quot) r` can be seen as the set of equivalence classes of `α` modulo `r`.
Functions from `[Quot]](#manual-Quot) r` must prove that they respect `r`: to define a function `f : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r → β`,
it is necessary to provide `f' : α → β` and prove that for all `x : α` and `y : α`,
`r x y → f' x = f' y`.

`[Quot]](#manual-Quot)` is a built-in primitive:

- `[Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk)` places elements of the underlying type `α` into the quotient.
- `[Quot.lift]](#manual-Quot___lift)` allows the definition of functions from the quotient to some other type.
- `[Quot.sound]](#manual-Quot___sound)` asserts the equality of elements related by `r`.
- `[Quot.ind]](#manual-Quot___ind)` is used to write proofs about quotients by assuming that all elements are constructed
  with `[Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk)`.

The relation `r` is not required to be an equivalence relation; the resulting quotient type's
equality extends `r` to an equivalence as a consequence of the rules for equality and quotients.
When `r` is an equivalence relation, it can be more convenient to use the higher-level type
`[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)`.

primitive

```lean
[Quot.mk.{u}]](#manual-Quot___mk) {α : Sort u} (r : α → α → Prop) (a : α) : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r



[Quot.mk.{u}]](#manual-Quot___mk) {α : Sort u}
  (r : α → α → Prop) (a : α) : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r
```

Places an element of a type into the quotient that equates terms according to the provided relation.

Given `v : α` and relation `r : α → α → Prop`, `[Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r v : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r` is like `v`, except all
observations of `v`'s value must respect `r`.

`[Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk)` is a built-in primitive:

- `[Quot]](#manual-Quot)` is the built-in quotient type.
- `[Quot.lift]](#manual-Quot___lift)` allows the definition of functions from the quotient to some other type.
- `[Quot.sound]](#manual-Quot___sound)` asserts the equality of elements related by `r`.
- `[Quot.ind]](#manual-Quot___ind)` is used to write proofs about quotients by assuming that all elements are constructed
  with `[Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk)`.

primitive

```lean
[Quot.lift.{u, v}]](#manual-Quot___lift) {α : Sort u} {r : α → α → Prop} {β : Sort v}
  (f : α → β) (a : ∀ (a b : α), r a b → f a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f b) : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r → β



[Quot.lift.{u, v}]](#manual-Quot___lift) {α : Sort u}
  {r : α → α → Prop} {β : Sort v}
  (f : α → β)
  (a : ∀ (a b : α), r a b → f a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f b) :
  [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r → β
```

Lifts a function from an underlying type to a function on a quotient, requiring that it respects the
quotient's relation.

Given a relation `r : α → α → Prop` and a quotient `[Quot]](#manual-Quot) r`, applying a function `f : α → β`
requires a proof `a` that `f` respects `r`. In this case, `Quot.lift f a : Quot r → β` computes the
same values as `f`.

Lean's type theory includes a [definitional reduction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=type-theory) from
`[Quot.lift]](#manual-Quot___lift) f h ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r v)` to `f v`.

`[Quot.lift]](#manual-Quot___lift)` is a built-in primitive:

- `[Quot]](#manual-Quot)` is the built-in quotient type.
- `[Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk)` places elements of the underlying type `α` into the quotient.
- `[Quot.sound]](#manual-Quot___sound)` asserts the equality of elements related by `r`
- `[Quot.ind]](#manual-Quot___ind)` is used to write proofs about quotients by assuming that all elements are constructed
  with `[Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk)`; it is analogous to the [recursor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=recursors) for a
  structure.

primitive

```lean
[Quot.ind.{u}]](#manual-Quot___ind) {α : Sort u} {r : α → α → Prop} {β : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r → Prop}
  (mk : ∀ (a : α), β ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r a)) (q : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r) : β q



[Quot.ind.{u}]](#manual-Quot___ind) {α : Sort u}
  {r : α → α → Prop} {β : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r → Prop}
  (mk : ∀ (a : α), β ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r a))
  (q : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r) : β q
```

A reasoning principle for quotients that allows proofs about quotients to assume that all values are
constructed with `[Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk)`.

`[Quot.rec]](#manual-Quot___rec)` is analogous to the [recursor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=recursors) for a structure, and can
be used when the resulting type is not necessarily a proposition.

`[Quot.ind]](#manual-Quot___ind)` is a built-in primitive:

- `[Quot]](#manual-Quot)` is the built-in quotient type.
- `[Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk)` places elements of the underlying type `α` into the quotient.
- `[Quot.lift]](#manual-Quot___lift)` allows the definition of functions from the quotient to some other type.
- `[Quot.sound]](#manual-Quot___sound)` asserts the equality of elements related by `r`.

axiom

```lean
[Quot.sound.{u}]](#manual-Quot___sound) {α : Sort u} {r : α → α → Prop} {a b : α} :
  r a b → [Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r b



[Quot.sound.{u}]](#manual-Quot___sound) {α : Sort u}
  {r : α → α → Prop} {a b : α} :
  r a b → [Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r b
```

The **quotient axiom**, which asserts the equality of elements related by the quotient's relation.

The relation `r` does not need to be an equivalence relation to use this axiom. When `r` is not an
equivalence relation, the quotient is with respect to the equivalence relation generated by `r`.

`[Quot.sound]](#manual-Quot___sound)` is part of the built-in primitive quotient type:

- `[Quot]](#manual-Quot)` is the built-in quotient type.
- `[Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk)` places elements of the underlying type `α` into the quotient.
- `[Quot.lift]](#manual-Quot___lift)` allows the definition of functions from the quotient to some other type.
- `[Quot.ind]](#manual-Quot___ind)` is used to write proofs about quotients by assuming that all elements are constructed
  with `[Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk)`; it is analogous to the [recursor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=recursors) for a
  structure.

[Quotient types](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=quotients) are described in more detail in the Lean Language
Reference.

#### 4.5.5.1. Quotient Reduction {#manual-quotient-reduction}

In addition to the above constants, Lean's kernel contains a reduction rule for `[Quot.lift]](#manual-Quot___lift)` that causes it to reduce when used with `[Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk)`, analogous to [ι-reduction]](#manual---tech-term-___-reduction) for inductive types.
Given a relation `r` over `α`, a function `f` from `α` to `β`, and a proof `resp` that `f` respects `r`, the term `[Quot.lift]](#manual-Quot___lift) f resp ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r x)` is [definitionally equal]](#manual---tech-term-definitional-equality) to `f x`.

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable)
(r : α → α → Prop)
(f : α → β)
(ok : ∀ x y, r x y → f x = f y)
(x : α)
example : [Quot.lift]](#manual-Quot___lift) f ok ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r x) = f x := [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
```

#### 4.5.5.2. Quotients and Inductive Types {#manual-quotients-nested-inductives}

Because `[Quot]](#manual-Quot)` is not an inductive type, types implemented as quotients may not occur around [nested occurrences]](#manual-nested-inductive-types) in inductive type declarations.
These types declarations must be rewritten to remove the nested quotient, which can often be done by defining a quotient-free version and then separately defining an equivalence relation that implements the desired equality relation.

**Example: Nested Inductive Types and Quotients**

The nested inductive type of rose trees nests the recursive occurrence of `[RoseTree]](#manual-RoseTree-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-and-Quotients_RPAR_)` under `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`:

```lean
inductive RoseTree (α : Type u) where
| leaf : α → [RoseTree]](#manual-RoseTree-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-and-Quotients_RPAR_) α
| branch : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) ([RoseTree]](#manual-RoseTree-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-and-Quotients_RPAR_) α) → [RoseTree]](#manual-RoseTree-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-and-Quotients_RPAR_) α
```

However, taking a quotient of the `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` that identifies all elements in the style of [squash types]](#manual-squash-types) causes Lean to reject the declaration:

```lean
inductive SetTree (α : Type u) where
| leaf : α → [SetTree]](#manual-SetTree-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-and-Quotients_RPAR_) α
| branch :
[Quot]](#manual-Quot) (fun (xs ys : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) ([SetTree]](#manual-SetTree-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-and-Quotients_RPAR_) α)) => [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)) →
[SetTree]](#manual-SetTree-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-and-Quotients_RPAR_) α
```

```lean
(kernel) arg #2 of 'SetTree.branch' contains a non valid occurrence of the datatypes being declared
```

#### 4.5.5.3. Low-Level Quotient API {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The-Type-System--Quotients--Logical-Model--Low-Level-Quotient-API}

`[Quot.liftOn]](#manual-Quot___liftOn)` is an version of `[Quot.lift]](#manual-Quot___lift)` that takes the quotient type's value first, by analogy to `[Quotient.liftOn]](#manual-Quotient___liftOn)`.

def

```lean
[Quot.liftOn.{u, v}]](#manual-Quot___liftOn) {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} {r : α → α → Prop}
  (q : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r) (f : α → β) (c : ∀ (a b : α), r a b → f a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f b) : β



[Quot.liftOn.{u, v}]](#manual-Quot___liftOn) {α : Sort u}
  {β : Sort v} {r : α → α → Prop}
  (q : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r) (f : α → β)
  (c : ∀ (a b : α), r a b → f a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f b) : β
```

Lifts a function from an underlying type to a function on a quotient, requiring that it respects the
quotient's relation.

Given a relation `r : α → α → Prop` and a quotient's value `q : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r`, applying a `f : α → β`
requires a proof `c` that `f` respects `r`. In this case, `[Quot.liftOn]](#manual-Quot___liftOn) q f h : β` evaluates
to the result of applying `f` to the underlying value in `α` from `q`.

`[Quot.liftOn]](#manual-Quot___liftOn)` is a version of the built-in primitive `[Quot.lift]](#manual-Quot___lift)` with its parameters re-ordered.

[Quotient types](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=quotients) are described in more detail in the Lean Language
Reference.

Lean also provides convenient elimination from `[Quot]](#manual-Quot)` into any subsingleton without further proof obligations, along with dependent elimination principles that correspond to those used for `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)`.

def

```lean
[Quot.recOnSubsingleton.{u, v}]](#manual-Quot___recOnSubsingleton) {α : Sort u} {r : α → α → Prop}
  {motive : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r → Sort v}
  [h : ∀ (a : α), [Subsingleton](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Subsingleton___intro) (motive ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r a))] (q : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r)
  (f : (a : α) → motive ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r a)) : motive q



[Quot.recOnSubsingleton.{u, v}]](#manual-Quot___recOnSubsingleton) {α : Sort u}
  {r : α → α → Prop}
  {motive : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r → Sort v}
  [h :
    ∀ (a : α),
      [Subsingleton](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Subsingleton___intro) (motive ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r a))]
  (q : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r)
  (f : (a : α) → motive ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r a)) :
  motive q
```

An alternative induction principle for quotients that can be used when the target type is a
subsingleton, in which all elements are equal.

In these cases, the proof that the function respects the quotient's relation is trivial, so any
function can be lifted.

`[Quot.rec]](#manual-Quot___rec)` does not assume that the type is a subsingleton.

def

```lean
[Quot.rec.{u, v}]](#manual-Quot___rec) {α : Sort u} {r : α → α → Prop}
  {motive : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r → Sort v} (f : (a : α) → motive ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r a))
  (h : ∀ (a b : α) (p : r a b), ⋯ ▸ f a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f b) (q : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r) : motive q



[Quot.rec.{u, v}]](#manual-Quot___rec) {α : Sort u}
  {r : α → α → Prop}
  {motive : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r → Sort v}
  (f : (a : α) → motive ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r a))
  (h :
    ∀ (a b : α) (p : r a b),
      ⋯ ▸ f a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f b)
  (q : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r) : motive q
```

A dependent recursion principle for `[Quot]](#manual-Quot)`. It is analogous to the
[recursor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=recursors) for a structure, and can be used when the resulting type
is not necessarily a proposition.

While it is very general, this recursor can be tricky to use. The following simpler alternatives may
be easier to use:

- `[Quot.lift]](#manual-Quot___lift)` is useful for defining non-dependent functions.
- `[Quot.ind]](#manual-Quot___ind)` is useful for proving theorems about quotients.
- `[Quot.recOnSubsingleton]](#manual-Quot___recOnSubsingleton)` can be used whenever the target type is a `[Subsingleton](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Subsingleton___intro)`.
- `[Quot.hrecOn]](#manual-Quot___hrecOn)` uses [heterogeneous equality](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=HEq) instead of rewriting with
  `[Quot.sound]](#manual-Quot___sound)`.

`[Quot.recOn]](#manual-Quot___recOn)` is a version of this recursor that takes the quotient parameter first.

def

```lean
[Quot.recOn.{u, v}]](#manual-Quot___recOn) {α : Sort u} {r : α → α → Prop}
  {motive : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r → Sort v} (q : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r)
  (f : (a : α) → motive ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r a))
  (h : ∀ (a b : α) (p : r a b), ⋯ ▸ f a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f b) : motive q



[Quot.recOn.{u, v}]](#manual-Quot___recOn) {α : Sort u}
  {r : α → α → Prop}
  {motive : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r → Sort v} (q : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r)
  (f : (a : α) → motive ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r a))
  (h :
    ∀ (a b : α) (p : r a b),
      ⋯ ▸ f a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f b) :
  motive q
```

A dependent recursion principle for `[Quot]](#manual-Quot)` that takes the quotient first. It is analogous to the
[recursor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=recursors) for a structure, and can be used when the resulting type
is not necessarily a proposition.

While it is very general, this recursor can be tricky to use. The following simpler alternatives may
be easier to use:

- `[Quot.lift]](#manual-Quot___lift)` is useful for defining non-dependent functions.
- `[Quot.ind]](#manual-Quot___ind)` is useful for proving theorems about quotients.
- `[Quot.recOnSubsingleton]](#manual-Quot___recOnSubsingleton)` can be used whenever the target type is a `[Subsingleton](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Subsingleton___intro)`.
- `[Quot.hrecOn]](#manual-Quot___hrecOn)` uses [heterogeneous equality](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=HEq) instead of rewriting with
  `[Quot.sound]](#manual-Quot___sound)`.

`[Quot.rec]](#manual-Quot___rec)` is a version of this recursor that takes the quotient parameter last.

def

```lean
[Quot.hrecOn.{u, v}]](#manual-Quot___hrecOn) {α : Sort u} {r : α → α → Prop}
  {motive : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r → Sort v} (q : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r)
  (f : (a : α) → motive ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r a))
  (c : ∀ (a b : α), r a b → f a [≍](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#HEq___refl) f b) : motive q



[Quot.hrecOn.{u, v}]](#manual-Quot___hrecOn) {α : Sort u}
  {r : α → α → Prop}
  {motive : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r → Sort v} (q : [Quot]](#manual-Quot) r)
  (f : (a : α) → motive ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r a))
  (c : ∀ (a b : α), r a b → f a [≍](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#HEq___refl) f b) :
  motive q
```

A dependent recursion principle for `[Quot]](#manual-Quot)` that uses [heterogeneous
equality](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=HEq), analogous to a [recursor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=recursors) for
a structure.

`[Quot.recOn]](#manual-Quot___recOn)` is a version of this recursor that uses `[Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl)` instead of `[HEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#HEq___refl)`.

### 4.5.6. Quotients and Function Extensionality {#manual-quotient-funext}

Because Lean's definitional equality includes a computational reduction rule for `[Quot.lift]](#manual-Quot___lift)`, quotient types are used in the standard library to prove function extensionality, which would need to be an [axiom](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Axioms/#axioms) otherwise.
This is done by first defining a type of functions quotiented by extensional equality, for which extensional equality holds by definition.

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) {α : Sort u} {β : α → Sort v}
def extEq (f g : (x : α) → β x) : Prop :=
∀ x, f x = g x
def ExtFun (α : Sort u) (β : α → Sort v) :=
[Quot]](#manual-Quot) (@[extEq]](#manual-extEq) α β)
```

Extensional functions can be applied just like ordinary functions.
Application respects extensional equality by definition: if applying to functions gives equal results, then applying them gives equal results.

```lean
def extApp
(f : [ExtFun]](#manual-ExtFun) α β)
(x : α) :
β x :=
f.[lift]](#manual-Quot___lift) (· x) fun g g' h => byα:Sort uβ:α → Sort vf:[ExtFun]](#manual-ExtFun) α βx:αg:(x : α) → β xg':(x : α) → β xh:[extEq]](#manual-extEq) g g'⊢ g x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) g' x
[exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) h xAll goals completed! 🐙
```

To show that two functions that are extensionally equal are in fact equal, it suffices to show that the functions that result from extensionally applying the corresponding extensional functions are equal.
This is because

```lean
[extApp]](#manual-extApp) ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) _ f)
```

is definitionally equal to

```lean
fun x => ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) [extEq]](#manual-extEq) f).[lift]](#manual-Quot___lift) (· x) (fun _ _ h => h x)
```

which is definitionally equal to `fun x => f x`, which is definitionally equal (by [η-equivalence]](#manual---tech-term-___-equivalence)) to `f`.
A propositional version of the computation rule for `[Quot.lift]](#manual-Quot___lift)` would not suffice, because the reducible expression occurs in the body of a function and rewriting by an equality in a function would already require function extensionality.

From here, it is enough to show that the extensional versions of the two functions are equal.
This is true due to `[Quot.sound]](#manual-Quot___sound)`: the fact that they are in the quotient's equivalence relation is an assumption.
This proof is a much more explicit version of the one in the standard library:

```lean

(h : ∀ x, f x = g x) :
f = g := byα:Sort uβ:α → Sort vf:(x : α) → β xg:(x : α) → β xh:∀ (x : α), f x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) g x⊢ f [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) g
[suffices](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#suffices) [extApp]](#manual-extApp) ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) _ f) = [extApp]](#manual-extApp) ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) _ g) byα:Sort uβ:α → Sort vf:(x : α) → β xg:(x : α) → β xh:∀ (x : α), f x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) g xthis:[extApp]](#manual-extApp) ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) [extEq]](#manual-extEq) f) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [extApp]](#manual-extApp) ([Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) [extEq]](#manual-extEq) g)⊢ f [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) g
```

### 4.5.7. Squash Types {#manual-squash-types}

Squash types are a quotient by the relation that relates all elements, transforming it into a [subsingleton]](#manual---tech-term-subsingleton).
In other words, if `α` is inhabited, then `[Squash]](#manual-Squash) α` has a single element, and if `α` is uninhabited, then `[Squash]](#manual-Squash) α` is also uninhabited.
Unlike `[Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) α`, which is a proposition stating that `α` is inhabited and is thus represented by a dummy value at runtime, `[Squash]](#manual-Squash) α` is a type that is represented identically to `α`.
Because `[Squash]](#manual-Squash) α` is in the same universe as `α`, it is not subject to the restrictions on computing data from propositions.

def

```lean
[Squash.{u}]](#manual-Squash) (α : Sort u) : Sort u



[Squash.{u}]](#manual-Squash) (α : Sort u) : Sort u
```

The quotient of `α` by the universal relation. The elements of `[Squash]](#manual-Squash) α` are those of `α`, but all
of them are equal and cannot be distinguished.

`[Squash]](#manual-Squash) α` is a `[Subsingleton](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Subsingleton___intro)`: it is empty if `α` is empty, otherwise it has just one element. It
is the “universal `[Subsingleton](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Subsingleton___intro)`” mapped from `α`.

`[Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) α` also has these properties. It is a proposition, which means that its elements (i.e.
proofs) are erased from compiled code and represented by a dummy value. `[Squash]](#manual-Squash) α` is a `Type u`,
and its representation in compiled code is identical to that of `α`.

Consequently, `[Squash.lift]](#manual-Squash___lift)` may extract an `α` value into any subsingleton type `β`, while
`Nonempty.rec` can only do the same when `β` is a proposition.

`[Squash]](#manual-Squash)` is defined in terms of `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)`, so `[Squash]](#manual-Squash)` can be used when a `[Quotient]](#manual-Quotient)` argument is
expected.

def

```lean
[Squash.mk.{u}]](#manual-Squash___mk) {α : Sort u} (x : α) : [Squash]](#manual-Squash) α



[Squash.mk.{u}]](#manual-Squash___mk) {α : Sort u} (x : α) :
  [Squash]](#manual-Squash) α
```

Places a value into its squash type, in which it cannot be distinguished from any other.

def

```lean
[Squash.lift.{u_1, u_2}]](#manual-Squash___lift) {α : Sort u_1} {β : Sort u_2} [[Subsingleton](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Subsingleton___intro) β]
  (s : [Squash]](#manual-Squash) α) (f : α → β) : β



[Squash.lift.{u_1, u_2}]](#manual-Squash___lift) {α : Sort u_1}
  {β : Sort u_2} [[Subsingleton](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Subsingleton___intro) β]
  (s : [Squash]](#manual-Squash) α) (f : α → β) : β
```

Extracts a squashed value into any subsingleton type.

If `β` is a subsingleton, a function `α → β` cannot distinguish between elements of `α` and thus
automatically respects the universal relation that `[Squash]](#manual-Squash)` quotients with.

theorem

```lean
[Squash.ind.{u}]](#manual-Squash___ind) {α : Sort u} {motive : [Squash]](#manual-Squash) α → Prop}
  (h : ∀ (a : α), motive ([Squash.mk]](#manual-Squash___mk) a)) (q : [Squash]](#manual-Squash) α) : motive q



[Squash.ind.{u}]](#manual-Squash___ind) {α : Sort u}
  {motive : [Squash]](#manual-Squash) α → Prop}
  (h : ∀ (a : α), motive ([Squash.mk]](#manual-Squash___mk) a))
  (q : [Squash]](#manual-Squash) α) : motive q
```

A reasoning principle that allows proofs about squashed types to assume that all values are
constructed with `[Squash.mk]](#manual-Squash___mk)`.
