Nonetheless, the proof of the theorem `incr_eq_plus1` can unfold its definition.
This is because proofs of theorems are in the private scope.
This is the case both for public and private theorems.

The option `[backward.privateInPublic]](#manual-backward___privateInPublic)` can be used while transitioning from ordinary source files to modules.
When it is set to `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, private definitions are exported, though their names are not accessible in importing modules.
However, references to them in the public part of their defining module are allowed.
Such references result in a warning unless the option `[backward.privateInPublic.warn]](#manual-backward___privateInPublic___warn)` is set to `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.
These warnings can be used to locate and eventually eliminate these references, allowing `[backward.privateInPublic]](#manual-backward___privateInPublic)` to be disabled.
Similarly, `[backward.proofsInPublic]](#manual-backward___proofsInPublic)` causes proofs created with `by` to be public, rather than private; this can enable `by` to fill in metavariables in its expected type.
Most use cases for `[backward.proofsInPublic]](#manual-backward___proofsInPublic)` also require that `[backward.privateInPublic]](#manual-backward___privateInPublic)` is enabled.

option

```lean
backward.privateInPublic
```

Default value: `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

(module system) Export `private` declarations, allowing for arbitrary access to them while code is being ported to the module system. Such accesses will generate warnings
unless `[backward.privateInPublic.warn]](#manual-backward___privateInPublic___warn)` is disabled.

option

```lean
backward.privateInPublic.warn
```

Default value: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

(module system) Warn on accesses to `private` declarations that are allowed only by `[backward.privateInPublic]](#manual-backward___privateInPublic)` being enabled.

option

```lean
backward.proofsInPublic
```

Default value: `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

(module system) Do not abstract proofs used in the public scope into auxiliary theorems. Enabling this option may lead to failures or, when `[backward.privateInPublic]](#manual-backward___privateInPublic)` and its `warn` sub-option are enabled, additional warnings from private accesses.

**Example: Exporting Private Definitions**

In the module `L.Defs`, the public definition of `f` refers to the private definition `drop2` in its signature.
Because `[backward.privateInPublic]](#manual-backward___privateInPublic)` is `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, this is allowed, resulting in a warning:

`L/Defs.lean`

```lean
module
set_option [backward.privateInPublic]](#manual-backward___privateInPublic) true
def drop2 (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α := xs.[drop](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___drop) 2
public def f (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (transform : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α:= [drop2]](#manual-_private___0___drop2-_LPAR_in-Exporting-Private-Definitions_RPAR_)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α :=
transform xs
```

```lean
Private declaration `[drop2]](#manual-_private___0___drop2-_LPAR_in-Exporting-Private-Definitions_RPAR_)` accessed publicly; this is allowed only because the `backward.privateInPublic` option is enabled. 

Disable `backward.privateInPublic.warn` to silence this warning.
```

When the module is imported, references to `f` use `drop2` as a default argument value; however, its name is inaccessible in the module `L`:

`L.lean`

```lean
module
import L.Defs
def xs := [1, 2, 3]
set_option pp.explicit true [in](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___in)
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Exporting-Private-Definitions_RPAR_) [xs]](#manual-_private___0___xs-_LPAR_in-Exporting-Private-Definitions_RPAR_)
```

```lean
@[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Exporting-Private-Definitions_RPAR_) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [xs]](#manual-_private___0___xs-_LPAR_in-Exporting-Private-Definitions_RPAR_) (@drop2✝ [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

**Example: Proofs in Public**

In the plain source file `NotMod`, the definition of `two` uses the content of the proof to fill out the numeric value in the definition by solving a [`metavariable`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Reading-Proof-States/#--tech-term-metavariables):

`NotMod.lean`

```lean
structure Half (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) where
val : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
ok : val + val = n
abbrev two := Half.mk _ <| by⊢ ?m.3 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) ?m.3 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) ?m.5
[show](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#show) 2 + 2 = 4⊢ 2 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 4
[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rfl)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Converting this file to a module results in an error, because the body of the definition is exposed in the public part but the proof is private and thus cannot change the public type:

`Mod.lean`

```lean
module
[public](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___sectionHeader-next) [section](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___section)
structure Half (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) where
val : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
ok : val + val = n
abbrev two := Half.mk _ <| by
[show](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#show) 2 + 2 = 4
[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rfl)
```

```lean
tactic execution is stuck, goal contains metavariables
  ?m.3 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) ?m.3 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) ?m.5
```

Setting the option `[backward.proofsInPublic]](#manual-backward___proofsInPublic)` causes the proof to be in the public part of the module so it can solve the metavariable:

`Mod.lean`

```lean
module
[public](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___sectionHeader-next) [section](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___section)
structure Half (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) where
val : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
ok : val + val = n
set_option [backward.proofsInPublic]](#manual-backward___proofsInPublic) true [in](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___in)
abbrev two := Half.mk _ <| by⊢ ?m.3 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) ?m.3 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) ?m.5
[show](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#show) 2 + 2 = 4⊢ 2 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 4
[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rfl)All goals completed! 🐙
```

However, it is typically better style to reformulate the definition so that the proof has a complete goal:

`Mod.lean`

```lean
module
[public](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___sectionHeader-next) [section](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___section)
structure Half (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) where
val : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
ok : val + val = n
abbrev two : Half 4 := Half.mk 2 <| by⊢ 2 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 4
[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rfl)All goals completed! 🐙
```

The private scope of a module may be imported into another module using the `all` modifier.
By default, this is only allowed if the imported module and the current module are from the same Lake [package](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Lake/#--tech-term-package), as its main purpose is to allow for separating definitions and proofs into separate modules for internal organization of a library.
The Lake package or library option [`allowImportAll`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Lake/#Lake___PackageConfig-allowImportAll) can be set to allow other packages to access to the current package's private scopes via `import all`.
The imported private scope includes private imports of the imported module, including nested `import all`s.
As a consequence, the set of private scopes accessible to the current module is the transitive closure of `import all` declarations.

The module system's `import all` is more powerful than `import` without the module system.
It makes imported private definitions accessible directly by name, as if they were defined in the current module.
A secondary use case for `import all` is to access code in multiple modules within a library that should nonetheless not be provided to downstream consumers, as well as to allow tests to access information that is not part of the public API.

**Example: Importing Private Information**

This library separates a module of definitions from a module of lemmas.
This is a common pattern in Lean code.

`Tree/Basic.lean`

```lean
module
public inductive Tree (α : Type u) : Type u where
| leaf
| branch (left : Tree α) (val : α) (right : Tree α)
public def Tree.count : Tree α → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| .leaf => 0
| .branch left _ right => left.count + 1 + right.count
```

However, because `Tree.count` is not exposed, the proof in the lemma file cannot unfold it:

`Tree/Lemmas.lean`

```lean
module
public import Tree.Basic
theorem Tree.count_leaf_eq_zero : count (.leaf : Tree α) = 0 := byα:Type u_1⊢ leaf.count [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [count]α:Type u_1⊢ leaf.count [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0
```

```lean
Invalid simp theorem `count`: Expected a definition with an exposed body
```

Importing the private scope from `Tree.Basic` into the lemma module allows the definition to be unfolded in the proof.

`Tree/Basic.lean`

```lean
module
public inductive Tree (α : Type u) : Type u where
| leaf
| branch (left : Tree α) (val : α) (right : Tree α)
public def Tree.count : Tree α → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| .leaf => 0
| .branch left _ right => left.count + 1 + right.count
```

`Tree/Lemmas.lean`

```lean
module
import all Tree.Basic
public import Tree.Basic
theorem Tree.count_leaf_eq_zero : count (.leaf : Tree α) = 0 := byα:Type u_1⊢ leaf.count [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [count]All goals completed! 🐙
```

#### 5.4.1. The Meta Phase {#manual-meta-phase}

Definitions in Lean result in both a representation in the type theory that is designed for formal reasoning and a compiled representation that is designed for execution.
This compiled representation is used to generate machine code, but it can also be executed directly using an interpreter.
The code that runs during [elaboration]](#manual---tech-term-elaboration), such as [tactics](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/#tactics) or [macros](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#macros), is the compiled form of definitions.
If this compiled representation changes, then any code created by it may no longer be up to date, and it must be re-run.
Because the compiler performs non-trivial optimizations, changes to any definition in the transitive dependency chain of a function could in principle invalidate its compiled representation.
This means that metaprograms exported by modules induce a much stronger coupling than ordinary definitions.
Furthermore, metaprograms run *during* the construction of ordinary terms; thus, they must be fully defined and compiled before use.
After all, a function definition without a body cannot be run.
The time at which metaprograms are run is referred to as the *metaprogramming phase*, frequently just called the *meta phase*.

Just as they distinguish between public and private information, modules additionally distinguish code that is available in the meta phase from ordinary code.
Any declaration used as an entry point to compile-time execution has to be tagged with the `meta` modifier, which indicates that the declaration is available for use as a metaprogram.
This is automatically done in built-in metaprogramming syntax such as [`syntax`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Command___syntax), [`macro`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#Lean___Parser___Command___macro), and `elab` but may need to be done explicitly when manually applying metaprogramming attributes such as `app_delab` or when defining helper declarations.
A `meta` definition may only access (and thus invoke) other `meta` definitions in execution-relevant positions; a non-`meta` definition likewise may only access other non-`meta` definitions.

**Example: Meta Definitions**

In this module, the helper function `revArrays` reverses the order of the elements in each array literal in a term.
This is called by the macro `rev!`.

`Main.lean`

```lean
module
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] [MonadRef m] [MonadQuotation m]
partial def revArrays : [Syntax](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___missing) → m [Term](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___Term)
| `(#[$xs,*]) => `(#[$((xs : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [Term](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___Term)).[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___reverse)),*])
| other => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match other with
| [.node](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___missing) k i args =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ⟨[.node](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___missing) k i (← args.[mapM](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mapM) revArrays)⟩
| _ => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ⟨other⟩
[macro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#Lean___Parser___Command___macro) "rev!" e:term : term => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
revArrays e
```

The error message indicates that `revArrays` cannot be used from the macro because it is not defined in the module's [metaprogramming phase]](#manual---tech-term-metaprogramming-phase):

```lean
Invalid `meta` definition `_aux___macroRules_termRev!__1`, `revArrays` not marked `meta`
```

Marking `revArrays` with the [`meta`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Modifiers/#Lean___Parser___Command___declModifiers) modifier allows the macro definition to call it:

`Main.lean`

```lean
module
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] [MonadRef m] [MonadQuotation m]
meta partial def revArrays : [Syntax](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___missing) → m [Term](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___Term)
| `(#[$xs,*]) => `(#[$((xs : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [Term](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___Term)).[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___reverse)),*])
| other => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match other with
| [.node](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___missing) k i args =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ⟨[.node](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___missing) k i (← args.[mapM](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mapM) revArrays)⟩
| _ => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ⟨other⟩
[macro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#Lean___Parser___Command___macro) "rev!" e:term : term => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
revArrays e
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) rev! #[1, 2, 3]
```

```lean
#[3, 2, 1]
```

Libraries that were not originally part of the meta phase can be brought into it by importing a module with `meta import`.
When a module is imported at the meta phase, all of its definitions are made available at that phase, whether or not they were marked `meta`.
There is no meta-meta phase.
In addition to making the imported module's public contents available at the meta phase, `meta import` indicates that the current module should be rebuilt if the compiled representation of the imported module changes, ensuring that modified metaprograms are re-run.
If a definition should be usable in both phases, then it must be defined in a separate module and imported at both phases.

**Example: Cross-Phase Code Reuse**

In this module, the function `toPalindrome` is defined in the meta phase, which allows it to be used in a macro but not in an ordinary definition:

`Phases.lean`

```lean
module
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] [MonadRef m] [MonadQuotation m]
meta def toPalindrome (xs : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α) : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α := xs ++ xs.[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___reverse)
meta partial def palArrays : [Syntax](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___missing) → m [Term](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___Term)
| `(#[$xs,*]) => `(#[$([toPalindrome]](#manual-_private___0___toPalindrome-_LPAR_in-Cross-Phase-Code-Reuse_RPAR_) (xs : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [Term](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___Term))),*])
| other => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match other with
| [.node](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___missing) k i args =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ⟨[.node](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___missing) k i (← args.[mapM](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mapM) palArrays)⟩
| _ => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ⟨other⟩
[macro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#Lean___Parser___Command___macro) "pal!" e:term : term => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
palArrays e
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) pal! (#[1, 2, 3] ++ [6, 7, 8])
public def colors := [toPalindrome]](#manual-_private___0___toPalindrome-_LPAR_in-Cross-Phase-Code-Reuse_RPAR_) #["red", "green", "blue"]
```

```lean
Invalid definition `colors`, may not access declaration `[toPalindrome]](#manual-_private___0___toPalindrome-_LPAR_in-Cross-Phase-Code-Reuse_RPAR_)` marked as `meta`
```

Moving `toPalindrome` to its own module, `Phases.Pal`, allows this module to be imported at both phases:

`Phases/Pal.lean`

```lean
module
public def toPalindrome (xs : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α) : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α := xs ++ xs.[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___reverse)
```

`Phases.lean`

```lean
module
meta import Phases.Pal
import Phases.Pal
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] [MonadRef m] [MonadQuotation m]
meta partial def palArrays : [Syntax](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___missing) → m [Term](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___Term)
| `(#[$xs,*]) => `(#[$([toPalindrome]](#manual-toPalindrome-_LPAR_in-Cross-Phase-Code-Reuse_RPAR_) (xs : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [Term](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___Term))),*])
| other => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match other with
| [.node](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___missing) k i args =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ⟨[.node](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___missing) k i (← args.[mapM](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mapM) palArrays)⟩
| _ => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ⟨other⟩
local [macro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#Lean___Parser___Command___macro) "pal!" e:term : term => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
palArrays e
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) pal! (#[1, 2, 3] ++ [6, 7, 8])
public def colors := [toPalindrome]](#manual-toPalindrome-_LPAR_in-Cross-Phase-Code-Reuse_RPAR_) #["red", "green", "blue"]
```

If the macro `pal!` were public (that is, if it was not declared with the `local` modifier) then the `meta import` of `Phases.Pal` would need to be declared `public` as well.

In addition, the import must be public if the imported definition may be executed at compile time outside the current module, i.e. if it is reachable from some public `meta` definition in the current module.
Use `public meta import`.
If the declaration is already declared `meta`, then `public import` is sufficient.

Unlike definitions, most metaprograms are public by default.
Thus, most `meta import` are also `public` in practice.
The exception is when a definition is imported solely for use in local metaprograms, such as those declared with `local syntax`, `local macro`, or `local elab`.

As a guideline, it is usually preferable to keep the amount of [`meta`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Modifiers/#Lean___Parser___Command___declModifiers) annotations as small as possible.
This avoids locking otherwise-reusable declarations into the [meta phase]](#manual---tech-term-meta-phase) and it helps the build system avoid more rebuilds.
Thus, when a metaprogram depends on other code that does not itself need to be marked [`meta`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Modifiers/#Lean___Parser___Command___declModifiers), this other code should be placed in a separate module and not marked [`meta`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Modifiers/#Lean___Parser___Command___declModifiers).
Only the final module that actually registers a metaprogram needs the helpers to be in the meta phase.
This module should use `public meta import` to import those helpers and then define its metaprograms using built-in syntax like `elab`, using `meta def`, or using [`meta section`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___section).

### 5.5. Elaborated Modules {#manual-module-contents}

When Lean elaborates a source file, the result is an [environment]](#manual---tech-term-environments).
The environment includes the constants, [inductive types]](#manual---tech-term-Inductive-types), [theorems](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Theorems/#--tech-term-theorems), [type classes](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/#--tech-term-type-class), [instances](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/#--tech-term-instances), and everything else declared in the file, along with side tables that track data as diverse as [simp sets](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Simp-sets/#--tech-term-simp-set), namespace aliases, and [documentation comments](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Modifiers/#--tech-term-Documentation-comments).
If the file contains a module, then the environment additionally tracks which information is public and private, and the phase at which definitions are available.

As the source file is processed by Lean, commands add content to the environment.
After elaboration, the environment is serialized to a `.olean` file, which contains both the environment and a compacted heap region with the run-time objects needed by the environment.
This means that an imported source file can be loaded without re-executing all of its commands.
Environments that result from elaborating modules are serialized into three [`.olean` files]](#manual---tech-term-___olean-file-next), containing the private, public, and server information in the environment.
The server information consists of data such as API documentation and source positions of definitions that is only needed when using the Lean language server and does not need to be loaded along with the public information in other contexts.

### 5.6. Module System Errors and Patterns {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Source-Files-and-Modules--Module-System-Errors-and-Patterns}

The following list contains common errors one might encounter when using the module system and especially porting existing files to the module system:

Unknown constant errors
:   Check whether a private definition is being accessed in the [public scope]](#manual---tech-term-public-scope).
    If so, the problem can be solved by making the current declaration private as well, or by placing the reference into the private scope using the `private` modifier on a field or `by` for a proof.

Definitional equality errors, especially after porting
:   Failures of expected definitional equalities are usually due to a missing `expose` attribute on a definition or alternatively, if imported, an `import all`.
    Prefer the former if anyone outside your library might feasibly require the same access.
    The error message should list non-exposed definitions that could not be unfolded.
    This may also appear as a kernel error when a tactic directly emits proof terms that reference specific declarations without going through the elaborator, such as for proof by reflection.
    In this case, there is no readily available trace for debugging; consider using `[@[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)expose[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)`‍` ``section`s generously on the closure of relevant modules.

#### 5.6.1. Recipe for Porting Existing Files {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Source-Files-and-Modules--Module-System-Errors-and-Patterns--Recipe-for-Porting-Existing-Files}

To gain the benefits of the module system, source files must be made into modules.
Start by enabling the module system throughout all files with minimal breaking changes:

1. Prefix all files with `module`.
2. Make all existing imports [`public`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Modifiers/#Lean___Parser___Command___declModifiers) unless they will be used only in proofs.

- Add `import all` when errors that mention references to private data occur.
- Add `public meta import` when errors that mention “must be `meta`” occur.
  The `public` may be omitted when defining local-only metaprograms.

3. Prefix the remainder of the file with `@[expose] public section` or, for programming-focused files, with [`public section`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___section).
   The latter should be used for programs that will be run but not reasoned about.

After an initial build under the module system succeeds, the dependencies between modules can be iteratively minimized.
In particular, removing uses of [`public`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Modifiers/#Lean___Parser___Command___declModifiers) and `[@[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)expose[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)` will help avoid unnecessary rebuilds.

### 5.7. Packages, Libraries, and Targets {#manual-code-distribution}

Lean modules are organized into [*packages*](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Lake/#--tech-term-package), which are units of code distribution.
A [package](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Lake/#--tech-term-package) may contain multiple libraries or executables.

Code in a package that is intended for use by other Lean packages is organized into libraries.
Code that is intended to be compiled and run as independent programs is organized into executables.
Packages, libraries, and executables are described in detail in the section on [Lake, the standard Lean build tool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Lake/#lake).

---



## Namespaces and Sections {#manual-namespaces-and-sections}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/

Names are organized into hierarchical *namespaces*, which are collections of names.
Namespaces are the primary means of organizing APIs in Lean: they provide an ontology of operations, grouping related items.
Additionally, while this is not done by giving them names in the namespace, the effects of features such as [syntax extensions](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/#language-extension), [instances](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/#--tech-term-instances), and [attributes](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#--tech-term-Attributes) can be attached to a namespace.

Sorting operations into namespaces organizes libraries conceptually, from a global perspective.
Any given Lean file will, however, typically not use all names equally.
[Sections]](#manual---tech-term-section) provide a means of ordering a local view of the globally-available collection of names, as well as a way to precisely control the scope of compiler options along with language extensions, instances, and attributes.
They also allow parameters shared by many declarations to be declared centrally and propagated as needed using the [`variable`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___variable) command.

### 6.1. Namespaces {#manual-namespaces}

Names that contain periods (that aren't inside [guillemets]](#manual---tech-term-guillemets)) are hierarchical names; the periods separate the *components* of a name.
All but the final component of a name are the namespace, while the final component is the name itself.

Namespaces serve to group related definitions, theorems, types, and other declarations.
When a namespace corresponds to a type's name, [generalized field notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Function-Application/#--tech-term-generalized-field-notation) can be used to access its contents.
In addition to organizing names, namespaces also group [syntax extensions](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/#language-extension), [attributes](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#attributes), and [instances](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/#type-classes).

Namespaces are orthogonal to [modules]](#manual---tech-term-module): a module is a unit of code that is elaborated, compiled, and loaded together, but there is no necessary connection between a module's name and the names that it provides.
A module may contain names in any namespace, and the nesting structure of hierarchical modules is unrelated to that of hierarchical namespaces.

There is a root namespace, ordinarily denoted by simply omitting a namespace.
It can be explicitly indicated by beginning a name with `_root_`.
This can be necessary in contexts where a name would otherwise be interpreted relative to an ambient namespace (e.g. from a [section scope]](#manual---tech-term-section-scope)) or local scope.

**Example: Explicit Root Namespace**

Names in the current namespace take precedence over names in the root namespace.
In this example, `[color]](#manual-Forest___color-_LPAR_in-Explicit-Root-Namespace_RPAR_)` in the definition of `[Forest.statement]](#manual-Forest___statement-_LPAR_in-Explicit-Root-Namespace_RPAR_)` refers to `[Forest.color]](#manual-Forest___color-_LPAR_in-Explicit-Root-Namespace_RPAR_)`:

```lean
def color := "yellow"
[namespace]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Forest
def color := "green"
def statement := s!"Lemons are {[color]](#manual-Forest___color-_LPAR_in-Explicit-Root-Namespace_RPAR_)}"
end Forest
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [Forest.statement]](#manual-Forest___statement-_LPAR_in-Explicit-Root-Namespace_RPAR_)
```

```lean
"Lemons are green"
```

Within the `Forest` namespace, references to `[color]](#manual-color-_LPAR_in-Explicit-Root-Namespace_RPAR_)` in the root namespace must be qualified with `_root_`:

```lean
[namespace]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Forest
def nextStatement :=
s!"Ripe lemons are {[_root_.color]](#manual-color-_LPAR_in-Explicit-Root-Namespace_RPAR_)}, not {[color]](#manual-Forest___color-_LPAR_in-Explicit-Root-Namespace_RPAR_)}"
end Forest
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [Forest.nextStatement]](#manual-Forest___nextStatement-_LPAR_in-Explicit-Root-Namespace_RPAR_)
```

```lean
"Ripe lemons are yellow, not green"
```

#### 6.1.1. Namespaces and Section Scopes {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Namespaces-and-Sections--Namespaces--Namespaces-and-Section-Scopes}

Every [section scope]](#manual---tech-term-section-scope) has a [current namespace]](#manual---tech-term-current-namespace), which is determined by the [`namespace`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) command.The [`namespace`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) command is described in the [section on commands that introduce section scopes]](#manual-scope-commands).
Names that are declared within the section scope are added to the current namespace.
If the declared name has more than one component, then its namespace is nested within the current namespace; the body of the declaration's current namespace is the nested namespace.
Section scopes also include a set of *opened namespaces*, which are namespaces whose contents are in scope without additional qualification.
[Resolving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Identifiers/#--tech-term-resolving) an identifier to a particular name takes the current namespace and opened namespaces into account.
However, protected declarations (that is, those with the `protected` [modifier](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Modifiers/#declaration-modifiers)) are not brought into scope when their namespace is opened.
The rules for resolving identifiers into names that take the current namespace and opened namespaces into account are described in the [section on identifiers as terms](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Identifiers/#identifiers-and-resolution).

**Example: Current Namespace**

Defining an inductive type results in the type's constructors being placed in its namespace, in this case as `[HotDrink.coffee]](#manual-HotDrink___coffee-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_)`, `[HotDrink.tea]](#manual-HotDrink___tea-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_)`, and `[HotDrink.cocoa]](#manual-HotDrink___cocoa-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_)`.

```lean
inductive HotDrink where
| coffee
| tea
| cocoa
```

Outside the namespace, these names must be qualified unless the namespace is opened:

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) [HotDrink.tea]](#manual-HotDrink___tea-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[HotDrink.tea]](#manual-HotDrink___tea-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_) : [HotDrink]](#manual-HotDrink-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) tea
```

```lean
Unknown identifier `tea`
```

```lean
[section]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___section)
[open]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) HotDrink
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) [tea]](#manual-HotDrink___tea-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_)
end
```

```lean
[HotDrink.tea]](#manual-HotDrink___tea-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_) : [HotDrink]](#manual-HotDrink-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_)
```

If a function is defined directly inside the `HotDrink` namespace, then the body of the function is elaborated with the current namespace set to `HotDrink`.
The constructors are in scope:

```lean
def HotDrink.ofString? : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [HotDrink]](#manual-HotDrink-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_)
| "coffee" => [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [coffee]](#manual-HotDrink___coffee-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_)
| "tea" => [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [tea]](#manual-HotDrink___tea-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_)
| "cocoa" => [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [cocoa]](#manual-HotDrink___cocoa-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_)
| _ => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
```

Defining another inductive type creates a new namespace:

```lean
inductive ColdDrink where
| water
| juice
```

From within the `HotDrink` namespace, `[HotDrink.toString]](#manual-HotDrink___toString-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_)` can be defined without an explicit prefix.
Defining a function in the `ColdDrink` namespace requires an explicit `_root_` qualifier to avoid defining `HotDrink.ColdDrink.toString`:

```lean
[namespace]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) HotDrink
def toString : [HotDrink]](#manual-HotDrink-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_) → [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
| [coffee]](#manual-HotDrink___coffee-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_) => "coffee"
| [tea]](#manual-HotDrink___tea-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_) => "tea"
| [cocoa]](#manual-HotDrink___cocoa-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_) => "cocoa"
def _root_.ColdDrink.toString : [ColdDrink]](#manual-ColdDrink-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_) → [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
| [.water]](#manual-ColdDrink___water-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_) => "water"
| [.juice]](#manual-ColdDrink___juice-_LPAR_in-Current-Namespace_RPAR_) => "juice"
end HotDrink
```

The [`open`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) command opens a namespace, making its contents available in the current section scope.
There are many variations on opening namespaces, providing flexibility in managing the local scope.

syntaxOpening Namespaces

The [`open`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) command is used to open a namespace:

```lean
command ::= ...
    | open openDecl
```

open declarationOpening Entire Namespaces

A sequence of one or more identifiers results in each namespace in the sequence being opened:

```lean
openDecl ::= ...
    | ident ident*
```

Each namespace in the sequence is considered relative to all currently-open namespaces, yielding a set of namespaces.
Every namespace in this set is opened before the next namespace in the sequence is processed.

**Example: Opening Nested Namespaces**

Namespaces to be opened are considered relative to the currently-open namespaces.
If the same component occurs in different namespace paths, a single [`open`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) command can be used to open all of them by iteratively bringing each into scope.
This example defines names in a variety of namespaces:

```lean
[namespace]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) A -- _root_.A
def a1 := 0
[namespace]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) B -- _root_.A.B
def a2 := 0
[namespace]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) C -- _root_.A.B.C
def a3 := 0
end C
end B
end A
[namespace]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) B -- _root_.B
def a4 := 0
[namespace]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) C -- _root_.B.C
def a5 := 0
end C
end B
[namespace]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) C -- _root_.C
def a6 := 0
end C
```

The names are:

- `[A.a1]](#manual-A___a1-_LPAR_in-Opening-Nested-Namespaces_RPAR_)`
- `[A.B.a2]](#manual-A___B___a2-_LPAR_in-Opening-Nested-Namespaces_RPAR_)`
- `[A.B.C.a3]](#manual-A___B___C___a3-_LPAR_in-Opening-Nested-Namespaces_RPAR_)`
- `[B.a4]](#manual-B___a4-_LPAR_in-Opening-Nested-Namespaces_RPAR_)`
- `[B.C.a5]](#manual-B___C___a5-_LPAR_in-Opening-Nested-Namespaces_RPAR_)`
- `[C.a6]](#manual-C___a6-_LPAR_in-Opening-Nested-Namespaces_RPAR_)`

All six names can be brought into scope with a single iterated [`open`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) command:

```lean
[section]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___section)
[open]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) A B C
example := [[a1]](#manual-A___a1-_LPAR_in-Opening-Nested-Namespaces_RPAR_), [a2]](#manual-A___B___a2-_LPAR_in-Opening-Nested-Namespaces_RPAR_), [a3]](#manual-A___B___C___a3-_LPAR_in-Opening-Nested-Namespaces_RPAR_), [a4]](#manual-B___a4-_LPAR_in-Opening-Nested-Namespaces_RPAR_), [a5]](#manual-B___C___a5-_LPAR_in-Opening-Nested-Namespaces_RPAR_), [a6]](#manual-C___a6-_LPAR_in-Opening-Nested-Namespaces_RPAR_)]
end
```

If the initial namespace in the command is `A.B` instead, then neither `_root_.A`, `_root_.B`, nor `_root_.B.C` is opened:

```lean
[section]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___section)
[open]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) A.B C
example := [a1, [a2]](#manual-A___B___a2-_LPAR_in-Opening-Nested-Namespaces_RPAR_), [a3]](#manual-A___B___C___a3-_LPAR_in-Opening-Nested-Namespaces_RPAR_), a4, a5, [a6]](#manual-C___a6-_LPAR_in-Opening-Nested-Namespaces_RPAR_)]
end
```

```lean
Unknown identifier `a1`
```

```lean
Unknown identifier `a4`
```

```lean
Unknown identifier `a5`
```

Opening `A.B` makes `A.B.C` visible as `C` along with `_root_.C`, so the subsequent `C` opens both.

open declarationHiding Names

A `hiding` declaration specifies a set of names that should *not* be brought into scope.
In contrast to opening an entire namespace, the provided identifier must uniquely designate a namespace to be opened.

```lean
openDecl ::= ...
    | ident hiding ident ident*
```

open declarationRenaming

A `renaming` declaration allows some names from the opened namespace to be renamed; they are accessible under the new name in the current section scope.
The provided identifier must uniquely designate a namespace to be opened.

```lean
openDecl ::= ...
    | ident renaming (ident → ident),*
```

An ASCII arrow (`->`) may be used instead of the Unicode arrow (`→`).

open declarationRestricted Opening

Parentheses indicate that *only* the names listed in the parentheses should be brought into scope.

```lean
openDecl ::= ...
    | ident (ident ident*)
```

The indicated namespace is added to each currently-opened namespace, and each name is considered in each resulting namespace.
All of the listed names must be unambiguous; that is, they must exist in exactly one of the considered namespaces.

open declarationScoped Declarations Only

The `scoped` keyword indicates that all scoped attributes, instances, and syntax from the provided namespaces should be opened, while not making any of the names available.

```lean
openDecl ::= ...
    | scoped ident ident*
```

**Example: Opening Scoped Declarations**

In this example, a scoped [notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/#--tech-term-notation) and a definition are created in the namespace `NS`:

```lean
[namespace]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) NS
scoped [notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/#Lean___Parser___Command___notation) "{!{" e "}!}" => (e, e)
def three := 3
end NS
```

Outside of the namespace, the notation is not available:

```lean
```lean
def x := {!{ "pear" }!}
```
```

```lean
<example>:1:21-1:22: unexpected token '!'; expected '}'
```

An `open scoped` command makes the notation available:

```lean
[open]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) [scoped]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___openScoped) NS
def x := {!{ "pear" }!}
```

However, the name `[NS.three]](#manual-NS___three-_LPAR_in-Opening-Scoped-Declarations_RPAR_)` is not in scope:

```lean
def y := three
```

```lean
Unknown identifier `three`
```

#### 6.1.2. Exporting Names {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Namespaces-and-Sections--Namespaces--Exporting-Names}

*Exporting* a name makes it available in the current namespace.
Unlike a definition, this alias is completely transparent: uses are resolved directly to the original name.
Exporting a name to the root namespace makes it available without qualification; the Lean standard library does this for names such as the constructors of `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` and key type class methods such as `get`.

syntaxExporting Names

The `export` command adds names from other namespaces to the current namespace, as if they had been declared in it.
When the current namespace is opened, these exported names are also brought into scope.

```lean
command ::= ...
    | export ident (ident*)
```

Internally, exported names are registered as aliases of their targets.
From the perspective of the kernel, only the original name exists; the elaborator resolves aliases as part of [resolving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Identifiers/#--tech-term-resolving) identifiers to names.

**Example: Exported Names**

The declaration of the [inductive type]](#manual---tech-term-Inductive-types) `[Veg.Leafy]](#manual-Veg___Leafy-_LPAR_in-Exported-Names_RPAR_)` establishes the constructors `[Veg.Leafy.spinach]](#manual-Veg___Leafy___spinach-_LPAR_in-Exported-Names_RPAR_)` and `[Veg.Leafy.cabbage]](#manual-Veg___Leafy___cabbage-_LPAR_in-Exported-Names_RPAR_)`:

```lean
[namespace]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Veg
inductive Leafy where
| spinach
| cabbage
[export]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___export) Leafy ([spinach]](#manual-Veg___Leafy___spinach-_LPAR_in-Exported-Names_RPAR_))
end Veg
[export]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___export) Veg.Leafy ([cabbage]](#manual-Veg___Leafy___cabbage-_LPAR_in-Exported-Names_RPAR_))
```

The first `export` command makes `[Veg.Leafy.spinach]](#manual-Veg___Leafy___spinach-_LPAR_in-Exported-Names_RPAR_)` accessible as `[Veg.spinach]](#manual-Veg___Leafy___spinach-_LPAR_in-Exported-Names_RPAR_)` because the [current namespace]](#manual---tech-term-current-namespace) is `Veg`.
The second makes `[Veg.Leafy.cabbage]](#manual-Veg___Leafy___cabbage-_LPAR_in-Exported-Names_RPAR_)` accessible as `[cabbage]](#manual-Veg___Leafy___cabbage-_LPAR_in-Exported-Names_RPAR_)`, because the current namespace is the root namespace.

### 6.2. Section Scopes {#manual-scopes}

Many commands have an effect for the current *section scope* (sometimes just called “scope” when clear).
Every Lean module has a section scope.
Nested scopes are created via the [`namespace`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) and [`section`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___section) commands, as well as the [`in`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in) command combinator.

The following data are tracked in section scopes:

The Current Namespace
:   The *current namespace* is the namespace into which new declarations will be defined.
    Additionally, [name resolution](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Identifiers/#--tech-term-resolving) includes all prefixes of the current namespace in the scope for global names.

Opened Namespaces
:   When a namespace is *opened*, its names become available without an explicit prefix in the current scope.
    Additionally, scoped attributes and [scoped syntax extensions](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#syntax-rules) in namespaces that have been opened are active in the current section scope.

Options
:   Compiler options are reverted to their original values at the end of the scope in which they were modified.

Section Variables
:   [Section variables]](#manual---tech-term-Section-variables) are names (or [instance implicit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/#--tech-term-instance-implicit) parameters) that are automatically added as parameters to definitions.
    They are also added as universally-quantified assumptions to theorems when they occur in the theorem's statement.

#### 6.2.1. Controlling Section Scopes {#manual-scope-commands}

The [`section`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___section) command creates a new section scope, but does not modify the current namespace, opened namespaces, or section variables.
Changes made to the section scope are reverted when the section ends.
Additionally, a section may cause a set of modifiers to be applied by default to all declarations in the section.
Sections may optionally be named; the `end` command that closes a named section must use the same name.
If section names have multiple components (that is, if they contain `.`-separated names), then multiple nested sections are introduced.
Section names have no other effect, and are a readability aid.

syntaxSections

The [`section`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___section) command creates a section scope that lasts either until an `end` command or the end of the file.
The section header, if present, modifies the declarations in the section.

```lean
command ::= ...
    | [sectionHeader]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___sectionHeader-next) section ident?
```

syntaxSection Headers

A section header, if present, modifies the declarations in the section.

```lean
[sectionHeader]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___sectionHeader-next) ::= ...
    | (@[expose])?
      public? noncomputable? meta?
```

If the header includes `noncomputable`, then the definitions in the section are all considered to be noncomputable, and no compiled code is generated for them.
This is needed for definitions that rely on noncomputational reasoning principles such as the Axiom of Choice.

The remaining modifiers are only useful in [modules]](#manual---tech-term-module).
If the header includes `[@[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)expose[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)`, then all definitions in the section are [exposed]](#manual---tech-term-exposed).
If it includes `public`, then the declarations in such a public section are public, rather than private, by default.
If it includes `meta`, then the section's declarations are all placed in the [meta phase]](#manual---tech-term-meta-phase).

**Example: Named Section**

The name `[english]](#manual-Greetings___english-_LPAR_in-Named-Section_RPAR_)` is defined in the `Greetings` namespace.

```lean
def Greetings.english := "Hello"
```

Outside its namespace, it cannot be evaluated.

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) english
```

```lean
Unknown identifier `english`
```

Opening a section allows modifications to the global scope to be contained.
This section is named `Greetings`.

```lean
[section]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___section) Greetings
```

Even though the section name matches the definition's namespace, the name is not in scope because section names are purely for readability and ease of refactoring.

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) english
```

```lean
Unknown identifier `english`
```

Opening the namespace `Greetings` brings `[Greetings.english]](#manual-Greetings___english-_LPAR_in-Named-Section_RPAR_)` as `[english]](#manual-Greetings___english-_LPAR_in-Named-Section_RPAR_)`:

```lean
[open]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) Greetings
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [english]](#manual-Greetings___english-_LPAR_in-Named-Section_RPAR_)
```

```lean
"Hello"
```

The section's name must be used to close it.

```lean
end
```

```lean
Missing name after `end`: Expected the current scope name `Greetings`

Hint: To end the current scope `Greetings`, specify its name:
  end ̲G̲r̲e̲e̲t̲i̲n̲g̲s̲
```

```lean
end Greetings
```

When the section is closed, the effects of the [`open`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) command are reverted.

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) english
```

```lean
Unknown identifier `english`
```

The [`namespace`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) command creates a new section scope.
Within this section scope, the current namespace is the name provided in the command, interpreted relative to the current namespace in the surrounding section scope.
Like sections, changes made to the section scope are reverted when the namespace's scope ends.

To close a namespace, the `end` command requires a suffix of the current namespace, which is removed.
All section scopes introduced by the [`namespace`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) command that introduced part of that suffix are closed.

syntaxNamespace Declarations

The `namespace` command modifies the current namespace by appending the provided identifier.
It creates a section scope that lasts either until an `end` command or the end of the file.

```lean
command ::= ...
    | namespace ident
```

syntaxSection and Namespace Terminators

Without an identifier, `end` closes the most recently opened section, which must be anonymous.

```lean
command ::= ...
    | end
```

With an identifier, it closes the most recently opened section or namespace.
If it is a section, the identifier must be a suffix of the concatenated names of the sections opened since the most recent [`namespace`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) command.
If it is a namespace, then the identifier must be a suffix of the current namespace's extensions since the most recent [`section`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___section) that is still open; afterwards, the current namespace will have had this suffix removed.

```lean
command ::= ...
    | end ident
```

The [`end`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual) that closes a [`mutual`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual) block is part of the syntax of [`mutual`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual), rather than the `end` command.

**Example: Nesting Namespaces and Sections**

Namespaces and sections may be nested.
A single `end` command may close one or more namespaces or one or more sections, but not a mix of the two.

After setting the current namespace to `A.B.C` with two separate commands, `B.C` may be removed with a single `end`:

```lean
[namespace]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) A.B
[namespace]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) C
end B.C
```

At this point, the current namespace is `A`.

Next, an anonymous section and the namespace `D.E` are opened:

```lean
[section]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___section)
[namespace]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) D.E
```

At this point, the current namespace is `A.D.E`.
An `end` command cannot close all three due to the intervening section:

```lean
end A.D.E
```

```lean
Invalid name after `end`: Expected `D.E`, but found `A.D.E`
```

Instead, namespaces and sections must be ended separately.

```lean
end D.E
end
end A
```

Rather than opening a section for a single command, the [`in`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in) combinator can be used to create single-command section scope.
The [`in`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in) combinator is right-associative, allowing multiple scope modifications to be stacked.

syntaxLocal Section Scopes

The `in` command combinator introduces a section scope for a single command.

```lean
command ::= ...
    | command in
      command
```

**Example: Using in for Local Scopes**

The contents of a namespace can be made available for a single command using [`in`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in).

```lean
def Dessert.cupcake := "delicious"
[open]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) Dessert [in]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in)
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [cupcake]](#manual-Dessert___cupcake-_LPAR_in-Using--in--for-Local-Scopes_RPAR_)
```

After the single command, the effects of [`open`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) are reverted.

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) cupcake
```

```lean
Unknown identifier `cupcake`
```

#### 6.2.2. Section Variables {#manual-section-variables}

*Section variables* are parameters that are automatically added to declarations that mention them.
This occurs whether or not the option `[autoImplicit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Headers-and-Signatures/#autoImplicit)` is `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.
Section variables may be implicit, strict implicit, or explicit; instance implicit section variables are treated specially.

When the name of a section variable is encountered in a non-theorem declaration, it is added as a parameter.
Any instance implicit section variables that mention the variable are also added.
If any of the variables that were added depend on other variables, then those variables are added as well; this process is iterated until no more dependencies remain.
All section variables are added in the order in which they are declared, before all other parameters.
Section variables are added only when they occur in the *statement* of a theorem.
Otherwise, modifying the proof of a theorem could change its statement if the proof term made use of a section variable.

Section variables are not added as definition parameters until after the definition's body has been elaborated.
This means that they cannot vary in recursive definitions, and their values are fixed.
Explicit parameters may shadow section variables and can be used for definitions in which the value must vary.

Variables are declared using the [`variable`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___variable) command.

syntaxVariable Declarations

```lean
command ::= ...
    | variable bracketedBinder bracketedBinder*
```

The bracketed binders allowed after `variable` match the [syntax used in definition headers](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Headers-and-Signatures/#bracketed-parameter-syntax).

**Example: Section Variables**

In this section, automatic implicit parameters are disabled, but a number of section variables are defined.

```lean
[section]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___section)
set_option [autoImplicit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Headers-and-Signatures/#autoImplicit) false
[universe]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___universe-next) u
[variable]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___variable) {α : Type u} (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) [[Zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Zero___mk) α] [[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) α]
```

Because automatic implicit parameters are disabled and `β` is neither a section variable nor bound as a parameter of the function, the following definition fails:

```lean
def addAll (lst : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) β) : β :=
lst.[foldr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___foldr) (init := 0) (· + ·)
```

```lean
Unknown identifier `β`

Note: It is not possible to treat `β` as an implicitly bound variable here because the `autoImplicit` option is set to `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.
```

On the other hand, not even `xs` needs to be written directly in the definition when it uses the section variables:

```lean
def addAll :=
xs.[foldr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___foldr) (init := 0) (· + ·)
```

**Example: Section Variables and Recursion**

Section variables are fixed in recursive functions.
The variable `length` represents a number that should decrease:

```lean
[variable]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (length : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

However, it cannot be used directly to define recursive functions, because the body of the function does not treat the section variable as a parameter:

```lean
def copies (x : α) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) length [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => []
| length' + 1 => x :: copies length' x
```

The error arises because `copies` expects only one explicit argument but has received two:

```lean
Function expected at
  copies length'
but this term has type
  [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)

Note: Expected a function because this term is being applied to the argument
  x
```

Even though `length` is already a section variable, it can be shadowed in order to define the function:

```lean
def copies (length : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (x : α) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) length [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => []
| length' + 1 => x :: copies length' x
```

To add a section variable to a theorem even if it is not explicitly mentioned in the statement, mark the variable with the `include` command.
All variables marked for inclusion are added to all theorems.
The `omit` command removes the inclusion mark from a variable; it's typically a good idea to use it with [`in`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in).

**Example: Included and Omitted Section Variables**

This section's variables include a predicate as well as everything needed to prove that it holds universally, along with a useless extra assumption.

```lean
[section]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___section)
[variable]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___variable) {p : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prop}
[variable]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (pZero : p 0) (pStep : ∀ n, p n → p (n + 1))
[variable]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (pFifteen : p 15)
```

However, only `p` is added to this theorem's assumptions, so it cannot be proved.

```lean
theorem p_all : ∀ n, p n := byp:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prop⊢ ∀ (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)), p n
[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro) np:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Propn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ p n
[induction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#induction) nzerop:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prop⊢ p 0succp:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Propn✝:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)a✝:p n✝⊢ p [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)n✝ [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
```

Because the spurious assumption `pFifteen` was inserted, Lean issues a warning:

```lean
automatically included section variable(s) unused in theorem `p_all`:
  pFifteen
consider restructuring your `variable` declarations so that the variables are not in scope or explicitly omit them:
  omit pFifteen in theorem ...

Note: This linter can be disabled with `set_option linter.unusedSectionVars false`
```

## Definitions {#manual-definitions}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/

The following commands in Lean are definition-like:

- `def`
- `abbrev`
- `example`
- `theorem`
- `opaque`

All of these commands cause Lean to [elaborate](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Elaborators/#--tech-term-elaborators) a term based on a [signature](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Headers-and-Signatures/#--tech-term-signature).
With the exception of `example`, which discards the result, the resulting expression in Lean's core language is saved for future use in the environment.
The `instance` command is described in the [section on instance declarations](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Instance-Declarations/#instance-declarations).

1. [7.1. Modifiers](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Modifiers/#declaration-modifiers)
2. [7.2. Headers and Signatures](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Headers-and-Signatures/#signature-syntax)
3. [7.3. Definitions](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Definitions/#The-Lean-Language-Reference--Definitions--Definitions)
4. [7.4. Theorems](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Theorems/#The-Lean-Language-Reference--Definitions--Theorems)
5. [7.5. Example Declarations](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Example-Declarations/#The-Lean-Language-Reference--Definitions--Example-Declarations)
6. [7.6. Recursive Definitions](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#recursive-definitions)
