## Definitions — 7.6. Recursive Definitions {#manual-definitions-76-recursive-definitions}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/

Allowing arbitrary recursive function definitions would make Lean's logic inconsistent.
General recursion makes it possible to write circular proofs: “[proposition]](#manual---tech-term-Propositions) `P` is true because proposition `P` is true”.
Outside of proofs, an infinite loop could be assigned the type `[Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty)`, which can be used with [`nomatch`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___nomatch) or `Empty.rec` to prove any theorem.

Banning recursive function definitions outright would render Lean far less useful: [inductive types]](#manual---tech-term-Inductive-types) are key to defining both predicates and data, and they have a recursive structure.
Furthermore, most useful recursive functions do not threaten soundness, and infinite loops usually indicate mistakes in definitions rather than intentional behavior.
Instead of banning recursive functions, Lean requires that each recursive function is defined safely.
While elaborating recursive definitions, the Lean elaborator also produces a justification that the function being defined is safe.The section on [the elaborator's output]](#manual-elaboration-results) in the overview of elaboration contextualizes the elaboration of recursive definitions in the overall context of the elaborator.

There are six main kinds of recursive functions that can be defined:

Structurally recursive functions
:   Structurally recursive functions take an argument such that the function makes recursive calls only on strict sub-components of said argument.Strictly speaking, arguments whose types are [indexed families]](#manual---tech-term-indexed-families) are grouped together with their indices, with the whole collection considered as a unit.
    The elaborator translates the recursion into uses of the argument's [recursor]](#manual---tech-term-recursor).
    Because every type-correct use of a recursor is guaranteed to avoid infinite regress, this translation is evidence that the function terminates.
    Applications of functions defined via recursors are definitionally equal to the result of the recursion, and are typically relatively efficient inside the kernel.

Recursion over well-founded relations
:   Many functions are also difficult to convert to structural recursion; for instance, a function may terminate because the difference between an array index and the size of the array decreases as the index increases, but `Nat.rec` isn't applicable because the index that increases is the function's argument.
    Here, there is a [measure]](#manual---tech-term-measure) of termination that decreases at each recursive call, but the measure is not itself an argument to the function.
    In these cases, [well-founded recursion]](#manual---tech-term-well-founded-recursion) can be used to define the function.
    Well-founded recursion is a technique for systematically transforming recursive functions with a decreasing measure into recursive functions over proofs that every sequence of reductions to the measure eventually terminates at a minimum.
    Applications of functions defined via well-founded recursion are not necessarily definitionally equal to their return values, but this equality can be proved as a proposition.
    Even when definitional equalities exist, these functions are frequently slow to compute with because they require reducing proof terms that are often very large.

Recursive functions as partial fixpoints
:   The definition of a function can be understood as an equation that specifies its behavior.
    In certain cases, the existence of a function that satisfies this specification can be proven even when the recursive function does not necessarily terminate for all inputs.
    This strategy is even applicable in some cases where the function definition does not necessarily terminate for all inputs.
    These partial functions emerge as fixed points of these equations are called [*partial fixpoints*]](#manual---tech-term-partial-fixpoint).

    In particular, any function whose return type is in certain monads (e.g. `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`) can be defined using this strategy.
    Lean generates additional partial correctness theorems for these monadic functions.
    As with well-founded recursion, applications of functions defined as partial fixpoints are not definitionally equal to their return values, but Lean generates theorems that propositionally equate the function to its unfolding and to the reduction behavior specified in its definition.

Coinductive and inductive predicates as fixpoints
:   Recursive `Prop`-valued functions can be defined as greatest or least fixpoints of monotone operators on complete lattices.
    Coinductive predicates, defined using `coinductive_fixpoint` or the `coinductive` command, describe potentially infinite behavior such as infinite sequences or bisimulation.
    Inductive predicates, defined using `inductive_fixpoint`, provide an alternative to standard inductive types that is compatible with mixed inductive-coinductive mutual blocks.

Partial functions with nonempty codomains
:   For many applications, it's not important to reason about the implementation of certain functions.
    A recursive function might be used only as part of the implementation of proof automation steps, or it might be an ordinary program that will never be formally proved correct.
    In these cases, the Lean kernel does not need either definitional or propositional equalities to hold for the definition; it suffices that soundness is maintained.
    Functions marked `partial` are treated as opaque constants by the kernel and are neither unfolded nor reduced.
    All that is required for soundness is that their return type is inhabited.
    Partial functions may still be used in compiled code as usual, and they may appear in propositions and proofs; their equational theory in Lean's logic is simply very weak.

Unsafe recursive definitions
:   Unsafe definitions have none of the restrictions of partial definitions.
    They may freely make use of general recursion, and they may use features of Lean that break assumptions about its equational theory, such as primitives for casting (`[unsafeCast]](#manual-unsafeCast)`), checking pointer equality (`[ptrAddrUnsafe]](#manual-ptrAddrUnsafe)`), and observing [reference counts](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Run-Time-Code/Reference-Counting/#--tech-term-reference-counting) (`[isExclusiveUnsafe]](#manual-isExclusiveUnsafe)`).
    However, any declaration that refers to an unsafe definition must itself be marked `unsafe`, making it clear when logical soundness is not guaranteed.
    Unsafe operations can be used to replace the implementations of other functions with more efficient variants in compiled code, while the kernel still uses the original definition.
    The replaced function may be opaque, which results in the function name having a trivial equational theory in the logic, or it may be an ordinary function, in which case the function is used in the logic.
    Use this feature with care: logical soundness is not at risk, but the behavior of programs written in Lean may diverge from their verified logical models if the unsafe implementation is incorrect.

As described in the [overview of the elaborator's output]](#manual-elaboration-results), elaboration of recursive functions proceeds in two phases:

1. The definition is elaborated as if Lean's core type theory had recursive definitions.
   Aside from using recursion, this provisional definition is fully elaborated.
   The compiler generates code from these provisional definitions.
2. A termination analysis attempts to use the five techniques to justify the function to Lean's kernel.
   If the definition is marked `unsafe` or `partial`, then that technique is used.
   If an explicit `termination_by`, `partial_fixpoint`, `coinductive_fixpoint`, or `inductive_fixpoint` clause is present, then the indicated technique is the only one attempted.
   If there is no such clause, then the elaborator performs a search, testing each parameter to the function as a candidate for structural recursion, and attempting to find a measure with a well-founded relation that decreases at each recursive call.

This section describes the rules that govern recursive functions.
After a description of mutual recursion, each of the five kinds of recursive definitions is specified, along with the tradeoffs between reasoning power and flexibility that go along with each.

### 7.6.1. Mutual Recursion {#manual-mutual-syntax}

Just as a recursive definition is one that mentions the name being defined in the body of the definition, *mutually recursive* definitions are definitions that may be recursive or mention one another.
To use mutual recursion between multiple declarations, they must be placed in a mutual block.

syntaxMutual Declaration Blocks

The general syntax for mutual recursion is:

```lean
command ::= ...
    | mutual
        declaration*
      end
```

where the declarations must be definitions or theorems.

The declarations in a mutual block are not in scope in each others' signatures, but they are in scope in each others' bodies.
Even though the names are not in scope in signatures, they will not be inserted as auto-bound implicit parameters.

**Example: Mutual Block Scope**

Names defined in a mutual block are not in scope in each others' signatures.

```lean
[mutual]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
abbrev NaturalNum : Type := [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
def n : NaturalNum := 5
[end]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

```lean
Unknown identifier `NaturalNum`
```

Without the mutual block, the definition succeeds:

```lean
abbrev NaturalNum : Type := [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
def n : NaturalNum := 5
```

**Example: Mutual Block Scope and Automatic Implicit Parameters**

Names defined in a mutual block are not in scope in each others' signatures.
Nonetheless, they cannot be used as automatic implicit parameters:

```lean
[mutual]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
abbrev α : Type := [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
def identity (x : α) : α := x
[end]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

```lean
Unknown identifier `α`
```

With a different name, the implicit parameter is automatically added:

```lean
[mutual]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
abbrev α : Type := [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
def identity (x : β) : β := x
[end]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

Elaborating recursive definitions always occurs at the granularity of mutual blocks, as if there were a singleton mutual block around every declaration that is not itself part of such a block.
Local definitions introduced via `let rec` and
`where` are lifted out of their context, introducing parameters for captured free variables as necessary, and treated as if they were separate definitions within the [`mutual`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___mutual) block as well.
Thus, helpers defined in a `where` block may use mutual recursion both with one another and with the definition in which they occur, but they may not mention each other in their type signatures.

After the first step of elaboration, in which definitions are still recursive, and before translating recursion using the techniques above, Lean identifies the actually (mutually) recursive cliques among the definitions in the mutual block and processes them separately and in dependency order.

### 7.6.2. Structural Recursion {#manual-structural-recursion}

Structurally recursive functions are those in which each recursive call is on a structurally smaller term than the argument.
The same parameter must decrease in all recursive calls; this parameter is called the *decreasing parameter*.
Structural recursion is stronger than the primitive recursion that recursors provide, because the recursive call can use more deeply nested sub-terms of the argument, rather than only an immediate sub-term.
The constructions used to implement structural recursion are, however, implemented using the recursor; these helper constructions are described in the [section on inductive types]](#manual-recursor-elaboration-helpers).

The rules that govern structural recursion are fundamentally *syntactic* in nature.
There are many recursive definitions that exhibit structurally recursive computational behavior, but which are not accepted by these rules; this is a fundamental consequence of the analysis being fully automatic.
[Well-founded recursion]](#manual---tech-term-well-founded-recursion) provides a semantic approach to demonstrating termination that can be used in situations where a recursive function is not structurally recursive, but it can also be used when a function that computes according to structural recursion doesn't satisfy the syntactic requirements.

**Example: Structural Recursion vs Subtraction**

The function `[countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Structural-Recursion-vs-Subtraction_RPAR_)` is structurally recursive.
The parameter `n` was matched against the pattern `n' + 1`, which means that `n'` is a direct subterm of `n` in the second branch of the pattern match:

```lean
def countdown (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => []
| n' + 1 => n' :: [countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Structural-Recursion-vs-Subtraction_RPAR_) n'
```

Replacing pattern matching with an equivalent Boolean test and subtraction results in an error:

```lean
def countdown' (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) n == 0 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) []
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
let n' := n - 1
n' :: countdown' n'
```

```lean
fail to show termination for
  countdown'
with errors
failed to infer structural recursion:
Cannot use parameter n:
  failed to eliminate recursive application
    countdown' n'


failed to prove termination, possible solutions:
  - Use `have`-expressions to prove the remaining goals
  - Use `termination_by` to specify a different well-founded relation
  - Use `decreasing_by` to specify your own tactic for discharging this kind of goal
n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h✝:[¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)[(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)n [==](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) 0[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)n':[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := n [-](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk) 1⊢ n [-](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk) 1 [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) n
```

This is because there was no pattern matching on the parameter `n`.
While this function indeed terminates, the argument that it does so is based on properties of if, the equality test, and subtraction, rather than being a generic feature of `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` being an [inductive type]](#manual---tech-term-Inductive-types).
These arguments are expressed using [well-founded recursion]](#manual---tech-term-well-founded-recursion), and a slight change to the function definition allows Lean's automatic support for well-founded recursion to construct an alternative termination proof.
This version branches on the decidability of [propositional equality](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#--tech-term-Propositional-equality) for `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` rather than the result of a Boolean equality test:

```lean
def countdown' (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) n = 0 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) []
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
let n' := n - 1
n' :: countdown' n'
```

Here, Lean's automation automatically constructs a termination proof from facts about propositional equality and subtraction.
It uses well-founded recursion rather than structural recursion behind the scenes.

Structural recursion may be used explicitly or automatically.
With explicit structural recursion, the function definition declares which parameter is the [decreasing parameter]](#manual---tech-term-decreasing-parameter).
If no termination strategy is explicitly declared, Lean performs a search for a decreasing parameter as well as a decreasing measure for use with [well-founded recursion]](#manual---tech-term-well-founded-recursion).
Explicitly annotating structural recursion has the following benefits:

- It can speed up elaboration, because no search occurs.
- It documents the termination argument for readers.
- In situations where structural recursion is explicitly desired, it prevents the accidental use of well-founded recursion.

#### 7.6.2.1. Explicit Structural Recursion {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Definitions--Recursive-Definitions--Structural-Recursion--Explicit-Structural-Recursion}

To explicitly use structural recursion, a function or theorem definition can be annotated with a `termination_by structural` clause that specifies the [decreasing parameter]](#manual---tech-term-decreasing-parameter).
The decreasing parameter may be a reference to a parameter named in the signature.
When the signature specifies a function type, the decreasing parameter may additionally be a parameter not named in the signature; in this case, names for the remaining parameters may be introduced by writing them before an arrow (`=>`).

**Example: Specifying Decreasing Parameters**

When the decreasing parameter is a named parameter to the function, it can be specified by referring to its name.

```lean
def half (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 | 1 => 0
| n + 2 => half n + 1
termination_by structural n
```

When the decreasing parameter is not named in the signature, a name can be introduced locally in the `termination_by` clause.

```lean
def half : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0 | 1 => 0
| n + 2 => half n + 1
termination_by structural n => n
```

syntaxExplicit Structural Recursion

The `termination_by structural` clause introduces a decreasing parameter.

```lean
terminationBy ::= ...
    | termination_by structural (ident* =>)? term
```

The identifiers before the optional `=>` can bring function parameters into scope that are not
already bound in the declaration header, and the mandatory term must indicate one of the function's parameters, whether introduced in the header or locally in the clause.

The decreasing parameter must satisfy the following conditions:

- Its type must be an [inductive type]](#manual---tech-term-Inductive-types).
- If its type is an [indexed family]](#manual---tech-term-indexed-families), then all indices must be parameters of the function.
- If the inductive or indexed family of the decreasing parameter has data type parameters, then these data type parameters may themselves only depend on function parameters that are part of the [fixed prefix]](#manual---tech-term-fixed-prefix).

A *fixed parameter* is a function parameter that is passed unmodified in all recursive calls and is not an index of the recursive parameter's type.
The *fixed prefix* is the longest prefix of the function's parameters in which all are fixed.

**Example: Ineligible decreasing parameters**

The decreasing parameter's type must be an inductive type.
In `[notInductive]](#manual-notInductive-_LPAR_in-Ineligible-decreasing-parameters_RPAR_)`, a function is specified as the decreasing parameter:

```lean
def notInductive (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[notInductive]](#manual-notInductive-_LPAR_in-Ineligible-decreasing-parameters_RPAR_) (fun n => x (n+1))
termination_by structural x
```

```lean
cannot use specified measure for structural recursion:
  its type is not an inductive
```

If the decreasing parameter is an indexed family, all the indices must be variables.
In `[constantIndex]](#manual-constantIndex-_LPAR_in-Ineligible-decreasing-parameters_RPAR_)`, the indexed family `[Fin']](#manual-Fin___-_LPAR_in-Ineligible-decreasing-parameters_RPAR_)` is instead applied to a constant value:

```lean
inductive Fin' : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Type where
| zero : [Fin']](#manual-Fin___-_LPAR_in-Ineligible-decreasing-parameters_RPAR_) (n+1)
| succ : [Fin']](#manual-Fin___-_LPAR_in-Ineligible-decreasing-parameters_RPAR_) n → [Fin']](#manual-Fin___-_LPAR_in-Ineligible-decreasing-parameters_RPAR_) (n+1)
def constantIndex (x : [Fin']](#manual-Fin___-_LPAR_in-Ineligible-decreasing-parameters_RPAR_) 100) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [constantIndex]](#manual-constantIndex-_LPAR_in-Ineligible-decreasing-parameters_RPAR_) [.zero]](#manual-Fin______zero-_LPAR_in-Ineligible-decreasing-parameters_RPAR_)
termination_by structural x
```

```lean
cannot use specified measure for structural recursion:
  its type Fin' is an inductive family and indices are not variables
    [Fin']](#manual-Fin___-_LPAR_in-Ineligible-decreasing-parameters_RPAR_) 100
```

The parameters of the decreasing parameter's type must not depend on function parameters that come after varying parameters or indices.
In `[afterVarying]](#manual-afterVarying-_LPAR_in-Ineligible-decreasing-parameters_RPAR_)`, the [fixed prefix]](#manual---tech-term-fixed-prefix) is empty, because the first parameter `n` varies, so `p` is not part of the fixed prefix:

```lean
inductive WithParam' (p : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Type where
| zero : [WithParam']](#manual-WithParam___-_LPAR_in-Ineligible-decreasing-parameters_RPAR_) p (n+1)
| succ : [WithParam']](#manual-WithParam___-_LPAR_in-Ineligible-decreasing-parameters_RPAR_) p n → [WithParam']](#manual-WithParam___-_LPAR_in-Ineligible-decreasing-parameters_RPAR_) p (n+1)
def afterVarying (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (p : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (x : [WithParam']](#manual-WithParam___-_LPAR_in-Ineligible-decreasing-parameters_RPAR_) p n) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[afterVarying]](#manual-afterVarying-_LPAR_in-Ineligible-decreasing-parameters_RPAR_) (n+1) p [.zero]](#manual-WithParam______zero-_LPAR_in-Ineligible-decreasing-parameters_RPAR_)
termination_by structural x
```

```lean
failed to infer structural recursion:
Cannot use parameter x:
  failed to eliminate recursive application
    [afterVarying]](#manual-afterVarying-_LPAR_in-Ineligible-decreasing-parameters_RPAR_) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) p [WithParam'.zero]](#manual-WithParam______zero-_LPAR_in-Ineligible-decreasing-parameters_RPAR_)
```

Furthermore, every recursive call of the functions must be on a *strict sub-term* of the decreasing
parameter.

- The decreasing parameter itself is a sub-term, but not a strict sub-term.
- If a sub-term is the [discriminant](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#--tech-term-match-discriminants) of a [`match`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) expression or other pattern-matching syntax, the pattern that matches the discriminant is a sub-term in the [right-hand side](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#--tech-term-right-hand-side) of each [match alternative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#--tech-term-match-alternatives).
  In particular, the rules of [match generalization](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#match-generalization) are used to connect the discriminant to the occurrences of the pattern term in the right-hand side; thus, it respects [definitional equality]](#manual---tech-term-definitional-equality).
  The pattern is a *strict* sub-term if and only if the discriminant is a strict sub-term.
- If a sub-term is a constructor applied to arguments, then its recursive arguments are strict sub-terms.

**Example: Nested Patterns and Sub-Terms**

In the following example, the decreasing parameter `n` is matched against the nested pattern `[.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ([.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n)`. Therefore `[.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ([.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n)` is a (non-strict) sub-term of `n`, and consequently both `n` and `[.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n` are strict sub-terms, and the definition is accepted.

```lean
def fib : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0 | 1 => 1
| [.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ([.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n) => [fib]](#manual-fib-_LPAR_in-Nested-Patterns-and-Sub-Terms_RPAR_) n + [fib]](#manual-fib-_LPAR_in-Nested-Patterns-and-Sub-Terms_RPAR_) ([.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n)
termination_by structural n => n
```

For clarity, this example uses `[.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n` and `[.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ([.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n)` instead of the equivalent `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`-specific `n+1` and `n+2`.

**Example: Matching on Complex Expressions Can Prevent Elaboration**

In the following example, the decreasing parameter `n` is not directly the [discriminant](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#--tech-term-match-discriminants) of the [`match`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) expression.
Therefore, `n'` is not considered a sub-term of `n`.

```lean
def half (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) [Option.some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) n [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [.some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (n' + 2) => half n' + 1
| _ => 0
termination_by structural n
```

```lean
failed to infer structural recursion:
Cannot use parameter n:
  failed to eliminate recursive application
    half n'
```

Using [well-founded recursion]](#manual---tech-term-well-founded-recursion), and explicitly connecting the discriminant to the pattern of the match, this definition can be accepted.

```lean
def half (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) h : [Option.some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) n [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [.some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (n' + 2) => half n' + 1
| _ => 0
termination_by n
decreasing_by [simp_all](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp_all)n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)n':[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n' [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1⊢ n' [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) n' [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1; [omega](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#omega)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Similarly, the following example fails: although `xs.[tail](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___tail)` would reduce to a strict sub-term of `xs`, this is not visible to Lean according to the rules above.
In particular, `xs.[tail](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___tail)` is not [definitionally equal]](#manual---tech-term-definitional-equality) to a strict sub-term of `xs`.

```lean
def listLen : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| [] => 0
| xs => [listLen]](#manual-listLen-_LPAR_in-Matching-on-Complex-Expressions-Can-Prevent-Elaboration_RPAR_) xs.[tail](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___tail) + 1
termination_by structural xs => xs
```

**Example: Simultaneous Matching vs Matching Pairs for Structural Recursion**

An important consequence of the strategies that are used to prove termination is that **simultaneous matching of two [discriminants](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#--tech-term-match-discriminants) is not equivalent to matching a pair**.
Simultaneous matching maintains the connection between the discriminants and the patterns, allowing the pattern matching to refine the types of the assumptions in the local context as well as the expected type of the [`match`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match).
Essentially, the elaboration rules for [`match`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) treat the discriminants specially, and changing discriminants in a way that preserves the run-time meaning of a program does not necessarily preserve the compile-time meaning.

This function that finds the minimum of two natural numbers is defined by structural recursion on its first parameter:

```lean
def min' (n k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) n, k [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0, _ => 0
| _, 0 => 0
| n' + 1, k' + 1 => min' n' k' + 1
termination_by structural n
```

Replacing the simultaneous pattern match on both parameters with a match on a pair causes termination analysis to fail:

```lean
def min' (n k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) (n, k) [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| (0, _) => 0
| (_, 0) => 0
| (n' + 1, k' + 1) => min' n' k' + 1
termination_by structural n
```

```lean
failed to infer structural recursion:
Cannot use parameter n:
  failed to eliminate recursive application
    min' n' k'
```

This is because the analysis only considers direct pattern matching on parameters when matching recursive calls to strictly-smaller argument values.
Wrapping the discriminants in a pair breaks the connection.

**Example: Structural Recursion Under Pairs**

This function that finds the minimum of the two components of a pair can't be elaborated via structural recursion.

```lean
def min' (nk : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) nk [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| (0, _) => 0
| (_, 0) => 0
| (n' + 1, k' + 1) => min' (n', k') + 1
termination_by structural nk
```

```lean
failed to infer structural recursion:
Cannot use parameter nk:
  the type [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [×](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) does not have a `.brecOn` recursor
```

This is because the parameter's type, `[Prod](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)`, is not recursive.
Thus, its constructor has no recursive parameters that can be exposed by pattern matching.

This definition is accepted using [well-founded recursion]](#manual---tech-term-well-founded-recursion), however:

```lean
def min' (nk : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) nk [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| (0, _) => 0
| (_, 0) => 0
| (n' + 1, k' + 1) => min' (n', k') + 1
termination_by nk
```

**Example: Structural Recursion and Definitional Equality**

Even though the recursive occurrence of `[countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Structural-Recursion-and-Definitional-Equality_RPAR_)` is applied to a term that is not a strict sub-term of the decreasing parameter, the following definition is accepted:

```lean
def countdown (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => []
| n' + 1 => n' :: [countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Structural-Recursion-and-Definitional-Equality_RPAR_) (n' + 0)
termination_by structural n
```

This is because `n' + 0` is [definitionally equal]](#manual---tech-term-definitional-equality) to `n'`, which is a strict sub-term of `n`.
[Sub-terms]](#manual---tech-term-strict-sub-term) that result from pattern matching are connected to the [discriminant](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#--tech-term-match-discriminants) using the rules for [match generalization](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#match-generalization), which respect definitional equality.

In `[countdown']](#manual-countdown___-_LPAR_in-Structural-Recursion-and-Definitional-Equality_RPAR_)`, the recursive occurrence is applied to `0 + n'`, which is not definitionally equal to `n'` because addition on natural numbers is structurally recursive in its second parameter:

```lean
def countdown' (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => []
| n' + 1 => n' :: [countdown']](#manual-countdown___-_LPAR_in-Structural-Recursion-and-Definitional-Equality_RPAR_) (0 + n')
termination_by structural n
```

```lean
failed to infer structural recursion:
Cannot use parameter n:
  failed to eliminate recursive application
    [countdown']](#manual-countdown___-_LPAR_in-Structural-Recursion-and-Definitional-Equality_RPAR_) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)0 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) n'[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
```

#### 7.6.2.2. Mutual Structural Recursion {#manual-mutual-structural-recursion}

Lean supports the definition of [mutually recursive]](#manual---tech-term-mutually-recursive) functions using structural recursion.
Mutual recursion may be introduced using a [mutual block]](#manual---tech-term-mutual-block), but it also results from `let rec` expressions and `where` blocks.
The rules for mutual structural recursion are applied to a group of actually mutually recursive, lifted definitions, that results from the [elaboration steps]](#manual-mutual-syntax) for mutual groups.
If every function in the mutual group has a `termination_by structural` annotation indicating that function’s decreasing argument, then structural recursion is used to translate the definitions.

The requirements on the decreasing argument above are extended:

- All the types of all the decreasing arguments must be from the same inductive type, or more generally from the same [mutual group of inductive types]](#manual-mutual-inductive-types).
- The parameters of the decreasing parameter's types must be the same for all functions, and may depend only on the *common* fixed prefix of function arguments.

The functions do not have to be in a one-to-one correspondence to the mutual inductive types.
Multiple functions can have a decreasing argument of the same type, and not all types that are mutually recursive with the decreasing argument need have a corresponding function.

**Example: Mutual Structural Recursion Over Non-Mutual Types**

The following example demonstrates mutual recursion over a non-mutual inductive data type:

```lean
[mutual]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
def even : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prop
| 0 => [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)
| n+1 => [odd]](#manual-odd-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Non-Mutual-Types_RPAR_) n
termination_by structural n => n
def odd : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prop
| 0 => [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)
| n+1 => [even]](#manual-even-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Non-Mutual-Types_RPAR_) n
termination_by structural n => n
[end]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

**Example: Mutual Structural Recursion Over Mutual Types**

The following example demonstrates recursion over mutually inductive types.
The functions `[Exp.size]](#manual-Exp___size-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_)` and `[App.size]](#manual-App___size-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_)` are mutually recursive.

```lean
[mutual]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
inductive Exp where
| var : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → [Exp]](#manual-Exp-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_)
| app : [App]](#manual-App-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_) → [Exp]](#manual-Exp-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_)
inductive App where
| fn : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → [App]](#manual-App-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_)
| app : [App]](#manual-App-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_) → [Exp]](#manual-Exp-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_) → [App]](#manual-App-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_)
[end]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
[mutual]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
def Exp.size : [Exp]](#manual-Exp-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| [.var]](#manual-Exp___var-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_) _ => 1
| [.app]](#manual-Exp___app-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_) a => a.[size]](#manual-App___size-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_)
termination_by structural e => e
def App.size : [App]](#manual-App-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| [.fn]](#manual-App___fn-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_) _ => 1
| [.app]](#manual-App___app-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_) a e => a.[size]](#manual-App___size-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_) + e.[size]](#manual-Exp___size-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_) + 1
termination_by structural a => a
[end]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

The definition of `[App.numArgs]](#manual-App___numArgs-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_)` is structurally recursive over type `[App]](#manual-App-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_)`.
It demonstrates that not all inductive types in the mutual group need to be handled.

```lean
def App.numArgs : [App]](#manual-App-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| [.fn]](#manual-App___fn-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_) _ => 0
| [.app]](#manual-App___app-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_) a _ => a.[numArgs]](#manual-App___numArgs-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Structural-Recursion-Over-Mutual-Types_RPAR_) + 1
termination_by structural a => a
```

#### 7.6.2.3. Inferring Structural Recursion {#manual-inferring-structural-recursion}

If no `termination_by` clauses are present in a recursive or mutually recursive function definition, then Lean attempts to infer a suitable structurally decreasing argument, effectively by trying all suitable parameters in sequence.
If this search fails, Lean then attempts to infer [well-founded recursion]](#manual---tech-term-well-founded-recursion).

For mutually recursive functions, all combinations of parameters are tried, up to a limit to avoid combinatorial explosion.
If only some of the mutually recursive functions have `termination_by structural` clauses, then only those parameters are considered, while for the other functions all parameters are considered for structural recursion.

A `termination_by?` clause causes the inferred termination annotation to be shown.
It can be automatically added to the source file using the offered suggestion or code action.

**Example: Inferred Termination Annotations**

Lean automatically infers that the function `[half]](#manual-half-_LPAR_in-Inferred-Termination-Annotations_RPAR_)` is structurally recursive.
The `termination_by?` clause causes the inferred termination annotation to be displayed, and it can be automatically added to the source file with a single click.

```lean
def half : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0 | 1 => 0
| n + 2 => [half]](#manual-half-_LPAR_in-Inferred-Termination-Annotations_RPAR_) n + 1
termination_by?
```

```lean
Try this:
  [apply] termination_by structural x => x
```

#### 7.6.2.4. Elaboration Using Course-of-Values Recursion {#manual-elab-as-course-of-values}

In this section, the construction used to elaborate structurally recursive functions is explained in more detail.
This elaboration uses the [`below` and `brecOn` constructions]](#manual-recursor-elaboration-helpers) that are automatically generated from inductive types' recursors.

**Example: Recursion vs Recursors**

Addition of natural numbers can be defined via recursion on the second argument.
This function is straightforwardly structurally recursive.

```lean
def add (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| [.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => n
| [.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) k => [.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ([add]](#manual-add-_LPAR_in-Recursion-vs-Recursors_RPAR_) n k)
```

Defined using `Nat.rec`, it is much further from the notations that most people are used to.

```lean
def add' (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :=
Nat.rec (motive := fun _ => [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
n
(fun k soFar => [.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) soFar)
```

Structural recursive calls made on data that isn't the immediate child of the function parameter requires either creativity or a complex yet systematic encoding.

```lean
def half : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0 | 1 => 0
| n + 2 => [half]](#manual-half-_LPAR_in-Recursion-vs-Recursors_RPAR_) n + 1
```

One way to think about this function is as a structural recursion that flips a bit at each call, only incrementing the result when the bit is set.

```lean
def helper : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
Nat.rec (motive := fun _ => [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
(fun _ => 0)
(fun _ soFar =>
fun b =>
([if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) b [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) id) (soFar !b))
def half' (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [helper]](#manual-helper-_LPAR_in-Recursion-vs-Recursors_RPAR_) n [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8].[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) [half']](#manual-half___-_LPAR_in-Recursion-vs-Recursors_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)0[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 0[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 3[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 3[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 4[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

Instead of creativity, a general technique called course-of-values recursion can be used.
Course-of-values recursion uses helpers that can be systematically derived for every inductive type, defined in terms of the recursor; Lean derives them automatically.
For every `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` `n`, the type `n.below (motive := mot)` provides a value of type `mot k` for all `k < n`, represented as an iterated dependent pair type.
The course-of-values recursor `Nat.brecOn` allows a function to use the result for any smaller `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
Using it to define the function is inconvenient:

```lean
noncomputable def half'' (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
Nat.brecOn n (motive := fun _ => [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
fun k soFar =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) k, soFar [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0, _ | 1, _ => 0
| _ + 2, ⟨_, ⟨h, _⟩⟩ => h + 1
```

The function is marked `noncomputable` because the compiler doesn't support generating code for course-of-values recursion, which is intended for reasoning rather that efficient code.
The kernel can still be used to test the function, however:

```lean
[#reduce]](#manual-Lean___reduceCmd) [0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8].[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) [half'']](#manual-half______-_LPAR_in-Recursion-vs-Recursors_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)0[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 0[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 3[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 3[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 4[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

The dependent pattern matching in the body of `[half'']](#manual-half______-_LPAR_in-Recursion-vs-Recursors_RPAR_)` can also be encoded using recursors (specifically, `Nat.casesOn`), if necessary:

```lean
noncomputable def half''' (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
n.brecOn (motive := fun _ => [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
fun k =>
k.casesOn
(motive :=
fun k' =>
(k'.below (motive := fun _ => [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))) →
[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
(fun _ => 0)
(fun k' =>
k'.casesOn
(motive :=
fun k'' =>
(k''.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero).below (motive := fun _ => [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))) →
[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
(fun _ => 0)
(fun _ soFar => soFar.[2](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#PProd___mk).[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#PProd___mk).[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)))
```

This definition still works.

```lean
[#reduce]](#manual-Lean___reduceCmd) [0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8].[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) [half'']](#manual-half______-_LPAR_in-Recursion-vs-Recursors_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)0[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 0[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 3[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 3[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 4[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

However, it is now far from the original definition and it has become difficult for most people to understand.
Recursors are an excellent logical foundation, but not an easy way to write programs or proofs.

The structural recursion analysis attempts to translate the recursive [pre-definition]](#manual---tech-term-pre-definition) into a use of the appropriate structural recursion constructions.
At this step, pattern matching has already been translated into the use of matcher functions; these are treated specially by the termination checker.
Next, for each group of parameters, a translation using `brecOn` is attempted.

**Example: Course-of-Values Tables**

This definition is equivalent to `List.below`:

```lean
def List.below' {α : Type u} {motive : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → Sort u} :
[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → Sort (max (u + 1) u)
| [] => [PUnit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit)
| _ :: xs => motive xs ×' xs.[below']](#manual-List___below___-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) (motive := motive)
```

In other words, for a given [motive]](#manual---tech-term-motive), `[List.below']](#manual-List___below___-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_)` is a type that contains a realization of the motive for all suffixes of the list.

More recursive arguments require further nested iterations of the product type.
For instance, binary trees have two recursive occurrences.

```lean
inductive Tree (α : Type u) : Type u where
| leaf
| branch (left : [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) α) (val : α) (right : [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) α)
```

Its corresponding course-of-values table contains the realizations of the motive for all subtrees:

```lean
def Tree.below' {α : Type u} {motive : [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) α → Sort u} :
[Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) α → Sort (max (u + 1) u)
| [.leaf]](#manual-Tree___leaf-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) => [PUnit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit)
| [.branch]](#manual-Tree___branch-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) left _val right =>
(motive left ×' left.[below']](#manual-Tree___below___-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) (motive := motive)) ×'
(motive right ×' right.[below']](#manual-Tree___below___-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) (motive := motive))
```

For both lists and trees, the `brecOn` operator expects just a single case, rather than one per constructor.
This case accepts a list or tree along with a table of results for all smaller values; from this, it should satisfy the motive for the provided value.
Dependent case analysis of the provided value automatically refines the type of the memo table, providing everything needed.

The following definitions are equivalent to `List.brecOn` and `Tree.brecOn`, respectively.
The primitive recursive helpers `[List.brecOnTable]](#manual-List___brecOnTable-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_)` and `[Tree.brecOnTable]](#manual-Tree___brecOnTable-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_)` compute the course-of-values tables along with the final results, and the actual definitions of the `brecOn` operators simply project out the result.

```lean
def List.brecOnTable {α : Type u}
{motive : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → Sort u}
(xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α)
(step :
(ys : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) →
ys.[below']](#manual-List___below___-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) (motive := motive) →
motive ys) :
motive xs ×' xs.[below']](#manual-List___below___-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) (motive := motive) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [] => ⟨step [] [PUnit.unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit), [PUnit.unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit)⟩
| x :: xs =>
let res := xs.[brecOnTable]](#manual-List___brecOnTable-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) (motive := motive) step
let val := step (x :: xs) res
⟨val, res⟩
```

```lean
def Tree.brecOnTable {α : Type u}
{motive : [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) α → Sort u}
(t : [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) α)
(step :
(ys : [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) α) →
ys.[below']](#manual-Tree___below___-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) (motive := motive) →
motive ys) :
motive t ×' t.[below']](#manual-Tree___below___-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) (motive := motive) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) t [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [.leaf]](#manual-Tree___leaf-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) => ⟨step [.leaf]](#manual-Tree___leaf-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) [PUnit.unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit), [PUnit.unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit)⟩
| [.branch]](#manual-Tree___branch-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) left val right =>
let resLeft := left.[brecOnTable]](#manual-Tree___brecOnTable-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) (motive := motive) step
let resRight := right.[brecOnTable]](#manual-Tree___brecOnTable-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) (motive := motive) step
let branchRes := ⟨resLeft, resRight⟩
let val := step ([.branch]](#manual-Tree___branch-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) left val right) branchRes
⟨val, branchRes⟩
```

```lean
def List.brecOn' {α : Type u}
{motive : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → Sort u}
(xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α)
(step :
(ys : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) →
ys.[below']](#manual-List___below___-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) (motive := motive) →
motive ys) :
motive xs :=
(xs.[brecOnTable]](#manual-List___brecOnTable-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) (motive := motive) step).[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#PProd___mk)
```

```lean
def Tree.brecOn' {α : Type u}
{motive : [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) α → Sort u}
(t : [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) α)
(step :
(ys : [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) α) →
ys.[below']](#manual-Tree___below___-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) (motive := motive) →
motive ys) :
motive t :=
(t.[brecOnTable]](#manual-Tree___brecOnTable-_LPAR_in-Course-of-Values-Tables_RPAR_) (motive := motive) step).[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#PProd___mk)
```

The `below` construction is a mapping from each value of a type to the results of some function call on *all* smaller values; it can be understood as a memoization table that already contains the results for all smaller values.
The notion of “smaller value” that is expressed in the `below` construction corresponds directly to the definition of [strict sub-terms]](#manual---tech-term-strict-sub-term).

Recursors expect an argument for each of the inductive type's constructors; these arguments are called with the constructor's arguments (and the result of recursion on recursive parameters) during [ι-reduction]](#manual---tech-term-___-reduction).
The course-of-values recursion operator `brecOn`, on the other hand, expects just a single case that covers all constructors at once.
This case is provided with a value and a `below` table that contains the results of recursion on all values smaller than the given value; it should use the contents of the table to satisfy the motive for the provided value.
If the function is structurally recursive over a given parameter (or parameter group), then the results of all recursive calls will be present in this table already.

When the body of the recursive function is transformed into an invocation of `brecOn` on one of the function's parameters, the parameter and its course-of-values table are in scope.
The analysis traverses the body of the function, looking for recursive calls.
If the parameter is matched against, then its occurrences in the local context are [generalized](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#match-generalization) and then instantiated with the pattern; this is also true for the type of the course-of-values table.
Typically, this pattern matching results in the type of the course-of-values table becoming more specific, which gives access to the recursive results for smaller values.
This generalization process implements the rule that patterns are [sub-terms]](#manual---tech-term-strict-sub-term) of match discriminants.
When an recursive occurrence of the function is detected, the course-of-values table is consulted to see whether it contains a result for the argument being checked.
If so, the recursive call can be replaced with a projection from the table.
If not, then the parameter in question doesn't support structural recursion.

**Example: Elaboration Walkthrough**

The first step in walking through the elaboration of `half` is to manually desugar it to a simpler form.
This doesn't match the way Lean works, but its output is much easier to read when there are fewer `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` instances present.
This readable definition:

```lean
def half : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0 | 1 => 0
| n + 2 => half n + 1
```

can be rewritten to this somewhat lower-level version:

```lean
def half : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| [.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) | [.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => .zero
| [.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ([.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n) => half n |>.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

The elaborator begins by elaborating a pre-definition in which recursion is still present but the definition is otherwise in Lean's core type theory.
Turning on the compiler's tracing of pre-definitions, as well as making the pretty printer more explicit, makes the resulting pre-definition visible:

```lean

| [.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) | [.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => .zero

```

The returned trace message is:

```

    fun (x : Nat) =>
```

The actual elaborator keeps track of the relationship between the parameter being checked for structural recursion and the positions in the course-of-values tables by inserting sentinel types with fresh names into the motive.

### 7.6.3. Well-Founded Recursion {#manual-well-founded-recursion}

Functions defined by *well-founded recursion* are those in which each recursive call has arguments that are *smaller* (in a [suitable sense]](#manual-wf-rel)) than the functions' parameters.
In contrast to [structural recursion]](#manual-structural-recursion), in which recursive definitions must satisfy particular *syntactic* requirements, definitions that use well-founded recursion employ *semantic* arguments.
This allows a larger class of recursive definitions to be accepted.
Furthermore, when Lean's automation fails to construct a termination proof, it is possible to specify one manually.

All definitions are treated identically by the Lean compiler.
In Lean's logic, definitions that use well-founded recursion typically do not reduce [definitionally]](#manual---tech-term-definitional-equality).
The reductions do hold as propositional equalities, however, and Lean automatically proves them.
This does not typically make it more difficult to prove properties of definitions that use well-founded recursion, because the propositional reductions can be used to reason about the behavior of the function.
It does mean, however, that using these functions in types typically does not work well.
Even when the reduction behavior happens to hold definitionally, it is often much slower than structurally recursive definitions in the kernel, which must unfold the termination proof along with the definition.
When possible, recursive function that are intended for use in types or in other situations where definitional equality is important should be defined with structural recursion.

To explicitly use well-founded recursion, a function or theorem definition can be annotated with a `termination_by` clause that specifies the *measure* by which the function terminates.
The measure should be a term that decreases at each recursive call; it may be one of the function's parameters or a tuple of the parameters, but it may also be any other term.
The measure's type must be equipped with a [well-founded relation]](#manual---tech-term-well-founded-relation), which determines what it means for the measure to decrease.

syntaxExplicit Well-Founded Recursion

The `termination_by` clause introduces the termination argument.

```lean
terminationBy ::= ...
    | termination_by (ident* =>)? term
```

The identifiers before the optional `=>` can bring function parameters into scope that are not
already bound in the declaration header, and the mandatory term must indicate one of the function's parameters, whether introduced in the header or locally in the clause.

**Example: Division by Iterated Subtraction**

Division can be specified as the number of times the divisor can be subtracted from the dividend.
This operation cannot be elaborated using structural recursion because subtraction is not pattern matching.
The value of `n` does decrease with each recursive call, so well-founded recursion can be used to justify the definition of division by iterated subtraction.

```lean
def div (n k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) k = 0 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) 0
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) k > n [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) 0
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) 1 + [div]](#manual-div-_LPAR_in-Division-by-Iterated-Subtraction_RPAR_) (n - k) k
termination_by n
```

#### 7.6.3.1. Well-Founded Relations {#manual-wf-rel}

A relation `≺` is a *well-founded relation* if there exists no infinitely descending chain

` x_0 ≻ x_1 ≻ \cdots`

In Lean, types that are equipped with a canonical well-founded relation are instances of the `[WellFoundedRelation]](#manual-WellFoundedRelation___mk)` type class.

type class

```lean
[WellFoundedRelation.{u}]](#manual-WellFoundedRelation___mk) (α : Sort u) : Sort (max 1 u)



[WellFoundedRelation.{u}]](#manual-WellFoundedRelation___mk) (α : Sort u) :
  Sort (max 1 u)
```

A type that has a standard well-founded relation.

Instances are used to prove that functions terminate using well-founded recursion by showing that
recursive calls reduce some measure according to a well-founded relation. This relation can combine
well-founded relations on the recursive function's parameters.

Instance Constructor

```lean
[WellFoundedRelation.mk]](#manual-WellFoundedRelation___mk).{u}
```

Methods

```lean
rel : α → α → Prop
```

A well-founded relation on `α`.

```lean
wf : [WellFounded]](#manual-WellFounded___intro) [WellFoundedRelation.rel]](#manual-WellFoundedRelation___mk)
```

A proof that `rel` is, in fact, well-founded.

The most important instances are:

- `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, ordered by `(· < ·)`.
- `[Prod](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)`, ordered lexicographically: `(a₁, b₁) ≺ (a₂, b₂)` if and only if `a₁ ≺ a₂` or `a₁ = a₂` and `b₁ ≺ b₂`.
- Every type that is an instance of the `[SizeOf]](#manual-SizeOf___mk)` type class, which provides a method `[SizeOf.sizeOf]](#manual-SizeOf___mk)`, has a well-founded relation.
  For these types, `x₁ ≺ x₂` if and only if `[sizeOf]](#manual-SizeOf___mk) x₁ < [sizeOf]](#manual-SizeOf___mk) x₂`. For [inductive types]](#manual---tech-term-Inductive-types), a `[SizeOf]](#manual-SizeOf___mk)` instance is automatically derived by Lean.

Note that there exists a low-priority instance `instSizeOfDefault` that provides a `[SizeOf]](#manual-SizeOf___mk)` instance for any type, and always returns `0`.
This instance cannot be used to prove that a function terminates using well-founded recursion because `0 < 0` is false.

**Example: Default Size Instance**

Function types in general do not have a well-founded relation that's useful for termination proofs.
[Instance synthesis](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#instance-synth) thus selects `instSizeOfDefault` and the corresponding well-founded relation.
If the measure is a function, the default `[SizeOf]](#manual-SizeOf___mk)` instance is selected and the proof cannot succeed.

```lean
termination_by b
```
