#### 7.6.3.2. Termination proofs {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Definitions--Recursive-Definitions--Well-Founded-Recursion--Termination-proofs}

Once a [measure]](#manual---tech-term-measure) is specified and its [well-founded relation]](#manual---tech-term-well-founded-relation) is determined, Lean determines the termination proof obligation for every recursive call.

The proof obligation for each recursive call is of the form `g a₁ a₂ … ≺ g p₁ p₂ …`, where:

- `g` is the measure as a function of the parameters,
- `[≺]](#manual-WellFoundedRelation___mk)` is the inferred well-founded relation,
- `a₁` `a₂` `…` are the arguments of the recursive call and
- `p₁` `p₂` `…` are the parameters of the function definition.

The context of the proof obligation is the local context of the recursive call.
In particular, local assumptions (such as those introduced by `if h : _`, `match h : _ with ` or `have`) are available.
If a function parameter is the [discriminant](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#--tech-term-match-discriminants) of a pattern match (e.g. by a [`match`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) expression), then this parameter is refined to the matched pattern in the proof obligation.

The overall termination proof obligation consists of one goal for each recursive call.
By default, the tactic `[decreasing_trivial]](#manual-decreasing_trivial)` is used to prove each proof obligation.
A custom tactic script can be provided using the optional `decreasing_by` clause, which comes after the `termination_by` clause.
This tactic script is run once, with one goal for each proof obligation, rather than separately on each proof obligation.

**Example: Termination Proof Obligations**

The following recursive definition of the Fibonacci numbers has two recursive calls, which results in two goals in the termination proof.

```lean
def fib (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : n ≤ 1 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
1
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
fib (n - 1) + fib (n - 2)
termination_by n
decreasing_by
[skip](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#skip)n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:[¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)n [≤](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) 1⊢ n [-](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk) 1 [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) nn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:[¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)n [≤](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) 1⊢ n [-](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk) 2 [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) n
```

n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:[¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)n [≤](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) 1⊢ n [-](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk) 1 [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) nn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:[¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)n [≤](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) 1⊢ n [-](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk) 2 [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) n

Here, the [measure]](#manual---tech-term-measure) is simply the parameter itself, and the well-founded order is the less-than relation on natural numbers.
The first proof goal requires the user to prove that the argument of the first recursive call, namely `n - 1`, is strictly smaller than the function's parameter, `n`.

Both termination proofs can be easily discharged using the `[omega](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#omega)` tactic.

```lean
def fib (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : n ≤ 1 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
1
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
fib (n - 1) + fib (n - 2)
termination_by n
decreasing_by
·n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:[¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)n [≤](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) 1⊢ n [-](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk) 1 [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) n [omega](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#omega)All goals completed! 🐙

```

**Example: Refined Parameters**

If a parameter of the function is the [discriminant](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#--tech-term-match-discriminants) of a pattern match, then the proof obligations mention the refined parameter.

```lean
def fib : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0 | 1 => 1
| [.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ([.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n) => [fib]](#manual-fib-_LPAR_in-Refined-Parameters_RPAR_) (n + 1) + [fib]](#manual-fib-_LPAR_in-Refined-Parameters_RPAR_) n
termination_by n => n
decreasing_by

```

Additionally, the context is enriched with additional assumptions that can make it easier to prove termination.
Some examples include:

- In the branches of an [if-then-else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#if-then-else) expression, a hypothesis that asserts the current branch's condition is added, much as if the dependent if-then-else syntax had been used.
- In the function argument to certain higher-order functions, the context of the function's body is enriched with assumptions about the argument.

This list is not exhaustive, and the mechanism is extensible.
It is described in detail in [the section on preprocessing]](#manual-well-founded-preprocessing).

**Example: Enriched Proof Obligation Contexts**

Here, the [`if`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) does not add a local assumption about the condition (that is, whether `n ≤ 1`) to the local contexts in the branches.

```lean
def fib (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) n ≤ 1 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
1
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[fib]](#manual-fib-_LPAR_in-Enriched-Proof-Obligation-Contexts_RPAR_) (n - 1) + [fib]](#manual-fib-_LPAR_in-Enriched-Proof-Obligation-Contexts_RPAR_) (n - 2)
termination_by n
decreasing_by

```

Termination proof obligations in body of a `for`​`…`​`in` loop are also enriched, in this case with a `Std.Legacy.Range` membership hypothesis:

```lean
def f (xs : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [Id.run](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id___run) [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut s := xs.[sum](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___sum)
for i in [:xs.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)] do
s := s + f (xs.[take](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___take) i)
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) s
termination_by xs
decreasing_by
```

```lean
[List.sum](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___sum) (xs.[myMap]](#manual-List___myMap-_LPAR_in-Enriched-Proof-Obligation-Contexts_RPAR_) (fun x => f x []))
```

#### 7.6.3.3. Default Termination Proof Tactic {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Definitions--Recursive-Definitions--Well-Founded-Recursion--Default-Termination-Proof-Tactic}

If no `decreasing_by` clause is given, then the `[decreasing_tactic]](#manual-decreasing_tactic)` is used implicitly, and applied to each proof obligation separately.

tactic

```lean
[decreasing_tactic]](#manual-decreasing_tactic)
```

The tactic `[decreasing_tactic]](#manual-decreasing_tactic)` mainly deals with lexicographic ordering of tuples, applying `Prod.Lex.right` if the left components of the product are [definitionally equal]](#manual---tech-term-definitional-equality), and `Prod.Lex.left` otherwise.
After preprocessing tuples this way, it calls the `[decreasing_trivial]](#manual-decreasing_trivial)` tactic.

tactic

```lean
[decreasing_trivial]](#manual-decreasing_trivial)
```

Extensible helper tactic for `[decreasing_tactic]](#manual-decreasing_tactic)`. This handles the "base case"
reasoning after applying lexicographic order lemmas.
It can be extended by adding more macro definitions, e.g.

```
macro_rules | `(tactic| decreasing_trivial) => `(tactic| linarith)
```

The tactic `[decreasing_trivial]](#manual-decreasing_trivial)` is an extensible tactic that applies a few common heuristics to solve a termination goal.
In particular, it tries the following tactics and theorems:

- `[simp_arith](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp_arith)`
- `[assumption](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#assumption)`
- theorems `Nat.sub_succ_lt_self`, `Nat.pred_lt_of_lt`, and `Nat.pred_lt`, which handle common arithmetic goals
- `[omega](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#omega)`
- `array_get_dec` and `array_mem_dec`, which prove that the size of array elements is less than the size of the array
- `sizeOf_list_dec` that the size of list elements is less than the size of the list
- `String.Legacy.Iterator.sizeOf_next_lt_of_hasNext` and `String.Legacy.Iterator.sizeOf_next_lt_of_atEnd`, to handle iteration through a string using `for`

This tactic is intended to be extended with further heuristics using [`macro_rules`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules).

**Example: No Backtracking of Lexicographic Order**

A classic example of a recursive function that needs a more complex [measure]](#manual---tech-term-measure) is the Ackermann function:

```lean
def ack : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0, n => n + 1
| m + 1, 0 => [ack]](#manual-ack-_LPAR_in-No-Backtracking-of-Lexicographic-Order_RPAR_) m 1
| m + 1, n + 1 => [ack]](#manual-ack-_LPAR_in-No-Backtracking-of-Lexicographic-Order_RPAR_) m ([ack]](#manual-ack-_LPAR_in-No-Backtracking-of-Lexicographic-Order_RPAR_) (m + 1) n)
termination_by m n => (m, n)
```

The measure is a tuple, so every recursive call has to be on arguments that are lexicographically smaller than the parameters.
The default `[decreasing_tactic]](#manual-decreasing_tactic)` can handle this.

In particular, note that the third recursive call has a second argument that is smaller than the second parameter and a first argument that is definitionally equal to the first parameter.
This allowed `[decreasing_tactic]](#manual-decreasing_tactic)` to apply `Prod.Lex.right`.

```lean
Prod.Lex.right {α β} {ra : α → α → Prop} {rb : β → β → Prop}
(a : α) {b₁ b₂ : β}
(h : rb b₁ b₂) :
Prod.Lex ra rb (a, b₁) (a, b₂)
```

It fails, however, with the following modified function definition, where the third recursive call's first argument is provably smaller or equal to the first parameter, but not syntactically equal:

```lean
def synack : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0, n => n + 1
| m + 1, 0 => synack m 1
| m + 1, n + 1 => synack m (synack (m / 2 + 1) n)
termination_by m n => (m, n)
```

Because `Prod.Lex.right` is not applicable, the tactic used `Prod.Lex.left`, which resulted in the unprovable goal above.

This function definition may require a manual proof that uses the more general theorem `Prod.Lex.right'`, which allows the first component of the tuple (which must be of type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`) to be less or equal instead of strictly equal:

#### 7.6.3.4. Inferring Well-Founded Recursion {#manual-inferring-well-founded-recursion}

If a recursive function definition does not indicate a termination [measure]](#manual---tech-term-measure), Lean will attempt to discover one automatically.
If neither `termination_by` nor `decreasing_by` is provided, Lean will try to [infer structural recursion]](#manual-inferring-structural-recursion) before attempting well-founded recursion.
If a `decreasing_by` clause is present, only well-founded recursion is attempted.

To infer a suitable termination [measure]](#manual---tech-term-measure), Lean considers multiple *basic termination measures*, which are termination measures of type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, and then tries all tuples of these measures.

The basic termination measures considered are:

- all parameters whose type have a non-trivial `[SizeOf]](#manual-SizeOf___mk)` instance
- the expression `e₂ - e₁` whenever the local context of a recursive call has an assumption of type `e₁ < e₂` or `e₁ ≤ e₂`, where `e₁` and `e₂` are of type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and depend only on the function's parameters. This approach is based on work by Panagiotis Manolios and Daron Vroon, 2006. [“Termination Analysis with Calling Context Graphs”](https://doi.org/10.1007/11817963_36). In *Proceedings of the International Conference on Computer Aided Verification (CAV 2006).* (LNCS 4144).
- in a mutual group, an additional basic measure is used to distinguish between recursive calls to other functions in the group and recursive calls to the function being defined (for details, see [the section on mutual well-founded recursion]](#manual-mutual-well-founded-recursion))

*Candidate measures* are basic measures or tuples of basic measures.
If any of the candidate measures allow all proof obligations to be discharged by the termination proof tactic (that is, the tactic specified by `decreasing_by`, or `[decreasing_trivial]](#manual-decreasing_trivial)` if there is no `decreasing_by` clause), then an arbitrary such candidate measure is selected as the automatic termination measure.

A `termination_by?` clause causes the inferred termination annotation to be shown.
It can be automatically added to the source file using the offered suggestion or code action.

To avoid the combinatorial explosion of trying all tuples of measures, Lean first tabulates all [basic termination measures]](#manual---tech-term-basic-termination-measures), determining whether the basic measure is decreasing, strictly decreasing, or non-decreasing.
A decreasing measure is smaller for at least one recursive call and never increases at any recursive call, while a strictly decreasing measure is smaller at all recursive calls.
A non-decreasing measure is one that the termination tactic could not show to be decreasing or strictly decreasing.
A suitable tuple is chosen based on the table.This approach is based on Lukas Bulwahn, Alexander Krauss, and Tobias Nipkow, 2007. [“Finding Lexicographic Orders for Termination Proofs in Isabelle/HOL”](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-74591-4_5). In *Proceedings of the International Conference on Theorem Proving in Higher Order Logics (TPHOLS 2007).* (LNTCS 4732).
This table shows up in the error message when no automatic measure could be found.

**Example: Termination failure**

If there is no `termination_by` clause, Lean attempts to infer a measure for well-founded recursion.
If it fails, then it prints the table mentioned above.
In this example, the `decreasing_by` clause simply prevents Lean from also attempting structural recursion; this keeps the error message specific.

```lean
def f : (n m l : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| n+1, m+1, l+1 => [
[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Termination-failure_RPAR_) (n+1) (m+1) (l+1),
[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Termination-failure_RPAR_) (n+1) (m-1) (l),
[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Termination-failure_RPAR_) (n) (m+1) (l) ].[sum](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___sum)
| _, _, _ => 0
decreasing_by [all_goals](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#all_goals) [decreasing_tactic]](#manual-decreasing_tactic)
```

```lean
Could not find a decreasing measure.
The basic measures relate at each recursive call as follows:
(<, ≤, =: relation proved, ? all proofs failed, _: no proof attempted)
           n m l
1) 32:6-25 = = =
2) 33:6-23 = < _
3) 34:6-23 < _ _
Please use `termination_by` to specify a decreasing measure.
```

The three recursive calls are identified by their source positions.
This message conveys the following facts:

- In the first recursive call, all arguments are (provably) equal to the parameters
- In the second recursive call, the first argument is equal to the first parameter and the second argument is provably smaller than the second parameter.
  The third parameter was not checked for this recursive call, because it was not necessary to determine that no suitable termination argument exists.
- In the third recursive call, the first argument decreases strictly, and the other arguments were not checked.

When termination proofs fail in this manner, a good technique to discover the problem is to explicitly indicate the expected termination argument using `termination_by`.
This will surface the messages from the failing tactic.

**Example: Array Indexing**

The purpose of considering expressions of the form `e₂ - e₁` as measures is to support the common idiom of counting up to some upper bound, in particular when traversing arrays in possibly interesting ways.
In the following function, which performs binary search on a sorted array, this heuristic helps Lean to find the `j - i` measure.

```lean
def binarySearch (x : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) (xs : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[go]](#manual-binarySearch___go-_LPAR_in-Array-Indexing_RPAR_) 0 xs.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)
where
go (i j : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (hj : j ≤ xs.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) := by [omega](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#omega)) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : i < j [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
let mid := (i + j) / 2
let y := xs[mid]
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) x = y [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) mid
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) x < y [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[go]](#manual-binarySearch___go-_LPAR_in-Array-Indexing_RPAR_) i mid
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[go]](#manual-binarySearch___go-_LPAR_in-Array-Indexing_RPAR_) (mid + 1) j
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
termination_by?
```

The fact that the inferred termination argument uses some arbitrary measure, rather than an optimal or minimal one, is visible in the inferred measure, which contains a redundant `j`:

```lean
Try this:
  [apply] termination_by (j, j - i)
```

**Example: Termination Proof Tactics During Inference**

The tactic indicated by `decreasing_by` is used slightly differently when inferring the termination [measure]](#manual---tech-term-measure) than it is in the actual termination proof.

- During inference, it is applied to a *single* goal, attempting to prove `[<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk)` or `[≤](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk)` on `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
- During the termination proof, it is applied to many simultaneous goals (one per recursive call), and the goals may involve the lexicographic ordering of pairs.

A consequence is that a `decreasing_by` block that addresses goals individually and which works successfully with an explicit termination argument can cause inference of the termination measure to fail:

```lean
def ack : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0, n => n + 1
| m + 1, 0 => [ack]](#manual-ack-_LPAR_in-Termination-Proof-Tactics-During-Inference_RPAR_) m 1
| m + 1, n + 1 => [ack]](#manual-ack-_LPAR_in-Termination-Proof-Tactics-During-Inference_RPAR_) m ([ack]](#manual-ack-_LPAR_in-Termination-Proof-Tactics-During-Inference_RPAR_) (m + 1) n)
decreasing_by
· [apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) Prod.Lex.left
[omega](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#omega)
· [apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) Prod.Lex.right
[omega](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#omega)
· [apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) Prod.Lex.left
[omega](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#omega)
```

It is advisable to always include a `termination_by` clause whenever an explicit `decreasing_by` proof is given.

**Example: Inference too powerful**

Because `[decreasing_tactic]](#manual-decreasing_tactic)` avoids the need to backtrack by being incomplete with regard to lexicographic ordering, Lean may infer a termination [measure]](#manual---tech-term-measure) that leads to goals that the tactic cannot prove.
In this case, the error message is the one that results from the failing tactic rather than the one that results from being unable to find a measure.
This is what happens in `[notAck]](#manual-notAck-_LPAR_in-Inference-too-powerful_RPAR_)`:

```lean
def notAck : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0, n => n + 1
| m + 1, 0 => [notAck]](#manual-notAck-_LPAR_in-Inference-too-powerful_RPAR_) m 1
| m + 1, n + 1 => [notAck]](#manual-notAck-_LPAR_in-Inference-too-powerful_RPAR_) m ([notAck]](#manual-notAck-_LPAR_in-Inference-too-powerful_RPAR_) (m / 2 + 1) n)
decreasing_by [all_goals](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#all_goals) [decreasing_tactic]](#manual-decreasing_tactic)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
failed to prove termination, possible solutions:
  - Use `have`-expressions to prove the remaining goals
  - Use `termination_by` to specify a different well-founded relation
  - Use `decreasing_by` to specify your own tactic for discharging this kind of goal
m n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ m [/](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HDiv___mk) 2 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) m [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1
```

In this case, explicitly stating the termination [measure]](#manual---tech-term-measure) helps.

#### 7.6.3.5. Mutual Well-Founded Recursion {#manual-mutual-well-founded-recursion}

Lean supports the definition of [mutually recursive]](#manual---tech-term-mutually-recursive) functions using [well-founded recursion]](#manual---tech-term-well-founded-recursion).
Mutual recursion may be introduced using a [mutual block]](#manual---tech-term-mutual-block), but it also results from `let rec` expressions and `where` blocks.
The rules for mutual well-founded recursion are applied to a group of actually mutually recursive, lifted definitions, that results from the [elaboration steps]](#manual-mutual-syntax) for mutual groups.

If any function in the mutual group has a `termination_by` or `decreasing_by` clause, well-founded recursion is attempted.
If a termination [measure]](#manual---tech-term-measure) is specified using `termination_by` for *any* function in the mutual group, then *all* functions in the group must specify a termination measure, and they have to have the same type.

If no termination argument is specified, the termination argument is [inferred, as described above]](#manual-inferring-well-founded-recursion). In the case of mutual recursion, a third class of basic measures is considered during inference, namely for each function in the mutual group the measure that is `1` for that function and `0` for the others. This allows Lean to order the functions so that some calls from one function to another are allowed even if the parameters do not decrease.

**Example: Mutual recursion without parameter decrease**

In the following mutual function definitions, the parameter does not decrease in the call from `[g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-Mutual-recursion-without-parameter-decrease_RPAR_)` to `[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Mutual-recursion-without-parameter-decrease_RPAR_)`.
Nonetheless, the definition is accepted due to the ordering imposed on the functions themselves by the additional basic measure.

```lean
[mutual]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
def f : (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0 => 0
| n + 1 => [g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-Mutual-recursion-without-parameter-decrease_RPAR_) n
termination_by?
def g (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := ([f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Mutual-recursion-without-parameter-decrease_RPAR_) n) + 1
termination_by?
[end]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

The inferred termination argument for `[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Mutual-recursion-without-parameter-decrease_RPAR_)` is:

```lean
Try this:
  [apply] termination_by n => (n, 0)
```

The inferred termination argument for `[g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-Mutual-recursion-without-parameter-decrease_RPAR_)` is:

```lean
Try this:
  [apply] termination_by (n, 1)
```

#### 7.6.3.6. Preprocessing Function Definitions {#manual-well-founded-preprocessing}

Lean *preprocesses* the function's body before determining the proof obligations at each call site, transforming it into an equivalent definition that may include additional information.
This preprocessing step is primarily used to enrich the local context with additional assumptions that may be necessary in order to solve the termination proof obligations, freeing users from the need to perform equivalent transformations by hand.
Preprocessing uses the [simplifier](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/#the-simplifier) and is extensible by the user.

The preprocessing happens in three steps:

1. Lean annotates occurrences of a function's parameter, or a subterm of a parameter, with the `[wfParam]](#manual-wfParam)` [gadget](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Class-Declarations/#--tech-term-gadgets).

   ```lean
   [wfParam]](#manual-wfParam) {α} (a : α) : α
   ```

   More precisely, every occurrence of the function's parameters is wrapped in `[wfParam]](#manual-wfParam)`.
   Whenever a [`match`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) expression has *any* discriminant wrapped in `[wfParam]](#manual-wfParam)`, the gadget is removed and every occurrence of a pattern match variable (regardless of whether it comes from the discriminant with the `[wfParam]](#manual-wfParam)` gadget) is wrapped in `[wfParam]](#manual-wfParam)`.
   The `[wfParam]](#manual-wfParam)` gadget is additionally floated out of [projection function]](#manual---tech-term-projection-function) applications.
2. The annotated function body is simplified using [the simplifier](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/#the-simplifier), using only simplification rules from the `wf_preprocess` [custom simp set](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Simp-sets/#--tech-term-Custom-simp-sets).
3. Finally, any left-over `[wfParam]](#manual-wfParam)` markers are removed.

Annotating function parameters that are used for well-founded recursion allows the preprocessing simplification rules to distinguish between parameters and other terms.

attributePreprocessing Simp Set for Well-Founded Recursion

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | wf_preprocess
```

Theorems tagged with the `[wf_preprocess]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___wf_preprocess)` attribute are used during the processing of functions defined
by well-founded recursion. They are applied to the function's body to add additional hypotheses,
such as replacing `[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#if) c [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#if) _ [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#if) _` with `if h : c then _ else _` or `xs.map` with
`xs.attach.map`. Also see `[wfParam]](#manual-wfParam)`.

Warning: These rewrites are only applied to the declaration for the purpose of the logical
definition, but do not affect the compiled code. In particular they can cause a function definition
that diverges as compiled to be accepted without an explicit `partial` keyword, for example if they
remove irrelevant subterms or change the evaluation order by hiding terms under binders. Therefore
avoid tagging theorems with `[[wf_preprocess]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___wf_preprocess)]` unless they preserve also operational behavior.

def

```lean
[wfParam.{u}]](#manual-wfParam) {α : Sort u} (a : α) : α



[wfParam.{u}]](#manual-wfParam) {α : Sort u} (a : α) : α
```

The `[wfParam]](#manual-wfParam)` gadget is used internally during the construction of recursive functions by
wellfounded recursion, to keep track of the parameter for which the automatic introduction
of `[List.attach](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___attach)` (or similar) is plausible.

Some rewrite rules in the `wf_preprocess` simp set apply generally, without heeding the `[wfParam]](#manual-wfParam)` marker.
In particular, the theorem `ite_eq_dite` is used to extend the context of an [if-then-else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#if-then-else) expression branch with an assumption about the condition:This assumption's name should be an inaccessible name based on `h`, as is indicated by using `[binderNameHint](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Naming-Bound-Variables/#binderNameHint)` with the term `()`. Binder name hints are described in the [tactic language reference](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Naming-Bound-Variables/#bound-variable-name-hints).

```lean
ite_eq_dite {P : Prop} {α : Sort u} {a b : α} [[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) P] :
([if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) P [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) a [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) b) =
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : P [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
[binderNameHint](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Naming-Bound-Variables/#binderNameHint) h () a
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
[binderNameHint](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Naming-Bound-Variables/#binderNameHint) h () b
```

Other rewrite rules use the `[wfParam]](#manual-wfParam)` marker to restrict their applicability; they are used only when a function (like `[List.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map)`) is applied to a parameter or subterm of a parameter, but not otherwise.
This is typically done in two steps:

1. A theorem such as `List.map_wfParam` recognizes a call of `[List.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map)` on a function parameter (or subterm), and uses `[List.attach](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___attach)` to enrich the type of the list elements with the assertion that they are indeed elements of that list:

   ```lean
   List.map_wfParam (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (f : α → β) :
   ([wfParam]](#manual-wfParam) xs).[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) f = xs.[attach](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___attach).[unattach](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___unattach).[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) f
   ```
2. A theorem such as `List.map_unattach` makes that assertion available to the function parameter of `[List.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map)`.

   ```lean
   List.map_unattach (P : α → Prop)
   (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) { x : α // P x }) (f : α → β) :
   xs.[unattach](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___unattach).[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) f = xs.[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) fun ⟨x, h⟩ =>
   [binderNameHint](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Naming-Bound-Variables/#binderNameHint) x f <|
   [binderNameHint](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Naming-Bound-Variables/#binderNameHint) h () <|
   f ([wfParam]](#manual-wfParam) x)
   ```

   This theorem uses the `[binderNameHint](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Naming-Bound-Variables/#binderNameHint)` gadget to preserve a user-chosen binder name, should `f` be a lambda expression.

By separating the introduction of `[List.attach](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___attach)` from the propagation of the introduced assumption, the desired the `x ∈ xs` assumption is made available to `f` even in chains such as `(xs.reverse.filter p).map f`.

This preprocessing can be disabled by setting the option `wf.preprocess` to `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.
To see the preprocessed function definition, before and after the removal of `[wfParam]](#manual-wfParam)` markers, set the option `[trace.Elab.definition.wf]](#manual-trace___Elab___definition___wf)` to `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.

option

```lean
trace.Elab.definition.wf
```

Default value: `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

enable/disable tracing for the given module and submodules

**Example: Preprocessing for a custom data type**

This example demonstrates what is necessary to enable automatic well-founded recursion for a custom container type.
The structure type `[Pair]](#manual-Pair-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)` is a homogeneous pair: it contains precisely two elements, both of which have the same type.
It can be thought of as being similar to a list or array that always contains precisely two elements.

As a container, `[Pair]](#manual-Pair-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)` can support a `[map]](#manual-Pair___map-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)` operation.
To support well-founded recursion in which recursive calls occur in the body of a function being mapped over a `[Pair]](#manual-Pair-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)`, some additional definitions are required, including a membership predicate, a theorem that relates the size of a member to the size of the containing pair, helpers to introduce and eliminate assumptions about membership, `wf_preprocess` rules to insert these helpers, and an extension to the `[decreasing_trivial]](#manual-decreasing_trivial)` tactic.
Each of these steps makes it easier to work with `[Pair]](#manual-Pair-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)`, but none are strictly necessary; there's no need to immediately implement all steps for every type.

```lean
/-- A homogeneous pair -/
structure Pair (α : Type u) where
fst : α
snd : α
/-- Mapping a function over the elements of a pair -/
def Pair.map (f : α → β) (p : [Pair]](#manual-Pair-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) α) : [Pair]](#manual-Pair-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) β where
[fst]](#manual-Pair___fst-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) := f p.[fst]](#manual-Pair___fst-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)
[snd]](#manual-Pair___snd-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) := f p.[snd]](#manual-Pair___snd-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)
```

Defining a nested inductive data type of binary trees that uses `[Pair]](#manual-Pair-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)` and attempting to define its `map` function demonstrates the need for preprocessing rules.

```lean
/-- A binary tree defined using `Pair` -/
inductive Tree (α : Type u) where
| leaf : α → [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) α
| node : [Pair]](#manual-Pair-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) ([Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) α) → [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) α
```

A straightforward definition of the `map` function fails:

```lean
def Tree.map (f : α → β) : [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) α → [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) β
| [leaf]](#manual-Tree___leaf-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) x => [leaf]](#manual-Tree___leaf-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) (f x)
| [node]](#manual-Tree___node-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) p => [node]](#manual-Tree___node-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) (p.[map]](#manual-Pair___map-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) (fun t' => t'.map f))
termination_by t => t
```

```lean
failed to prove termination, possible solutions:
  - Use `have`-expressions to prove the remaining goals
  - Use `termination_by` to specify a different well-founded relation
  - Use `decreasing_by` to specify your own tactic for discharging this kind of goal
α:Type u_1p:[Pair]](#manual-Pair-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) ([Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) α)t':[Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) α⊢ [sizeOf]](#manual-SizeOf___mk) t' [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) 1 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) [sizeOf]](#manual-SizeOf___mk) p
```

Clearly the proof obligation is not solvable, because nothing connects `t'` to `p`.

The standard idiom to enable this kind of function definition is to have a function that enriches each element of a collection with a proof that they are, in fact, elements of the collection.
Stating this property requires a membership predicate.

```lean
inductive Pair.Mem (p : [Pair]](#manual-Pair-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) α) : α → Prop where
| fst : [Mem]](#manual-Pair___Mem-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) p p.[fst]](#manual-Pair___fst-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)
| snd : [Mem]](#manual-Pair___Mem-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) p p.[snd]](#manual-Pair___snd-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)
instance : Membership α ([Pair]](#manual-Pair-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) α) where
mem := [Pair.Mem]](#manual-Pair___Mem-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)
```

Every inductive type automatically has a `[SizeOf]](#manual-SizeOf___mk)` instance.
An element of a collection should be smaller than the collection, but this fact must be proved before it can be used to construct a termination proof:

The next step is to define `[attach]](#manual-Pair___attach-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)` and `[unattach]](#manual-Pair___unattach-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)` functions that enrich the elements of the pair with a proof that they are elements of the pair, or remove said proof.
Here, the type of `[Pair.unattach]](#manual-Pair___unattach-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)` is more general and can be used with any [subtype](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Subtypes/#Subtype); this is a typical pattern.

```lean
def Pair.attach (p : [Pair]](#manual-Pair-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) α) : [Pair]](#manual-Pair-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) {x : α // x ∈ p} where
[fst]](#manual-Pair___fst-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) := ⟨p.[fst]](#manual-Pair___fst-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_), [.fst]](#manual-Pair___Mem___fst-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)⟩
[snd]](#manual-Pair___snd-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_) := ⟨p.[snd]](#manual-Pair___snd-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_), [.snd]](#manual-Pair___Mem___snd-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)⟩
def Pair.unattach {P : α → Prop} :
```

This transformation can be made fully automatic.
The preprocessing feature of well-founded recursion can be used to automate the introduction of the `[Pair.attach]](#manual-Pair___attach-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)` function.
This is done in two stages.
First, when `[Pair.map]](#manual-Pair___map-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)` is applied to one of the function's parameters, it is rewritten to an `[attach]](#manual-Pair___attach-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)`/`[unattach]](#manual-Pair___unattach-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)` composition.
Then, when a function is mapped over the result of `[Pair.unattach]](#manual-Pair___unattach-_LPAR_in-Preprocessing-for-a-custom-data-type_RPAR_)`, the function is rewritten to accept the proof of membership and bring it into scope.


To keep the example short, the `sizeOf_pair_dec` tactic is tailored to this particular recursion pattern and isn't really general enough for a general-purpose container library.
It does, however, demonstrate that libraries can be just as convenient in practice as the container types in the standard library.

#### 7.6.3.7. Theory and Construction {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Definitions--Recursive-Definitions--Well-Founded-Recursion--Theory-and-Construction}

This section gives a very brief glimpse into the mathematical constructions that underlie termination proofs via [well-founded recursion]](#manual---tech-term-well-founded-recursion), which may surface occasionally.
The elaboration of functions defined by well-founded recursion is based on the `[WellFounded.fix]](#manual-WellFounded___fix)` operator.

def

```lean
[WellFounded.fix.{u, v}]](#manual-WellFounded___fix) {α : Sort u} {C : α → Sort v} {r : α → α → Prop}
  (hwf : [WellFounded]](#manual-WellFounded___intro) r) (F : (x : α) → ((y : α) → r y x → C y) → C x)
  (x : α) : C x



[WellFounded.fix.{u, v}]](#manual-WellFounded___fix) {α : Sort u}
  {C : α → Sort v} {r : α → α → Prop}
  (hwf : [WellFounded]](#manual-WellFounded___intro) r)
  (F :
    (x : α) →
      ((y : α) → r y x → C y) → C x)
  (x : α) : C x
```

A well-founded fixpoint. If satisfying the motive `C` for all values that are smaller according to a
well-founded relation allows it to be satisfied for the current value, then it is satisfied for all
values.

This function is used as part of the elaboration of well-founded recursion.

The type `α` is instantiated with the function's (varying) parameters, packed into one type using `[PSigma](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#PSigma___mk)`.
The `[WellFounded]](#manual-WellFounded___intro)` relation is constructed from the termination [measure]](#manual---tech-term-measure) via `[invImage]](#manual-invImage)`.

def

```lean
[invImage.{u_1, u_2}]](#manual-invImage) {α : Sort u_1} {β : Sort u_2} (f : α → β)
  (h : [WellFoundedRelation]](#manual-WellFoundedRelation___mk) β) : [WellFoundedRelation]](#manual-WellFoundedRelation___mk) α



[invImage.{u_1, u_2}]](#manual-invImage) {α : Sort u_1}
  {β : Sort u_2} (f : α → β)
  (h : [WellFoundedRelation]](#manual-WellFoundedRelation___mk) β) :
  [WellFoundedRelation]](#manual-WellFoundedRelation___mk) α
```

The inverse image of a well-founded relation is well-founded.

The function's body is passed to `[WellFounded.fix]](#manual-WellFounded___fix)`, with parameters suitably packed and unpacked, and recursive calls are replaced with a call to the value provided by `[WellFounded.fix]](#manual-WellFounded___fix)`.
The termination proofs generated by the `decreasing_by` tactics are inserted in the right place.

Finally, the equational and unfolding theorems for the recursive function are proved from `WellFounded.fix_eq`.
These theorems hide the details of packing and unpacking arguments and describe the function's behavior in terms of the original definition.

In the case of mutual recursion, an equivalent non-mutual function is constructed by combining the function's arguments using `[PSum](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#PSum___inl)`, and pattern-matching on that sum type in the result type and the body.

The definition of `[WellFounded]](#manual-WellFounded___intro)` builds on the notion of *accessible elements* of the relation:

inductive predicate

```lean
[WellFounded.{u}]](#manual-WellFounded___intro) {α : Sort u} (r : α → α → Prop) : Prop



[WellFounded.{u}]](#manual-WellFounded___intro) {α : Sort u}
  (r : α → α → Prop) : Prop
```

A relation `r` is `[WellFounded]](#manual-WellFounded___intro)` if all elements of `α` are accessible within `r`.
If a relation is `[WellFounded]](#manual-WellFounded___intro)`, it does not allow for an infinite descent along the relation.

If the arguments of the recursive calls in a function definition decrease according to
a well founded relation, then the function terminates.
Well-founded relations are sometimes called *Artinian* or said to satisfy the “descending chain condition”.

Constructors

```lean
[WellFounded.intro.{u}]](#manual-WellFounded___intro) {α : Sort u} {r : α → α → Prop}
  (h : ∀ (a : α), [Acc]](#manual-Acc___intro) r a) : [WellFounded]](#manual-WellFounded___intro) r
```

If all elements are accessible via `r`, then `r` is well-founded.

inductive predicate

```lean
[Acc.{u}]](#manual-Acc___intro) {α : Sort u} (r : α → α → Prop) : α → Prop



[Acc.{u}]](#manual-Acc___intro) {α : Sort u} (r : α → α → Prop) :
  α → Prop
```

`[Acc]](#manual-Acc___intro)` is the accessibility predicate. Given some relation `r` (e.g. `<`) and a value `x`,
`[Acc]](#manual-Acc___intro) r x` means that `x` is accessible through `r`:

`x` is accessible if there exists no infinite sequence `... < y₂ < y₁ < y₀ < x`.

Constructors

```lean
[Acc.intro.{u}]](#manual-Acc___intro) {α : Sort u} {r : α → α → Prop} (x : α)
  (h : ∀ (y : α), r y x → [Acc]](#manual-Acc___intro) r y) : [Acc]](#manual-Acc___intro) r x
```

A value is accessible if for all `y` such that `r y x`, `y` is also accessible.
Note that if there exists no `y` such that `r y x`, then `x` is accessible. Such an `x` is called a
*base case*.

**Example: Division by Iterated Subtraction: Termination Proof**

The definition of division by iterated subtraction can be written explicitly using well-founded recursion.

```lean
noncomputable def div (n k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
([inferInstance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance) : [WellFoundedRelation]](#manual-WellFoundedRelation___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)).[wf]](#manual-WellFoundedRelation___mk).[fix]](#manual-WellFounded___fix)
(fun n r =>
```

The definition must be marked `noncomputable` because well-founded recursion is not supported by the compiler.
Like [recursors]](#manual---tech-term-recursor), it is part of Lean's logic.

The definition of division should satisfy the following equations:

- `∀{n k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)}, (k = 0) → [div]](#manual-div-_LPAR_in-Division-by-Iterated-Subtraction___-Termination-Proof_RPAR_) n k = 0`
- `∀{n k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)}, (k > n) → [div]](#manual-div-_LPAR_in-Division-by-Iterated-Subtraction___-Termination-Proof_RPAR_) n k = 0`
- `∀{n k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)}, (k ≠ 0) → (¬ k > n) → [div]](#manual-div-_LPAR_in-Division-by-Iterated-Subtraction___-Termination-Proof_RPAR_) n k = 1 + [div]](#manual-div-_LPAR_in-Division-by-Iterated-Subtraction___-Termination-Proof_RPAR_) (n - k) k`

This reduction behavior does not hold [definitionally]](#manual---tech-term-definitional-equality):

```lean
theorem div.eq0 : [div]](#manual-div-_LPAR_in-Division-by-Iterated-Subtraction___-Termination-Proof_RPAR_) n 0 = 0 := byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [div]](#manual-div-_LPAR_in-Division-by-Iterated-Subtraction___-Termination-Proof_RPAR_) n 0 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rfl)n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [div]](#manual-div-_LPAR_in-Division-by-Iterated-Subtraction___-Termination-Proof_RPAR_) n 0 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0
```

```lean

is not definitionally equal to the right-hand side
  0

n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [div]](#manual-div-_LPAR_in-Division-by-Iterated-Subtraction___-Termination-Proof_RPAR_) n 0 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0
```
