### 7.6.4. Partial Fixpoint Recursion {#manual-partial-fixpoint}

All definitions are fundamentally equations: the new constant being defined is equal to the right-hand side of the definition.
For functions defined by [structural recursion]](#manual-structural-recursion), this equation holds [definitionally]](#manual---tech-term-definitional-equality), and there is a unique value returned by application of the function.
For functions defined by [well-founded recursion]](#manual-well-founded-recursion), the equation may hold only [propositionally]](#manual---tech-term-Propositions), but all type-correct applications of the function to arguments are equal to the respective values prescribed by the definition.
In both cases, the fact that the function terminates for all inputs means that the value computed by applying the function is always uniquely determined.

In some cases where a function does not terminate for all arguments, the equation may not *uniquely* determine the function's return value for each input, but there are nonetheless functions for which the defining equation holds.
In these cases, a definition as a *partial fixpoint* may still be possible.
Any function that satisfies the defining equation can be used to demonstrate that the equation does not create a logical contradiction, and the equation can then be proven as a theorem about this function.
As with the other strategies for defining recursive functions, compiled code uses the function as it was originally written; like definitions in terms of eliminators or recursion over accessibility proofs, the function used to define the partial fixpoint is used only to justify the function's equations in Lean's logic for purposes of mathematical reasoning.

The term [*partial fixpoint*]](#manual---tech-term-partial-fixpoint) is specific to Lean.
Functions declared `partial` do not require termination proofs, so long as the type of their return values is inhabited, but they are completely opaque from the perspective of Lean's logic.
Partial fixpoints, on the other hand, can be rewritten using their defining equations while writing proofs.
Logically speaking, partial fixpoints are total functions that don't reduce [definitionally]](#manual---tech-term-definitional-equality) when applied, but for which equational rewrite rule are provided.
They are *partial* in the sense that the defining equation does not necessarily specify a value for all possible arguments.

While partial fixpoints do allow functions to be defined that cannot be expressed using structural or well-founded recursion, the technique is also useful in other cases.
Even in cases where the defining equation fully describes the function's behavior and a termination proof using [well-founded recursion]](#manual-well-founded-recursion) would be possible, it may simply be more convenient to define the function as a partial fixpoint to avoid a having to write a termination proof.

Defining recursive functions as partial fixpoints only occurs when explicitly requested by annotating the definition with `partial_fixpoint`.

There are two classes of functions that can be defined as partial fixpoints:

- Tail-recursive functions whose return type is inhabited type
- Functions that return values in a suitable monad, such as the `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` monad

Both classes are backed by the same theory and construction: least fixpoints of monotone equations in chain-complete partial orders.

Just as with structural and well-founded recursion, Lean allows [mutually recursive]](#manual---tech-term-mutually-recursive) functions to be defined as partial fixpoints.
To use this feature, every function definition in a [mutual block]](#manual---tech-term-mutual-block) must be annotated with the `partial_fixpoint` modifier.

**Example: Definition by Partial Fixpoint**

The following function finds the least natural number for which the predicate `p` holds.
If `p` never holds, then this equation does not specify the behavior: the function `[find]](#manual-find-_LPAR_in-Definition-by-Partial-Fixpoint_RPAR_)` could return `42` or any other `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` in that case and still satisfy the equation.

```lean
def find (p : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) (i : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := 0) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) p i [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
i
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[find]](#manual-find-_LPAR_in-Definition-by-Partial-Fixpoint_RPAR_) p (i + 1)
partial_fixpoint
```

The elaborator can prove that functions satisfying the equation exist.
Within Lean's logic, `[find]](#manual-find-_LPAR_in-Definition-by-Partial-Fixpoint_RPAR_)` is defined to be an arbitrary such function.

#### 7.6.4.1. Tail-Recursive Functions {#manual-partial-fixpoint-tailrec}

A recursive function can be defined as a partial fixpoint if the following two conditions hold:

1. The function's return type is inhabited (as with [functions marked `partial`]](#manual-partial-unsafe))—either a `[Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro)` or `[Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk)` instance works.
2. All recursive calls are in [tail position]](#manual---tech-term-tail-position) of the function.

An expression is in *tail position* in the function body if it is:

- the function body itself,
- the branches of a [`match`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) expression that is in tail position,
- the branches of an [`if`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) expression that is in tail position, and
- the body of a `let` expression that is in tail position.

In particular, the [discriminant](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#--tech-term-match-discriminants) of a [`match`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) expression, the condition of an [`if`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) expression and the arguments of functions are not tail positions.

**Example: Loops are Tail Recursive Functions**

Because the function body itself is a [tail position]](#manual---tech-term-tail-position), the infinitely looping function `[loop]](#manual-loop-_LPAR_in-Loops-are-Tail-Recursive-Functions_RPAR_)` is tail recursive.
It can be defined as a partial fixpoint.

```lean
def loop (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [loop]](#manual-loop-_LPAR_in-Loops-are-Tail-Recursive-Functions_RPAR_) (x + 1)
partial_fixpoint
```

**Example: Tail Recursion with Branching**

`[Array.find]](#manual-Array___find-_LPAR_in-Tail-Recursion-with-Branching_RPAR_)` could also be constructed using well-founded recursion with a termination proof, but may be more convenient to define using `partial_fixpoint`, where no termination proof is needed.

```lean
def Array.find (xs : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α) (p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false))
(i : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := 0) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : i < xs.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) p xs[i] [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) xs[i]
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[Array.find]](#manual-Array___find-_LPAR_in-Tail-Recursion-with-Branching_RPAR_) xs p (i + 1)
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
partial_fixpoint
```

If the result of the recursive call is not just returned, but passed to another function, it is not in tail position and this definition fails.

```lean
def List.findIndex (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [] => -1
| x::ys =>
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) p x [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
0
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
have r := [List.findIndex]](#manual-List___findIndex-_LPAR_in-Tail-Recursion-with-Branching_RPAR_) ys p
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) r = -1 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) -1 [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) r + 1
partial_fixpoint
```

The error message on the recursive call is:

```lean
Could not prove 'List.findIndex' to be monotone in its recursive calls:
  Cannot eliminate recursive call `List.findIndex ys p` enclosed in
    if ys✝.[findIndex]](#manual-List___findIndex-_LPAR_in-Tail-Recursion-with-Branching_RPAR_) p [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) -1 then -1 else ys✝.[findIndex]](#manual-List___findIndex-_LPAR_in-Tail-Recursion-with-Branching_RPAR_) p [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1
  Tried to apply 'monotone_ite', but failed.
  Possible cause: A missing `MonoBind` instance.
  Use `set_option trace.Elab.Tactic.monotonicity true` to debug.
```

#### 7.6.4.2. Monadic functions {#manual-partial-fixpoint-monadic}

Defining a function as a partial fixpoint is more powerful if the function's return type is a monad that is an instance of `Lean.Order.MonoBind`, such as `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`.
In this case, recursive call are not restricted to tail-positions, but may also occur inside higher-order monadic functions such as `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)` and `[List.mapM](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___mapM)`.

The set of higher-order functions for which this works is [extensible]](#manual-partial-fixpoint-theory), so no exhaustive list is given here.
The aspiration is that a monadic recursive function definition that is built using abstract monadic operations like `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)`, but that does not open the abstraction of the monad (e.g. by matching on the `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` value), is accepted.
In particular, using [[`do`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)-notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#--tech-term-do-notation) should work.

**Example: Monadic functions**

The following function implements the Ackermann function in the `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` monad, and is accepted without an (explicit or implicit) termination proof:

```lean
def ack : (n m : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0, y => [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (y+1)
| x+1, 0 => [ack]](#manual-ack-_LPAR_in-Monadic-functions_RPAR_) x 1
| x+1, y+1 => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do) [ack]](#manual-ack-_LPAR_in-Monadic-functions_RPAR_) x (← [ack]](#manual-ack-_LPAR_in-Monadic-functions_RPAR_) (x+1) y)
partial_fixpoint
```

Recursive calls may also occur within higher-order functions such as `[List.mapM](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___mapM)`, if they are set up appropriately, and [[`do`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)-notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#--tech-term-do-notation):

```lean
structure Tree where cs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Monadic-functions_RPAR_)
def Tree.rev (t : [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Monadic-functions_RPAR_)) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Monadic-functions_RPAR_) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
Tree.mk (← t.[cs]](#manual-Tree___cs-_LPAR_in-Monadic-functions_RPAR_).[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse).[mapM](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___mapM) ([Tree.rev]](#manual-Tree___rev-_LPAR_in-Monadic-functions_RPAR_) ·))
partial_fixpoint
def Tree.rev' (t : [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Monadic-functions_RPAR_)) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Monadic-functions_RPAR_) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut cs := []
for c in t.[cs]](#manual-Tree___cs-_LPAR_in-Monadic-functions_RPAR_) do
cs := (← c.[rev']](#manual-Tree___rev___-_LPAR_in-Monadic-functions_RPAR_)) :: cs
return Tree.mk cs
partial_fixpoint
```

Pattern matching on the result of the recursive call will prevent the definition by partial fixpoint from going through:

```lean
def List.findIndex (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [] => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| x::ys =>
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) p x [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) 0
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) List.findIndex ys p [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) r => [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (r + 1)
partial_fixpoint
```

```lean
Could not prove 'List.findIndex' to be monotone in its recursive calls:
  Cannot eliminate recursive call `List.findIndex ys p` enclosed in
    match ys✝.findIndex p with
    | [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
    | [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) r => [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)r [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
  
```

In this particular case, using `[Functor.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` instead of explicit pattern matching helps:

```lean
def List.findIndex (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [] => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| x::ys =>
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) p x [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) 0
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
(· + 1) <$> List.findIndex ys p
partial_fixpoint
```

#### 7.6.4.3. Partial Correctness Theorems {#manual-partial-correctness-theorem}

For every function defined as a partial fixpoint, Lean proves that the defining equation is satisfied.
This enables proofs by rewriting.
However, these equational theorems are not sufficient for reasoning about the behavior of the function on arguments for which the function specification does not terminate.
Code paths that lead to infinite recursion at runtime would end up as infinite chains of rewrites in a potential proof.

Partial fixpoints in suitable monads, on the other hand, provide additional theorems that map the undefined values from non-termination to suitable values in the monad.
In the `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` monad, then partial fixpoint equals `[Option.none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` on all function inputs for which the defining equation specifies non-termination.
From this fact, Lean proves a *partial correctness theorem* for the function which allows facts to be concluded when the function's result is `[Option.some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`.

**Example: Partial Correctness Theorem**

Recall `[List.findIndex]](#manual-List___findIndex-_LPAR_in-Partial-Correctness-Theorem_RPAR_)` from an earlier example:

```lean
def List.findIndex (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [] => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| x::ys =>
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) p x [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) 0
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
(· + 1) <$> [List.findIndex]](#manual-List___findIndex-_LPAR_in-Partial-Correctness-Theorem_RPAR_) ys p
partial_fixpoint
```

With this function definition, Lean automatically proves the following partial correctness theorem:

```lean
List.findIndex.partial_correctness.{u_1} {α : Type u_1}
(p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false))
(motive : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prop)
(h :
∀ (findIndex : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)),
(∀ (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (r : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)), findIndex xs = [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) r → motive xs r) →
∀ (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (r : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)),
([match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [] => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| x :: ys =>
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) p x = [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) 0
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) (fun x => x + 1) <$> findIndex ys) = [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) r →
motive xs r)
(xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (r : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :
xs.[findIndex]](#manual-List___findIndex-_LPAR_in-Partial-Correctness-Theorem_RPAR_) p = [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) r →
motive xs r
```

Here, the motive is a relation between the parameter and return types of `[List.findIndex]](#manual-List___findIndex-_LPAR_in-Partial-Correctness-Theorem_RPAR_)`, with the `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` removed from the return type.
If, when given an arbitrary partial function with a signature that's compatible with `[List.findIndex]](#manual-List___findIndex-_LPAR_in-Partial-Correctness-Theorem_RPAR_)`, the following hold:

- the motive is satisfied for all inputs for which the arbitrary function returns a value (rather than `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`),
- taking one rewriting step with the defining equation, in which the recursive calls are replaced by the arbitrary function, also implies the satisfaction of the motive

then the motive is satisfied for all inputs for which the `[List.findIndex]](#manual-List___findIndex-_LPAR_in-Partial-Correctness-Theorem_RPAR_)` returns `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`.

The partial correctness theorem is a reasoning principle.
It can be used to prove that the resulting number is a valid index in the list and that the predicate holds for that index:

#### 7.6.4.4. Mutual Recursion with Partial Fixpoints {#manual-mutual-partial-fixpoint}

Lean supports the definition of [mutually recursive]](#manual---tech-term-mutually-recursive) functions using [partial fixpoint]](#manual---tech-term-partial-fixpoint).
Mutual recursion may be introduced using a [mutual block]](#manual---tech-term-mutual-block), but it also results from `let rec` expressions and `where` blocks.
The rules for mutual recursion with partial fixpoints are applied to a group of actually mutually recursive, lifted definitions, that results from the [elaboration steps]](#manual-mutual-syntax) for mutual groups.

If all functions in the mutual group have the `partial_fixpoint` clause, then this strategy is used.

#### 7.6.4.5. Theory and Construction {#manual-partial-fixpoint-theory}

The construction builds on a variant of the Knaster–Tarski theorem: In a chain-complete partial order, every monotone function has a least fixed point.

The necessary theory is found in the `Lean.Order` namespace.
This is not meant to be a general purpose library of order theoretic results.
Instead, the definitions and theorems in `Lean.Order` are only intended as implementation details of the `partial_fixpoint` feature, and they should be considered a private API that may change without notice.

The notion of a partial order, and that of a chain-complete partial order, are represented by the type classes `[Lean.Order.PartialOrder]](#manual-Lean___Order___PartialOrder___mk)` and `[Lean.Order.CCPO]](#manual-Lean___Order___CCPO___mk)`, respectively.

type class

```lean
  Sort (max 1 u)
```

A function is monotone if it preserves partial orders.
That is, if `x ⊑ y` then `f x ⊑ f y`.
The operator `⊑` represent `[Lean.Order.PartialOrder.rel]](#manual-Lean___Order___PartialOrder___mk)`.

```lean

  [[PartialOrder]](#manual-Lean___Order___PartialOrder___mk) β] (f : α → β) : Prop



[Lean.Order.monotone.{u, v}]](#manual-Lean___Order___monotone) {α : Sort u}
  [[PartialOrder]](#manual-Lean___Order___PartialOrder___mk) α] {β : Sort v}
  [[PartialOrder]](#manual-Lean___Order___PartialOrder___mk) β] (f : α → β) : Prop
```

A function is monotone if it maps related elements to related elements.

This is intended to be used in the construction of `partial_fixpoint`, and not meant to be used otherwise.

The fixpoint of a monotone function can be taken using `[fix]](#manual-Lean___Order___fix)`, which indeed constructs a fixpoint, as shown by `[fix_eq]](#manual-Lean___Order___fix_eq)`,

def

```lean
[Lean.Order.fix.{u}]](#manual-Lean___Order___fix) {α : Sort u} [[CCPO]](#manual-Lean___Order___CCPO___mk) α] (f : α → α)
  (hmono : [monotone]](#manual-Lean___Order___monotone) f) : α



[Lean.Order.fix.{u}]](#manual-Lean___Order___fix) {α : Sort u} [[CCPO]](#manual-Lean___Order___CCPO___mk) α]
  (f : α → α) (hmono : [monotone]](#manual-Lean___Order___monotone) f) : α
```

The least fixpoint of a monotone function is the least upper bound of its transfinite iteration.

The `[monotone]](#manual-Lean___Order___monotone) f` assumption is not strictly necessarily for the definition, but without this the
definition is not very meaningful and it simplifies applying theorems like `[fix_eq]](#manual-Lean___Order___fix_eq)` if every use of
`[fix]](#manual-Lean___Order___fix)` already has the monotonicity requirement.

This is intended to be used in the construction of `partial_fixpoint`, and not meant to be used otherwise.

theorem

```lean
[Lean.Order.fix_eq.{u}]](#manual-Lean___Order___fix_eq) {α : Sort u} [[CCPO]](#manual-Lean___Order___CCPO___mk) α] {f : α → α}
  (hf : [monotone]](#manual-Lean___Order___monotone) f) : [fix]](#manual-Lean___Order___fix) f hf [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f ([fix]](#manual-Lean___Order___fix) f hf)



[Lean.Order.fix_eq.{u}]](#manual-Lean___Order___fix_eq) {α : Sort u}
  [[CCPO]](#manual-Lean___Order___CCPO___mk) α] {f : α → α} (hf : [monotone]](#manual-Lean___Order___monotone) f) :
  [fix]](#manual-Lean___Order___fix) f hf [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f ([fix]](#manual-Lean___Order___fix) f hf)
```

The main fixpoint theorem for fixed points of monotone functions in chain-complete partial orders.

This is intended to be used in the construction of `partial_fixpoint`, and not meant to be used otherwise.

To construct the partial fixpoint, Lean first synthesizes a suitable `[CCPO]](#manual-Lean___Order___CCPO___mk)` instance.

- If the function's result type has a dedicated instance, like `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` has with `instCCPOOption`, this is used together with the instance for the function type, `instCCPOPi`, to construct an instance for the whole function's type.
- Otherwise, if the function's type can be shown to be inhabited by a witness `w`, then the instance `FlatOrder.instCCPO` for the wrapper type `FlatOrder w` is used. In this order, `w` is a least element and all other elements are incomparable.

Next, the recursive calls in the right-hand side of the function definitions are abstracted; this turns into the argument `f` of `[fix]](#manual-Lean___Order___fix)`. The monotonicity requirement is solved by the `monotonicity` tactic, which applies compositional monotonicity lemmas in a syntax-driven way.

The tactic solves goals of the form `[monotone]](#manual-Lean___Order___monotone) (fun x => … x …)` using the following steps:

- Applying `monotone_const` when there is no dependency on `x` left.
- Splitting on [`match`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) expressions.
- Splitting on [`if`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) expressions.
- Moving `let` expression to the context, if the value and type do not depend on `x`.
- Zeta-reducing a `let` expression when value and type do depend on `x`.
- Applying lemmas annotated with `partial_fixpoint_monotone`

The following monotonicity lemmas are registered, and should allow recursive calls under the given higher-order functions in the arguments indicated by `·` (but not the other arguments, shown as `_`).

The order-theoretic framework described here also underpins [coinductive and inductive predicates]](#manual-coinductive-predicates).
For `Prop`-valued functions, the `[Lean.Order.CompleteLattice]](#manual-Lean___Order___CompleteLattice___mk)` instance provides both least and greatest fixpoints, enabling definitions with `inductive_fixpoint` and `coinductive_fixpoint` clauses.

### 7.6.5. Coinductive and Inductive Predicates {#manual-coinductive-predicates}

Lean's type theory does not support coinductive types directly.
However, coinductive predicates, that is, recursive definitions valued in `Prop`, can be defined using the complete lattice structure on propositions.
These predicates provide a coinductive reasoning principle, where something can be shown to satisfy a predicate by showing that it satisfies some smaller predicate that is itself consistent with the definition of the coinductive predicate.
This is the dual of inductive reasoning, in which a known fact can be decomposed via a potentially recursive case analysis.
Coinductive predicates allow infinite domains to be specified and reasoned about.
Some examples from computer science include:

- bisimilarity of state transition systems that admit cycles
- divergence of small-step operational semantics
- liveness properties

Dually, inductive predicates can also be defined via least fixpoints using the same machinery.
Because it uses the same underlying mechanisms, this alternative to ordinary [inductive types]](#manual---tech-term-Inductive-types) is compatible with mixed inductive-coinductive mutual blocks.

**Example: Infinite Sequences**

Given a relation `R` on `α` (that is, with type `α → α → Prop`), there is an infinite sequence of values in `α` starting at `x` if:

- there exists some `y` such that `R x y`, and
- there exists an infinite sequence from `y`.

This is a quintessential coinductive predicate: it describes a potentially infinite behavior that can be presented as a single inference rule with no base cases.

This recursive specification is well-defined, but it cannot be defined as an ordinary recursive function because the recursive part of the definition does not decrease.
However, it is a perfectly sensible coinductive definition:

```lean
coinductive InfSeq (R : α → α → Prop) : α → Prop where
| step (y : α) : R x y → [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_) R y → [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_) R x
```

The coinductive reasoning principle takes a predicate `pred`.
To prove that `a` is the start of an infinite `R`-sequence, it suffices to show that `R` relates each element that satisfies `pred` to some other such element.
In other words, it that the presence of an infinite sequence can be demonstrated by providing one:

```lean
InfSeq.coinduct (R : α → α → Prop) (pred : α → Prop) :
(∀ (a : α), pred a → ∃ y, R a y ∧ pred y) →
∀ (a : α), pred a → [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_) R a
```

There are two ways to define coinductive predicates in Lean:

1. Using the `coinductive_fixpoint` termination clause on a recursive `def` valued in `Prop`, which takes the greatest fixpoint. Equivalently, the `inductive_fixpoint` clause defines inductive predicates as least fixpoints.
2. Using the `coinductive` command, which provides a declarative syntax mirroring `inductive` declarations.

#### 7.6.5.1. Fixpoint Termination Clauses {#manual-fixpoint-clauses}

A recursive `Prop`-valued function can be defined as a fixpoint by annotating it with `coinductive_fixpoint` for coinductive definitions (greatest fixpoint) or `inductive_fixpoint` for inductive definitions (least fixpoint).
These termination clauses play the same role as `partial_fixpoint` but use the [complete lattice structure on `Prop`]](#manual-lattice-prop) to compute the appropriate fixpoint.

##### 7.6.5.1.1. Coinductive Fixpoint {#manual-coinductive-fixpoint-clause}

The `coinductive_fixpoint` clause defines a predicate as the greatest fixpoint of its defining equation.
The function must be monotone with respect to `Lean.Order.ReverseImplicationOrder`, in which `P ⊑ Q` means `Q → P`.

This ordering is extended pointwise over the predicate's domain.
Given predicates `P` and `Q` over `α`, `P ⊑ Q` means `∀ x : α, P x ⊑ Q x` (that is, `∀ x, Q x → P x`).

**Example: Monotonicity of Infinite Sequences**

The proposition `[InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Monotonicity-of-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_) R a` is true when there exists an infinite chain of `R`-related elements starting from `a`.
This can be written using `coinductive_fixpoint`:

```lean
def InfSeq (R : α → α → Prop) (a : α) : Prop :=
∃ b, R a b ∧ [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Monotonicity-of-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_) R b
coinductive_fixpoint
```

During elaboration, the first step is to abstract this recursive definition over the recursive calls, yielding a definition equivalent to `[F]](#manual-F-_LPAR_in-Monotonicity-of-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_)`:

```lean
def F (R : α → α → Prop) (a : α) (P : α → Prop) : Prop :=
∃ b, R a b ∧ P b
```

For this function to be monotone with respect to reverse implication, it must preserve the reverse implication ordering between `P` and `Q`.
That is, `∀ (x : α), Q x → P x` must imply `∀ (x : α), [F]](#manual-F-_LPAR_in-Monotonicity-of-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_) R x Q → [F]](#manual-F-_LPAR_in-Monotonicity-of-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_) R x P`:

```lean
theorem F_monotone
(h : ∀ (x : α), Q x → P x) :
∀ (x : α), [F]](#manual-F-_LPAR_in-Monotonicity-of-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_) R x Q → [F]](#manual-F-_LPAR_in-Monotonicity-of-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_) R x P := byα:Sort u_1R:α → α → PropQ:α → PropP:α → Proph:∀ (x : α), Q x → P x⊢ ∀ (x : α), [F]](#manual-F-_LPAR_in-Monotonicity-of-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_) R x Q → [F]](#manual-F-_LPAR_in-Monotonicity-of-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_) R x P
```

**Example: Failure of Monotonicity**

An element is accessible in a relation if there is no infinite chain leading to the element.
This property is inductively defined as `[Acc]](#manual-Acc___intro)` in the standard library.
This attempt to define it coinductively fails:

```lean
def NoInfChain (R : α → α → Prop) (x : α) : Prop :=
∀ y, R x y → ¬[NoInfChain]](#manual-NoInfChain-_LPAR_in-Failure-of-Monotonicity_RPAR_) R y
coinductive_fixpoint
```

```lean
Could not prove 'NoInfChain' to be monotone in its recursive calls:
  Cannot eliminate recursive call in
    [NoInfChain]](#manual-NoInfChain-_LPAR_in-Failure-of-Monotonicity_RPAR_) R y✝
  
```

The corresponding function is:

```lean
def F (R : α → α → Prop) (x : α) (P : α → Prop) : Prop :=
∀ y, R x y → ¬P y
```

**Example: Non-Predicates**

An infinite conjunction of some proposition can be defined as a coinductive fixpoint:

```lean
def InfConj (p : Prop) : Prop := p ∧ [InfConj]](#manual-InfConj-_LPAR_in-Non-Predicates_RPAR_) p
coinductive_fixpoint
```

This cannot be used to define an infinite product, however:

```lean
def InfProd (α : Type) : Prop := α × [InfProd]](#manual-InfProd-_LPAR_in-Non-Predicates_RPAR_) α
coinductive_fixpoint
```

The error message indicates that a proposition was expected:

```lean
Application type mismatch: The argument
  InfProd α
has type
  Prop
of sort `Type` but is expected to have type
  Type ?u.3
of sort `Type (?u.3 + 1)` in the application
  α [×](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) InfProd α
```

Just as with definitions via partial fixpoints, the coinductive predicate's defining equations do not hold definitionally.
However, the elaborator proves equational lemmas that allow the predicate to be rewritten to its unfolding.

**Example: Definitional Equality and Coinductive Predicates**

```lean
coinductive_fixpoint
```

In addition to equational lemmas, Lean generates a coinduction principle.
The coinduction principle states that the coinductive predicate can be proved by exhibiting some other predicate that is a post-fixpoint of the monotone function.

**Example: Coinduction Principles for Infinite Sequences**

`[InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinduction-Principles-for-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_)` is the coinductive statement that an relation starts an infinite chain:

```lean
def InfSeq (R : α → α → Prop) (a : α) : Prop :=
∃ b, R a b ∧ [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinduction-Principles-for-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_) R b
coinductive_fixpoint
```

The corresponding monotone function is:

```lean
def F (R : α → α → Prop) (a : α) (P : α → Prop) : Prop :=
∃ b, R a b ∧ P b
```

Because `[InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinduction-Principles-for-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_)` is the *greatest* fixpoint of `[F]](#manual-F-_LPAR_in-Coinduction-Principles-for-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_)`, the existence of *any* predicate that is less than its image in `[F]](#manual-F-_LPAR_in-Coinduction-Principles-for-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_)` suffices to show that every element that satisfies the predicate also satisfies `[InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinduction-Principles-for-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_)`.
In other words, to prove `[InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinduction-Principles-for-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_) R a`, it suffices to demonstrate a predicate `P` such that `∀ (a : α), P a → [F]](#manual-F-_LPAR_in-Coinduction-Principles-for-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_) R a P`, or `∀ (a : α), P a → ∃ b, R a b ∧ P b`, and then show `P a`.

This coinduction principle is named `InfSeq.coinduct`:

```lean
InfSeq.coinduct {α} (R : α → α → Prop) (pred : α → Prop) :
(∀ (a : α), pred a → ∃ b, R a b ∧ pred b) →
∀ (a : α), pred a → [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinduction-Principles-for-Infinite-Sequences_RPAR_) R a
```

**Example: Simple Proof by Coinduction**

`[InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Simple-Proof-by-Coinduction_RPAR_)` states that there is an infinite sequence of elements in a relation, with a given starting point:

```lean

∃ b, R a b ∧ [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Simple-Proof-by-Coinduction_RPAR_) R b
coinductive_fixpoint
```

**Example: DFA Language Equivalence**

Coinductive predicates naturally capture bisimulation-like notions.

A deterministic finite automaton is given by a set of states `Q`, an alphabet `A`, a start state `q` in `Q`, a subset of `Q` that defines accepting states, and a transition function that takes a state and an element of the alphabet to a new state:

```lean
structure DFA (Q : Type) (A : Type) : Type where
q₀ : Q
δ : Q → A → Q
accepting : Q → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

Two automata over the same alphabet have equivalent languages from a given pair of states when they agree as to whether these states are accepting and they furthermore have equivalent languages from all successor states according to their transition functions:

```lean
def languageEquivalent (M : [DFA]](#manual-DFA-_LPAR_in-DFA-Language-Equivalence_RPAR_) Q A) (M' : [DFA]](#manual-DFA-_LPAR_in-DFA-Language-Equivalence_RPAR_) Q' A)
(q : Q) (q' : Q') : Prop :=
M.[accepting]](#manual-DFA___accepting-_LPAR_in-DFA-Language-Equivalence_RPAR_) q = M'.[accepting]](#manual-DFA___accepting-_LPAR_in-DFA-Language-Equivalence_RPAR_) q' ∧
∀ (a : A), [languageEquivalent]](#manual-languageEquivalent-_LPAR_in-DFA-Language-Equivalence_RPAR_) M M' (M.[δ]](#manual-DFA______-_LPAR_in-DFA-Language-Equivalence_RPAR_) q a) (M'.[δ]](#manual-DFA______-_LPAR_in-DFA-Language-Equivalence_RPAR_) q' a)
coinductive_fixpoint
```

The coinduction principle captures the standard notion of bisimulation of deterministic automata:

```lean
languageEquivalent.coinduct {Q A Q' : Type}
(M : [DFA]](#manual-DFA-_LPAR_in-DFA-Language-Equivalence_RPAR_) Q A) (M' : [DFA]](#manual-DFA-_LPAR_in-DFA-Language-Equivalence_RPAR_) Q' A) (pred : Q → Q' → Prop) :
(∀ (q : Q) (q' : Q'), pred q q' →
M.[accepting]](#manual-DFA___accepting-_LPAR_in-DFA-Language-Equivalence_RPAR_) q = M'.[accepting]](#manual-DFA___accepting-_LPAR_in-DFA-Language-Equivalence_RPAR_) q' ∧
∀ (a : A), pred (M.[δ]](#manual-DFA______-_LPAR_in-DFA-Language-Equivalence_RPAR_) q a) (M'.[δ]](#manual-DFA______-_LPAR_in-DFA-Language-Equivalence_RPAR_) q' a)) →
∀ (q : Q) (q' : Q'), pred q q' →
[languageEquivalent]](#manual-languageEquivalent-_LPAR_in-DFA-Language-Equivalence_RPAR_) M M' q q'
```

##### 7.6.5.1.2. Inductive Fixpoint {#manual-inductive-fixpoint-clause}

The `inductive_fixpoint` clause defines a predicate as the least fixpoint of its defining equation.
The function must be monotone with respect to `Lean.Order.ImplicationOrder`, the order on `Prop` where `P ⊑ Q` means `P → Q`.
This provides an alternative to ordinary `inductive` type declarations for predicates, and is the dual of `coinductive_fixpoint`.

In most cases, an ordinary inductive type declaration is more convenient.
However, inductive fixpoint definitions have two key advantages over ordinary inductive type declarations that make them more suitable for certain specialized use cases:

- Ordinary inductive type declarations have a *syntactic* positivity condition, where recursive occurrences of the inductive type cannot occur in negative positions. Inductive fixpoints instead require monotonicity, which is a *semantic* condition.
- Inductive fixpoints can be defined mutually with coinductive fixpoints, allowing mixed inductive-codinductive predicates.

For each inductive fixpoint definition, an induction principle is automatically proven.
This induction principle has the same logical strength as the corresponding induction principle that would be generated for an inductive type declaration, but it is formulated somewhat differently and must be explicitly applied.

Just as with coinductive fixpoints, inductive fixpoint definitions do not definitionally reduce.
They can be unfolded using their generated equational lemmas, and their induction principles allow them to be used in proofs.

**Example: Reflexive Transitive Closures as Inductive Fixpoints**

The reflexive transitive closure of a relation can be defined as an inductive predicate:

```lean
inductive Star (R : α → α → Prop) : α → α → Prop where
| refl : ∀ x : α, [Star]](#manual-Star-_LPAR_in-Reflexive-Transitive-Closures-as-Inductive-Fixpoints_RPAR_) R x x
| step : ∀ x y z, R x y → [Star]](#manual-Star-_LPAR_in-Reflexive-Transitive-Closures-as-Inductive-Fixpoints_RPAR_) R y z → [Star]](#manual-Star-_LPAR_in-Reflexive-Transitive-Closures-as-Inductive-Fixpoints_RPAR_) R x z
```

The same predicate can be defined as a least fixpoint.

```lean
def StarInd (tr : α → α → Prop) (q₁ q₂ : α) : Prop :=
q₁ = q₂ ∨ ∃ (z : α), (tr q₁ z ∧ [StarInd]](#manual-StarInd-_LPAR_in-Reflexive-Transitive-Closures-as-Inductive-Fixpoints_RPAR_) tr z q₂)
inductive_fixpoint
```

An induction principle is generated:

```lean
StarInd.induct (tr : α → α → Prop) (q₂ : α) (pred : α → Prop)
(hyp : ∀ (q₁ : α), (q₁ = q₂ ∨ ∃ z, tr q₁ z ∧ pred z) → pred q₁)
(q₁ : α) :
[StarInd]](#manual-StarInd-_LPAR_in-Reflexive-Transitive-Closures-as-Inductive-Fixpoints_RPAR_) tr q₁ q₂ → pred q₁
```

The induction principle can be used to prove that the two formulations are equivalent:

##### 7.6.5.1.3. Mixed Inductive-Coinductive Predicates in Mutual Blocks {#manual-mixed-mutual-fixpoint}

A [mutual block]](#manual---tech-term-mutual-block) can mix `coinductive_fixpoint` and `inductive_fixpoint` clauses.
Every definition in the block must use one of these two clauses.
The construction uses two [lattice structures on `Prop`]](#manual-lattice-prop): `ImplicationOrder` for inductive definitions and `ReverseImplicationOrder` for coinductive definitions.
In both cases, the least fixpoint of the corresponding lattice is computed; using the reverse implication order, the least fixpoint coincides with the greatest fixpoint in the standard order.
This is possible because [monotonicity]](#manual-coinductive-monotonicity) lemmas flip between the two orders when negation or implication is encountered.

**Example: Mixed Inductive-Coinductive Mutual Block**

This mutual block contains mutually-recursive coinductive and inductive predicates:

```lean
[mutual]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
def tick : Prop :=
¬[tock]](#manual-tock-_LPAR_in-Mixed-Inductive-Coinductive-Mutual-Block_RPAR_)
coinductive_fixpoint
def tock : Prop :=
¬[tick]](#manual-tick-_LPAR_in-Mixed-Inductive-Coinductive-Mutual-Block_RPAR_)
inductive_fixpoint
[end]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

A mutual induction principle is generated for the first definition in the mutual block:

```lean
tick.mutual_induct (pred_1 pred_2 : Prop) :
(pred_1 → pred_2 → [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)) → ((pred_1 → [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)) → pred_2) →
(pred_1 → [tick]](#manual-tick-_LPAR_in-Mixed-Inductive-Coinductive-Mutual-Block_RPAR_)) ∧ ([tock]](#manual-tock-_LPAR_in-Mixed-Inductive-Coinductive-Mutual-Block_RPAR_) → pred_2)
```

#### 7.6.5.2. Further Examples {#manual-coinductive-predicate-examples}

**Example: Infinite Chains from Universal Reachability**

The reflexive transitive closure of a relation is specified inductively:

```lean
inductive Star (R : α → α → Prop) : α → α → Prop where
| refl : ∀ x : α, [Star]](#manual-Star-_LPAR_in-Infinite-Chains-from-Universal-Reachability_RPAR_) R x x
| step : ∀ x y z, R x y → [Star]](#manual-Star-_LPAR_in-Infinite-Chains-from-Universal-Reachability_RPAR_) R y z → [Star]](#manual-Star-_LPAR_in-Infinite-Chains-from-Universal-Reachability_RPAR_) R x z
```

Infinite sequences are specified coinductively:

```lean
def InfSeq (R : α → α → Prop) (a : α) : Prop :=
∃ b, R a b ∧ [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Infinite-Chains-from-Universal-Reachability_RPAR_) R b
coinductive_fixpoint
```

If every state reachable from a starting state `a` via the reflexive transitive closure has a successor, then there is an infinite chain from `a`.
The predicate `[AllSeqInf]](#manual-AllSeqInf-_LPAR_in-Infinite-Chains-from-Universal-Reachability_RPAR_)` states that every reachable state has a successor:

```lean
def AllSeqInf (R : α → α → Prop) (x : α) : Prop :=
∀ y : α, [Star]](#manual-Star-_LPAR_in-Infinite-Chains-from-Universal-Reachability_RPAR_) R x y → ∃ z, R y z
```

Proving that this implies that there is an infinite chain is done via coinduction:

```lean

∀ x, [AllSeqInf]](#manual-AllSeqInf-_LPAR_in-Infinite-Chains-from-Universal-Reachability_RPAR_) R x → [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Infinite-Chains-from-Universal-Reachability_RPAR_) R x := byα:Sort u_1R:α → α → Prop⊢ ∀ (x : α), [AllSeqInf]](#manual-AllSeqInf-_LPAR_in-Infinite-Chains-from-Universal-Reachability_RPAR_) R x → [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Infinite-Chains-from-Universal-Reachability_RPAR_) R x
```

**Example: Coinduction Up-To Transitive Closure**

A strengthened coinduction principle allows the coinduction hypothesis to be applied up to transitive closure.
Given a predicate `X` such that every `X`-state leads via one-or-more `R`-steps to another `X`-state, then every `X`-state satisfies `[InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinduction-Up-To-Transitive-Closure_RPAR_) R`:

```lean
inductive Star (R : α → α → Prop) : α → α → Prop where
| refl : ∀ x : α, [Star]](#manual-Star-_LPAR_in-Coinduction-Up-To-Transitive-Closure_RPAR_) R x x
| step : ∀ x y z, R x y → [Star]](#manual-Star-_LPAR_in-Coinduction-Up-To-Transitive-Closure_RPAR_) R y z → [Star]](#manual-Star-_LPAR_in-Coinduction-Up-To-Transitive-Closure_RPAR_) R x z
```

```lean
def InfSeq (R : α → α → Prop) (a : α) : Prop :=
∃ b, R a b ∧ [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinduction-Up-To-Transitive-Closure_RPAR_) R b
coinductive_fixpoint
```

#### 7.6.5.3. The `coinductive` Command {#manual-coinductive-command}

The `coinductive` command provides a syntax for defining [coinductive predicates]](#manual---tech-term-coinductive-predicates) that mirrors the syntax of `inductive` declarations.
Rather than writing a recursive function with `coinductive_fixpoint`, the declaration is written in terms of constructors, just as it would be for an inductive type.

syntaxCoinductive Predicates

```lean
command ::= ...
    | coinductive declId (ident | [hole](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Holes/#Lean___Parser___Term___hole) | bracketedBinder)* : term where
        ctor*
```

The `coinductive` command defines a coinductive predicate by specifying its constructors.
It can only be used to define predicates, that is, types valued in `Prop`.

The `coinductive` command defines the same predicate as the corresponding `coinductive_fixpoint` definition.
It additionally generates constructors and a case analysis principle, much like an ordinary `inductive` declaration.

**Example: Coinductive Predicate via coinductive**

The predicate `[InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinductive-Predicate-via--coinductive_RPAR_)` from prior examples can equivalently be defined using the `coinductive` command:

```lean
[variable]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (α : Type)
coinductive InfSeq (r : α → α → Prop) : α → Prop where
| step : r a b → [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinductive-Predicate-via--coinductive_RPAR_) r b → [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinductive-Predicate-via--coinductive_RPAR_) r a
```

This generates a constructor and a [coinduction principle]](#manual---tech-term-coinduction-principle):

```lean
[InfSeq.step]](#manual-InfSeq___step-_LPAR_in-Coinductive-Predicate-via--coinductive_RPAR_) (α : Type) (r : α → α → Prop) {a b : α} :
r a b → [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinductive-Predicate-via--coinductive_RPAR_) α r b → [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinductive-Predicate-via--coinductive_RPAR_) α r a
```

```lean
InfSeq.coinduct (α : Type) (r : α → α → Prop) (pred : α → Prop) :
(∀ (a : α), pred a → ∃ b, r a b ∧ pred b) →
∀ (a : α), pred a → [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinductive-Predicate-via--coinductive_RPAR_) α r a
```

A case analysis principle is also generated:

```lean
InfSeq.casesOn (α : Type) (r : α → α → Prop)
{motive : (a : α) → [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinductive-Predicate-via--coinductive_RPAR_) α r a → Prop} {a : α} (t : [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinductive-Predicate-via--coinductive_RPAR_) α r a) :
(∀ {a b} (a_1 : r a b) (a_2 : [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinductive-Predicate-via--coinductive_RPAR_) α r b),
motive a ([InfSeq.step]](#manual-InfSeq___step-_LPAR_in-Coinductive-Predicate-via--coinductive_RPAR_) α r a_1 a_2)) →
motive a t
```

Case analysis can be used in proofs via the `[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases)` tactic:

```lean
theorem InfSeq.casesOnTest (r : α → α → Prop)
(a : α) : [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinductive-Predicate-via--coinductive_RPAR_) α r a → ∃ b, r a b := byα:Typer:α → α → Propa:α⊢ [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinductive-Predicate-via--coinductive_RPAR_) α r a → [∃](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) b[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) r a b
[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro) hα:Typer:α → α → Propa:αh:[InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinductive-Predicate-via--coinductive_RPAR_) α r a⊢ [∃](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) b[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) r a b
[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases) hstepα:Typer:α → α → Propa:αb✝:αa✝¹:[InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinductive-Predicate-via--coinductive_RPAR_) α r b✝a✝:r a b✝⊢ [∃](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) b[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) r a b
[case](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case) step b _ hr =>α:Typer:α → α → Propa:αb:αa✝:[InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Coinductive-Predicate-via--coinductive_RPAR_) α r b✝hr:r a b✝⊢ [∃](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) b[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) r a b [exists](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exists) bAll goals completed! 🐙
```

##### 7.6.5.3.1. Elaboration {#manual-coinductive-elaboration}

Under the hood, the `coinductive` command is elaborated in several steps.
First, it is processed as if it were an ordinary `inductive` declaration.
Before registering the types with the kernel, however, a *flat inductive* (also called a *functor*) is created: each recursive occurrence of the coinductive predicate in the premises of a constructor is replaced by an explicit parameter.

**Example: Flat Inductive**

This example uses the coinductive specification of infinite sequences:

```lean
coinductive InfSeq (r : α → α → Prop) : α → Prop where
| step : r a b → [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Flat-Inductive_RPAR_) r b → [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Flat-Inductive_RPAR_) r a
```

For `[InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Flat-Inductive_RPAR_)`, the generated flat inductive is:

```lean
InfSeq._functor : (α : Type) → (α → α → Prop) → (α → Prop) → α → Prop
```

Its constructor takes the predicate parameter in place of recursive calls:

```lean
set_option [pp.proofs](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Reading-Proof-States/#pp___proofs) true [in]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in)
#print InfSeq._functor
```

```lean
inductive InfSeq._functor : (α : Type) → (α → α → Prop) → (α → Prop) → α → Prop
number of parameters: 3
constructors:
InfSeq._functor.step : ∀ (α : Type) (r : α → α → Prop) (InfSeq._functor.call : α → Prop) {a b : α},
  r a b → InfSeq._functor.call b → InfSeq._functor α r InfSeq._functor.call a
```

An equivalent *existential form* is then constructed, expressing each constructor as a disjunction of dependent products (that is, existential quantifiers and conjunctions).
This form is used for monotonicity checking and for generating readable coinduction principles.

**Example: Existential Form**

```lean
coinductive InfSeq (r : α → α → Prop) : α → Prop where
| step : r a b → [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Existential-Form_RPAR_) r b → [InfSeq]](#manual-InfSeq-_LPAR_in-Existential-Form_RPAR_) r a
```

```lean
set_option [pp.proofs](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Reading-Proof-States/#pp___proofs) true [in]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in)
#print InfSeq._functor.existential
```

```lean
def InfSeq._functor.existential : (α : Type) → (α → α → Prop) → (α → Prop) → α → Prop :=
fun α r InfSeq._functor.call a => [∃](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) b[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) r a b [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) InfSeq._functor.call b
```

The two forms are connected by an equivalence theorem:

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) @InfSeq._functor.existential_equiv
```

```lean
InfSeq._functor.existential_equiv : ∀ (α : Type) (r : α → α → Prop) (InfSeq._functor.call : α → Prop) (a : α),
  InfSeq._functor α r InfSeq._functor.call a [↔](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Iff___intro) [∃](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) b[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) r a b [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) InfSeq._functor.call b
```

The existential form is then registered as a coinductive predicate using the [partial fixpoint]](#manual-partial-fixpoint) machinery with the `Lean.Order.ReverseImplicationOrder` complete lattice instance.
Using the correspondence between the flat inductive and the existential form, constructors and a case analysis eliminator are generated, just as for regular inductive types.

The following declarations are generated for a coinductive predicate named `P`:

- `P._functor`: the [flat inductive]](#manual---tech-term-flat-inductive)
- `P._functor.existential`: the [existential form]](#manual---tech-term-existential-form)
- `P._functor.existential_equiv`: equivalence between the two forms
- `P.functor_unfold`: theorem connecting the coinductive predicate to its flat inductive
- Constructors (e.g., `P.step`): corresponding to each constructor in the declaration
- `P.casesOn`: case analysis principle
- `P.coinduct`: [coinduction principle]](#manual---tech-term-coinduction-principle)

##### 7.6.5.3.2. Mutual Coinductive and Inductive Blocks {#manual-mutual-coinductive-syntax}

In a [mutual block]](#manual---tech-term-mutual-block) containing `coinductive` definitions, the `inductive` keyword is reinterpreted: instead of being registered as an ordinary kernel inductive type, it is elaborated via the lattice-theoretic [inductive fixpoint]](#manual---tech-term-inductive-predicates) machinery.
This allows mixing coinductive and inductive predicates in the same mutual block.

**Example: Mutual Coinductive-Inductive Block**

The predicates `[Tick]](#manual-Tick-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Coinductive-Inductive-Block_RPAR_)` and `[Tock]](#manual-Tock-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Coinductive-Inductive-Block_RPAR_)` are defined mutually, with `[Tick]](#manual-Tick-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Coinductive-Inductive-Block_RPAR_)` as a coinductive predicate and `[Tock]](#manual-Tock-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Coinductive-Inductive-Block_RPAR_)` as an inductive predicate:

```lean
[mutual]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
coinductive Tick : Prop where
| mk : ¬[Tock]](#manual-Tock-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Coinductive-Inductive-Block_RPAR_) → [Tick]](#manual-Tick-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Coinductive-Inductive-Block_RPAR_)
inductive Tock : Prop where
| mk : ¬[Tick]](#manual-Tick-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Coinductive-Inductive-Block_RPAR_) → [Tock]](#manual-Tock-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Coinductive-Inductive-Block_RPAR_)
[end]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

Both constructors are available:

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) @[Tick.mk]](#manual-Tick___mk-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Coinductive-Inductive-Block_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[Tick.mk]](#manual-Tick___mk-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Coinductive-Inductive-Block_RPAR_) : [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)[Tock]](#manual-Tock-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Coinductive-Inductive-Block_RPAR_) → [Tick]](#manual-Tick-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Coinductive-Inductive-Block_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) @[Tock.mk]](#manual-Tock___mk-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Coinductive-Inductive-Block_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[Tock.mk]](#manual-Tock___mk-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Coinductive-Inductive-Block_RPAR_) : [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)[Tick]](#manual-Tick-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Coinductive-Inductive-Block_RPAR_) → [Tock]](#manual-Tock-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Coinductive-Inductive-Block_RPAR_)
```

A mutual induction principle is generated:

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) @Tick.mutual_induct
```

```lean
Tick.mutual_induct : ∀ (pred_1 pred_2 : Prop),
  (pred_1 → pred_2 → [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)) → ((pred_1 → [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)) → pred_2) → (pred_1 → [Tick]](#manual-Tick-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Coinductive-Inductive-Block_RPAR_)) [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) ([Tock]](#manual-Tock-_LPAR_in-Mutual-Coinductive-Inductive-Block_RPAR_) → pred_2)
```

##### 7.6.5.3.3. Restrictions {#manual-coinductive-restrictions}

The `coinductive` command has the following restrictions:

- It can only define predicates, that is, types valued in `Prop`.
  Attempting to define a coinductive type in `Type` or higher universes results in an error.
- The predicate being defined may not have [macro scopes](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#--tech-term-macro-scopes).
- Pattern matching via [`match`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) is not yet supported; use the `[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases)` tactic instead.

**Example: Restriction to Predicates**

Attempting to define a coinductive type that is not a predicate results in an error:

```lean
coinductive MyNat where
| zero : MyNat
| succ : MyNat → MyNat
```

```lean
`coinductive` keyword can only be used to define predicates
```

#### 7.6.5.4. Theory and Construction {#manual-coinductive-theory}

The construction of coinductive and inductive predicates builds on the Knaster-Tarski fixpoint theorem for complete lattices.
While [partial fixpoint recursion]](#manual-partial-fixpoint-theory) relies on chain-complete partial orders (`[Lean.Order.CCPO]](#manual-Lean___Order___CCPO___mk)`), coinductive and inductive predicates use the stronger notion of a *complete lattice*.

The key idea is that `Prop` carries a [complete lattice]](#manual-complete-lattices) structure ordered by implication (`P ⊑ Q` when `P → Q`), and any monotone endofunction on a complete lattice has both a least and a greatest fixpoint by the Knaster-Tarski theorem.
Coinductive predicates use the [reverse implication order]](#manual-lattice-prop) (`P ⊑ Q` when `Q → P`), so that the least fixpoint in this reversed order is the greatest fixpoint in the standard order.
For predicates of the form `α → Prop`, the pointwise lifting of this lattice structure to function types provides the necessary setting.
For mutual blocks, the product of complete lattices is again a complete lattice.
This construction shares its internals with the [partial fixpoint]](#manual-partial-fixpoint) machinery.

##### 7.6.5.4.1. Complete Lattices {#manual-complete-lattices}

A [complete lattice]](#manual---tech-term-complete-lattice) is a partial order where every subset has a least upper bound, not just every chain.

type class

```lean
[Lean.Order.CompleteLattice.{u}]](#manual-Lean___Order___CompleteLattice___mk) (α : Sort u) : Sort (max 1 u)



[Lean.Order.CompleteLattice.{u}]](#manual-Lean___Order___CompleteLattice___mk)
  (α : Sort u) : Sort (max 1 u)
```




```lean
rel_trans : ∀ {x y z : α}, x [⊑]](#manual-Lean___Order___PartialOrder___mk) y → y [⊑]](#manual-Lean___Order___PartialOrder___mk) z → x [⊑]](#manual-Lean___Order___PartialOrder___mk) z
```

The least upper bound of an arbitrary subset exists.

Every complete lattice gives rise to a CCPO, since every chain is in particular a subset, but the converse does not hold in general.
For instance, the flat order on an inhabited type (used by [partial fixpoints]](#manual-partial-fixpoint) for tail-recursive functions) is a CCPO but not a complete lattice.

In a complete lattice, the least fixpoint of a monotone function can be constructed directly as the infimum of all pre-fixpoints, following the Knaster-Tarski theorem:

def

```lean
[Lean.Order.lfp.{u}]](#manual-Lean___Order___lfp) {α : Sort u} [[CompleteLattice]](#manual-Lean___Order___CompleteLattice___mk) α] (f : α → α) : α

  [[CompleteLattice]](#manual-Lean___Order___CompleteLattice___mk) α] (f : α → α) : α
```

```lean
  [[CompleteLattice]](#manual-Lean___Order___CompleteLattice___mk) α] {f : α → α}
  (hm : [monotone]](#manual-Lean___Order___monotone) f) : [lfp]](#manual-Lean___Order___lfp) f [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f ([lfp]](#manual-Lean___Order___lfp) f)
```

The corresponding induction principle is Park induction: to show that a property holds for all elements of the least fixpoint, it suffices to show that the property is preserved by one application of the defining function.

```lean
[Lean.Order.lfp_le_of_le_monotone.{u}]](#manual-Lean___Order___lfp_le_of_le_monotone) {α : Sort u} [[CompleteLattice]](#manual-Lean___Order___CompleteLattice___mk) α]
  (f : α → α) {hm : [monotone]](#manual-Lean___Order___monotone) f} (x : α) :
  f x [⊑]](#manual-Lean___Order___PartialOrder___mk) x → lfp_monotone f hm [⊑]](#manual-Lean___Order___PartialOrder___mk) x



[Lean.Order.lfp_le_of_le_monotone.{u}]](#manual-Lean___Order___lfp_le_of_le_monotone)
  {α : Sort u} [[CompleteLattice]](#manual-Lean___Order___CompleteLattice___mk) α]
```
