Takes an explicit witness of `f` being monotone.

##### 7.6.5.4.2. Lattice Structure on Propositions {#manual-lattice-prop}

The type `Prop` admits two natural complete lattice structures, each giving rise to a different kind of fixpoint:

- `Lean.Order.ImplicationOrder` orders propositions by implication: `P ⊑ Q` means `P → Q`.
  The least fixpoint in this order yields the smallest predicate closed under the defining rules, corresponding to an [*inductive predicate*]](#manual---tech-term-inductive-predicates).
  This is the order used by `inductive_fixpoint`.
- `Lean.Order.ReverseImplicationOrder` orders propositions by reverse implication: `P ⊑ Q` means `Q → P`.
  The least fixpoint in this *reversed* order is the *greatest* fixpoint in the standard order, yielding the largest predicate consistent with the defining rules.
  This corresponds to a [*coinductive predicate*]](#manual---tech-term-coinductive-predicates).
  This is the order used by `coinductive_fixpoint`.

Arrow types into a complete lattice inherit a complete lattice structure, and products of complete lattices are complete lattices.
These closure properties allow the construction to be extended to predicates of arbitrary arity and to mutual blocks.

##### 7.6.5.4.3. Monotonicity {#manual-coinductive-monotonicity}

Defining a predicate as a fixpoint requires the defining equation to be monotone with respect to the appropriate order.
For both the `coinductive` command and the `coinductive_fixpoint` and `inductive_fixpoint` termination clauses, the monotonicity requirement is semantic rather than syntactic.
The `monotonicity` tactic proves monotonicity by composing lemmas registered with the `partial_fixpoint_monotone` attribute.
This approach is more permissive than strict positivity.
For example, negation and implication are handled correctly by flipping the order between `Lean.Order.ImplicationOrder` and `Lean.Order.ReverseImplicationOrder`.
This is what allows mixing inductive and coinductive fixpoints in the same [mutual block]](#manual---tech-term-mutual-block).

The set of constructs handled by the `monotonicity` tactic is extensible: registering additional `partial_fixpoint_monotone` lemmas teaches the tactic to handle new logical connectives or higher-order functions.
Alternatively, an explicit monotonicity proof term can be provided when using `coinductive_fixpoint` via a `monotonicity` clause.

See the [theory section of partial fixpoints]](#manual-partial-fixpoint-theory) for the full list of registered monotonicity lemmas and for more detail on the monotonicity tactic.

### 7.6.6. Partial and Unsafe Definitions {#manual-partial-unsafe}

While most Lean functions can be reasoned about in Lean's type theory as well as compiled and run, definitions marked `partial` or `unsafe` cannot be meaningfully reasoned about.
From the perspective of the logic, `partial` functions are opaque constants, and theorems that refer to `unsafe` definitions are summarily rejected.
In exchange for the inability to use these functions for reasoning, there are far fewer requirements placed on them; this can make it possible to write programs that would be impractical or cost-prohibitive to prove anything about, while not giving up formal reasoning for the rest.
In essence, the `partial` subset of Lean is a traditional functional programming language that is nonetheless deeply integrated with the theorem proving features, and the `unsafe` subset features the ability to break Lean's runtime invariants in certain rare situations, at the cost of less integration with Lean's theorem-proving features.
Analogously, `noncomputable` definitions may use features that don't make sense in programs, but are meaningful in the logic.

#### 7.6.6.1. Partial Functions {#manual-partial-functions}

The `partial` modifier may only be applied to function definitions.
Partial functions are not required to demonstrate termination, and Lean does not attempt to do so.
These functions are “partial” in the sense that they do not necessarily specify a mapping from each element of the domain to an element of the codomain, because they might fail to terminate for some or all elements of the domain.
They are elaborated into [pre-definitions]](#manual---tech-term-pre-definition) that contain explicit recursion, and type checked using the kernel; however, they are subsequently treated as opaque constants by the logic.

The function's return type must be inhabited; this ensures soundness.
Otherwise, a partial function could have a type such as `[Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) → [Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty)`.
Together with `[Empty.elim](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty___elim)`, the existence of such a function could be used to prove `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)` even if it does not reduce.

With partial definitions, the kernel is responsible for the following:

- It ensures that the pre-definition's type is indeed a well-formed type.
- It checks that the pre-definition's type is a function type.
- It ensures that the function's codomain is inhabited by demanding a `[Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro)` or `[Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk)` instance.
- It checks that the resulting term would be type-correct if Lean had recursive definitions.

Even though recursive definitions are not part of the kernel's type theory, the kernel can still be used to check that the body of the definition has the right type.
This works the same way as in other functional languages: uses of recursion are type checked by checking the body in an environment in which the definition is already associated with its type.
Having ensured that it type checks, the body is discarded and only the opaque constant is retained by the kernel.
As with all Lean functions, the compiler generates code from the elaborated [pre-definition]](#manual---tech-term-pre-definition).

Even though partial functions are not unfolded by the kernel, it is still possible to reason about other functions that call them so long as this reasoning doesn't depend on the implementation of the partial function itself.

**Example: Partial Functions in Proofs**

The recursive function `[nextPrime]](#manual-nextPrime-_LPAR_in-Partial-Functions-in-Proofs_RPAR_)` inefficiently computes the next prime number after a given number by repeatedly testing candidates with trial division.
Because there are infinitely many prime numbers, it always terminates; however, formulating this proof would be nontrivial.
It is thus marked `partial`.

```lean
def isPrime (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) := [Id.run](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id___run) [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
for i in [2:n] do
if i * i > n then return [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
if n % i = 0 then return [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
return [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
partial def nextPrime (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
let n := n + 1
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [isPrime]](#manual-isPrime-_LPAR_in-Partial-Functions-in-Proofs_RPAR_) n [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) n [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [nextPrime]](#manual-nextPrime-_LPAR_in-Partial-Functions-in-Proofs_RPAR_) n
```

It is nonetheless possible to prove that the following two functions are equal:

```lean
def answerUser (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
s!"The next prime is {[nextPrime]](#manual-nextPrime-_LPAR_in-Partial-Functions-in-Proofs_RPAR_) n}"
def answerOtherUser (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
" ".[intercalate](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___intercalate) [
"The",
"next",
"prime",
"is",
toString ([nextPrime]](#manual-nextPrime-_LPAR_in-Partial-Functions-in-Proofs_RPAR_) n)
]
```

In fact, the proof is by `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rfl)`:

```lean
theorem answer_eq_other : [answerUser]](#manual-answerUser-_LPAR_in-Partial-Functions-in-Proofs_RPAR_) = [answerOtherUser]](#manual-answerOtherUser-_LPAR_in-Partial-Functions-in-Proofs_RPAR_) := by⊢ [answerUser]](#manual-answerUser-_LPAR_in-Partial-Functions-in-Proofs_RPAR_) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [answerOtherUser]](#manual-answerOtherUser-_LPAR_in-Partial-Functions-in-Proofs_RPAR_)
[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rfl)All goals completed! 🐙
```

#### 7.6.6.2. Unsafe Definitions {#manual-unsafe}

Unsafe definitions have even fewer safeguards than partial functions.
Their codomains do not need to be inhabited, they are not restricted to function definitions, and they have access to features of Lean that might violate internal invariants or break abstractions.
As a result, they cannot be used at all as part of mathematical reasoning.

While partial functions are treated as opaque constants by the type theory, unsafe definitions may only be referenced from other unsafe definitions.
As a consequence, any function that calls an unsafe function must be unsafe itself.
Theorems are not allowed to be declared unsafe.

In addition to unrestricted use of recursion, unsafe functions can cast from one type to another, check whether two values are the very same object in memory, retrieve pointer values, and run `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions from otherwise-pure code.
Using these operators requires a thorough understanding of the Lean implementation.

unsafe def

```lean
[unsafeCast.{u, v}]](#manual-unsafeCast) {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} (a : α) : β



[unsafeCast.{u, v}]](#manual-unsafeCast) {α : Sort u}
  {β : Sort v} (a : α) : β
```

This function will cast a value of type `α` to type `β`, and is a no-op in the
compiler. This function is **extremely dangerous** because there is no guarantee
that types `α` and `β` have the same data representation, and this can lead to
memory unsafety. It is also logically unsound, since you could just cast
`[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)` to `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)`. For all those reasons this function is marked as `unsafe`.

It is implemented by lifting both `α` and `β` into a common universe, and then
using `cast (lcProof : ULift (PLift α) = ULift (PLift β))` to actually perform
the cast. All these operations are no-ops in the compiler.

Using this function correctly requires some knowledge of the data representation
of the source and target types. Some general classes of casts which are safe in
the current runtime:

- `[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α` to `[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) β` where `α` and `β` have compatible representations,
  or more generally for other inductive types.
- `[Quot]](#manual-Quot) α r` and `α`.
- `@[Subtype](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Subtypes/#Subtype___mk) α p` and `α`, or generally any structure containing only one
  non-`Prop` field of type `α`.
- Casting `α` to/from `NonScalar` when `α` is a boxed generic type
  (i.e. a function that accepts an arbitrary type `α` and is not specialized to
  a scalar type like `[UInt8](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt8___ofBitVec)`).

unsafe def

```lean
[ptrEq.{u_1}]](#manual-ptrEq) {α : Type u_1} (a b : α) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)



[ptrEq.{u_1}]](#manual-ptrEq) {α : Type u_1} (a b : α) :
  [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

Compares two objects for pointer equality.

Two objects are pointer-equal if, at runtime, they are allocated at exactly the same address. This
function is unsafe because it can distinguish between definitionally equal values.

unsafe def

```lean
[ptrEqList.{u_1}]](#manual-ptrEqList) {α : Type u_1} (as bs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)



[ptrEqList.{u_1}]](#manual-ptrEqList) {α : Type u_1}
  (as bs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

Compares two lists of objects for element-wise pointer equality. Returns `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` if both lists are
the same length and the objects at the corresponding indices of each list are pointer-equal.

Two objects are pointer-equal if, at runtime, they are allocated at exactly the same address. This
function is unsafe because it can distinguish between definitionally equal values.

unsafe opaque

```lean
[ptrAddrUnsafe.{u}]](#manual-ptrAddrUnsafe) {α : Type u} (a : α) : [USize](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#USize___ofBitVec)



[ptrAddrUnsafe.{u}]](#manual-ptrAddrUnsafe) {α : Type u} (a : α) :
  [USize](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#USize___ofBitVec)
```

Returns the address at which an object is allocated.

This function is unsafe because it can distinguish between definitionally equal values.

unsafe opaque

```lean
[isExclusiveUnsafe.{u}]](#manual-isExclusiveUnsafe) {α : Type u} (a : α) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)



[isExclusiveUnsafe.{u}]](#manual-isExclusiveUnsafe) {α : Type u}
  (a : α) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

Returns `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` if `a` is an exclusive object.

An object is exclusive if it is single-threaded and its reference counter is 1. This function is
unsafe because it can distinguish between definitionally equal values.

unsafe def

```lean
[unsafeIO]](#manual-unsafeIO) {α : Type} (fn : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) α) : [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [IO.Error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#IO___Error___alreadyExists) α



[unsafeIO]](#manual-unsafeIO) {α : Type} (fn : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) α) :
  [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [IO.Error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#IO___Error___alreadyExists) α
```

Executes arbitrary side effects in a pure context, with exceptions indicated via `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`. This a
**dangerous** operation that can easily undermine important assumptions about the meaning of Lean
programs, and it should only be used with great care and a thorough understanding of compiler
internals, and even then only to implement observationally pure operations.

This function is not a good way to convert an `[EIO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#EIO) α` or `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) α` into an `α`. Instead, use
[`do`-notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=do-notation).

Because the resulting value is treated as a side-effect-free term, the compiler may re-order,
duplicate, or delete calls to this function. The side effect may even be hoisted into a constant,
causing the side effect to occur at initialization time, even if it would otherwise never be called.

unsafe def

```lean
[unsafeEIO]](#manual-unsafeEIO) {ε α : Type} (fn : [EIO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#EIO) ε α) : [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) ε α



[unsafeEIO]](#manual-unsafeEIO) {ε α : Type} (fn : [EIO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#EIO) ε α) :
  [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) ε α
```

Executes arbitrary side effects in a pure context, with exceptions indicated via `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`. This a
**dangerous** operation that can easily undermine important assumptions about the meaning of Lean
programs, and it should only be used with great care and a thorough understanding of compiler
internals, and even then only to implement observationally pure operations.

This function is not a good way to convert an `[EIO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#EIO) α` or `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) α` into an `α`. Instead, use
[`do`-notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=do-notation).

Because the resulting value is treated as a side-effect-free term, the compiler may re-order,
duplicate, or delete calls to this function. The side effect may even be hoisted into a constant,
causing the side effect to occur at initialization time, even if it would otherwise never be called.

unsafe def

```lean
[unsafeBaseIO]](#manual-unsafeBaseIO) {α : Type} (fn : [BaseIO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#BaseIO) α) : α



[unsafeBaseIO]](#manual-unsafeBaseIO) {α : Type} (fn : [BaseIO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#BaseIO) α) :
  α
```

Executes arbitrary side effects in a pure context. This a **dangerous** operation that can easily
undermine important assumptions about the meaning of Lean programs, and it should only be used with
great care and a thorough understanding of compiler internals, and even then only to implement
observationally pure operations.

This function is not a good way to convert a `[BaseIO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#BaseIO) α` into an `α`. Instead, use
[`do`-notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=do-notation).

Because the resulting value is treated as a side-effect-free term, the compiler may re-order,
duplicate, or delete calls to this function. The side effect may even be hoisted into a constant,
causing the side effect to occur at initialization time, even if it would otherwise never be called.

Frequently, unsafe operators are used to write fast code that takes advantage of low-level details.
Just as Lean code may be replaced at runtime with C code via the FFI, safe Lean code may be replaced with unsafe Lean code for runtime programs.
This is accomplished by adding the `implemented_by` attribute to the function that is to be replaced, which is often an `opaque` definition.
While this does not threaten Lean's soundness as a logic because the constant to be replaced has already been checked by the kernel and the unsafe replacement is only used in run-time code, it is still risky.
Both C code and unsafe code may execute arbitrary side effects.

attributeReplacing Run-Time Implementations

The `implemented_by` attribute instructs the compiler to replace one constant with another in compiled code.
The replacement constant may be unsafe.

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | implemented_by ident
```

**Example: Checking Equality with Pointers**

Ordinarily, a `[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)` instance's equality predicate must fully traverse both of its arguments to determine whether they are equal.
If they are, in fact, the very same object in memory, this is wasteful indeed.
A pointer equality test can be used prior to the traversal to catch this case.

The type being compared is `[Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Checking-Equality-with-Pointers_RPAR_)`, a type of binary trees.

```lean
inductive Tree α where
| empty
| branch (left : [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Checking-Equality-with-Pointers_RPAR_) α) (val : α) (right : [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Checking-Equality-with-Pointers_RPAR_) α)
```

An unsafe function may use pointer equality to terminate the structural equality test more quickly, falling back to structural checks when pointer equality fails.

```lean
unsafe def Tree.fastBEq [[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) α] (t1 t2 : [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Checking-Equality-with-Pointers_RPAR_) α) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [ptrEq]](#manual-ptrEq) t1 t2 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) t1, t2 [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [.empty]](#manual-Tree___empty-_LPAR_in-Checking-Equality-with-Pointers_RPAR_), [.empty]](#manual-Tree___empty-_LPAR_in-Checking-Equality-with-Pointers_RPAR_) => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [.branch]](#manual-Tree___branch-_LPAR_in-Checking-Equality-with-Pointers_RPAR_) l1 x r1, [.branch]](#manual-Tree___branch-_LPAR_in-Checking-Equality-with-Pointers_RPAR_) l2 y r2 =>
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [ptrEq]](#manual-ptrEq) x y || x == y [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
l1.[fastBEq]](#manual-Tree___fastBEq-_LPAR_in-Checking-Equality-with-Pointers_RPAR_) l2 && r1.[fastBEq]](#manual-Tree___fastBEq-_LPAR_in-Checking-Equality-with-Pointers_RPAR_) r2
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| _, _ => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

An `implemented_by` attribute on an opaque definition bridges the worlds of safe and unsafe code.

```lean
@[implemented_by [Tree.fastBEq]](#manual-Tree___fastBEq-_LPAR_in-Checking-Equality-with-Pointers_RPAR_)]
opaque Tree.beq [[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) α] (t1 t2 : [Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Checking-Equality-with-Pointers_RPAR_) α) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
instance [[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) α] : [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) ([Tree]](#manual-Tree-_LPAR_in-Checking-Equality-with-Pointers_RPAR_) α) where
[beq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) := [Tree.beq]](#manual-Tree___beq-_LPAR_in-Checking-Equality-with-Pointers_RPAR_)
```

**Example: Taking Advantage of Run-Time Representations**

Because a `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)` is represented identically to its underlying `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, `[List.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) [Fin.val](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)` can be replaced by `[unsafeCast]](#manual-unsafeCast)` to avoid a linear-time traversal that, in practice, does nothing:

```lean
unsafe def unFinImpl (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) ([Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[unsafeCast]](#manual-unsafeCast) xs
@[implemented_by [unFinImpl]](#manual-unFinImpl-_LPAR_in-Taking-Advantage-of-Run-Time-Representations_RPAR_)]
def unFin (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) ([Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
xs.[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) [Fin.val](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)
```

From the perspective of the Lean kernel, `[unFin]](#manual-unFin-_LPAR_in-Taking-Advantage-of-Run-Time-Representations_RPAR_)` is defined using `[List.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map)`:

```lean
theorem unFin_length_eq_length {xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) ([Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n)} :
([unFin]](#manual-unFin-_LPAR_in-Taking-Advantage-of-Run-Time-Representations_RPAR_) xs).[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) = xs.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) := byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)xs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) ([Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n)⊢ ([unFin]](#manual-unFin-_LPAR_in-Taking-Advantage-of-Run-Time-Representations_RPAR_) xs).[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) xs.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length)
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [[unFin]](#manual-unFin-_LPAR_in-Taking-Advantage-of-Run-Time-Representations_RPAR_)]All goals completed! 🐙
```

In compiled code, there is no traversal of the list.

This kind of replacement is risky: the correspondence between the proof and the compiled code depends fully on the equivalence of the two implementations, which cannot be proved in Lean.
The correspondence relies on details of Lean's implementation.
These “escape hatches” should be used very carefully.

### 7.6.7. Controlling Reduction {#manual-reducibility}

While checking proofs and programs, Lean takes *reducibility*, also known as *transparency*, into account.
A definition's reducibility controls the contexts in which it is unfolded during elaboration and proof execution.

There are five levels of reducibility:

Irreducible
:   Irreducible definitions are not unfolded at all during elaboration.
    Definitions can be made irreducible by applying the `irreducible` attribute.

Semireducible
:   Semireducible definitions are not unfolded by potentially expensive automation such as type class instance synthesis or `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)`, but they are unfolded while checking definitional equality and while resolving [generalized field notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Function-Application/#--tech-term-generalized-field-notation).
    The `def` command generally creates semireducible definitions unless a different reducibility level is specified with an attribute; however, definitions that use [well-founded recursion]](#manual---tech-term-well-founded-recursion) are irreducible by default.

Implicit reducible
:   Implicit-reducible definitions are unfolded while checking [definitional equality]](#manual---tech-term-definitional-equality) of implicit arguments to functions.
    This includes ordinary [implicit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Functions/#--tech-term-implicit) arguments, [instance implicit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/#--tech-term-instance-implicit) arguments, and [strict implicit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Functions/#--tech-term-Strict-implicit) arguments.
    Definitions that appear in the types of implicit arguments and are intended to reduce should be implicit-reducible.

Instance reducible
:   Instance-reducible definitions are unfolded during type class [instance synthesis](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/#--tech-term-synthesizes).
    All type class instances should be instance-reducible or reducible.
    Instances that are created by the `instance` command are automatically marked instance-reducible.

Reducible
:   Reducible definitions are unfolded essentially everywhere, on demand.
    Type class instance synthesis, definitional equality checks, and the rest of the language treat the definition as being essentially an abbreviation.
    This is the setting applied by the `abbrev` command.

**Example: Reducibility and Instance Synthesis**

These three aliases for `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)` are respectively reducible, semireducible, and irreducible.

```lean
abbrev Phrase := [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
def Clause := [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
@[irreducible]
def Utterance := [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
```

The reducible and semireducible aliases are unfolded during the elaborator's definitional equality check, causing them to be considered equivalent to `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)`:

```lean
def hello : [Phrase]](#manual-Phrase-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Instance-Synthesis_RPAR_) := "Hello"
def goodMorning : [Clause]](#manual-Clause-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Instance-Synthesis_RPAR_) := "Good morning"
```

The irreducible alias, on the other hand, is rejected as the type for a string, because the elaborator's definitional equality test does not unfold it:

```lean
def goodEvening : [Utterance]](#manual-Utterance-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Instance-Synthesis_RPAR_) := "Good evening"
```

```lean
Type mismatch
  "Good evening"
has type
  [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
but is expected to have type
  [Utterance]](#manual-Utterance-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Instance-Synthesis_RPAR_)
```

Because `[Phrase]](#manual-Phrase-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Instance-Synthesis_RPAR_)` is reducible, the `ToString [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)` instance can be used as a `ToString [Phrase]](#manual-Phrase-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Instance-Synthesis_RPAR_)` instance:

```lean
[#synth]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___synth) ToString [Phrase]](#manual-Phrase-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Instance-Synthesis_RPAR_)
```

However, `[Clause]](#manual-Clause-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Instance-Synthesis_RPAR_)` is semireducible, so the `ToString [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)` instance cannot be used:

```lean
[#synth]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___synth) ToString [Clause]](#manual-Clause-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Instance-Synthesis_RPAR_)
```

```lean
failed to synthesize
  ToString [Clause]](#manual-Clause-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Instance-Synthesis_RPAR_)

Hint: Additional diagnostic information may be available using the `set_option diagnostics true` command.
```

The instance can be explicitly enabled by creating a `ToString [Clause]](#manual-Clause-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Instance-Synthesis_RPAR_)` instance that reduces to the `ToString [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)` instance.
This example works because semireducible definitions are unfolded while checking definitional equality:

```lean
instance : ToString [Clause]](#manual-Clause-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Instance-Synthesis_RPAR_) := inferInstanceAs (ToString [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray))
```

**Example: Reducibility and Generalized Field Notation**

[Generalized field notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Function-Application/#--tech-term-generalized-field-notation) unfolds reducible and semireducible declarations while searching for matching names.
Given the semireducible alias `[Sequence]](#manual-Sequence-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Generalized-Field-Notation_RPAR_)` for `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`:

```lean
def Sequence := [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
def Sequence.ofList (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Sequence]](#manual-Sequence-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Generalized-Field-Notation_RPAR_) α := xs
```

generalized field notation allows `[List.reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse)` to be accessed from a term of type `[Sequence]](#manual-Sequence-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Generalized-Field-Notation_RPAR_) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) let xs : [Sequence]](#manual-Sequence-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Generalized-Field-Notation_RPAR_) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [.ofList]](#manual-Sequence___ofList-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Generalized-Field-Notation_RPAR_) [1,2,3]; xs.[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse)
```

However, declaring `[Sequence]](#manual-Sequence-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Generalized-Field-Notation_RPAR_)` to be irreducible prevents the unfolding:

```lean
[attribute](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Command___attribute) [irreducible] [Sequence]](#manual-Sequence-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Generalized-Field-Notation_RPAR_)
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) let xs : [Sequence]](#manual-Sequence-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Generalized-Field-Notation_RPAR_) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [.ofList]](#manual-Sequence___ofList-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Generalized-Field-Notation_RPAR_) [1,2,3]; xs.reverse
```

```lean
Invalid field `reverse`: The environment does not contain `Sequence.reverse`, so it is not possible to project the field `reverse` from an expression
  xs
of type `[Sequence]](#manual-Sequence-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Generalized-Field-Notation_RPAR_) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`
```

attributeReducibility Annotations

A definition's reducibility can be set using one of the five reducibility attributes:

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | reducible
```

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | instance_reducible
```

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | implicit_reducible
```

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | semireducible
```

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | irreducible
```

These attributes can only be applied globally in the same file as the definition being modified, but they may be `local`ly applied anywhere.

#### 7.6.7.1. Reducibility and Tactics {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Definitions--Recursive-Definitions--Controlling-Reduction--Reducibility-and-Tactics}

The tactics `with_reducible`, `with_reducible_and_instances`, and `with_unfolding_all` control which definitions are unfolded by most tactics.

**Example: Reducibility and Tactics**

The functions `[plus]](#manual-plus-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Tactics_RPAR_)`, `[sum]](#manual-sum-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Tactics_RPAR_)`, and `[tally]](#manual-tally-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Tactics_RPAR_)` are all synonyms for `[Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add)` that are respectively reducible, semireducible, and irreducible:

```lean
abbrev plus := [Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add)
def sum := [Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add)
@[irreducible]
def tally := [Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add)
```

The reducible synonym is unfolded by `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)`:

```lean
theorem plus_eq_add : [plus]](#manual-plus-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Tactics_RPAR_) x y = x + y := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [plus]](#manual-plus-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Tactics_RPAR_) x y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y [simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)All goals completed! 🐙
```

The semireducible synonym is not, however, unfolded by `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)`:

```lean
theorem sum_eq_add : [sum]](#manual-sum-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Tactics_RPAR_) x y = x + y := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [sum]](#manual-sum-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Tactics_RPAR_) x y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y [simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)x:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [sum]](#manual-sum-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Tactics_RPAR_) x y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y
```

Nonetheless, the definitional equality check induced by `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rfl)` unfolds the `[sum]](#manual-sum-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Tactics_RPAR_)`:

```lean
theorem sum_eq_add : [sum]](#manual-sum-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Tactics_RPAR_) x y = x + y := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [sum]](#manual-sum-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Tactics_RPAR_) x y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rfl)All goals completed! 🐙
```

The irreducible `[tally]](#manual-tally-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Tactics_RPAR_)`, however, is not reduced by definitional equality.

```lean
theorem tally_eq_add : [tally]](#manual-tally-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Tactics_RPAR_) x y = x + y := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [tally]](#manual-tally-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Tactics_RPAR_) x y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rfl)x:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [tally]](#manual-tally-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Tactics_RPAR_) x y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y
```

The `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` tactic can unfold any definition, even irreducible ones, when they are explicitly provided:

```lean
theorem tally_eq_add : [tally]](#manual-tally-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Tactics_RPAR_) x y = x + y := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [tally]](#manual-tally-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Tactics_RPAR_) x y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y [simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [[tally]](#manual-tally-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Tactics_RPAR_)]All goals completed! 🐙
```

Similarly, part of a proof can be instructed to ignore irreducibility by placing it in a `with_unfolding_all` block:

```lean
theorem tally_eq_add : [tally]](#manual-tally-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Tactics_RPAR_) x y = x + y := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [tally]](#manual-tally-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Tactics_RPAR_) x y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y with_unfolding_all [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rfl)All goals completed! 🐙
```

**Example: Reducibility and Implicit Arguments**

The functions `[plus]](#manual-plus-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_)`, `[sum]](#manual-sum-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_)`, and `[tally]](#manual-tally-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_)` are synonyms for `[Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add)` that are respectively reducible, implicit-reducible, and irreducible:

```lean
abbrev plus := [Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add)
@[instance_reducible]
def sum := [Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add)
def tally := [Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add)
```

An instances of `[Nonzero]](#manual-Nonzero-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_)` contains a proof that the given number is not equal to zero.
The function `[notZero]](#manual-notZero-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_)` extracts this proof from a synthesized instance:

```lean
class Nonzero (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) where
non_zero : n ≠ 0
instance Nonzero.instSucc : [Nonzero]](#manual-Nonzero-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_) (n + 1) where
[non_zero]](#manual-Nonzero___non_zero-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_) := byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 ≠ 0 [grind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#grind)All goals completed! 🐙
def notZero (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) [[Nonzero]](#manual-Nonzero-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_) n] : n ≠ 0 := [Nonzero.non_zero]](#manual-Nonzero___non_zero-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_)
```

The instance is found for the reducible definition `[plus]](#manual-plus-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_)`:

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) [notZero]](#manual-notZero-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_) ([plus]](#manual-plus-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_) 2 2)
```

It is also found for the instance-reducible definition `[sum]](#manual-sum-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_)`.
This is because the type `[Nonzero]](#manual-Nonzero-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_) ([sum]](#manual-sum-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_) 2 2)` is the type of an [instance implicit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/#--tech-term-instance-implicit) parameter to `[notZero]](#manual-notZero-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_)`.
In particular, `[sum]](#manual-sum-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_)` is reduced to `[Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add)` which is itself instance-reducible, so the type is reduced to `[Nonzero]](#manual-Nonzero-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_) 4`:

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) [notZero]](#manual-notZero-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_) ([sum]](#manual-sum-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_) 2 2)
```

Instance synthesis fails for `[tally]](#manual-tally-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_)` because it is not reduced:

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) [notZero]](#manual-notZero-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_) ([tally]](#manual-tally-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_) 2 2)
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [Nonzero]](#manual-Nonzero-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_) ([tally]](#manual-tally-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_) 2 2)

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

In other contexts, such as calls to `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)`, `[plus]](#manual-plus-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_)` is unfolded:

```lean
theorem plus_eq_add : [plus]](#manual-plus-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_) x y = x + y := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [plus]](#manual-plus-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_) x y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y [simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)All goals completed! 🐙
```

The implicit reducible synonym is not, however, unfolded by `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)`:

```lean
theorem sum_eq_add : [sum]](#manual-sum-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_) x y = x + y := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [sum]](#manual-sum-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_) x y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y [simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)x:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [sum]](#manual-sum-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Implicit-Arguments_RPAR_) x y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y
```

```lean
`simp` made no progress
```

#### 7.6.7.2. Modifying Reducibility {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Definitions--Recursive-Definitions--Controlling-Reduction--Modifying-Reducibility}

The reducibility of a definition can be globally modified in the module in which it is defined by applying the appropriate attribute with the [`attribute`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Command___attribute) command.
In other modules, the reducibility of imported definitions can be modified by applying the attribute with the `local` modifier.
The [`seal`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___commandSeal__) and [`unseal`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___commandUnseal__) commands are a shorthand for this process.

syntaxLocal Irreducibility

The `seal foo` command ensures that the definition of `foo` is sealed, meaning it is marked as `[irreducible]`.
This command is particularly useful in contexts where you want to prevent the reduction of `foo` in proofs.

In terms of functionality, `seal foo` is equivalent to `attribute [local irreducible] foo`.
This attribute specifies that `foo` should be treated as irreducible only within the local scope,
which helps in maintaining the desired abstraction level without affecting global settings.

```lean
command ::= ...
    | seal ident ident*
```

syntaxLocal Reducibility

The `unseal foo` command ensures that the definition of `foo` is unsealed, meaning it is marked as `[semireducible]`, the
default reducibility setting. This command is useful when you need to allow some level of reduction of `foo` in proofs.

Functionally, `unseal foo` is equivalent to `attribute [local semireducible] foo`.
Applying this attribute makes `foo` semireducible only within the local scope.

```lean
command ::= ...
    | unseal ident ident*
```

#### 7.6.7.3. Options {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Definitions--Recursive-Definitions--Controlling-Reduction--Options}

For performance, the elaborator and many tactics construct indices and caches.
Many of these take reducibility into account, and there's no way to invalidate and regenerate them if reducibility changes globally.
Unsafe changes to reducibility settings that could have unpredictable results are disallowed by default, but they can be enabled by using the `[allowUnsafeReducibility]](#manual-allowUnsafeReducibility)` option.

option

```lean
allowUnsafeReducibility
```

Default value: `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

enables users to modify the reducibility settings for declarations even when such changes are deemed potentially hazardous. For example, `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` and type class resolution maintain term indices where reducible declarations are expanded.

---



## Axioms {#manual-axioms}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Axioms/

*Axioms* are postulated constants.
While the axiom's type must itself be a type (that is, it must have type `Sort u`), there are no further requirements.
Axioms do not [reduce]](#manual---tech-term-reduction) to other terms.

Axioms can be used to experiment with the consequences of an idea before investing the time required to construct a model or prove a theorem.
They can also be used to adopt reasoning principles that can't otherwise be accessed in Lean's type theory; Lean itself provides [three such axioms]](#manual-standard-axioms) that are known to be consistent.
However, axioms should be used with caution: axioms that are inconsistent with one another, or just false, undermine the very foundations of proofs.
Lean automatically tracks the axioms that each proof depends on so that they can be audited.

### 8.1. Axiom Declarations {#manual-axiom-declarations}

Axioms declarations include a name and a type:

syntaxAxiom Declarations

```lean
[axiom]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) ::= ...
    | axiom declId [declSig]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___declSig)
```

Axioms declarations may be modified with all possible [declaration modifiers]](#manual-declaration-modifiers).
Documentation comments, attributes, `private`, and `protected` have the same meaning as for other declarations.
The modifiers `partial`, `nonrec`, `noncomputable` and `unsafe` have no effect.

### 8.2. Consistency {#manual-axiom-consistency}

Using axioms is risky.
Because they introduce a new constant of any type, and an inhabitant of a type that is a proposition counts as a proof of the proposition, axioms can be used to prove even false propositions.
Any proof that relies on an axiom can be trusted only to the extent that the axiom is both true and consistent with the other axioms used.
By their very nature, Lean cannot check whether new axioms are consistent; please exercise care when adding axioms.

**Example: Inconsistencies From Axioms**

Axioms may introduce inconsistency, either alone or in combination with other axioms.

Assuming a false statement allows any statement at all to be proved:

```lean
[axiom]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) false_is_true : [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)
theorem two_eq_five : 2 = 5 := [false_is_true]](#manual-false_is_true-_LPAR_in-Inconsistencies-From-Axioms_RPAR_).[elim](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False___elim)
```

Inconsistency may also arise from axioms that are incompatible with other properties of Lean.
For example, parametricity is a powerful reasoning technique when used in languages that support it, but it is not compatible with Lean's standard axioms.
If parametricity held, then the “free theorem” from the introduction to Wadler's [*Theorems for Free*](https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/99370.99404) (1989), which describes a technique for using parametricity to derive theorems about polymorphic functions, would be true.
As an axiom, it reads:

```lean
[axiom]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) List.free_theorem {α β}
(f : {α : _} → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (g : α → β) :
f ∘ ([List.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) g) = ([List.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) g) ∘ f
```

However, a consequence of excluded middle is that all propositions are decidable; this means that a function can *check* whether they are true or false.
This function can't be compiled, but it still exists.
This can be used to define polymorphic functions that are not parametric:

```lean
[open]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) Classical [in]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in)
noncomputable def nonParametric
{α : _} (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) :
[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) α = [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [] [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) xs
```

The existence of this function contradicts the “free theorem”:

```lean

[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro) eqeq:[Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)

### 8.3. Reduction {#manual-axiom-reduction}

Even consistent axioms can cause difficulties.
[Definitional equality]](#manual---tech-term-definitional-equality) identifies terms modulo reduction rules.
The [ι-reduction]](#manual---tech-term-___-reduction) rule specifies the interaction of recursors and constructors; because axioms are not constructors, it does not apply to them.
Ordinarily, terms without free variables reduce to applications of constructors, but axioms can cause them to get “stuck,” resulting in large terms.

**Example: Axioms and Stuck Reduction**

Adding an additional `0` to `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` with an axiom results in some definitional reductions getting stuck.
In this example, two `[Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` constructors are successfully moved to the outside of the term by reduction, but `Nat.rec` is unable to make further progress after encountering `[Nat.otherZero]](#manual-Nat___otherZero-_LPAR_in-Axioms-and-Stuck-Reduction_RPAR_)`.

```lean
[axiom]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) Nat.otherZero : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
[#reduce]](#manual-Lean___reduceCmd) 4 + ([Nat.otherZero]](#manual-Nat___otherZero-_LPAR_in-Axioms-and-Stuck-Reduction_RPAR_) + 2)
```

```lean
((Nat.rec ⟨fun x => x, [PUnit.unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit)⟩ (fun n n_ih => ⟨fun x => (n_ih.1 x).[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero), n_ih⟩) [Nat.otherZero]](#manual-Nat___otherZero-_LPAR_in-Axioms-and-Stuck-Reduction_RPAR_)).1 4).[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero).[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

Furthermore, the Lean compiler is not able to generate code for axioms.
At runtime, Lean values must be represented by concrete data in memory, but axioms do not have a concrete representation.
Definitions that contain non-proof code that relies on axioms must be marked `noncomputable` and can't be compiled.

**Example: Axioms and Compilation**

Adding an additional `0` to `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` with an axiom makes it so functions that use it can't be compiled.
In particular, `List.length'` returns the axiom `[Nat.otherZero]](#manual-Nat___otherZero-_LPAR_in-Axioms-and-Compilation_RPAR_)` instead of `[Nat.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` as the length of the empty list.

```lean
[axiom]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) Nat.otherZero : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
def List.length' : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| [] => [Nat.otherZero]](#manual-Nat___otherZero-_LPAR_in-Axioms-and-Compilation_RPAR_)
| _ :: _ => xs.length
```

```lean
`Nat.otherZero` not supported by code generator; consider marking definition as `noncomputable`
```

Axioms used in proofs rather than programs do not prevent a function from being compiled.
The compiler does not generate code for proofs, so axioms in proofs are no problem.
`[nextOdd]](#manual-nextOdd-_LPAR_in-Axioms-and-Compilation_RPAR_)` computes the next odd number from a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, which may be the number itself or one greater:

```lean

The tactic proof generates a term that transitively relies on three axioms:

```lean
[#print]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) [axioms]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) [nextOdd]](#manual-nextOdd-_LPAR_in-Axioms-and-Compilation_RPAR_)
```

```lean
'nextOdd' depends on axioms: [[propext]](#manual-propext), Classical.choice, [Quot.sound]](#manual-Quot___sound)]
```

Because they occur only in a proof, the compiler has no problem generating code:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ([nextOdd]](#manual-nextOdd-_LPAR_in-Axioms-and-Compilation_RPAR_) 4, [nextOdd]](#manual-nextOdd-_LPAR_in-Axioms-and-Compilation_RPAR_) 5)
```

```lean
(5, 5)
```

### 8.4. Standard Axioms {#manual-standard-axioms}

There are seven standard axioms in Lean. The first three axioms are important parts of how mathematics is done in Lean:

- ```lean
  Classical.choice.{u} {α : Sort u} : [Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) α → α
  ```
- ```lean
  [propext]](#manual-propext) {a b : Prop} : (a ↔ b) → a = b
  ```
- ```lean
  [Quot.sound]](#manual-Quot___sound).{u} {α : Sort u}
  {r : α → α → Prop} {a b : α} :
  r a b → [Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r a = [Quot.mk]](#manual-Quot___mk) r b
  ```

All three of these axioms are discussed in the book [Theorem Proving in Lean](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=axioms-and-computation).

The axiom `sorryAx` is used as part of the implementation of the `[sorry](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#sorry)` tactic and `sorry` term.
Uses of this axiom are not intended to occur in finished proofs, as it can be used to prove anything:

- ```lean
  sorryAx {α : Sort u} (synthetic := [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : α
  ```

Three final axioms do not truly exist for their *mathematical* content; from a mathematical perspective they prove trivial statements:

- ```lean
  Lean.trustCompiler : [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)
  ```
- ```lean
  Lean.ofReduceBool (a b : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : Lean.reduceBool a = b → a = b
  ```
- ```lean
  Lean.ofReduceNat (a b : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : Lean.reduceNat a = b → a = b
  ```

These axioms instead track proofs that depend on the correctness of the entire compiler, and not just on the much smaller [`kernel`]](#manual---tech-term-kernel).

**Example: Creating and Tracking Proofs That Trust the Compiler**

The functions `Lean.reduceBool` and `Lean.reduceNat` can be invoked to have the compiler perform a calculation; this can greatly improve performance of implementations of proof by reflection.

```lean
def largeNumber : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := Lean.reduceNat (230_000 + 4_500 + 1_000_067)
```

The resulting term depends on the axiom `Lean.trustCompiler` in order to track the fact that this calculation depends on the correctness of the compiler.

```lean
[#print]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) [axioms]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) [largeNumber]](#manual-largeNumber-_LPAR_in-Creating-and-Tracking-Proofs-That-Trust-the-Compiler_RPAR_)
```

```lean
'largeNumber' depends on axioms: [Lean.trustCompiler]
```

**Example: Axioms and the native\_decide Tactic**

Instead of appealing to `Lean.trustCompiler`, the `[native_decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#native_decide)` tactic creates a bespoke axiom for each invocation.
This allows each axiom to be audited for the precise statement that it proves.

```lean
def bigSum : ([List.range](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___range) 1_001).[sum](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___sum) = 500_500 := by⊢ ([List.range](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___range) 1001).[sum](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___sum) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 500500 [native_decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#native_decide)All goals completed! 🐙
[#print]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) [axioms]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) [bigSum]](#manual-bigSum-_LPAR_in-Axioms-and-the--native_decide--Tactic_RPAR_)
```

```lean
'bigSum' depends on axioms: [bigSum._native.native_decide.ax_1]
```

The axiom's type can be checked directly:

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) bigSum._native.native_decide.ax_1
```

```lean
bigSum._native.native_decide.ax_1 : [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___decide) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl)([List.range](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___range) 1001).[sum](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___sum) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 500500[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

### 8.5. Displaying Axiom Dependencies {#manual-print-axioms}

The command [`#print axioms`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms), followed by a defined identifier, displays all the axioms that a definition transitively relies on.
In other words, if a proof uses another proof, which itself uses an axiom, then the axiom is reported by [`#print axioms`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) for both.

This can be used to audit the assumptions made by a proof, for instance detecting that a proof transitively depends on the `[sorry](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#sorry)` tactic.

```lean
def lazy : 4 == 2 + 1 + 1 := by⊢ [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)4 [==](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) 2 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) [sorry](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#sorry)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
[#print]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) [axioms]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) [lazy]](#manual-lazy)
```

```lean
'lazy' depends on axioms: [sorryAx]
```

**Example: Printing Axioms of Simple Definitions**

Consider the following three constants:

```lean
def addThree (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := 1 + n + 2
theorem excluded_middle (P : Prop) : P ∨ ¬ P := Classical.em P
theorem simple_equality (P : Prop) : (P ∨ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)) = P := or_false P
```

Regular functions like `[addThree]](#manual-addThree-_LPAR_in-Printing-Axioms-of-Simple-Definitions_RPAR_)` that we might want to actually evaluation typically do not depend on any axioms:

```lean
[#print]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) [axioms]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) [addThree]](#manual-addThree-_LPAR_in-Printing-Axioms-of-Simple-Definitions_RPAR_)
```

```lean
'addThree' does not depend on any axioms
```

The excluded middle theorem is only true if we use classical reasoning, so the foundation for classical reasoning shows up alongside other axioms:

```lean
[#print]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) [axioms]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) [excluded_middle]](#manual-excluded_middle-_LPAR_in-Printing-Axioms-of-Simple-Definitions_RPAR_)
```

```lean
'excluded_middle' depends on axioms: [[propext]](#manual-propext), Classical.choice, [Quot.sound]](#manual-Quot___sound)]
```

Finally, the idea that two equivalent propositions are equal directly relies on [propositional extensionality]](#manual---tech-term-Extensionality).

```lean
[#print]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) [axioms]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) [simple_equality]](#manual-simple_equality-_LPAR_in-Printing-Axioms-of-Simple-Definitions_RPAR_)
```

```lean
'simple_equality' depends on axioms: [[propext]](#manual-propext)]
```

**Example: Using #print axioms with #guard\_msgs**

You can use [`#print axioms`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms)
together with [`#guard_msgs`]](#manual-Lean___guardMsgsCmd) to ensure
that updates to libraries from other projects cannot silently
introduce unwanted dependencies on axioms.

For example, if the proof of `[double_neg_elim]](#manual-double_neg_elim-_LPAR_in-Using--___print-axioms--with--___guard_msgs_RPAR_)` below changed in such a way that it used more
axioms than those listed, then the [`#guard_msgs`]](#manual-Lean___guardMsgsCmd) command would report an error.

```lean
theorem double_neg_elim (P : Prop) : (¬ ¬ P) = P :=
[propext]](#manual-propext) Classical.not_not
/--
info: 'double_neg_elim' depends on axioms:
[propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
-/
[#guard_msgs]](#manual-Lean___guardMsgsCmd) (whitespace := lax) [in]](#manual-Lean___guardMsgsCmd)
[#print]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) [axioms]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) [double_neg_elim]](#manual-double_neg_elim-_LPAR_in-Using--___print-axioms--with--___guard_msgs_RPAR_)
```
