## Attributes {#manual-attributes}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/

*Attributes* are an extensible set of compile-time annotations on declarations.
They can be added as a [declaration modifier]](#manual-declaration-modifiers) or using the [`attribute`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___attribute) command.

Attributes can associate information with declarations in compile-time tables (including [custom simp sets](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Simp-sets/#--tech-term-Custom-simp-sets), [macros](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#--tech-term-Macros), and [instances](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/#--tech-term-instances)), impose additional requirements on definitions (e.g. rejecting them if their type is not a type class), or generate additional code.
As with [macros](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#--tech-term-Macros) and custom [elaborators](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Elaborators/#--tech-term-elaborators) for terms, commands, and tactics, the [syntax category](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#--tech-term-syntax-categories) `attr` of attributes is designed to be extended, and there is a table that maps each extension to a compile-time program that interprets it.

Attributes are applied as *attribute instances* that pair a scope indicator with an attribute.
These may occur either in attributes as declaration modifiers or the stand-alone [`attribute`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___attribute) command.

syntaxAttribute Instances

```lean
[attrInstance]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attrInstance-next) ::= ...
    | attrKind attr
```

An `attrKind` is the optional [attribute scope]](#manual-scoped-attributes) keywords `local` or `scoped`.
These control the visibility of the attribute's effects.
The attribute itself is anything from the extensible [syntax category](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#--tech-term-syntax-categories) `attr`.

The attribute system is very powerful: attributes can associate arbitrary information with declarations and generate any number of helpers.
This imposes some design trade-offs: storing this information takes space, and retrieving it takes time.
As a result, some attributes can only be applied to a declaration in the module where the declaration is defined.
This allows lookups to be much faster in large projects, because they don't need to examine data for all modules.
Each attribute determines how to store its own metadata and what the appropriate tradeoff between flexibility and performance is for a given use case.

### 9.1. Attributes as Modifiers {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Attributes--Attributes-as-Modifiers}

Attributes can be added to declarations as a [declaration modifier]](#manual-declaration-modifiers).
They are placed between the documentation comment and the visibility modifiers.

syntaxAttributes

```lean
[attributes]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next) ::=
    @[[attrInstance]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attrInstance-next),*]
```

### 9.2. The `attribute` Command {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Attributes--The--attribute--Command}

The [`attribute`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___attribute) command can be used to modify a declaration's attributes.
Some example uses include:

- registering a pre-existing declaration as an [instance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/#--tech-term-instances) in the local scope by adding `instance`,
- marking a pre-existing theorem as a simp lemma or an extensionality lemma, using `simp` or `ext`, and
- temporarily removing a simp lemma from the default [simp set](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Simp-sets/#--tech-term-simp-set).

syntaxAttribute Modification

The [`attribute`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___attribute) command adds or removes attributes from an existing declaration.
The identifier is the name whose attributes are being modified.

```lean
command ::= ...
    | attribute [([eraseAttr]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eraseAttr-next) | [attrInstance]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attrInstance-next)),*] ident
```

In addition to attribute instances that add an attribute to an existing declaration, some attributes can be removed; this is called *erasing* the attribute.
Attributes can be erased by preceding their name with `-`.
Not all attributes support erasure, however.

syntaxErasing Attributes

Attributes are erased by preceding their name with a `-`.

```lean
[eraseAttr]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eraseAttr-next) ::= ...
    | -ident
```

### 9.3. Scoped Attributes {#manual-scoped-attributes}

Many attributes can be applied in a particular scope.
This determines whether the attribute's effect is visible only in the current section scope, in namespaces that open the current namespace, or everywhere.
These scope indications are also used to control [syntax extensions](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#syntax-rules) and [type class instances](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Instance-Declarations/#instance-attribute).
Each attribute is responsible for defining precisely what these terms mean for its particular effect.

syntaxAttribute Scopes

Globally-scoped declarations (the default) are in effect whenever the [module]](#manual---tech-term-module) in which they're established is transitively imported.
They are indicated by the absence of another scope modifier.

```lean
attrKind ::=
    
```

Locally-scoped declarations are in effect only for the extent of the [section scope]](#manual---tech-term-section-scope) in which they are established.

```lean
attrKind ::= ...
    | local
```

Scoped declarations are in effect whenever the [namespace]](#manual---tech-term-current-namespace) in which they are established is opened.

```lean
attrKind ::= ...
    | scoped
```

---



## Type Classes {#manual-type-classes}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/

An operation is *polymorphic* if it can be used with multiple types.
In Lean, polymorphism comes in three varieties:

1. [universe polymorphism]](#manual---tech-term-universe-polymorphism), where the sorts in a definition can be instantiated in various ways,
2. functions that take types as (potentially implicit) parameters, allowing a single body of code to work with any type, and
3. *ad-hoc polymorphism*, implemented with type classes, in which operations to be overloaded may have different implementations for different types.

Because Lean does not allow case analysis of types, polymorphic functions implement operations that are uniform for any choice of type argument; for example, `[List.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map)` does not suddenly compute differently depending on whether the input list contains `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)`s or `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`s.
Ad-hoc polymorphic operations are useful when there is no “uniform” way to implement an operation; the canonical use case is for overloading arithmetic operators so that they work with `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)`, `[Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float___ofModel)`, and any other type that has a sensible notion of addition.
Ad-hoc polymorphism may also involve multiple types; looking up a value at a given index in a collection involves the collection type, the index type, and the type of member elements to be extracted.
A *type class*Type classes were first described in Philip Wadler and Stephen Blott, 1980. “How to make ad-hoc polymorphism less ad hoc”. In *Proceedings of the 16th Symposium on Principles of Programming Languages.* describes a collection of overloaded operations (called *methods*) together with the involved types.

Type classes are very flexible.
Overloading may involve multiple types; operations like indexing into a data structure can be overloaded for a specific choice of data structure, index type, element type, and even a predicate that asserts the presence of the key in the structure.
Due to Lean's expressive type system, overloading operations is not restricted only to types; type classes may be parameterized by ordinary values, by families of types, and even by predicates or propositions.
All of these possibilities are used in practice:

Natural number literals
:   The `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` type class is used to interpret natural number literals.
    Instances may depend not only on the type being instantiated, but also on the number literal itself.

Computational effects
:   Type classes such as `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)`, whose parameter is a function from one type to another, are used to provide [special syntax for programs with side effects.](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#monads-and-do)
    The “type” for which operations are overloaded is actually a type-level function, such as `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)`, or `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`.

Predicates and propositions
:   The `[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse)` type class allows a decision procedure for a proposition to be found automatically by Lean.
    This is used as the basis for [`if`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)-expressions, which may branch on any decidable proposition.

While ordinary polymorphic definitions simply expect instantiation with arbitrary parameters, the operators overloaded with type classes are to be instantiated with *instances* that define the overloaded operation for some specific set of parameters.
These instance-implicit parameters are indicated in square brackets.
At invocation sites, Lean either *synthesizes*   a suitable instance from the available candidates or signals an error.
Because instances may themselves have instance parameters, this search process may be recursive and result in a final composite instance value that combines code from a variety of instances.
Thus, type class instance synthesis is also a means of constructing programs in a type-directed manner.

Here are some typical use cases for type classes:

- Type classes may represent overloaded operators, such as arithmetic that can be used with a variety of types of numbers or a membership predicate that can be used for a variety of data structures. There is often a single canonical choice of operator for a given type—after all, there is no sensible alternative definition of addition for `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`—but this is not an essential property, and libraries may provide alternative instances if needed.
- Type classes can represent an algebraic structure, providing both the extra structure and the axioms required by the structure. For example, a type class that represents an Abelian group may contain methods for a binary operator, a unary inverse operator, an identity element, as well as proofs that the binary operator is associative and commutative, that the identity is an identity, and that the inverse operator yields the identity element on both sides of the operator. Here, there may not be a canonical choice of structure, and a library may provide many ways to instantiate a given set of axioms; there are two equally canonical monoid structures over the integers.
- A type class can represent a relation between two types that allows them to be used together in some novel way by a library.
  The `[Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Coercions/#Coe___mk)` class represents automatically-inserted coercions from one type to another, and `[MonadLift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Lifting-Monads/#MonadLift___mk)` represents a way to run operations with one kind of effect in a context that expects another kind.
- Type classes can represent a framework of type-driven code generation, where instances for polymorphic types each contribute some portion of a final program.
  The `[Repr]](#manual-Repr___mk)` class defines a canonical pretty printer for a type, and polymorphic types end up with polymorphic `[Repr]](#manual-Repr___mk)` instances.
  When pretty printing is finally invoked on an expression with a known concrete type, such as `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × ([String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) ⊕ [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)))`, the resulting pretty printer contains code assembled from the `[Repr]](#manual-Repr___mk)` instances for `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`, `[Prod](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)`, `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, `[Sum](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl)`, `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)`, and `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)`.

1. [10.1. Class Declarations](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Class-Declarations/#class)
2. [10.2. Instance Declarations](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Instance-Declarations/#instance-declarations)
3. [10.3. Instance Synthesis](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#instance-synth)
4. [10.4. Deriving Instances](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#deriving-instances)

## Type Classes — 10.1. Class Declarations {#manual-type-classes-101-class-declarations}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Class-Declarations/

Type classes are declared with the `class` keyword.

syntaxType Class Declarations

```lean
command ::= ...
    | [declModifiers]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___declModifiers)
      class declId bracketedBinder* (: term)?
        (extends (ident : )?term,*)?
        where
        ([declModifiers]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___declModifiers) ident ::)?
        structFields
      ([deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) ident,*)?
```

Declares a new type class.

The `class` declaration creates a new single-constructor inductive type, just as if the `structure` command had been used instead.
In fact, the results of the `class` and `structure` commands are almost identical, and features such as default values may be used the same way in both.
Please refer to [the documentation for structures]](#manual-structures) for more information about default values, inheritance, and other features of structures.
The differences between structure and class declarations are:

Methods instead of fields
:   Instead of creating field projections that take a value of the structure type as an explicit parameter, [methods]](#manual---tech-term-methods) are created. Each method takes the corresponding instance as an instance-implicit parameter.

Instance-implicit parent classes
:   The constructor of a class that extends other classes takes its class parents' instances as instance-implicit parameters, rather than explicit parameters.
    When instances of this class are defined, instance synthesis is used to find the values of inherited fields.
    Parents that are not classes are still explicit parameters to the underlying constructor.

Parent projections via instance synthesis
:   Structure field projections make use of [inheritance information]](#manual-structure-inheritance) to project parent structure fields from child structure values.
    Classes instead use instance synthesis: given a child class instance, synthesis will construct the parent; thus, methods are not added to child classes in the same way that projections are added to child structures.

Registered as class
:   The resulting inductive type is registered as a type class, for which instances may be defined and that may be used as the type of instance-implicit arguments.

Out and semi-out parameters are considered
:   The `[outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam)` and `[semiOutParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#semiOutParam)` [gadgets]](#manual---tech-term-gadgets) have no meaning in structure definitions, but they are used in class definitions to control instance search.

While `deriving` clauses are allowed for class definitions to maintain the parallel between class and structure elaboration, they are not frequently used and should be considered an advanced feature.

**Example: No Instances of Non-Classes**

Lean rejects instance-implicit parameters of types that are not classes:

```lean
def f [n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)] : n = n := rfl
```

```lean
invalid binder annotation, type is not a class instance
  [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)

Note: Use the command `set_option checkBinderAnnotations false` to disable the check
```

**Example: Class vs Structure Constructors**

A very small algebraic hierarchy can be represented either as structures (`[S.Magma]](#manual-S___Magma-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_)`, `[S.Semigroup]](#manual-S___Semigroup-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_)`, and `[S.Monoid]](#manual-S___Monoid-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_)` below), a mix of structures and classes (`[C1.Monoid]](#manual-C1___Monoid-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_)`), or only using classes (`[C2.Magma]](#manual-C2___Magma-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_)`, `[C2.Semigroup]](#manual-C2___Semigroup-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_)`, and `[C2.Monoid]](#manual-C2___Monoid-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_)`):

```lean
[namespace]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) S
structure Magma (α : Type u) where
op : α → α → α
structure Semigroup (α : Type u) extends [Magma]](#manual-S___Magma-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) α where
op_assoc : ∀ x y z, op (op x y) z = op x (op y z)
structure Monoid (α : Type u) extends [Semigroup]](#manual-S___Semigroup-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) α where
ident : α
ident_left : ∀ x, op ident x = x
ident_right : ∀ x, op x ident = x
end S
[namespace]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) C1
class Monoid (α : Type u) extends [S.Semigroup]](#manual-S___Semigroup-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) α where
ident : α
ident_left : ∀ x, op ident x = x
ident_right : ∀ x, op x ident = x
end C1
[namespace]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) C2
class Magma (α : Type u) where
op : α → α → α
class Semigroup (α : Type u) extends [Magma]](#manual-C2___Magma-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) α where
op_assoc : ∀ x y z, op (op x y) z = op x (op y z)
class Monoid (α : Type u) extends [Semigroup]](#manual-C2___Semigroup-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) α where
ident : α
ident_left : ∀ x, op ident x = x
ident_right : ∀ x, op x ident = x
end C2
```

`S.Monoid.mk` and `C1.Monoid.mk` have identical signatures, because the parent of the class `[C1.Monoid]](#manual-C1___Monoid-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_)` is not itself a class:

```lean
S.Monoid.mk.{u} {α : Type u}
(toSemigroup : [S.Semigroup]](#manual-S___Semigroup-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) α)
(ident : α)
(ident_left : ∀ (x : α), toSemigroup.[op]](#manual-S___Magma___op-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) ident x = x)
(ident_right : ∀ (x : α), toSemigroup.[op]](#manual-S___Magma___op-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) x ident = x) :
[S.Monoid]](#manual-S___Monoid-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) α
```

```lean
C1.Monoid.mk.{u} {α : Type u}
(toSemigroup : [S.Semigroup]](#manual-S___Semigroup-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) α)
(ident : α)
(ident_left : ∀ (x : α), toSemigroup.[op]](#manual-S___Magma___op-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) ident x = x)
(ident_right : ∀ (x : α), toSemigroup.[op]](#manual-S___Magma___op-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) x ident = x) :
[C1.Monoid]](#manual-C1___Monoid-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) α
```

Similarly, because neither `S.Magma` nor `C2.Magma` inherits from another structure or class, their constructors are identical:

```lean
S.Magma.mk.{u} {α : Type u} (op : α → α → α) : [S.Magma]](#manual-S___Magma-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) α
```

```lean
C2.Magma.mk.{u} {α : Type u} (op : α → α → α) : [C2.Magma]](#manual-C2___Magma-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) α
```

`S.Semigroup.mk`, however, takes its parent as an ordinary parameter, while `C2.Semigroup.mk` takes its parent as an instance implicit parameter:

```lean
S.Semigroup.mk.{u} {α : Type u}
(toMagma : [S.Magma]](#manual-S___Magma-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) α)
(op_assoc : ∀ (x y z : α),
toMagma.[op]](#manual-S___Magma___op-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) (toMagma.[op]](#manual-S___Magma___op-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) x y) z = toMagma.[op]](#manual-S___Magma___op-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) x (toMagma.[op]](#manual-S___Magma___op-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) y z)) :
[S.Semigroup]](#manual-S___Semigroup-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) α
```

```lean
C2.Semigroup.mk.{u} {α : Type u} [toMagma : [C2.Magma]](#manual-C2___Magma-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) α]
(op_assoc : ∀ (x y z : α),
toMagma.[op]](#manual-C2___Magma___op-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) (toMagma.[op]](#manual-C2___Magma___op-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) x y) z = toMagma.[op]](#manual-C2___Magma___op-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) x (toMagma.[op]](#manual-C2___Magma___op-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) y z)) :
[C2.Semigroup]](#manual-C2___Semigroup-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) α
```

Finally, `C2.Monoid.mk` takes its semigroup parent as an instance implicit parameter.
The references to `op` become references to the method `[C2.Magma.op]](#manual-C2___Magma___op-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_)`, relying on instance synthesis to recover the implementation from the `[C2.Semigroup]](#manual-C2___Semigroup-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_)` instance-implicit parameter via its parent projection:

```lean
C2.Monoid.mk.{u} {α : Type u}
[toSemigroup : [C2.Semigroup]](#manual-C2___Semigroup-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) α]
(ident : α)
(ident_left : ∀ (x : α), [C2.Magma.op]](#manual-C2___Magma___op-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) ident x = x)
(ident_right : ∀ (x : α), [C2.Magma.op]](#manual-C2___Magma___op-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) x ident = x) :
[C2.Monoid]](#manual-C2___Monoid-_LPAR_in-Class-vs-Structure-Constructors_RPAR_) α
```

Parameters to type classes may be marked with *gadgets*, which are special versions of the identity function that cause the elaborator to treat a value differently.
Gadgets never change the *meaning* of a term, but they may cause it to be treated differently in elaboration-time search procedures.
The gadgets `[outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam)` and `[semiOutParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#semiOutParam)` affect [instance synthesis](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#instance-synth), so they are documented in that section.

Whether a type is a class or not has no effect on definitional equality.
Two instances of the same class with the same parameters are not necessarily identical and may in fact be very different.

**Example: Instances are Not Unique**

This implementation of binary heap insertion is buggy:

```lean
structure Heap (α : Type u) where
contents : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr]](#manual-Repr___mk)
def Heap.bubbleUp [[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) α] (i : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (xs : [Heap]](#manual-Heap-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_) α) : [Heap]](#manual-Heap-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_) α :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : i = 0 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) xs
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) [if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : i ≥ xs.[contents]](#manual-Heap___contents-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_).[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) xs
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
let j := i / 2
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [Ord.compare](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) xs.[contents]](#manual-Heap___contents-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_)[i] xs.[contents]](#manual-Heap___contents-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_)[j] == [.lt](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ordering___lt) [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[Heap.bubbleUp]](#manual-Heap___bubbleUp-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_) j { xs with [contents]](#manual-Heap___contents-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_) := xs.[contents]](#manual-Heap___contents-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_).[swap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___swap) i j }
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) xs
def Heap.insert [[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) α] (x : α) (xs : [Heap]](#manual-Heap-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_) α) : [Heap]](#manual-Heap-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_) α :=
let i := xs.[contents]](#manual-Heap___contents-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_).[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)
{xs with [contents]](#manual-Heap___contents-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_) := xs.[contents]](#manual-Heap___contents-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_).[push](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___push) x}.[bubbleUp]](#manual-Heap___bubbleUp-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_) i
```

The problem is that a heap constructed with one `[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk)` instance may later be used with another, leading to the breaking of the heap invariant.

One way to correct this is to make the heap type depend on the selected `Ord` instance:

```lean
structure Heap' (α : Type u) [[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) α] where
contents : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α

@[Heap']](#manual-Heap___-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_) α inst :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : i = 0 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) xs
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) [if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : i ≥ xs.[contents]](#manual-Heap______contents-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_).[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) xs
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
let j := i / 2
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) inst.[compare](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) xs.[contents]](#manual-Heap______contents-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_)[i] xs.[contents]](#manual-Heap______contents-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_)[j] == [.lt](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ordering___lt) [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[Heap'.bubbleUp]](#manual-Heap______bubbleUp-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_) j {xs with [contents]](#manual-Heap______contents-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_) := xs.[contents]](#manual-Heap______contents-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_).[swap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___swap) i j}

def Heap'.insert [[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) α] (x : α) (xs : [Heap']](#manual-Heap___-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_) α) : [Heap']](#manual-Heap___-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_) α :=
let i := xs.[contents]](#manual-Heap______contents-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_).[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)
{xs with [contents]](#manual-Heap______contents-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_) := xs.[contents]](#manual-Heap______contents-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_).[push](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___push) x}.[bubbleUp]](#manual-Heap______bubbleUp-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_) i
```

In the improved definitions, `[Heap'.bubbleUp]](#manual-Heap______bubbleUp-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-Not-Unique_RPAR_)` is needlessly explicit; the instance does not need to be explicitly named here because Lean would select the indicated instances nonetheless, but it does bring the correctness invariant front and center for readers.

### 10.1.1. Sum Types as Classes {#manual-class-inductive}

Most type classes follow the paradigm of a set of overloaded methods from which clients may choose freely.
This is naturally modeled by a product type, from which the overloaded methods are projections.
Some classes, however, are sum types: they require that the recipient of the synthesized instance first check *which* of the available instance constructors was provided.
To account for these classes, a class declaration may consist of an arbitrary [inductive type]](#manual---tech-term-Inductive-types), not just an extended form of structure declaration.

syntaxClass Inductive Type Declarations

```lean
command ::= ...
    | [declModifiers]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___declModifiers)
      class inductive declId [optDeclSig]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___optDeclSig) where
        (| [declModifiers]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___declModifiers) ident [optDeclSig]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___optDeclSig))*
      ([deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) ident,*)?
```

Class inductive types are just like other inductive types, except they may participate in instance synthesis.
The paradigmatic example of a class inductive is `[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse)`: synthesizing an instance in a context with free variables amounts to synthesizing the decision procedure, but if there are no free variables, then the truth of the proposition can be established by instance synthesis alone (as is done by the `[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)` tactic).

### 10.1.2. Class Abbreviations {#manual-class-abbrev}

In some cases, many related type classes may co-occur throughout a codebase.
Rather than writing all the names repeatedly, it would be possible to define a class that extends all the classes in question, contributing no new methods itself.
However, this new class has a disadvantage: its instances must be declared explicitly.

The `class abbrev` command allows the creation of *class abbreviations* in which one name is short for a number of other class parameters.
Behind the scenes, a class abbreviation is represented by a class that extends all the others.
Its constructor is additionally declared to be an instance so the new class can be constructed by instance synthesis alone.

**Example: Class Abbreviations**

Both `[plusTimes1]](#manual-plusTimes1-_LPAR_in-Class-Abbreviations_RPAR_)` and `[plusTimes2]](#manual-plusTimes2-_LPAR_in-Class-Abbreviations_RPAR_)` require that their parameters' type have `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)` and `[Mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk)` instances:

```lean
class abbrev AddMul (α : Type u) := [Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) α, [Mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk) α
def plusTimes1 [[AddMul]](#manual-AddMul-_LPAR_in-Class-Abbreviations_RPAR_) α] (x y z : α) := x + y * z
class AddMul' (α : Type u) extends [Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) α, [Mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk) α
def plusTimes2 [[AddMul']](#manual-AddMul___-_LPAR_in-Class-Abbreviations_RPAR_) α] (x y z : α) := x + y * z
```

Because `[AddMul]](#manual-AddMul-_LPAR_in-Class-Abbreviations_RPAR_)` is a `class abbrev`, no additional declarations are necessary to use `[plusTimes1]](#manual-plusTimes1-_LPAR_in-Class-Abbreviations_RPAR_)` with `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [plusTimes1]](#manual-plusTimes1-_LPAR_in-Class-Abbreviations_RPAR_) 2 5 7
```

```lean
37
```

However, `[plusTimes2]](#manual-plusTimes2-_LPAR_in-Class-Abbreviations_RPAR_)` fails, because there is no `[AddMul']](#manual-AddMul___-_LPAR_in-Class-Abbreviations_RPAR_) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` instance—no instances whatsoever have yet been declared:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [plusTimes2]](#manual-plusTimes2-_LPAR_in-Class-Abbreviations_RPAR_) 2 5 7
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [AddMul']](#manual-AddMul___-_LPAR_in-Class-Abbreviations_RPAR_) ?m.8

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

Declaring a very general instance takes care of the problem for `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and every other type:

```lean
instance [[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) α] [[Mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk) α] : [AddMul']](#manual-AddMul___-_LPAR_in-Class-Abbreviations_RPAR_) α where
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [plusTimes2]](#manual-plusTimes2-_LPAR_in-Class-Abbreviations_RPAR_) 2 5 7
```

```lean
37
```

---



## Type Classes — 10.2. Instance Declarations {#manual-type-classes-102-instance-declarations}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Instance-Declarations/

The syntax of instance declarations is almost identical to that of definitions.
The only syntactic differences are that the keyword `def` is replaced by `instance` and the name is optional:

syntaxInstance Declarations

Most instances define each method using `where` syntax:

```lean
instance ::= ...
    | instance ((priority := prio))? declId? [declSig]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___declSig) where
        structInstField*
```

However, type classes are inductive types, so instances can be constructed using any expression with an appropriate type:

```lean
instance ::= ...
    | instance ((priority := prio))? declId? [declSig]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___declSig) :=
        term
```

Instances may also be defined by cases; however, this feature is rarely used outside of `[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse)` instances:

```lean
instance ::= ...
    | instance ((priority := prio))? declId? [declSig]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___declSig)
        (| term => term)*
```

Instances defined with explicit terms often consist of either anonymous constructors ([`⟨...⟩`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___anonymousCtor)) wrapping method implementations or of invocations of `[inferInstanceAs](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstanceAs)` on definitionally equal types.

Elaboration of instances is almost identical to the elaboration of ordinary definitions, with the exception of the caveats documented below.
If no name is provided, then one is created automatically.
It is possible to refer to this generated name directly, but the algorithm used to generate the names has changed in the past and may change in the future.
It's better to explicitly name instances that will be referred to directly.
After elaboration, the new instance is registered as a candidate for instance search.
Adding the attribute `instance` to a name can be used to mark any other defined name as a candidate.

**Example: Instance Name Generation**

Following these declarations:

```lean
structure NatWrapper where
val : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
instance : [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) [NatWrapper]](#manual-NatWrapper-_LPAR_in-Instance-Name-Generation_RPAR_) where
[beq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)
| ⟨x⟩, ⟨y⟩ => x == y
```

the name `instBEqNatWrapper` refers to the new instance.

**Example: Variations in Instance Definitions**

Given this structure type:

```lean
structure NatWrapper where
val : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

all of the following ways of defining a `[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)` instance are equivalent:

```lean
instance : [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) [NatWrapper]](#manual-NatWrapper-_LPAR_in-Variations-in-Instance-Definitions_RPAR_) where
[beq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)
| ⟨x⟩, ⟨y⟩ => x == y
instance : [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) [NatWrapper]](#manual-NatWrapper-_LPAR_in-Variations-in-Instance-Definitions_RPAR_) :=
⟨fun x y => x.[val]](#manual-NatWrapper___val-_LPAR_in-Variations-in-Instance-Definitions_RPAR_) == y.[val]](#manual-NatWrapper___val-_LPAR_in-Variations-in-Instance-Definitions_RPAR_)⟩
instance : [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) [NatWrapper]](#manual-NatWrapper-_LPAR_in-Variations-in-Instance-Definitions_RPAR_) :=
⟨fun ⟨x⟩ ⟨y⟩ => x == y⟩
```

Aside from introducing different names into the environment, the following are also equivalent:

```lean
@[[instance]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___instance)]
def instBeqNatWrapper : [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) [NatWrapper]](#manual-NatWrapper-_LPAR_in-Variations-in-Instance-Definitions_RPAR_) where
[beq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)
| ⟨x⟩, ⟨y⟩ => x == y
instance : [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) [NatWrapper]](#manual-NatWrapper-_LPAR_in-Variations-in-Instance-Definitions_RPAR_) :=
⟨fun x y => x.[val]](#manual-NatWrapper___val-_LPAR_in-Variations-in-Instance-Definitions_RPAR_) == y.[val]](#manual-NatWrapper___val-_LPAR_in-Variations-in-Instance-Definitions_RPAR_)⟩
instance : [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) [NatWrapper]](#manual-NatWrapper-_LPAR_in-Variations-in-Instance-Definitions_RPAR_) :=
⟨fun ⟨x⟩ ⟨y⟩ => x == y⟩
```

### 10.2.1. Recursive Instances {#manual-recursive-instances}

Functions defined in `where` structure definition syntax are not recursive.
Because instance declaration is a version of structure definition, type class methods are also not recursive by default.
Instances for recursive inductive types are common, however.
There is a standard idiom to work around this limitation: define a recursive function independently of the instance, and then refer to it in the instance definition.
By convention, these recursive functions have the name of the corresponding method, but are defined in the type's namespace.

**Example: Instances are not recursive**

Given this definition of `[NatTree]](#manual-NatTree-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_)`:

```lean
inductive NatTree where
| leaf
| branch (left : [NatTree]](#manual-NatTree-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_)) (val : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (right : [NatTree]](#manual-NatTree-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_))
```

the following `[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)` instance fails:

```lean
instance : [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) [NatTree]](#manual-NatTree-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_) where
[beq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)
| [.leaf]](#manual-NatTree___leaf-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_), [.leaf]](#manual-NatTree___leaf-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_) =>
[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [.branch]](#manual-NatTree___branch-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_) l1 v1 r1, [.branch]](#manual-NatTree___branch-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_) l2 v2 r2 =>
l1 == l2 && v1 == v2 && r1 == r2
| _, _ =>
[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

with errors in both the left and right recursive calls that read:

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) [NatTree]](#manual-NatTree-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_)

Hint: Adding the command `deriving instance BEq for NatTree` may allow Lean to derive the missing instance.
```

Given a suitable recursive function, such as `[NatTree.beq]](#manual-NatTree___beq-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_)`:

```lean
def NatTree.beq : [NatTree]](#manual-NatTree-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_) → [NatTree]](#manual-NatTree-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [.leaf]](#manual-NatTree___leaf-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_), [.leaf]](#manual-NatTree___leaf-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_) =>
[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [.branch]](#manual-NatTree___branch-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_) l1 v1 r1, [.branch]](#manual-NatTree___branch-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_) l2 v2 r2 =>
[NatTree.beq]](#manual-NatTree___beq-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_) l1 l2 && v1 == v2 && [NatTree.beq]](#manual-NatTree___beq-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_) r1 r2
| _, _ =>
[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

the instance can be created in a second step:

```lean
instance : [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) [NatTree]](#manual-NatTree-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_) where
[beq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) := [NatTree.beq]](#manual-NatTree___beq-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_)
```

or, equivalently, using anonymous constructor syntax:

```lean
instance : [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) [NatTree]](#manual-NatTree-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_) := ⟨[NatTree.beq]](#manual-NatTree___beq-_LPAR_in-Instances-are-not-recursive_RPAR_)⟩
```

Furthermore, instances are not available for instance synthesis during their own definitions.
They are first marked as being available for instance synthesis after they are defined.
Nested inductive types, in which the recursive occurrence of the type occurs as a parameter to some other inductive type, may require an instance to be available to write even the recursive function.
The standard idiom to work around this limitation is to create a local instance in a recursively-defined function that includes a reference to the function being defined, taking advantage of the fact that instance synthesis may use every binding in the local context with the right type.

**Example: Instances for nested types**

In this definition of `[NatRoseTree]](#manual-NatRoseTree-_LPAR_in-Instances-for-nested-types_RPAR_)`, the type being defined occurs nested under another inductive type constructor (`[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk)`):

```lean
inductive NatRoseTree where
| node (val : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (children : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [NatRoseTree]](#manual-NatRoseTree-_LPAR_in-Instances-for-nested-types_RPAR_))
```

Checking the equality of rose trees requires checking equality of arrays.
However, instances are not typically available for instance synthesis during their own definitions, so the following definition fails, even though `NatRoseTree.beq` is a recursive function and is in scope in its own definition.

```lean
def NatRoseTree.beq : (tree1 tree2 : [NatRoseTree]](#manual-NatRoseTree-_LPAR_in-Instances-for-nested-types_RPAR_)) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [.node]](#manual-NatRoseTree___node-_LPAR_in-Instances-for-nested-types_RPAR_) val1 children1, [.node]](#manual-NatRoseTree___node-_LPAR_in-Instances-for-nested-types_RPAR_) val2 children2 =>
val1 == val2 &&
children1 == children2
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) ([Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [NatRoseTree]](#manual-NatRoseTree-_LPAR_in-Instances-for-nested-types_RPAR_))

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

To solve this, a local `[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) [NatRoseTree]](#manual-NatRoseTree-_LPAR_in-Instances-for-nested-types_RPAR_)` instance may be `let`-bound:

```lean
partial def NatRoseTree.beq : (tree1 tree2 : [NatRoseTree]](#manual-NatRoseTree-_LPAR_in-Instances-for-nested-types_RPAR_)) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [.node]](#manual-NatRoseTree___node-_LPAR_in-Instances-for-nested-types_RPAR_) val1 children1, [.node]](#manual-NatRoseTree___node-_LPAR_in-Instances-for-nested-types_RPAR_) val2 children2 =>
let _ : [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) [NatRoseTree]](#manual-NatRoseTree-_LPAR_in-Instances-for-nested-types_RPAR_) := ⟨NatRoseTree.beq⟩
val1 == val2 &&
children1 == children2
```

The use of array equality on the children finds the let-bound instance during instance synthesis.

### 10.2.2. Instances of `class inductive`s {#manual-class-inductive-instances}

Many instances have function types: any instance that itself recursively invokes instance search is a function, as is any instance with implicit parameters.
While most instances only project method implementations from their own instance parameters, instances of class inductive types typically pattern-match one or more of their arguments, allowing the instance to select the appropriate constructor.
This is done using ordinary Lean function syntax.
Just as with other instances, the function in question is not available for instance synthesis in its own definition.

**Example: An instance for a sum class**

Because `[DecidableEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#DecidableEq) α` is an abbreviation for `(a b : α) → [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) ([Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a b)`, its arguments can be used directly, as in this example:

```lean
inductive ThreeChoices where
| yes | no | maybe
instance : [DecidableEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#DecidableEq) [ThreeChoices]](#manual-ThreeChoices-_LPAR_in-An-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_)
| [.yes]](#manual-ThreeChoices___yes-_LPAR_in-An-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_), [.yes]](#manual-ThreeChoices___yes-_LPAR_in-An-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_) =>
[.isTrue](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
| [.no]](#manual-ThreeChoices___no-_LPAR_in-An-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_), [.no]](#manual-ThreeChoices___no-_LPAR_in-An-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_) =>
[.isTrue](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
| [.maybe]](#manual-ThreeChoices___maybe-_LPAR_in-An-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_), [.maybe]](#manual-ThreeChoices___maybe-_LPAR_in-An-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_) =>
[.isTrue](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
| [.yes]](#manual-ThreeChoices___yes-_LPAR_in-An-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_), [.maybe]](#manual-ThreeChoices___maybe-_LPAR_in-An-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_) | [.yes]](#manual-ThreeChoices___yes-_LPAR_in-An-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_), [.no]](#manual-ThreeChoices___no-_LPAR_in-An-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_)
| [.maybe]](#manual-ThreeChoices___maybe-_LPAR_in-An-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_), [.yes]](#manual-ThreeChoices___yes-_LPAR_in-An-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_) | [.maybe]](#manual-ThreeChoices___maybe-_LPAR_in-An-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_), [.no]](#manual-ThreeChoices___no-_LPAR_in-An-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_)
| [.no]](#manual-ThreeChoices___no-_LPAR_in-An-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_), [.yes]](#manual-ThreeChoices___yes-_LPAR_in-An-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_) | [.no]](#manual-ThreeChoices___no-_LPAR_in-An-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_), [.maybe]](#manual-ThreeChoices___maybe-_LPAR_in-An-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_) =>
[.isFalse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) [nofun](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___nofun)
```

**Example: A recursive instance for a sum class**

The type `[StringList]](#manual-StringList-_LPAR_in-A-recursive-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_)` represents monomorphic lists of strings:

```lean
inductive StringList where
| nil
| cons (hd : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) (tl : [StringList]](#manual-StringList-_LPAR_in-A-recursive-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_))
```

In the following attempt at defining a `[DecidableEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#DecidableEq)` instance, instance synthesis invoked while elaborating the inner [`if`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) fails because the instance is not available for instance synthesis in its own definition:

```lean
instance : [DecidableEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#DecidableEq) [StringList]](#manual-StringList-_LPAR_in-A-recursive-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_)
| [.nil]](#manual-StringList___nil-_LPAR_in-A-recursive-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_), [.nil]](#manual-StringList___nil-_LPAR_in-A-recursive-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_) => [.isTrue](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
| [.cons]](#manual-StringList___cons-_LPAR_in-A-recursive-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_) h1 t1, [.cons]](#manual-StringList___cons-_LPAR_in-A-recursive-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_) h2 t2 =>
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : h1 = h2 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h' : t1 = t2 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
[.isTrue](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) (byh1:[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)t1:[StringList]](#manual-StringList-_LPAR_in-A-recursive-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_)h2:[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)t2:[StringList]](#manual-StringList-_LPAR_in-A-recursive-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_)h:h1 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) h2h':t1 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) t2⊢ [StringList.cons]](#manual-StringList___cons-_LPAR_in-A-recursive-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_) h1 t1 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [StringList.cons]](#manual-StringList___cons-_LPAR_in-A-recursive-instance-for-a-sum-class_RPAR_) h2 t2 [simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [*]All goals completed! 🐙)
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
[.isFalse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) ### 10.2.3. Instance Priorities {#manual-instance-priorities}
```

Instances may be assigned *priorities*.
During instance synthesis, higher-priority instances are preferred; see [the section on instance synthesis](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#instance-synth) for details of instance synthesis.

syntaxInstance Priorities

Priorities may be numeric:

```lean
prio ::=
    num
```

If no priority is specified, the default priority that corresponds to 1000 is used:

```lean
prio ::= ...
    | default
```

Three named priorities are available when numeric values are too fine-grained, corresponding to 100, 500, and 10000 respectively.
The [`mid`]](#manual-prioMid) priority is lower than [`default`]](#manual-prioDefault).

```lean
prio ::= ...
    | low
```

```lean
prio ::= ...
    | mid
```

```lean
prio ::= ...
    | high
```

Finally, priorities can be added and subtracted, so `default + 2` is a valid priority, corresponding to 1002:

```lean
prio ::= ...
    | (prio)
```

```lean
prio ::= ...
    | prio + prio
```

```lean
prio ::= ...
    | prio - prio
```

### 10.2.4. Default Instances {#manual-default-instances}

The `default_instance` attribute specifies that an instance [should be used as a fallback in situations where there is not enough information to select it otherwise](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#default-instance-synth).
If no priority is specified, then the default priority `default` is used.

attributeThe `default_instance` Attribute

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | default_instance prio?
```

**Example: Default Instances**

A default instance of `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is used to select `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` for natural number literals in the absence of other type information.
It is declared in the Lean standard library with priority 100.
Given this representation of even numbers, in which an even number is represented by half of it:

```lean
structure Even where
half : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

the following instances allow numeric literals to be used for small `[Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next)` values (a limit on the depth of type class instance search prevents them from being used for arbitrarily large literals):

```lean
instance ofNatEven0 : [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) 0 where
[ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) := ⟨0⟩
instance ofNatEvenPlusTwo [[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) n] : [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) (n + 2) where
[ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) := ⟨([OfNat.ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) n : [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next)).[half]](#manual-Even___half-_LPAR_in-Default-Instances_RPAR_) + 1⟩
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (0 : [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next))
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (34 : [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next))
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (254 : [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next))
```

```lean
{ half := 0 }
```

```lean
{ half := 17 }
```

```lean
{ half := 127 }
```

Specifying them as default instances with a priority greater than or equal to 100 causes them to be used instead of `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`:

```lean
[attribute]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___attribute) [[default_instance]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___default_instance) 100] [ofNatEven0]](#manual-ofNatEven0-_LPAR_in-Default-Instances_RPAR_)
[attribute]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___attribute) [[default_instance]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___default_instance) 100] [ofNatEvenPlusTwo]](#manual-ofNatEvenPlusTwo-_LPAR_in-Default-Instances_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) 0
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) 34
```

```lean
{ half := 0 }
```

```lean
{ half := 17 }
```

Non-even numerals still use the `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` instance:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) 5
```

```lean
5
```

### 10.2.5. The Instance Attribute {#manual-instance-attribute}

The `instance` attribute declares a name to be an instance, with the specified priority.
Like other attributes, `instance` can be applied globally, locally, or only when the current namespace is opened.
The `instance` declaration is a form of definition that automatically applies the `instance` attribute.

attributeThe `instance` Attribute

Declares the definition to which it is applied to be an instance.
If no priority is provided, then the default priority `default` is used.

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | instance prio?
```

---



## Type Classes — 10.3. Instance Synthesis {#manual-type-classes-103-instance-synthesis}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/

Instance synthesis is a recursive search procedure that either finds an instance for a given type class or fails.
In other words, given a type that is registered as a type class, instance synthesis attempts to construct a term with said type.
It respects [reducibility]](#manual---tech-term-reducibility): [semireducible]](#manual---tech-term-Semireducible) or [irreducible]](#manual---tech-term-Irreducible) definitions are not unfolded, so instances for a definition are not automatically treated as instances for its unfolding unless it is [reducible]](#manual---tech-term-Reducible).
There may be multiple possible instances for a given class; in this case, declared priorities and order of declaration are used as tiebreakers, in that order, with more recent instances taking precedence over earlier ones with the same priority.

This search procedure is efficient in the presence of diamonds and does not loop indefinitely when there are cycles.
*Diamonds* occur when there is more than one route to a given goal, and *cycles* are situations when two instances each could be solved if the other were solved.
Diamonds occur regularly in practice when encoding mathematical concepts using type classes, and Lean's coercion feature naturally leads to cycles, e.g. between finite sets and finite multisets.

Instance synthesis can be tested using the [`#synth`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___synth) command.
Additionally, `[inferInstance]](#manual-inferInstance)` and `[inferInstanceAs]](#manual-inferInstanceAs)` can be used to synthesize an instance in a position where the instance itself is needed.
`[inferInstance]](#manual-inferInstance)` with a type annotation and `[inferInstanceAs]](#manual-inferInstanceAs)` are not equivalent; `[inferInstanceAs]](#manual-inferInstanceAs)` [preprocesses the synthesized instance]](#manual-instance-wrapping) to prevent unintentional leakage of implementation details into interfaces.

def

```lean
[inferInstance.{u}]](#manual-inferInstance) {α : Sort u} [i : α] : α



[inferInstance.{u}]](#manual-inferInstance) {α : Sort u} [i : α] : α
```

`[inferInstance]](#manual-inferInstance)` synthesizes a value of any target type by typeclass
inference. This function has the same type signature as the identity
function, but the square brackets on the `[i : α]` argument means that it will
attempt to construct this argument by typeclass inference. (This will fail if
`α` is not a `class`.) Example:

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) ([inferInstance]](#manual-inferInstance) : [Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) -- Inhabited Nat
def foo : [Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :=
[inferInstance]](#manual-inferInstance)
example : foo.[default](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) = ([default](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk), [default](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk)) :=
[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
```

def

```lean
[«inferInstanceAs».{u}]](#manual-inferInstanceAs) (α : Sort u) [i : α] : α



[«inferInstanceAs».{u}]](#manual-inferInstanceAs) (α : Sort u)
  [i : α] : α
```

`inferInstanceAs α` synthesizes an instance of type `α` and then adjusts it to conform to the
expected type `β`, which must be inferable from context.

Example:

```lean
def D := [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
instance : [Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) D := inferInstanceAs ([Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

The adjustment will make sure that when the resulting instance will not "leak" the RHS `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` when
reduced at transparency levels below `semireducible`, i.e. where `D` would not be unfolded either,
preventing "defeq abuse".

More specifically, given the "source type" (the argument) and "target type" (the expected type),
`[inferInstanceAs]](#manual-inferInstanceAs)` synthesizes an instance for the source type and then unfolds and rewraps its
components (fields, nested instances) as necessary to make them compatible with the target type. The
individual steps are represented by the following options, which all default to enabled and can be
disabled to help with porting:

- `[backward.inferInstanceAs.wrap]](#manual-backward___inferInstanceAs___wrap)`: master switch for instance adjustment in both `[inferInstanceAs]](#manual-inferInstanceAs)`
  and the default deriving handler
- `[backward.inferInstanceAs.wrap.reuseSubInstances]](#manual-backward___inferInstanceAs___wrap___reuseSubInstances)`: reuse existing instances for the target type
  for sub-instance fields to avoid non-defeq instance diamonds
- `[backward.inferInstanceAs.wrap.instances]](#manual-backward___inferInstanceAs___wrap___instances)`: wrap non-reducible instances in auxiliary definitions
- `[backward.inferInstanceAs.wrap.data]](#manual-backward___inferInstanceAs___wrap___data)`: wrap data fields in auxiliary definitions (proof fields are
  always wrapped)

If you just need to synthesize an instance without transporting between types, use `[inferInstance]](#manual-inferInstance)`
instead, potentially with a type annotation for the expected type.

### 10.3.1. Instance Search Summary {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Type-Classes--Instance-Synthesis--Instance-Search-Summary}

Generally speaking, instance synthesis is a recursive search procedure that may, in general, backtrack arbitrarily.
Synthesis may *succeed* with an instance term, *fail* if no such term can be found, or get *stuck* if there is insufficient information.
A detailed description of the instance synthesis algorithm is available in Selsam, Ullrich, and de Moura (2020)Daniel Selsam, Sebastian Ullrich, and Leonardo de Moura, 2020. [“Tabled typeclass resolution”](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.04301). arXiv:2001.04301.
An instance search problem is given by a type class applied to concrete arguments; these argument values may or may not be known.
Instance search attempts every locally-bound variable whose type is a class, as well as each registered instance, in order of priority and definition.
When candidate instances themselves have instance-implicit parameters, they impose further synthesis tasks.

A problem is only attempted when all of the input parameters to the type class are known.
When a problem cannot yet be attempted, then that branch is stuck; progress in other subproblems may result in the problem becoming solvable.
Output or semi-output parameters may be either known or unknown at the start of instance search.
Output parameters are ignored when checking whether an instance matches the problem, while semi-output parameters are considered.

Every candidate solution for a given problem is saved in a table; this prevents infinite regress in case of cycles as well as exponential search overheads in the presence of diamonds (that is, multiple paths by which the same goal can be achieved).
A branch of the search fails when any of the following occur:

- All potential instances have been attempted, and the search space is exhausted.
- The instance size limit specified by the option `[synthInstance.maxSize]](#manual-synthInstance___maxSize)` is reached.
- The synthesized value of an output parameter does not match the specified value in the search problem.
  Failed branches are not retried.

If search would otherwise fail or get stuck, the search process attempts to use matching [default instances]](#manual---tech-term-default-instances) in order of priority.
For default instances, the input parameters do not need to be fully known, and may be instantiated by the instances parameter values.
Default instances may take instance-implicit parameters, which induce further recursive search.

Successful branches in which the problem is fully known (that is, in which there are no unsolved metavariables) are pruned, and further potentially-successful instances are not attempted, because no later instance could cause the previously-succeeding branch to fail.

### 10.3.2. Instance Search Problems {#manual-instance-search}

Instance search occurs during the elaboration of (potentially nullary) function applications.
Some of the implicit parameters' values are forced by others; for instance, an implicit type parameter may be solved using the type of a later value argument that is explicitly provided.
Implicit parameters may also be solved using information from the expected type at that point in the program.
The search for instance implicit arguments may make use of the implicit argument values that have been found, and may additionally solve others.

Instance synthesis begins with the type of the instance-implicit parameter.
This type must be the application of a type class to zero or more arguments; these argument values may be known or unknown when search begins.
If an argument to a class is unknown, the search process will not instantiate it unless the corresponding parameter is [marked as an output parameter]](#manual-class-output-parameters), explicitly making it an output of the instance synthesis routine.

Search may succeed, fail, or get stuck; a stuck search may occur when an unknown argument value becoming known might enable progress to be made.
Stuck searches may be re-invoked when the elaborator has discovered one of the previously-unknown implicit arguments.
If this does not occur, stuck searches become failures.

**Example: Tracing Instance Search**

Setting the `trace.Meta.synthInstance` option to `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` causes Lean to emit a trace of the process for synthesizing an instance of a type class.
This trace can be used to understand how instance synthesis succeeds and why it fails.

Here, we can see the steps Lean takes to conclude that there exists an element of the type `([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ⊕ [Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty))` (specifically the element `[Sum.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) 0`):
Clicking a `▶` symbol expands that branch of the trace, and clicking the `▼` collapses an expanded branch.

```lean
set_option pp.explicit true [in]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in)
set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true [in]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in)
[#synth]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___synth) [Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ⊕ [Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty))
```

```lean

- [Meta.synthInstance] ✅️ new goal [Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) ([Sum](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty))
```
