```lean
  - [Meta.synthInstance.resume] size: 2
  - [Meta.synthInstance.answer] ✅️ [Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) ([Sum](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty))
- [Meta.synthInstance] result @Sum.nonemptyLeft [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty) (@instNonemptyOfInhabited [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) instInhabitedNat)
```

By exploring the trace, it is possible to follow the depth-first, backtracking search that Lean uses for type class instance search.
This can take a little practice to get used to!
In the example above, Lean follows these steps:

- Lean considers the first goal, `[Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) ([Sum](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty))`. Lean sees four ways of possibly satisfying this goal:

  - The `Sum.nonemptyRight` instance, which would create a sub-goal `[Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) [Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty)`.
  - The `Sum.nonemptyLeft` instance, which would create a sub-goal `[Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
  - The `instNonemptyOfMonad` instance, which would create two sub-goals `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) ([Sum](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))` and `[Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
  - The `instNonemptyOfInhabited` instance, which would create a sub-goal `[Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) ([Sum](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty))`.
- It applies `Sum.nonemptyRight`, which succeeds, leaving a new goal: `[Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) [Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty)`.
- The first sub-goal, `[Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) [Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty)`, is considered. Lean sees two ways of possibly satisfying this goal:

  - The `instNonemptyOfMonad` instance, which is rejected.
    It can't be used because the type `[Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty)` is not the application of a monad to a type.
  - The `instNonemptyOfInhabited` instance, which would create a sub-goal `[Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) [Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty)`.
- The newly-generated sub-goal, `[Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) [Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty)`, is considered.
  Lean only sees one way of possibly satisfying this goal, `instInhabitedOfMonad`, which is rejected.
  As before, this is because the type `[Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty)` is not the application of a monad to a type.
- At this point, there are no remaining options for achieving the original first sub-goal.
  The search backtracks, using the instance `Sum.nonemptyLeft`, which requires an instance of `[Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
  This search eventually succeeds, via the `[Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` instance.

The third and fourth original candidates are never considered.
Once the search for `[Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` succeeds, the [`#synth`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___synth) command finishes and outputs the solution:

```lean
@Sum.nonemptyLeft [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty) (@instNonemptyOfInhabited [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) instInhabitedNat)
```

### 10.3.3. Candidate Instances {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Type-Classes--Instance-Synthesis--Candidate-Instances}

Instance synthesis uses both local and global instances in its search.
*Local instances* are those available in the local context; they may be either parameters to a function or locally defined with `let`.
Local instances do not need to be indicated specially; any local variable whose type is a type class is a candidate for instance synthesis.
*Global instances* are those available in the global environment; every global instance is a defined name with the `instance` attribute applied.`instance` declarations automatically apply the `instance` attribute.

**Example: Local Instances**

In this example, `[addPairs]](#manual-addPairs-_LPAR_in-Local-Instances_RPAR_)` contains a locally-defined instance of `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) [NatPair]](#manual-NatPair-_LPAR_in-Local-Instances_RPAR_)`:

```lean
structure NatPair where
x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
def addPairs (p1 p2 : [NatPair]](#manual-NatPair-_LPAR_in-Local-Instances_RPAR_)) : [NatPair]](#manual-NatPair-_LPAR_in-Local-Instances_RPAR_) :=
let _ : [Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) [NatPair]](#manual-NatPair-_LPAR_in-Local-Instances_RPAR_) :=
⟨fun ⟨x1, y1⟩ ⟨x2, y2⟩ => ⟨x1 + x2, y1 + y2⟩⟩
p1 + p2
```

The local instance is used for the addition, having been found by instance synthesis.

**Example: Local Instances Have Priority**

Here, `[addPairs]](#manual-addPairs-_LPAR_in-Local-Instances-Have-Priority_RPAR_)` contains a locally-defined instance of `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) [NatPair]](#manual-NatPair-_LPAR_in-Local-Instances-Have-Priority_RPAR_)`, even though there is a global instance:

```lean
structure NatPair where
x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
instance : [Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) [NatPair]](#manual-NatPair-_LPAR_in-Local-Instances-Have-Priority_RPAR_) where
[add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)
| ⟨x1, y1⟩, ⟨x2, y2⟩ => ⟨x1 + x2, y1 + y2⟩
def addPairs (p1 p2 : [NatPair]](#manual-NatPair-_LPAR_in-Local-Instances-Have-Priority_RPAR_)) : [NatPair]](#manual-NatPair-_LPAR_in-Local-Instances-Have-Priority_RPAR_) :=
let _ : [Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) [NatPair]](#manual-NatPair-_LPAR_in-Local-Instances-Have-Priority_RPAR_) :=
⟨fun _ _ => ⟨0, 0⟩⟩
p1 + p2
```

The local instance is selected instead of the global one:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [addPairs]](#manual-addPairs-_LPAR_in-Local-Instances-Have-Priority_RPAR_) ⟨1, 2⟩ ⟨5, 2⟩
```

```lean
{ x := 0, y := 0 }
```

### 10.3.4. Instance Parameters and Synthesis {#manual-instance-synth-parameters}

The search process for instances is largely governed by class parameters.
Type classes take a certain number of parameters, and instances are tried during the search when their choice of parameters is *compatible* with those in the class type for which the instance is being synthesized.

Instances themselves may also take parameters, but the role of instances' parameters in instance synthesis is very different.
Instances' parameters represent either variables that may be instantiated by instance synthesis or further synthesis work to be done before the instance can be used.
In particular, parameters to instances may be explicit, implicit, or instance-implicit.
If they are instance implicit, then they induce further recursive instance searching, while explicit or implicit parameters must be solved by unification.

**Example: Implicit and Explicit Parameters to Instances**

While instances typically take parameters either implicitly or instance-implicitly, explicit parameters may be filled out as if they were implicit during instance synthesis.
In this example, `[aNonemptySumInstance]](#manual-aNonemptySumInstance-_LPAR_in-Implicit-and-Explicit-Parameters-to-Instances_RPAR_)` is found by synthesis, applied explicitly to `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, which is needed to make it type-correct.

```lean
instance aNonemptySumInstance
(α : Type) {β : Type} [inst : [Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) α] :
[Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) (α ⊕ β) :=
let ⟨x⟩ := inst
⟨[.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) x⟩
```

```lean
set_option pp.explicit true [in]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in)
[#synth]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___synth) [Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ⊕ [Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty))
```

In the output, both the explicit argument `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and the implicit argument `[Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty)` were found by unification with the search goal, while the `[Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` instance was found via recursive instance synthesis.

```lean
@[aNonemptySumInstance]](#manual-aNonemptySumInstance-_LPAR_in-Implicit-and-Explicit-Parameters-to-Instances_RPAR_) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty) (@instNonemptyOfInhabited [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) instInhabitedNat)
```

### 10.3.5. Output Parameters {#manual-class-output-parameters}

By default, the parameters of a type class are considered to be *inputs* to the search process.
If the parameters are not known, then the search process gets stuck, because choosing an instance would require the parameters to have values that match those in the instance, which cannot be determined on the basis of incomplete information.
In most cases, guessing instances would make instance synthesis unpredictable.

In some cases, however, the choice of one parameter should cause an automatic choice of another.
For example, the overloaded membership predicate type class `Membership` treats the type of elements of a data structure as an output, so that the type of element can be determined by the type of data structure at a use site, instead of requiring that there be sufficient type annotations to determine *both* types prior to starting instance synthesis.
An element of a `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` can be concluded to be a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` simply on the basis of its membership in the list.

Type class parameters can be declared as outputs by wrapping their types in the `[outParam]](#manual-outParam)` [gadget]](#manual---tech-term-gadgets).
When a class parameter is an *output parameter*, instance synthesis will not require that it be known; in fact, any existing value is ignored completely.
The first instance that matches the input parameters is selected, and that instance's assignment of the output parameter becomes its value.
If there was a pre-existing value, then it is compared with the assignment after synthesis is complete, and it is an error if they do not match.

def

```lean
[outParam.{u}]](#manual-outParam) (α : Sort u) : Sort u



[outParam.{u}]](#manual-outParam) (α : Sort u) : Sort u
```

Gadget for marking output parameters in type classes.

For example, the `Membership` class is defined as:

```
class Membership (α : outParam (Type u)) (γ : Type v)
```

This means that whenever a typeclass goal of the form `Membership ?α ?γ` comes
up, Lean will wait to solve it until `?γ` is known, but then it will run
typeclass inference, and take the first solution it finds, for any value of `?α`,
which thereby determines what `?α` should be.

This expresses that in a term like `a ∈ s`, `s` might be a `Set α` or
`[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α` or some other type with a membership operation, and in each case
the "member" type `α` is determined by looking at the container type.

**Example: Output Parameters and Stuck Search**

This serialization framework provides a way to convert values to some underlying storage type:

```lean
class Serialize (input output : Type) where
ser : input → output
[export]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___export) Serialize (ser)
instance : Serialize [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) where
ser n := toString n
instance [Serialize α γ] [Serialize β γ] [[Append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Append___mk) γ] :
Serialize (α × β) γ where
ser
| (x, y) => ser x ++ ser y
```

In this example, the output type is unknown.

```lean
example := ser (2, 3)
```

Instance synthesis can't select the `Serialize [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)` instance, and thus the `[Append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Append___mk) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)` instance, because that would require instantiating the output type as `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)`, so the search gets stuck:

```lean
typeclass instance problem is stuck
  Serialize [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [×](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) ?m.5

Note: Lean will not try to resolve this typeclass instance problem because the second type argument to `Serialize` is a metavariable. This argument must be fully determined before Lean will try to resolve the typeclass.

Hint: Adding type annotations and supplying implicit arguments to functions can give Lean more information for typeclass resolution. For example, if you have a variable `x` that you intend to be a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, but Lean reports it as having an unresolved type like `?m`, replacing `x` with `(x : Nat)` can get typeclass resolution un-stuck.
```

As the message indicates, one way to fix the problem is to supply an expected type:

```lean
example : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) := ser (2, 3)
```

The other is to make the output type into an output parameter:

```lean
class Serialize (input : Type) (output : [outParam]](#manual-outParam) Type) where
ser : input → output
[export]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___export) Serialize (ser)
instance : Serialize [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) where
ser n := toString n
instance [Serialize α γ] [Serialize β γ] [[Append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Append___mk) γ] :
Serialize (α × β) γ where
ser
| (x, y) => ser x ++ ser y
```

Now, instance synthesis is free to select the `Serialize [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)` instance, which solves the unknown implicit `output` parameter of `ser`:

```lean
example := ser (2, 3)
```

**Example: Output Parameters with Pre-Existing Values**

The class `[OneSmaller]](#manual-OneSmaller-_LPAR_in-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_)` represents a way to transform non-maximal elements of a type into elements of a type that has one fewer elements.
There are two separate instances that can match an input type `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, with different outputs:

```lean
class OneSmaller (α : Type) (β : [outParam]](#manual-outParam) Type) where
biggest : α
shrink : (x : α) → x ≠ biggest → β
instance : [OneSmaller]](#manual-OneSmaller-_LPAR_in-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α) α where
[biggest]](#manual-OneSmaller___biggest-_LPAR_in-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_) := [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
[shrink]](#manual-OneSmaller___shrink-_LPAR_in-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x, _ => x
instance : [OneSmaller]](#manual-OneSmaller-_LPAR_in-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)) where
[biggest]](#manual-OneSmaller___biggest-_LPAR_in-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_) := [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
[shrink]](#manual-OneSmaller___shrink-_LPAR_in-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none), _ => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false), _ => [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ()
instance : [OneSmaller]](#manual-OneSmaller-_LPAR_in-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) where
[biggest]](#manual-OneSmaller___biggest-_LPAR_in-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_) := [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
[shrink]](#manual-OneSmaller___shrink-_LPAR_in-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_)
| [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false), _ => ()
```

Because instance synthesis selects the most recently defined instance, the following code is an error:

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) [OneSmaller.shrink]](#manual-OneSmaller___shrink-_LPAR_in-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_) (β := [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) sorry
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [OneSmaller]](#manual-OneSmaller-_LPAR_in-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

The `[OneSmaller]](#manual-OneSmaller-_LPAR_in-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit))` instance was selected during instance synthesis, without regard to the supplied value of `β`.

*Semi-output parameters* are like output parameters in that they are not required to be known prior to synthesis commencing; unlike output parameters, their values are taken into account when selecting instances.

def

```lean
[semiOutParam.{u}]](#manual-semiOutParam) (α : Sort u) : Sort u



[semiOutParam.{u}]](#manual-semiOutParam) (α : Sort u) : Sort u
```

Gadget for marking semi output parameters in type classes.

Semi-output parameters influence the order in which arguments to type class
instances are processed. Lean determines an order where all non-(semi-)output
parameters to the instance argument have to be figured out before attempting to
synthesize an argument (that is, they do not contain assignable metavariables
created during TC synthesis). This rules out instances such as `[Mul β] : Add α` (because `β` could be anything). Marking a parameter as semi-output is a
promise that instances of the type class will always fill in a value for that
parameter.

For example, the `[Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Coercions/#Coe___mk)` class is defined as:

```
class Coe (α : semiOutParam (Sort u)) (β : Sort v)
```

This means that all `[Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Coercions/#Coe___mk)` instances should provide a concrete value for `α`
(i.e., not an assignable metavariable). An instance like `[Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Coercions/#Coe___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)` or `[Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Coercions/#Coe___mk) α ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α)` is fine, but `[Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Coercions/#Coe___mk) α [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is not since it does not provide a value
for `α`.

Semi-output parameters impose a requirement on instances: each instance of a class with semi-output parameters should determine the values of its semi-output parameters.

**Example: Semi-Output Parameters with Pre-Existing Values**

The class `[OneSmaller]](#manual-OneSmaller-_LPAR_in-Semi-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_)` represents a way to transform non-maximal elements of a type into elements of a type that one fewer elements.
It has two separate instances that can match an input type `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, with different outputs:

```lean
class OneSmaller (α : Type) (β : [semiOutParam]](#manual-semiOutParam) Type) where
biggest : α
shrink : (x : α) → x ≠ biggest → β
instance : [OneSmaller]](#manual-OneSmaller-_LPAR_in-Semi-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α) α where
[biggest]](#manual-OneSmaller___biggest-_LPAR_in-Semi-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_) := [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
[shrink]](#manual-OneSmaller___shrink-_LPAR_in-Semi-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x, _ => x
instance : [OneSmaller]](#manual-OneSmaller-_LPAR_in-Semi-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)) where
[biggest]](#manual-OneSmaller___biggest-_LPAR_in-Semi-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_) := [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
[shrink]](#manual-OneSmaller___shrink-_LPAR_in-Semi-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none), _ => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false), _ => [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ()
instance : [OneSmaller]](#manual-OneSmaller-_LPAR_in-Semi-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) where
[biggest]](#manual-OneSmaller___biggest-_LPAR_in-Semi-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_) := [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
[shrink]](#manual-OneSmaller___shrink-_LPAR_in-Semi-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_)
| [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false), _ => ()
```

Because instance synthesis takes semi-output parameters into account when selecting instances, the `[OneSmaller]](#manual-OneSmaller-_LPAR_in-Semi-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit))` instance is passed over due to the supplied value for `β`:

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) [OneSmaller.shrink]](#manual-OneSmaller___shrink-_LPAR_in-Semi-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_) (β := [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) sorry
```

```lean
[OneSmaller.shrink]](#manual-OneSmaller___shrink-_LPAR_in-Semi-Output-Parameters-with-Pre-Existing-Values_RPAR_) ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) ⋯ : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

### 10.3.6. Default Instances {#manual-default-instance-synth}

When instance synthesis would otherwise fail, having not selected an instance, the *default instances* specified using the `default_instance` attribute are attempted in order of priority.
When priorities are equal, more recently-defined default instances are chosen before earlier ones.
The first default instance that causes the search to succeed is chosen.

Default instances may induce further recursive instance search if the default instances themselves have instance-implicit parameters.
If the recursive search fails, the search process backtracks and the next default instance is tried.

### 10.3.7. “Morally Canonical” Instances {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Type-Classes--Instance-Synthesis--___Morally-Canonical___-Instances}

During instance synthesis, if a goal is fully known (that is, contains no metavariables) and search succeeds, no further instances will be attempted for that same goal.
In other words, when search succeeds for a goal in a way that can't be refuted by a subsequent increase in information, the goal will not be attempted again, even if there are other instances that could potentially have been used.
This optimization can prevent a failure in a later branch of an instance synthesis search from causing spurious backtracking that replaces a fast solution from an earlier branch with a slow exploration of a large state space.

The optimization relies on the assumption that instances are *morally canonical*.
Even if there is more than one potential implementation of a given type class's overloaded operations, or more than one way to synthesize an instance due to diamonds, *any discovered instance should be considered as good as any other*.
In other words, there's no need to consider *all* potential instances so long as one of them has been guaranteed to work.
The optimization may be disabled with the backwards-compatibility option `[backward.synthInstance.canonInstances]](#manual-backward___synthInstance___canonInstances)`, which may be removed in a future version of Lean.

Code that uses instance-implicit parameters should be prepared to consider all instances as equivalent.
In other words, it should be robust in the face of differences in synthesized instances.
When the code relies on instances *in fact* being equivalent, it should either explicitly manipulate instances (e.g. via local definitions, by saving them in structure fields, or having a structure inherit from the appropriate class) or it should make this dependency explicit in the type, so that different choices of instance lead to incompatible types.

### 10.3.8. Wrapping Synthesized Instances {#manual-instance-wrapping}

After `[inferInstanceAs]](#manual-inferInstanceAs)` or the default `deriving` handler synthesize an instance, the instance body is processed to ensure that its type and the types of its fields match the expected types at `[instances](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#Lean___Meta___TransparencyMode___all)` transparency, which unfolds only [reducible]](#manual---tech-term-Reducible) and [implicit reducible]](#manual---tech-term-Implicit-reducible) definitions.
This processing prevents the internals of the instance's definition from being leaked when the instance is reduced at lower than [semireducible]](#manual---tech-term-Semireducible) transparency, which could induce unintended dependencies between different parts of a code base.

If the expected type is a proposition, the instance is wrapped in an auxiliary theorem.
Otherwise, the synthesized instance is reduced to weak head normal form at `[instances](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#Lean___Meta___TransparencyMode___all)` transparency.
If the result is a constructor application, each field is processed:

- Sub-instance fields are replaced by a freshly synthesized instance for their type when one can be found.
  This ensures that the instance is the same as that which would be found by client code that synthesized the instance, avoiding a situation in which multiple paths to an instance (called *diamonds*) yield instances that are not [definitionally equal]](#manual---tech-term-definitional-equality) to one another other.
  When synthesis does not find an instance, the field is recursively wrapped using this procedure.
- Proof fields whose types are not definitionally equal to the expected type are wrapped in auxiliary theorems that hide the difference in types.
- Data fields whose types do not match the expected type are wrapped in auxiliary definitions with the appropriate reducibility.

If the instance does not reduce to a constructor application and its type does not match the expected type, then it is wrapped in an auxiliary definition with the appropriate reducibility.

### 10.3.9. Options {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Type-Classes--Instance-Synthesis--Options}

option

```lean
backward.synthInstance.canonInstances
```

Default value: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

use optimization that relies on 'morally canonical' instances during type class resolution

option

```lean
synthInstance.maxHeartbeats
```

Default value: `20000`

maximum amount of heartbeats per typeclass resolution problem. A heartbeat is number of (small) memory allocations (in thousands), 0 means no limit

option

```lean
synthInstance.maxSize
```

Default value: `128`

maximum number of instances used to construct a solution in the type class instance synthesis procedure

option

```lean
backward.inferInstanceAs.wrap
```

Default value: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

wrap instance bodies in `[inferInstanceAs]](#manual-inferInstanceAs)` and the default `deriving` handler

option

```lean
backward.inferInstanceAs.wrap.reuseSubInstances
```

Default value: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

when recursing into sub-instances, reuse existing instances for the target type instead of re-wrapping them, which can be important to avoid non-defeq instance diamonds

option

```lean
backward.inferInstanceAs.wrap.instances
```

Default value: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

wrap non-reducible instances in auxiliary definitions to fix their types

option

```lean
backward.inferInstanceAs.wrap.data
```

Default value: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

wrap data fields in auxiliary definitions to fix their types

## Type Classes — 10.4. Deriving Instances {#manual-type-classes-104-deriving-instances}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/

Lean can automatically generate instances for many classes, a process known as *deriving* instances.
Instance deriving can be invoked either when defining a type or as a stand-alone command.

syntaxInstance Deriving (Optional)

As part of a command that creates a new inductive type, a `deriving` clause specifies a comma-separated list of class names for which instances should be generated:

```lean
[optDeriving]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) ::=
    (deriving derivingClass,*)?
```

syntaxStand-Alone Deriving of Instances

The stand-alone [`deriving`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___deriving-next) command specifies a number of class names and subject names.
Each of the specified classes are derived for each of the specified subjects.

```lean
command ::= ...
    | deriving instance derivingClass,* for term,*
```

**Example: Deriving Multiple Classes**

After specifying multiple classes to derive for multiple types, as in this code:

```lean
structure A where
structure B where
[deriving]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___deriving-next) [instance]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___deriving-next) [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk), [Repr]](#manual-Repr___mk) [for]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___deriving-next) [A]](#manual-A-_LPAR_in-Deriving-Multiple-Classes_RPAR_), [B]](#manual-B-_LPAR_in-Deriving-Multiple-Classes_RPAR_)
```

all the instances exist for all the types, so all four [`#synth`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___synth) commands succeed:

```lean
[#synth]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___synth) [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) [A]](#manual-A-_LPAR_in-Deriving-Multiple-Classes_RPAR_)
[#synth]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___synth) [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) [B]](#manual-B-_LPAR_in-Deriving-Multiple-Classes_RPAR_)
[#synth]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___synth) [Repr]](#manual-Repr___mk) [A]](#manual-A-_LPAR_in-Deriving-Multiple-Classes_RPAR_)
[#synth]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___synth) [Repr]](#manual-Repr___mk) [B]](#manual-B-_LPAR_in-Deriving-Multiple-Classes_RPAR_)
```

### 10.4.1. Deriving Handlers {#manual-deriving-handlers}

Instance deriving uses a table of *deriving handlers* that maps type class names to metaprograms that derive instances for them.
Deriving handlers may be added to the table using `[registerDerivingHandler]](#manual-Lean___Elab___registerDerivingHandler)`, which should be called in an `initialize` block.
Each deriving handler should have the type `[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) Name → CommandElabM [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.
When a user requests that an instance of a class be derived, its registered handlers are called one at a time.
They are provided with all of the names in the mutual block for which the instance is to be derived, and should either correctly derive an instance and return `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` or have no effect and return `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.
When a handler returns `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, no further handlers are called.

Lean includes deriving handlers for the following classes:

- `[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)`
- `[DecidableEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#DecidableEq)`
- `[Hashable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk)`
- `[Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk)`
- `[LawfulBEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LawfulBEq___mk)`
- `[Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro)`
- `[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk)`
- `[ReflBEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#ReflBEq___mk)`
- `[Repr]](#manual-Repr___mk)`
- `[SizeOf]](#manual-SizeOf___mk)`
- `TypeName`

def

```lean
[Lean.Elab.registerDerivingHandler]](#manual-Lean___Elab___registerDerivingHandler) (className : Name)
  (handler : DerivingHandler) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)



[Lean.Elab.registerDerivingHandler]](#manual-Lean___Elab___registerDerivingHandler)
  (className : Name)
  (handler : DerivingHandler) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)
```

Registers a deriving handler for a class. This function should be called in an `initialize` block.

A `DerivingHandler` is called on the fully qualified names of all types it is running for. For
example, `deriving instance Foo for Bar, Baz` invokes `fooHandler #[`Bar, `Baz]`.

**Example: Deriving Handlers**

Instances of the `[IsEnum]](#manual-IsEnum-_LPAR_in-Deriving-Handlers_RPAR_)` class demonstrate that a type is a finite enumeration by providing a bijection between the type and a suitably-sized `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)`:

```lean
class IsEnum (α : Type) where
size : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
toIdx : α → [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) size
fromIdx : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) size → α
to_from_id : ∀ (i : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) size), toIdx (fromIdx i) = i
from_to_id : ∀ (x : α), fromIdx (toIdx x) = x
```

For inductive types that are trivial enumerations, where no constructor expects any parameters, instances of this class are quite repetitive.
The instance for `Bool` is typical:

```lean
instance : [IsEnum]](#manual-IsEnum-_LPAR_in-Deriving-Handlers_RPAR_) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) where
[size]](#manual-IsEnum___size-_LPAR_in-Deriving-Handlers_RPAR_) := 2
[toIdx]](#manual-IsEnum___toIdx-_LPAR_in-Deriving-Handlers_RPAR_)
| [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => 0
| [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => 1
[fromIdx]](#manual-IsEnum___fromIdx-_LPAR_in-Deriving-Handlers_RPAR_)
| 0 => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| 1 => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
[to_from_id]](#manual-IsEnum___to_from_id-_LPAR_in-Deriving-Handlers_RPAR_)
| 0 => [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
| 1 => [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
[from_to_id]](#manual-IsEnum___from_to_id-_LPAR_in-Deriving-Handlers_RPAR_)
| [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
| [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
```

The deriving handler programmatically constructs each pattern case, by analogy to the `[IsEnum]](#manual-IsEnum-_LPAR_in-Deriving-Handlers_RPAR_) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` implementation:

```lean
[open]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) Lean Elab Parser Term Command
def deriveIsEnum (declNames : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) Name) : CommandElabM [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
if h : declNames.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) = 1 then
let env ← getEnv
if let [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (.inductInfo ind) := env.find? declNames[0] then
let mut tos : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) ([TSyntax](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___TSyntax___mk) ``matchAlt) := #[]
let mut froms := #[]
let mut to_froms := #[]
let mut from_tos := #[]
let mut i := 0
for ctorName in ind.ctors do
let c := [mkIdent](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___mkIdent) ctorName
let n := [Syntax.mkNumLit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___mkNumLit) (toString i)
tos := tos.[push](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___push) (← `(matchAltExpr| | $c => $n))
from_tos := from_tos.[push](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___push) (← `(matchAltExpr| | $c => rfl))
froms := froms.[push](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___push) (← `(matchAltExpr| | $n => $c))
to_froms := to_froms.[push](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___push) (← `(matchAltExpr| | $n => rfl))
i := i + 1
let cmd ← `(instance : IsEnum $([mkIdent](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___mkIdent) declNames[0]) where
size := $([quote](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Quote___mk) ind.ctors.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length))
toIdx $tos:matchAlt*
fromIdx $froms:matchAlt*
to_from_id $to_froms:matchAlt*
from_to_id $from_tos:matchAlt*)
elabCommand cmd
return [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
return [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
initialize
[registerDerivingHandler]](#manual-Lean___Elab___registerDerivingHandler) ``[IsEnum]](#manual-IsEnum-_LPAR_in-Deriving-Handlers_RPAR_) [deriveIsEnum]](#manual-deriveIsEnum-_LPAR_in-Deriving-Handlers_RPAR_)
```

## Type Classes — 10.5. Basic Classes {#manual-type-classes-105-basic-classes}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/

Many Lean type classes exist in order to allow built-in notations such as addition or array indexing to be overloaded.

### 10.5.1. Boolean Equality Tests {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Type-Classes--Basic-Classes--Boolean-Equality-Tests}

The Boolean equality operator `==` is overloaded by defining instances of `[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk)`.
The companion class `[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` specifies a hashing procedure for a type.
When a type has both `[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk)` and `[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` instances, then the hashes computed should respect the `[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk)` instance: two values equated by `[BEq.beq]](#manual-BEq___mk)` should always have the same hash.

type class

```lean
[BEq.{u}]](#manual-BEq___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u



[BEq.{u}]](#manual-BEq___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u
```

`[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α` is a typeclass for supplying a boolean-valued equality relation on
`α`, notated as `a == b`. Unlike `[DecidableEq]](#manual-DecidableEq) α` (which uses `a = b`), this
is `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` valued instead of `Prop` valued, and it also does not have any
axioms like being reflexive or agreeing with `=`. It is mainly intended for
programming applications. See `[LawfulBEq]](#manual-LawfulBEq___mk)` for a version that requires that
`==` and `=` coincide.

Typically we prefer to put the "more variable" term on the left,
and the "more constant" term on the right.

Instance Constructor

```lean
[BEq.mk]](#manual-BEq___mk).{u}
```

Methods

```lean
beq : α → α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

Boolean equality, notated as `a == b`.

Conventions for notations in identifiers:

- The recommended spelling of `==` in identifiers is `beq`.

type class

```lean
[Hashable.{u}]](#manual-Hashable___mk) (α : Sort u) : Sort (max 1 u)
```

### 10.5.2. Ordering {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Type-Classes--Basic-Classes--Ordering}

There are two primary ways to order the values of a type:

- The `[Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk)` type class provides a three-way comparison operator, `[compare]](#manual-Ord___mk)`, which can indicate that one value is less than, equal to, or greater than another. It returns an `[Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`.
- The `[LT]](#manual-LT___mk)` and `[LE]](#manual-LE___mk)` classes provide canonical `Prop`-valued ordering relations for a type that do not need to be decidable. These relations are used to overload the `<` and `≤` operators.

type class

```lean
[Ord.{u}]](#manual-Ord___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u



[Ord.{u}]](#manual-Ord___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u
```

`[Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) α` provides a computable total order on `α`, in terms of the
`compare : α → α → Ordering` function.

Typically instances will be transitive, reflexive, and antisymmetric,
but this is not enforced by the typeclass.

There is a derive handler, so appending `deriving Ord` to an inductive type or structure
will attempt to create an `[Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk)` instance.

Instance Constructor

```lean
[Ord.mk]](#manual-Ord___mk).{u}
```

Methods

```lean
compare : α → α → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)
```

Compare two elements in `α` using the comparator contained in an `[[Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) α]` instance.

The `[compare]](#manual-Ord___mk)` method is exported, so no explicit `Ord` namespace is required to use it.

def

```lean
[compareOn.{u_1, u_2}]](#manual-compareOn) {β : Type u_1} {α : Sort u_2} [ord : [Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) β]
  (f : α → β) (x y : α) : [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)



[compareOn.{u_1, u_2}]](#manual-compareOn) {β : Type u_1}
  {α : Sort u_2} [ord : [Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) β] (f : α → β)
  (x y : α) : [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)
```

Compares two values by comparing the results of applying a function.

In particular, `x` is compared to `y` by comparing `f x` and `f y`.

Examples:

- `[compareOn]](#manual-compareOn) (·.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___length)) "apple" "banana" = [.lt]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`
- `[compareOn]](#manual-compareOn) (· % 3) 5 6 = [.gt]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`
- `[compareOn]](#manual-compareOn) (·.[foldl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___foldl) [max]](#manual-Max___mk) 0) [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1] = [.eq]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`

def

```lean

[Ord.opposite.{u_1}]](#manual-Ord___opposite) {α : Type u_1}
  (ord : [Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) α) : [Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) α
```

Inverts the order of an `[Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk)` instance.

The result is an `[Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) α` instance that returns `[Ordering.lt]](#manual-Ordering___lt)` when `ord` would return `[Ordering.gt]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`
and that returns `[Ordering.gt]](#manual-Ordering___lt)` when `ord` would return `[Ordering.lt]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`.

inductive type

```lean
[Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt) : Type



[Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt) : Type
```

The result of a comparison according to a total order.

The relationship between the compared items may be:

- `[Ordering.lt]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`: less than
- `[Ordering.eq]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`: equal
- `[Ordering.gt]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`: greater than

Constructors

```lean
[Ordering.lt]](#manual-Ordering___lt) : [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)
```

Less than.

```lean
[Ordering.eq]](#manual-Ordering___lt) : [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)
```

Equal.

```lean
[Ordering.gt]](#manual-Ordering___lt) : [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)
```

Greater than.

def

```lean
[Ordering.swap]](#manual-Ordering___swap) : [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt) → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)



[Ordering.swap]](#manual-Ordering___swap) : [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt) → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)
```

Swaps less-than and greater-than ordering results.

Examples:

- `[Ordering.lt]](#manual-Ordering___lt).[swap]](#manual-Ordering___swap) = [Ordering.gt]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`
- `[Ordering.eq]](#manual-Ordering___lt).[swap]](#manual-Ordering___swap) = [Ordering.eq]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`
- `[Ordering.gt]](#manual-Ordering___lt).[swap]](#manual-Ordering___swap) = [Ordering.lt]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`

def

```lean
[Ordering.then]](#manual-Ordering___then) (a b : [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)) : [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)



[Ordering.then]](#manual-Ordering___then) (a b : [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)) : [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)
```

If `a` and `b` are `[Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`, then `a.[then]](#manual-Ordering___then) b` returns `a` unless it is `.eq`, in which case it
returns `b`. Additionally, it has “short-circuiting” behavior similar to boolean `&&`: if `a` is not
`.eq` then the expression for `b` is not evaluated.

This is a useful primitive for constructing lexicographic comparator functions. The `deriving Ord`
syntax on a structure uses the `[Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk)` instance to compare each field in order, combining the results
equivalently to `[Ordering.then]](#manual-Ordering___then)`.

Use `[compareLex]](#manual-compareLex)` to lexicographically combine two comparison functions.

Examples:

```lean
structure Person where
name : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
age : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
-- Sort people first by name (in ascending order), and people with the same name by age (in
-- descending order)
instance : [Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) Person where
[compare]](#manual-Ord___mk) a b := ([compare]](#manual-Ord___mk) a.name b.name).[then]](#manual-Ordering___then) ([compare]](#manual-Ord___mk) b.age a.age)
```

```
#eval Ord.compare (⟨"Gert", 33⟩ : Person) ⟨"Dana", 50⟩
```

```lean
[Ordering.gt]](#manual-Ordering___lt)
```

```
#eval Ord.compare (⟨"Gert", 33⟩ : Person) ⟨"Gert", 50⟩
```

```lean
[Ordering.gt]](#manual-Ordering___lt)
```

```
#eval Ord.compare (⟨"Gert", 33⟩ : Person) ⟨"Gert", 20⟩
```

```lean
[Ordering.lt]](#manual-Ordering___lt)
```

def

```lean
[compareOfLessAndEq.{u_1}]](#manual-compareOfLessAndEq) {α : Type u_1} (x y : α) [[LT]](#manual-LT___mk) α]
  [[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) [(]](#manual-LT___mk)x [<]](#manual-LT___mk) y[)]](#manual-LT___mk)] [[DecidableEq]](#manual-DecidableEq) α] : [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)



[compareOfLessAndEq.{u_1}]](#manual-compareOfLessAndEq) {α : Type u_1}
  (x y : α) [[LT]](#manual-LT___mk) α] [[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) [(]](#manual-LT___mk)x [<]](#manual-LT___mk) y[)]](#manual-LT___mk)]

```

Uses decidable less-than and equality relations to find an `[Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`.

In particular, if `x < y` then the result is `[Ordering.lt]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`. If `x = y` then the result is
`[Ordering.eq]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`. Otherwise, it is `[Ordering.gt]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`.

`[compareOfLessAndBEq]](#manual-compareOfLessAndBEq)` uses `[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk)` instead of `[DecidableEq]](#manual-DecidableEq)`.

def

```lean
[compareOfLessAndBEq.{u_1}]](#manual-compareOfLessAndBEq) {α : Type u_1} (x y : α) [[LT]](#manual-LT___mk) α]
  [[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) [(]](#manual-LT___mk)x [<]](#manual-LT___mk) y[)]](#manual-LT___mk)] [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α] : [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)



[compareOfLessAndBEq.{u_1}]](#manual-compareOfLessAndBEq) {α : Type u_1}
  (x y : α) [[LT]](#manual-LT___mk) α] [[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) [(]](#manual-LT___mk)x [<]](#manual-LT___mk) y[)]](#manual-LT___mk)]
  [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α] : [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)
```

Uses a decidable less-than relation and Boolean equality to find an `[Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`.

In particular, if `x < y` then the result is `[Ordering.lt]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`. If `x == y` then the result is
`[Ordering.eq]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`. Otherwise, it is `[Ordering.gt]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`.

`[compareOfLessAndEq]](#manual-compareOfLessAndEq)` uses `[DecidableEq]](#manual-DecidableEq)` instead of `[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk)`.

def

```lean
[compareLex.{u_1, u_2}]](#manual-compareLex) {α : Sort u_1} {β : Sort u_2}
  (cmp₁ cmp₂ : α → β → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)) (a : α) (b : β) : [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)



[compareLex.{u_1, u_2}]](#manual-compareLex) {α : Sort u_1}
  {β : Sort u_2}
  (cmp₁ cmp₂ : α → β → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)) (a : α)
  (b : β) : [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)
```

Compares `a` and `b` lexicographically by `cmp₁` and `cmp₂`.

`a` and `b` are first compared by `cmp₁`. If this returns `[Ordering.eq]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`, `a` and `b` are compared
by `cmp₂` to break the tie.

To lexicographically combine two `[Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`s, use `[Ordering.then]](#manual-Ordering___then)`.

syntaxOrdering Operators

The less-than operator is overloaded in the `[LT]](#manual-LT___mk)` class:

```lean
term ::= ...
    | term < term
```

The less-than-or-equal-to operator is overloaded in the `[LE]](#manual-LE___mk)` class:

```lean
term ::= ...
    | term ≤ term
```

The greater-than and greater-than-or-equal-to operators are the reverse of the less-than and less-than-or-equal-to operators, and cannot be independently overloaded:

```lean
term ::= ...
    | term > term
```

```lean
term ::= ...
    | term ≥ term
```

type class

```lean
[LT.{u}]](#manual-LT___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u



[LT.{u}]](#manual-LT___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u
```

`[LT]](#manual-LT___mk) α` is the typeclass which supports the notation `x < y` where `x y : α`.

```lean

```


Conventions for notations in identifiers:

- The recommended spelling of `<` in identifiers is `lt`.

```lean
[LE.{u}]](#manual-LE___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u

```

`[LE]](#manual-LE___mk) α` is the typeclass which supports the notation `x ≤ y` where `x y : α`.

```lean
le : α → α → Prop
```

Conventions for notations in identifiers:

- The recommended spelling of `≤` in identifiers is `le`.

**Example: Using Ord Instances for LT and LE Instances**

Lean can automatically derive an `[Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk)` instance.
In this case, the `[Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) [Vegetable]](#manual-Vegetable-_LPAR_in-Using--Ord--Instances-for--LT--and--LE--Instances_RPAR_)` instance compares vegetables lexicographically:

```lean
structure Vegetable where
color : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
size : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) 5
[deriving]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk)
```

```lean
def broccoli : [Vegetable]](#manual-Vegetable-_LPAR_in-Using--Ord--Instances-for--LT--and--LE--Instances_RPAR_) where
[color]](#manual-Vegetable___color-_LPAR_in-Using--Ord--Instances-for--LT--and--LE--Instances_RPAR_) := "green"
[size]](#manual-Vegetable___size-_LPAR_in-Using--Ord--Instances-for--LT--and--LE--Instances_RPAR_) := 2
def sweetPotato : [Vegetable]](#manual-Vegetable-_LPAR_in-Using--Ord--Instances-for--LT--and--LE--Instances_RPAR_) where
[color]](#manual-Vegetable___color-_LPAR_in-Using--Ord--Instances-for--LT--and--LE--Instances_RPAR_) := "orange"
[size]](#manual-Vegetable___size-_LPAR_in-Using--Ord--Instances-for--LT--and--LE--Instances_RPAR_) := 3
```

Using the helpers `[ltOfOrd]](#manual-ltOfOrd)` and `[leOfOrd]](#manual-leOfOrd)`, `[LT]](#manual-LT___mk) [Vegetable]](#manual-Vegetable-_LPAR_in-Using--Ord--Instances-for--LT--and--LE--Instances_RPAR_)` and `[LE]](#manual-LE___mk) [Vegetable]](#manual-Vegetable-_LPAR_in-Using--Ord--Instances-for--LT--and--LE--Instances_RPAR_)` instances can be defined.
These instances compare the vegetables using `[compare]](#manual-Ord___mk)` and logically assert that the result is as expected.

```lean
instance : [LT]](#manual-LT___mk) [Vegetable]](#manual-Vegetable-_LPAR_in-Using--Ord--Instances-for--LT--and--LE--Instances_RPAR_) := [ltOfOrd]](#manual-ltOfOrd)
instance : [LE]](#manual-LE___mk) [Vegetable]](#manual-Vegetable-_LPAR_in-Using--Ord--Instances-for--LT--and--LE--Instances_RPAR_) := [leOfOrd]](#manual-leOfOrd)
```

The resulting relations are decidable because equality is decidable for `[Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [broccoli]](#manual-broccoli-_LPAR_in-Using--Ord--Instances-for--LT--and--LE--Instances_RPAR_) < [sweetPotato]](#manual-sweetPotato-_LPAR_in-Using--Ord--Instances-for--LT--and--LE--Instances_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [broccoli]](#manual-broccoli-_LPAR_in-Using--Ord--Instances-for--LT--and--LE--Instances_RPAR_) ≤ [sweetPotato]](#manual-sweetPotato-_LPAR_in-Using--Ord--Instances-for--LT--and--LE--Instances_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [broccoli]](#manual-broccoli-_LPAR_in-Using--Ord--Instances-for--LT--and--LE--Instances_RPAR_) < [broccoli]](#manual-broccoli-_LPAR_in-Using--Ord--Instances-for--LT--and--LE--Instances_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [broccoli]](#manual-broccoli-_LPAR_in-Using--Ord--Instances-for--LT--and--LE--Instances_RPAR_) ≤ [broccoli]](#manual-broccoli-_LPAR_in-Using--Ord--Instances-for--LT--and--LE--Instances_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

#### 10.5.2.1. Instance Construction {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Type-Classes--Basic-Classes--Ordering--Instance-Construction}

def

```lean
[Ord.lex.{u_1, u_2}]](#manual-Ord___lex) {α : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} :
  [Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) α → [Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) β → [Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)α [×](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) β[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)



[Ord.lex.{u_1, u_2}]](#manual-Ord___lex) {α : Type u_1}
  {β : Type u_2} :
  [Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) α → [Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) β → [Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)α [×](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) β[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)
```

Constructs the lexicographic order on products `α × β` from orders for `α` and `β`.

def

```lean
[Ord.lex'.{u_1}]](#manual-Ord___lex___) {α : Type u_1} (ord₁ ord₂ : [Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) α) : [Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) α



[Ord.lex'.{u_1}]](#manual-Ord___lex___) {α : Type u_1}
  (ord₁ ord₂ : [Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) α) : [Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) α
```

Constructs an `[Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk)` instance from two existing instances by combining them lexicographically.

The resulting instance compares elements first by `ord₁` and then, if this returns `[Ordering.eq]](#manual-Ordering___lt)`, by
`ord₂`.

The function `[compareLex]](#manual-compareLex)` can be used to perform this comparison without constructing an
intermediate `[Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk)` instance. `[Ordering.then]](#manual-Ordering___then)` can be used to lexicographically combine the results of
comparisons.

def

```lean
[Ord.on.{u_1, u_2}]](#manual-Ord___on) {β : Type u_1} {α : Type u_2} :
  [Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) β → (f : α → β) → [Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) α



[Ord.on.{u_1, u_2}]](#manual-Ord___on) {β : Type u_1}
  {α : Type u_2} :
  [Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) β → (f : α → β) → [Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk) α
```

Constructs an `[Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk)` instance that compares values according to the results of `f`.

In particular, `ord.on f` compares `x` and `y` by comparing `f x` and `f y` according to `ord`.

The function `[compareOn]](#manual-compareOn)` can be used to perform this comparison without constructing an intermediate
`[Ord]](#manual-Ord___mk)` instance.

### 10.5.3. Minimum and Maximum Values {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Type-Classes--Basic-Classes--Minimum-and-Maximum-Values}

The classes `Max` and `Min` provide overloaded operators for choosing the greater or lesser of two values.
These should be in agreement with `Ord`, `LT`, and `LE` instances, if they exist, but there is no mechanism to enforce this.

type class

```lean
[Min.{u}]](#manual-Min___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u



[Min.{u}]](#manual-Min___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u
```

Instance Constructor

```lean
[Min.mk]](#manual-Min___mk).{u}
```

Methods

```lean

```

Returns the lesser of its two arguments.

type class

```lean
[Max.{u}]](#manual-Max___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u



[Max.{u}]](#manual-Max___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u
```

An overloaded operation to find the greater of two values of type `α`.

Instance Constructor

```lean
[Max.mk]](#manual-Max___mk).{u}
```

Methods

```lean
max : α → α → α
```

Returns the greater of its two arguments.

Given an `[LE]](#manual-LE___mk) α` instance for which `[LE.le]](#manual-LE___mk)` is decidable, the helpers `[minOfLe]](#manual-minOfLe)` and `[maxOfLe]](#manual-maxOfLe)` can be used to create suitable `[Min]](#manual-Min___mk) α` and `[Max]](#manual-Max___mk) α` instances.
They can be used as the right-hand side of an `instance` declaration.

def

```lean
[minOfLe.{u_1}]](#manual-minOfLe) {α : Type u_1} [[LE]](#manual-LE___mk) α] [[DecidableRel]](#manual-DecidableRel) [LE.le]](#manual-LE___mk)] : [Min]](#manual-Min___mk) α



[minOfLe.{u_1}]](#manual-minOfLe) {α : Type u_1} [[LE]](#manual-LE___mk) α]
  [[DecidableRel]](#manual-DecidableRel) [LE.le]](#manual-LE___mk)] : [Min]](#manual-Min___mk) α
```

Constructs a `[Min]](#manual-Min___mk)` instance from a decidable `≤` operation.

def

```lean
[maxOfLe.{u_1}]](#manual-maxOfLe) {α : Type u_1} [[LE]](#manual-LE___mk) α] [[DecidableRel]](#manual-DecidableRel) [LE.le]](#manual-LE___mk)] : [Max]](#manual-Max___mk) α



[maxOfLe.{u_1}]](#manual-maxOfLe) {α : Type u_1} [[LE]](#manual-LE___mk) α]
```
