
Constructs a `[Max]](#manual-Max___mk)` instance from a decidable `≤` operation.

### 10.5.4. Decidability {#manual-decidable-propositions}

A proposition is *decidable* if it can be checked algorithmically.
The Law of the Excluded Middle means that every proposition is true or false, but it provides no way to check which of the two cases holds, which can often be useful.
By default, only algorithmic `[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse)` instances for which code can be generated are in scope; opening the `Classical` namespace makes every proposition decidable.

inductive type

```lean
[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) (p : Prop) : Type



[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) (p : Prop) : Type
```

Either a proof that `p` is true or a proof that `p` is false. This is equivalent to a `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` paired
with a proof that the `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` is `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` if and only if `p` is true.

`[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse)` instances are primarily used via `[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#if)`-expressions and the tactic `[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)`. In
conditional expressions, the `[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse)` instance for the proposition is used to select a branch. At
run time, this case distinction code is identical to that which would be generated for a
`[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`-based conditional. In proofs, the tactic `[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)` synthesizes an instance of `[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) p`,
attempts to reduce it to `[isTrue]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) h`, and then succeeds with the proof `h` if it can.

Because `[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse)` carries data, when writing `@[simp]` lemmas which include a `[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse)` instance
on the LHS, it is best to use `{_ : Decidable p}` rather than `[[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) p]` so that non-canonical
instances can be found via unification rather than instance synthesis.

Constructors

```lean
[Decidable.isFalse]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) {p : Prop} (h : [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)p) : [Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) p
```

Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `¬p`

```lean
[Decidable.isTrue]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) {p : Prop} (h : p) : [Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) p
```

Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `p`

def

```lean
[DecidablePred.{u}]](#manual-DecidablePred) {α : Sort u} (r : α → Prop) : Sort (max 1 u)



[DecidablePred.{u}]](#manual-DecidablePred) {α : Sort u}
  (r : α → Prop) : Sort (max 1 u)
```

A decidable predicate.

A predicate is decidable if the corresponding proposition is `[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse)` for each possible argument.

def

```lean
[DecidableRel.{u, v}]](#manual-DecidableRel) {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} (r : α → β → Prop) :
  Sort (max (max 1 u) v)



[DecidableRel.{u, v}]](#manual-DecidableRel) {α : Sort u}
  {β : Sort v} (r : α → β → Prop) :
  Sort (max (max 1 u) v)
```

A decidable relation.

A relation is decidable if the corresponding proposition is `[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse)` for all possible arguments.

def

```lean
[DecidableEq.{u}]](#manual-DecidableEq) (α : Sort u) : Sort (max 1 u)



[DecidableEq.{u}]](#manual-DecidableEq) (α : Sort u) :
  Sort (max 1 u)
```

Propositional equality is `[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse)` for all elements of a type.

In other words, an instance of `[DecidableEq]](#manual-DecidableEq) α` is a means of deciding the proposition `a = b` is
for all `a b : α`.

def

```lean
[DecidableLT.{u}]](#manual-DecidableLT) (α : Type u) [[LT]](#manual-LT___mk) α] : Type u



[DecidableLT.{u}]](#manual-DecidableLT) (α : Type u) [[LT]](#manual-LT___mk) α] :
  Type u
```

Abbreviation for `[DecidableRel]](#manual-DecidableRel) (· < · : α → α → Prop)`.

def

```lean
[DecidableLE.{u}]](#manual-DecidableLE) (α : Type u) [[LE]](#manual-LE___mk) α] : Type u



[DecidableLE.{u}]](#manual-DecidableLE) (α : Type u) [[LE]](#manual-LE___mk) α] :
  Type u
```

Abbreviation for `[DecidableRel]](#manual-DecidableRel) (· ≤ · : α → α → Prop)`.

def

```lean
[Decidable.decide]](#manual-Decidable___decide) (p : Prop) [h : [Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) p] : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)



[Decidable.decide]](#manual-Decidable___decide) (p : Prop)
  [h : [Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) p] : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

Converts a decidable proposition into a `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.

If `p : Prop` is decidable, then `[decide]](#manual-Decidable___decide) p : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` is the Boolean value
that is `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` if `p` is true and `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` if `p` is false.

def

```lean
[Decidable.byCases.{u}]](#manual-Decidable___byCases) {p : Prop} {q : Sort u} [dec : [Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) p]
  (h1 : p → q) (h2 : [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)p → q) : q



[Decidable.byCases.{u}]](#manual-Decidable___byCases) {p : Prop}
  {q : Sort u} [dec : [Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) p]
  (h1 : p → q) (h2 : [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)p → q) : q
```

Construct a `q` if some proposition `p` is decidable, and both the truth and falsity of `p` are
sufficient to construct a `q`.

This is a synonym for `dite`, the dependent if-then-else operator.

**Example: Excluded Middle and Decidable**

The equality of functions from `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` to `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is not decidable:

```lean
example (f g : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) (f = g) := [inferInstance]](#manual-inferInstance)
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl)f [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) g[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl)

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

Opening `Classical` makes every proposition decidable; however, declarations and examples that use this fact must be marked `noncomputable` to indicate that code should not be generated for them.

```lean
[open]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) Classical
noncomputable example (f g : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) (f = g) :=
[inferInstance]](#manual-inferInstance)
```

### 10.5.5. Inhabited Types {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Type-Classes--Basic-Classes--Inhabited-Types}

type class

```lean
[Inhabited.{u}]](#manual-Inhabited___mk) (α : Sort u) : Sort (max 1 u)



[Inhabited.{u}]](#manual-Inhabited___mk) (α : Sort u) :
  Sort (max 1 u)
```

`[Inhabited]](#manual-Inhabited___mk) α` is a typeclass that says that `α` has a designated element,
called `([default]](#manual-Inhabited___mk) : α)`. This is sometimes referred to as a "pointed type".

This class is used by functions that need to return a value of the type
when called "out of domain". For example, `Array.get! arr i : α` returns
a value of type `α` when `arr : Array α`, but if `i` is not in range of
the array, it reports a panic message, but this does not halt the program,
so it must still return a value of type `α` (and in fact this is required
for logical consistency), so in this case it returns `[default]](#manual-Inhabited___mk)`.

Instance Constructor

```lean
[Inhabited.mk]](#manual-Inhabited___mk).{u}
```

Methods

```lean
default : α
```

`[default]](#manual-Inhabited___mk)` is a function that produces a "default" element of any
`[Inhabited]](#manual-Inhabited___mk)` type. This element does not have any particular specified
properties, but it is often an all-zeroes value.

inductive predicate

```lean
[Nonempty.{u}]](#manual-Nonempty___intro) (α : Sort u) : Prop



[Nonempty.{u}]](#manual-Nonempty___intro) (α : Sort u) : Prop
```

`[Nonempty]](#manual-Nonempty___intro) α` is a typeclass that says that `α` is not an empty type,
that is, there exists an element in the type. It differs from `[Inhabited]](#manual-Inhabited___mk) α`
in that `[Nonempty]](#manual-Nonempty___intro) α` is a `Prop`, which means that it does not actually carry
an element of `α`, only a proof that *there exists* such an element.
Given `[Nonempty]](#manual-Nonempty___intro) α`, you can construct an element of `α` *nonconstructively*
using `Classical.choice`.

Constructors

```lean
[Nonempty.intro.{u}]](#manual-Nonempty___intro) {α : Sort u} (val : α) : [Nonempty]](#manual-Nonempty___intro) α
```

If `val : α`, then `α` is nonempty.

### 10.5.6. Subsingleton Types {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Type-Classes--Basic-Classes--Subsingleton-Types}

type class

```lean
[Subsingleton.{u}]](#manual-Subsingleton___intro) (α : Sort u) : Prop



[Subsingleton.{u}]](#manual-Subsingleton___intro) (α : Sort u) : Prop
```

A *subsingleton* is a type with at most one element. It is either empty or has a unique element.

All propositions are subsingletons because of proof irrelevance: false propositions are empty, and
all proofs of a true proposition are equal to one another. Some non-propositional types are also
subsingletons.

Instance Constructor

```lean
[Subsingleton.intro]](#manual-Subsingleton___intro).{u}
```

Prove that `α` is a subsingleton by showing that any two elements are equal.

Methods

```lean
allEq : ∀ (a b : α), a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) b
```

Any two elements of a subsingleton are equal.

theorem

```lean
[Subsingleton.elim.{u}]](#manual-Subsingleton___elim) {α : Sort u} [h : [Subsingleton]](#manual-Subsingleton___intro) α] (a b : α) :
  a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) b

```

If a type is a subsingleton, then all of its elements are equal.

theorem

```lean
[Subsingleton.helim.{u}]](#manual-Subsingleton___helim) {α β : Sort u} [h₁ : [Subsingleton]](#manual-Subsingleton___intro) α] (h₂ : α [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) β)
  (a : α) (b : β) : a [≍](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#HEq___refl) b



[Subsingleton.helim.{u}]](#manual-Subsingleton___helim) {α β : Sort u}
  [h₁ : [Subsingleton]](#manual-Subsingleton___intro) α] (h₂ : α [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) β)
  (a : α) (b : β) : a [≍](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#HEq___refl) b
```

If two types are equal and one of them is a subsingleton, then all of their elements are
[heterogeneously equal](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=HEq).

Methods


`a / b` computes the result of dividing `a` by `b`.
The meaning of this notation is type-dependent.

- For most types like `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)`, `Rat`, `Real`, `a / 0` is defined to be `0`.
- For `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, `a / b` rounds downwards.
- For `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)`, `a / b` rounds downwards if `b` is positive or upwards if `b` is negative.
  It is implemented as `[Int.ediv](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ediv)`, the unique function satisfying
  `a % b + b * (a / b) = a` and `0 ≤ a % b < natAbs b` for `b ≠ 0`.
  Other rounding conventions are available using the functions
  `[Int.fdiv](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___fdiv)` (floor rounding) and `[Int.tdiv](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___tdiv)` (truncation rounding).
- For `[Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float___ofModel)`, `a / 0` follows the IEEE 754 semantics for division,
  usually resulting in `inf` or `nan`.

Conventions for notations in identifiers:

- The recommended spelling of `/` in identifiers is `div`.

(The right argument is not the same as the left since we often want this even
in the homogeneous case.)

Types can choose to subscribe to particular defaulting behavior by providing
an instance to either `[NatPow]](#manual-NatPow___mk)` or `[HomogeneousPow]](#manual-HomogeneousPow___mk)`:

- `[NatPow]](#manual-NatPow___mk)` is for types whose exponents is preferentially a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
- `[HomogeneousPow]](#manual-HomogeneousPow___mk)` is for types whose base and exponent are preferentially the same.

```lean
[NatPow.{u}]](#manual-NatPow___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u
```

The homogeneous version of `[Pow]](#manual-Pow___mk)` where the exponent is a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
The purpose of this class is that it provides a default `[Pow]](#manual-Pow___mk)` instance,
which can be used to specialize the exponent to `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` during elaboration.

For example, if `x ^ 2` should preferentially elaborate with `2 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` then `x`'s type should
provide an instance for this class.

Instance Constructor

```lean
[NatPow.mk]](#manual-NatPow___mk).{u}
```

Methods


`a ^ n` computes `a` to the power of `n` where `n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`. See `[Pow]](#manual-Pow___mk)`.

type class

```lean
[HomogeneousPow.{u}]](#manual-HomogeneousPow___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u



[HomogeneousPow.{u}]](#manual-HomogeneousPow___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u
```

The completely homogeneous version of `[Pow]](#manual-Pow___mk)` where the exponent has the same type as the base.
The purpose of this class is that it provides a default `[Pow]](#manual-Pow___mk)` instance,
which can be used to specialize the exponent to have the same type as the base's type during elaboration.
This is to say, a type should provide an instance for this class in case `x ^ y` should be elaborated
with both `x` and `y` having the same type.

For example, the `[Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float___ofModel)` type provides an instance of this class, which causes expressions
such as `(2.2 ^ 2.2 : [Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float___ofModel))` to elaborate.

Instance Constructor

```lean
[HomogeneousPow.mk]](#manual-HomogeneousPow___mk).{u}
```

Methods

```lean
pow : α → α → α
```

`a ^ b` computes `a` to the power of `b` where `a` and `b` both have the same type.

  truncated to the bit width.

### 10.5.9. Data Lookups {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Type-Classes--Basic-Classes--Data-Lookups}

type class

```lean
[GetElem.{u, v, w}]](#manual-GetElem___mk) (coll : Type u) (idx : Type v)
  (elem : [outParam]](#manual-outParam) (Type w)) (valid : [outParam]](#manual-outParam) (coll → idx → Prop)) :
  Type (max (max u v) w)



[GetElem.{u, v, w}]](#manual-GetElem___mk) (coll : Type u)
  (idx : Type v)
  (elem : [outParam]](#manual-outParam) (Type w))
  (valid : [outParam]](#manual-outParam) (coll → idx → Prop)) :
  Type (max (max u v) w)
```

The classes `[GetElem]](#manual-GetElem___mk)` and `[GetElem?]](#manual-GetElem______mk)` implement lookup notation,
specifically `xs[i]`, `xs[i]?`, `xs[i]!`, and `xs[i]'p`.

Both classes are indexed by types `coll`, `idx`, and `elem` which are
the collection, the index, and the element types.
A single collection may support lookups with multiple index
types. The relation `valid` determines when the index is guaranteed to be
valid; lookups of valid indices are guaranteed not to fail.

For example, an instance for arrays looks like
`[GetElem]](#manual-GetElem___mk) ([Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) α (fun xs i => i < xs.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size))`. In other words, given an
array `xs` and a natural number `i`, `xs[i]` will return an `α` when `valid xs i`
holds, which is true when `i` is less than the size of the array. `[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk)`
additionally supports indexing with `[USize](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#USize___ofBitVec)` instead of `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
In either case, because the bounds are checked at compile time,
no runtime check is required.

Given `xs[i]` with `xs : coll` and `i : idx`, Lean looks for an instance of
`[GetElem]](#manual-GetElem___mk) coll idx elem valid` and uses this to infer the type of the return
value `elem` and side condition `valid` required to ensure `xs[i]` yields
a valid value of type `elem`. The tactic `[get_elem_tactic](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#get_elem_tactic)` is
invoked to prove validity automatically. The `xs[i]'p` notation uses the
proof `p` to satisfy the validity condition.
If the proof `p` is long, it is often easier to place the
proof in the context using `[have](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#have)`, because `[get_elem_tactic](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#get_elem_tactic)` tries
`[assumption](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#assumption)`.

The proof side-condition `valid xs i` is automatically dispatched by the
`[get_elem_tactic](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#get_elem_tactic)` tactic; this tactic can be extended by adding more clauses to
`get_elem_tactic_extensible` using `macro_rules`.

`xs[i]?` and `xs[i]!` do not impose a proof obligation; the former returns
an `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) elem`, with `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` signalling that the value isn't present, and
the latter returns `elem` but panics if the value isn't there, returning
`default : elem` based on the `[Inhabited]](#manual-Inhabited___mk) elem` instance.
These are provided by the `[GetElem?]](#manual-GetElem______mk)` class, for which there is a default instance
generated from a `[GetElem]](#manual-GetElem___mk)` class as long as `valid xs i` is always decidable.

Important instances include:

- `arr[i] : α` where `arr : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α` and `i : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` or `i : USize`: does array
  indexing with no runtime bounds check and a proof side goal `i < arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)`.
- `l[i] : α` where `l : List α` and `i : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`: index into a list, with proof
  side goal `i < l.length`.

Instance Constructor

```lean
[GetElem.mk]](#manual-GetElem___mk).{u, v, w}
```

Methods

```lean
getElem : (xs : coll) → (i : idx) → valid xs i → elem
```

The syntax `arr[i]` gets the `i`'th element of the collection `arr`. If there
are proof side conditions to the application, they will be automatically
inferred by the `[get_elem_tactic](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#get_elem_tactic)` tactic.

Conventions for notations in identifiers:

- The recommended spelling of `xs[i]` in identifiers is `[getElem]](#manual-GetElem___mk)`.
- The recommended spelling of `xs[i]'h` in identifiers is `[getElem]](#manual-GetElem___mk)`.

## Coercions {#manual-coercions}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Coercions/

When the Lean elaborator is expecting one type but produces a term with a different type, it attempts to automatically insert a *coercion*, which is a specially designated function from the term's type to the expected type.
Coercions make it possible to use specific types to represent data while interacting with APIs that expect less-informative types.
They also allow mathematical developments to follow the usual practice of “punning”, where the same symbol is used to stand for both an algebraic structure and its carrier set, with the precise meaning determined by context.

Lean's standard library and metaprogramming APIs define many coercions.
Some examples include:

- A `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` may be used where an `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)` is expected.
- A `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)` may be used where a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is expected.
- An `α` may be used where an `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α` is expected. The coercion wraps the value in `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`.
- An `α` may be used where a `[Thunk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Lazy-Computations/#Thunk___mk) α` is expected. The coercion wraps the term in a function to delay its evaluation.
- When one syntax category `c1` embeds into another category `c2`, a coercion from `[TSyntax](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___TSyntax___mk) c1` to `[TSyntax](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___TSyntax___mk) c2` performs any necessary wrapping to construct a valid syntax tree.

Coercions are found using type class [synthesis]](#manual---tech-term-synthesizes).
The set of coercions can be extended by adding further instances of the appropriate type classes.

**Example: Coercions**

All of the following examples rely on coercions:

```lean
example (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) := n
example (n : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) k) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := n
example (x : α) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α := x
def th (f : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Thunk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Lazy-Computations/#Thunk___mk) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) := f x
[open]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) Lean [in]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in)
example (n : [Ident](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___Ident)) : [Term](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___Term) := n
```

In the case of `[th]](#manual-th-_LPAR_in-Coercions_RPAR_)`, using `#print` demonstrates that evaluation of the function application is delayed until the thunk's value is requested:

```lean
#print [th]](#manual-th-_LPAR_in-Coercions_RPAR_)
```

```lean
def th : ([Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Thunk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Lazy-Computations/#Thunk___mk) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
fun f x => [{](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Lazy-Computations/#Thunk___mk) [fn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Lazy-Computations/#Thunk___mk) [:=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Lazy-Computations/#Thunk___mk) fun x_1 => f ↑x [}](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Lazy-Computations/#Thunk___mk)
```

Coercions are not used to resolve [generalized field notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Function-Application/#--tech-term-generalized-field-notation): only the inferred type of the term is considered.
However, a [type ascription](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Type-Ascription/#--tech-term-Type-ascriptions) can be used to trigger a coercion to the type that has the desired generalized field.
Coercions are also not used to resolve `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` instances: even though there is a default instance for `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, a coercion from `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` to `α` does not allow natural number literals to be used for `α`.

**Example: Coercions and Generalized Field Notation**

The name `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero).bdiv` is not defined, but `[Int.bdiv](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___bdiv)` exists.
The coercion from `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` to `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)` is not considered when looking up the field `bdiv`:

```lean
example (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) := n.bdiv 2
```

```lean
Invalid field `bdiv`: The environment does not contain `Nat.bdiv`, so it is not possible to project the field `bdiv` from an expression
  n
of type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`
```

This is because coercions are only inserted when there is an expected type that differs from an inferred type, and generalized fields are resolved based on the inferred type of the term before the dot.
Coercions can be triggered by adding a type ascription, which additionally causes the inferred type of the entire ascription term to be `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)`, allowing the function `[Int.bdiv](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___bdiv)` to be found.

```lean
example (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) := (n : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)).[bdiv](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___bdiv) 2
```

**Example: Coercions and OfNat**

`[Bin]](#manual-Bin-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_)` is an inductive type that represents binary numbers.

```lean
inductive Bin where
| done
| zero : [Bin]](#manual-Bin-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) → [Bin]](#manual-Bin-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_)
| one : [Bin]](#manual-Bin-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) → [Bin]](#manual-Bin-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_)
def Bin.toString : [Bin]](#manual-Bin-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) → [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
| [.done]](#manual-Bin___done-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) => ""
| [.one]](#manual-Bin___one-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) b => b.[toString]](#manual-Bin___toString-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) ++ "1"
| [.zero]](#manual-Bin___zero-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) b => b.[toString]](#manual-Bin___toString-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) ++ "0"
instance : ToString [Bin]](#manual-Bin-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) where
toString
| [.done]](#manual-Bin___done-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) => "0"
| b => [Bin.toString]](#manual-Bin___toString-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) b
```

Binary numbers can be converted to natural numbers by repeatedly applying `[Bin.succ]](#manual-Bin___succ-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_)`:

```lean
def Bin.succ (b : [Bin]](#manual-Bin-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_)) : [Bin]](#manual-Bin-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) b [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [.done]](#manual-Bin___done-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) => [Bin.done]](#manual-Bin___done-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_).[one]](#manual-Bin___one-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_)
| [.zero]](#manual-Bin___zero-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) b => [.one]](#manual-Bin___one-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) b
| [.one]](#manual-Bin___one-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) b => [.zero]](#manual-Bin___zero-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) b.[succ]](#manual-Bin___succ-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_)
def Bin.ofNat (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Bin]](#manual-Bin-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => .done
| n + 1 => ([Bin.ofNat]](#manual-Bin___ofNat-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) n).[succ]](#manual-Bin___succ-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_)
```

Even if `[Bin.ofNat]](#manual-Bin___ofNat-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_)` is registered as a coercion, natural number literals cannot be used for `[Bin]](#manual-Bin-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_)`:

```lean
[attribute]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___attribute) [[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Coercions/Coercing-Between-Types/#Lean___Attr___coe)] [Bin.ofNat]](#manual-Bin___ofNat-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_)
instance : [Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Bin]](#manual-Bin-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) where
[coe]](#manual-Coe___mk) := [Bin.ofNat]](#manual-Bin___ofNat-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (9 : [Bin]](#manual-Bin-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_))
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [Bin]](#manual-Bin-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) 9
numerals are polymorphic in Lean, but the numeral `9` cannot be used in a context where the expected type is
  [Bin]](#manual-Bin-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_)
due to the absence of the instance above

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

This is because coercions are inserted in response to mismatched types, but a failure to synthesize an `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` instance is not a type mismatch.

The coercion can be used in the definition of the `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [Bin]](#manual-Bin-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_)` instance:

```lean
instance : [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [Bin]](#manual-Bin-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_) n where
[ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) := n
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (10 : [Bin]](#manual-Bin-_LPAR_in-Coercions-and--OfNat_RPAR_))
```

```lean
1010
```

Most new coercions can be defined by declaring an instance of the `[Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk)` [type class]](#manual---tech-term-type-class) and applying the `coe` attribute to the function that performs the coercion.
To enable more control over coercions or to enable them in more contexts, Lean provides further classes that can be implemented, described in the rest of this chapter.

**Example: Defining Coercions: Decimal Numbers**

Decimal numbers can be defined as arrays of digits.

```lean
structure Decimal where
digits : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) ([Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) 10)
```

Adding a coercion allows them to be used in contexts that expect `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, but also contexts that expect any type that `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` can be coerced to.

```lean
@[[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Coercions/Coercing-Between-Types/#Lean___Attr___coe)]
def Decimal.toNat (d : [Decimal]](#manual-Decimal-_LPAR_in-Defining-Coercions___-Decimal-Numbers_RPAR_)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
d.[digits]](#manual-Decimal___digits-_LPAR_in-Defining-Coercions___-Decimal-Numbers_RPAR_).[foldl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___foldl) (init := 0) fun n d => n * 10 + d.[val](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)
instance : [Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk) [Decimal]](#manual-Decimal-_LPAR_in-Defining-Coercions___-Decimal-Numbers_RPAR_) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) where
[coe]](#manual-Coe___mk) := [Decimal.toNat]](#manual-Decimal___toNat-_LPAR_in-Defining-Coercions___-Decimal-Numbers_RPAR_)
```

This can be demonstrated by treating a `[Decimal]](#manual-Decimal-_LPAR_in-Defining-Coercions___-Decimal-Numbers_RPAR_)` as an `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)` as well as a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`:

```lean
def twoHundredThirteen : [Decimal]](#manual-Decimal-_LPAR_in-Defining-Coercions___-Decimal-Numbers_RPAR_) where
[digits]](#manual-Decimal___digits-_LPAR_in-Defining-Coercions___-Decimal-Numbers_RPAR_) := #[2, 1, 3]
def one : [Decimal]](#manual-Decimal-_LPAR_in-Defining-Coercions___-Decimal-Numbers_RPAR_) where
[digits]](#manual-Decimal___digits-_LPAR_in-Defining-Coercions___-Decimal-Numbers_RPAR_) := #[1]
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ([one]](#manual-one-_LPAR_in-Defining-Coercions___-Decimal-Numbers_RPAR_) : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) - ([twoHundredThirteen]](#manual-twoHundredThirteen-_LPAR_in-Defining-Coercions___-Decimal-Numbers_RPAR_) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
-212
```

type class

```lean
[Coe.{u, v}]](#manual-Coe___mk) (α : [semiOutParam]](#manual-semiOutParam) (Sort u)) (β : Sort v) :
  Sort (max (max 1 u) v)



[Coe.{u, v}]](#manual-Coe___mk) (α : [semiOutParam]](#manual-semiOutParam) (Sort u))
  (β : Sort v) : Sort (max (max 1 u) v)
```

`[Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk) α β` is the typeclass for coercions from `α` to `β`. It can be transitively
chained with other `[Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk)` instances, and coercion is automatically used when
`x` has type `α` but it is used in a context where `β` is expected.
You can use the `↑x` operator to explicitly trigger coercion.

Instance Constructor

```lean
[Coe.mk]](#manual-Coe___mk).{u, v}
```

Methods

```lean
coe : α → β
```

Coerces a value of type `α` to type `β`. Accessible by the notation `↑x`,
or by double type ascription `((x : α) : β)`.

1. [11.1. Coercion Insertion](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Coercions/Coercion-Insertion/#coercion-insertion)
2. [11.2. Coercing Between Types](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Coercions/Coercing-Between-Types/#ordinary-coercion)
3. [11.3. Coercing to Sorts](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Coercions/Coercing-to-Sorts/#sort-coercion)
4. [11.4. Coercing to Function Types](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Coercions/Coercing-to-Function-Types/#fun-coercion)
5. [11.5. Implementation Details](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Coercions/Implementation-Details/#coercion-impl-details)

## Coercions — 11.1. Coercion Insertion {#manual-coercions-111-coercion-insertion}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Coercions/Coercion-Insertion/

The process of searching for a coercion from one type to another is called *coercion insertion*.
Coercion insertion is attempted in the following situations where an error would otherwise occur:

- The expected type for a term is not equal to the type found for the term.
- A type or proposition is expected, but the term's type is not a [universe]](#manual---tech-term-universes).
- A term is applied as though it were a function, but its type is not a function type.

Coercions are also inserted when they are explicitly requested.
Each situation in which coercions may be inserted has a corresponding prefix operator that triggers the appropriate insertion.

Because coercions are inserted automatically, nested [type ascriptions](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Type-Ascription/#--tech-term-Type-ascriptions) provide a way to precisely control the types involved in a coercion.
If `α` and `β` are not the same type, `((e : α) : β)` arranges for `e` to have type `α` and then inserts a coercion from `α` to `β`.

When a coercion is discovered, the instances used to find it are unfolded and removed from the resulting term.
To the extent possible, calls to `[Coe.coe]](#manual-Coe___mk)` and related functions do not occur in the final term.
This process of unfolding makes terms more readable.
Even more importantly, it means that coercions can control the evaluation of the coerced terms by wrapping them in functions.

**Example: Controlling Evaluation with Coercions**

The structure `[Later]](#manual-Later-_LPAR_in-Controlling-Evaluation-with-Coercions_RPAR_)` represents a term that can be evaluated in the future, by calling the contained function.

```lean
structure Later (α : Type u) where
get : [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) → α
```

A coercion from any value to a later value is performed by creating a function that wraps it.

```lean
instance : [CoeTail](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Coercions/Coercing-Between-Types/#CoeTail___mk) α ([Later]](#manual-Later-_LPAR_in-Controlling-Evaluation-with-Coercions_RPAR_) α) where
[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Coercions/Coercing-Between-Types/#CoeTail___mk) x := { [get]](#manual-Later___get-_LPAR_in-Controlling-Evaluation-with-Coercions_RPAR_) := fun () => x }
```

However, if coercion insertion resulted in an application of `[CoeTail.coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Coercions/Coercing-Between-Types/#CoeTail___mk)`, then this coercion would not have the desired effect at runtime, because the coerced value would be evaluated and then saved in the function's closure.
Because coercion implementations are unfolded, this instance is nonetheless useful.

```lean
def tomorrow : [Later]](#manual-Later-_LPAR_in-Controlling-Evaluation-with-Coercions_RPAR_) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
([Nat.fold](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___fold) 10000
(init := "")
(fun _ _ s => s ++ "tomorrow") : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray))
```

Printing the resulting definition shows that the computation is inside the function's body:

```lean
#print [tomorrow]](#manual-tomorrow-_LPAR_in-Controlling-Evaluation-with-Coercions_RPAR_)
```

```lean
def tomorrow : [Later]](#manual-Later-_LPAR_in-Controlling-Evaluation-with-Coercions_RPAR_) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
{ [get]](#manual-Later___get-_LPAR_in-Controlling-Evaluation-with-Coercions_RPAR_) := fun x => [Nat.fold](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___fold) 10000 (fun x x_1 s => s [++]](#manual-HAppend___mk) "tomorrow") "" }
```

**Example: Duplicate Evaluation in Coercions**

Because the contents of `[Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk)` instances are unfolded during coercion insertion, coercions that use their argument more than once should be careful to ensure that evaluation occurs just once.
This can be done by using a helper function that is not part of the instance, or by using `let` to evaluate the coerced term and then reuse its resulting value.

The structure `[Twice]](#manual-Twice-_LPAR_in-Duplicate-Evaluation-in-Coercions_RPAR_)` requires that both fields have the same value:

```lean
structure Twice (α : Type u) where
first : α
second : α
first_eq_second : first = second
```

One way to define a coercion from `α` to `[Twice]](#manual-Twice-_LPAR_in-Duplicate-Evaluation-in-Coercions_RPAR_) α` is with a helper function `[twice]](#manual-twice-_LPAR_in-Duplicate-Evaluation-in-Coercions_RPAR_)`.
The `coe` attribute marks it as a coercion so it can be shown correctly in proof goals and error messages.

```lean
@[[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Coercions/Coercing-Between-Types/#Lean___Attr___coe)]
def twice (x : α) : [Twice]](#manual-Twice-_LPAR_in-Duplicate-Evaluation-in-Coercions_RPAR_) α where
[first]](#manual-Twice___first-_LPAR_in-Duplicate-Evaluation-in-Coercions_RPAR_) := x
[second]](#manual-Twice___second-_LPAR_in-Duplicate-Evaluation-in-Coercions_RPAR_) := x
[first_eq_second]](#manual-Twice___first_eq_second-_LPAR_in-Duplicate-Evaluation-in-Coercions_RPAR_) := [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
instance : [Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk) α ([Twice]](#manual-Twice-_LPAR_in-Duplicate-Evaluation-in-Coercions_RPAR_) α) := ⟨[twice]](#manual-twice-_LPAR_in-Duplicate-Evaluation-in-Coercions_RPAR_)⟩
```

When the `[Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk)` instance is unfolded, the call to `[twice]](#manual-twice-_LPAR_in-Duplicate-Evaluation-in-Coercions_RPAR_)` remains, which causes its argument to be evaluated before the body of the function is executed.
As a result, the `dbg_trace` is included in the resulting term just once:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ((dbg_trace "hello"; 5 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Twice]](#manual-Twice-_LPAR_in-Duplicate-Evaluation-in-Coercions_RPAR_) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

This is used to demonstrate the effect:

```lean
hello
```

Inlining the helper into the `[Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk)` instance results in a term that duplicates the `dbg_trace`:

```lean
instance : [Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk) α ([Twice]](#manual-Twice-_LPAR_in-Duplicate-Evaluation-in-Coercions_RPAR_) α) where
[coe]](#manual-Coe___mk) x := ⟨x, x, [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)⟩
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ((dbg_trace "hello"; 5 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Twice]](#manual-Twice-_LPAR_in-Duplicate-Evaluation-in-Coercions_RPAR_) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
hello
hello
```

Introducing an intermediate name for the result of the evaluation prevents the duplication of `dbg_trace`:

```lean
instance : [Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk) α ([Twice]](#manual-Twice-_LPAR_in-Duplicate-Evaluation-in-Coercions_RPAR_) α) where
[coe]](#manual-Coe___mk) x := let y := x; ⟨y, y, [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)⟩
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ((dbg_trace "hello"; 5 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Twice]](#manual-Twice-_LPAR_in-Duplicate-Evaluation-in-Coercions_RPAR_) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
hello
```

## Coercions — 11.2. Coercing Between Types {#manual-coercions-112-coercing-between-types}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Coercions/Coercing-Between-Types/

Coercions between types are inserted when the Lean elaborator successfully constructs a term, inferring its type, in a context where a term of some other type was expected.
Before signaling an error, the elaborator attempts to insert a coercion from the inferred type to the expected type by synthesizing an instance of `[CoeT]](#manual-CoeT___mk)`.
There are two ways that this might succeed:

1. There could be a chain of coercions from the inferred type to the expected type through a number of intermediate types.
   These chained coercions are selected based on the inferred type and the expected type, but not the term being coerced.
2. There could be a single dependent coercion from the inferred type to the expected type.
   Dependent coercions take the term being coerced into account as well as the inferred and expected types, but they cannot be chained.

The simplest way to define a non-dependent coercion is by implementing a `[Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk)` instance, which is enough to synthesize a `[CoeT]](#manual-CoeT___mk)` instance.
This instance participates in chaining, and may be applied any number of times.
The expected type of the expression is used to drive synthesis of `[Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk)` instances, rather than the inferred type.
For instances that can be used at most once, or instances in which the inferred type should drive synthesis, one of the other coercion classes may be needed.

**Example: Defining Coercions**

The type `[Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next)` represents the even natural numbers.

```lean
structure Even where
number : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
isEven : number % 2 = 0
```

A coercion allows even numbers to be used where natural numbers are expected.
The `coe` attribute marks the projection as a coercion so that it can be shown accordingly in proof states and error messages, as described in the [section on implementing coercions]](#manual-coercion-impl).

```lean
[attribute]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___attribute) [[coe]](#manual-Lean___Attr___coe)] [Even.number]](#manual-Even___number-_LPAR_in-Defining-Coercions_RPAR_)
instance : [Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk) [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) where
[coe]](#manual-Coe___mk) := [Even.number]](#manual-Even___number-_LPAR_in-Defining-Coercions_RPAR_)
```

With this coercion in place, even numbers can be used where natural numbers are expected.

```lean
def four : [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) := ⟨4, by⊢ 4 [%]](#manual-HMod___mk) 2 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 [omega](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#omega)All goals completed! 🐙⟩
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ([four]](#manual-four-_LPAR_in-Defining-Coercions_RPAR_) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) + 1
```

```lean
5
```

Due to coercion chaining, there is also a coercion from `[Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next)` to `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)` formed by chaining the `[Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk) [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` instance with the existing coercion from `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` to `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)`:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ([four]](#manual-four-_LPAR_in-Defining-Coercions_RPAR_) : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) - 5
```

```lean
-1
```

Dependent coercions are needed when the specific term being coerced is required in order to determine whether or how to coerce the term: for example, only decidable propositions can be coerced to `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, so the proposition in question must occur as part of the instance's type so that it can require the `[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse)` instance.
Non-dependent coercions are used whenever all values of the inferred type can be coerced to the target type.

**Example: Defining Dependent Coercions**

The string `"four"` can be coerced into the natural number `4` with this instance declaration:

```lean
instance : [CoeDep]](#manual-CoeDep___mk) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) "four" [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) where
[coe]](#manual-CoeDep___mk) := 4
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ("four" : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
4
```

Ordinary type errors are produced for other strings:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ("three" : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
Type mismatch
  "three"
has type
  [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
but is expected to have type
  [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

Non-dependent coercions may be chained: if there is a coercion from `α` to `β` and from `β` to `γ`, then there is also a coercion from `α` to `γ`.
The chain should be in the form `[CoeHead]](#manual-CoeHead___mk)``?``[CoeOut]](#manual-CoeOut___mk)``*``[Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk)``*``[CoeTail]](#manual-CoeTail___mk)``?`, which is to say it may consist of:

- An optional instance of `[CoeHead]](#manual-CoeHead___mk) α α'`, followed by
- Zero or more instances of `[CoeOut]](#manual-CoeOut___mk) α' …`, …, `[CoeOut]](#manual-CoeOut___mk) … α''`, followed by
- Zero or more instances of `[Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk) α'' …`, …, `[Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk) … β'`, followed by
- An optional instance of `[CoeTail]](#manual-CoeTail___mk) β' γ`

Most coercions can be implemented as instances of `[Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk)`.
`[CoeHead]](#manual-CoeHead___mk)`, `[CoeOut]](#manual-CoeOut___mk)`, and `[CoeTail]](#manual-CoeTail___mk)` are needed in certain special situations.

`[CoeHead]](#manual-CoeHead___mk)` and `[CoeOut]](#manual-CoeOut___mk)` instances are chained from the inferred type towards the expected type.
In other words, information in the type found for the term is used to resolve a chain of instances.
`[Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk)` and `[CoeTail]](#manual-CoeTail___mk)` instances are chained from the expected type towards the inferred type, so information in the expected type is used to resolve a chain of instances.
If these chains meet in the middle, a coercion has been found.
This is reflected in their type signatures: `[CoeHead]](#manual-CoeHead___mk)` and `[CoeOut]](#manual-CoeOut___mk)` use [semi-output parameters]](#manual---tech-term-Semi-output-parameters) for the coercion's target, while `[Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk)` and `[CoeTail]](#manual-CoeTail___mk)` use [semi-output parameters]](#manual---tech-term-Semi-output-parameters) for the coercions' source.

When an instance provides a value for a [semi-output parameter]](#manual---tech-term-Semi-output-parameters), the value is used during instance synthesis.
However, if no value is provided, then a value may be assigned by the synthesis algorithm.
Consequently, every semi-output parameter should be assigned a type when an instance is selected.
This means that `[CoeOut]](#manual-CoeOut___mk)` should be used when the variables that occur in the coercion's output are a subset of those in its input, and `[Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk)` should be used when the variables in the input are a subset of those in the output.

**Example: CoeOut vs Coe instances**

A `[Truthy]](#manual-Truthy-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_)` value is a value paired with an indication of whether it should be considered to be true or false.
A `[Decision]](#manual-Decision-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_)` is either `[yes]](#manual-Decision___yes-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_)`, `[no]](#manual-Decision___no-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_)`, or `[maybe]](#manual-Decision___maybe-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_)`, with the latter containing further data for consideration.

```lean
structure Truthy (α : Type) where
val : α
isTrue : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
inductive Decision (α : Type) where
| yes
| maybe (val : α)
| no
```

“Truthy” values can be converted to `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`s by forgetting the contained value.
`[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`s can be converted to `[Decision]](#manual-Decision-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_)`s by discounting the `[maybe]](#manual-Decision___maybe-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_)` case.

```lean
@[[coe]](#manual-Lean___Attr___coe)]
def Truthy.toBool : [Truthy]](#manual-Truthy-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_) α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
[Truthy.isTrue]](#manual-Truthy___isTrue-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_)
@[[coe]](#manual-Lean___Attr___coe)]
def Decision.ofBool : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → [Decision]](#manual-Decision-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_) α
| [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => .yes
| [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => .no
```

`[Truthy.toBool]](#manual-Truthy___toBool-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_)` must be a `[CoeOut]](#manual-CoeOut___mk)` instance, because the target of the coercion contains fewer unknown type variables than the source, while `[Decision.ofBool]](#manual-Decision___ofBool-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_)` must be a `[Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk)` instance, because the source of the coercion contains fewer variables than the target:

```lean
instance : [CoeOut]](#manual-CoeOut___mk) ([Truthy]](#manual-Truthy-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_) α) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) := ⟨[Truthy.isTrue]](#manual-Truthy___isTrue-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_)⟩
instance : [Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) ([Decision]](#manual-Decision-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_) α) := ⟨[Decision.ofBool]](#manual-Decision___ofBool-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_)⟩
```

With these instances, coercion chaining works:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ({ [val]](#manual-Truthy___val-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_) := 1, [isTrue]](#manual-Truthy___isTrue-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_) := [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) : [Truthy]](#manual-Truthy-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) } : [Decision]](#manual-Decision-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray))
```

```lean
Decision.yes
```

Attempting to use the wrong class leads to an error:

```lean
instance : [Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk) ([Truthy]](#manual-Truthy-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_) α) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) := ⟨[Truthy.isTrue]](#manual-Truthy___isTrue-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_)⟩
```

```lean
instance does not provide concrete values for (semi-)out-params
  [Coe]](#manual-Coe___mk) ([Truthy]](#manual-Truthy-_LPAR_in-CoeOut--vs--Coe--instances_RPAR_) ?α) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

type class

```lean
[CoeHead.{u, v}]](#manual-CoeHead___mk) (α : Sort u) (β : [semiOutParam]](#manual-semiOutParam) (Sort v)) :
  Sort (max (max 1 u) v)



[CoeHead.{u, v}]](#manual-CoeHead___mk) (α : Sort u)
  (β : [semiOutParam]](#manual-semiOutParam) (Sort v)) :
  Sort (max (max 1 u) v)
```

`[CoeHead]](#manual-CoeHead___mk) α β` is for coercions that are applied from left-to-right at most once
at beginning of the coercion chain.

```lean
coe : α → β
```

or by double type ascription `((x : α) : β)`.

type class

```lean
[CoeOut.{u, v}]](#manual-CoeOut___mk) (α : Sort u) (β : [semiOutParam]](#manual-semiOutParam) (Sort v)) :
  Sort (max (max 1 u) v)



[CoeOut.{u, v}]](#manual-CoeOut___mk) (α : Sort u)
  (β : [semiOutParam]](#manual-semiOutParam) (Sort v)) :
  Sort (max (max 1 u) v)
```

`[CoeOut]](#manual-CoeOut___mk) α β` is for coercions that are applied from left-to-right.

